cardCatalog.noteEn: Docenas stays plural when it means an approximate large count. De is required before the following noun: docenas de cartas. The noun is normally plural when it names countable items.

example.en: We saw dozens of stars.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you refer to an organ donor?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Donante names the donor, and de introduces what is donated. Change the noun after de for other kinds of donation, such as donante de sangre.

example.es: Ana decidió ser donante de órganos.
example.en: Ana decided to be an organ donor.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you distinguish falling asleep from simply sleeping?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use dormirse for the change into sleep, with a matching short word such as me, te, or se.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dormir describes sleeping. Dormirse focuses on becoming asleep: duermo means “I sleep,” while me duermo means “I fall asleep.” The short word changes with the person.

example.en: The baby falls asleep quickly.

cardCatalog.promptEs: echar a alguien de un lugar
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone is forced to leave a place?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of echar for forcing the person out, then de before the place being left.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The person can follow echar with personal a: echaron a Leo del aula. A short object word instead goes before a changed form of echar: lo echaron del aula, me echó de casa. De introduces the place the person is forced to leave.

example.es: La directora lo echó del aula.
example.en: The principal threw him out of the classroom.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone suddenly starts running?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of echar or echarse, then a, then correr.
cardCatalog.noteEn: In this expression, echar does not keep its usual sense of throwing. The whole pattern marks the sudden beginning of running. Both echar a correr and echarse a correr are used.

example.es: Al oír el ruido, Pablo echó a correr.
example.en: When Pablo heard the noise, he started running.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes a quick look at something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of echar followed by un vistazo; use a before the thing being viewed when it is stated.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Echar has many literal meanings, but echar un vistazo is a conventional expression for looking briefly. Only echar changes for the person and time: echo, echas, echó, echaré. Un vistazo stays together.

example.es: Voy a echar un vistazo al mapa.
example.en: I'm going to take a look at the map.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How can echar mean that you estimate someone's age, time, or another amount?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use me, te, le, nos, or les with a form of echar, then give the approximate quantity.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The short object marker identifies the person or thing being estimated, while echar changes for the speaker and time. This estimating sense is different from the basic meaning “to throw”; it is common with ages, durations, distances, and similar quantities.

example.en: I estimate that person to be about thirty.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone steps aside or gets out of the way?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of echarse followed by a un lado.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Echar changes for the person and time, and the attached short word changes with the person: me echo, te echas, se echa, nos echamos. A un lado stays fixed. The expression can describe a physical move or, figuratively, letting someone or something else take over.

example.es: Nos echamos a un lado para dejarlos pasar.
example.en: We stepped aside to let them pass.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What historical period does Edad Moderna normally name?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Edad Moderna is the conventional Spanish name for the Early Modern period.
cardCatalog.noteEn: In common Spanish historical periodization, the Edad Moderna follows the Edad Media and precedes the Edad Contemporánea. Exact boundary dates vary, but the name is a conventional period label rather than simply any age that feels modern.

example.es: La imprenta transformó la Edad Moderna.
example.en: The printing press transformed the Early Modern period.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “next year” by describing the year that is coming?
cardCatalog.noteEn: The relative word que links año to viene, “comes.” The same pattern works with other time nouns: la semana que viene and el mes que viene. Viene stays singular because it describes one week, month, or year.

example.en: We will start next year.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you identify the opposite side of a place, street, or object?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use el otro lado de, then name the place or object.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al otro lado de often describes where something is; del otro lado de can identify something coming from that opposite side. Al combines a + el, and del combines de + el.

example.es: La farmacia está al otro lado de la plaza.
example.en: The pharmacy is on the other side of the square.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you introduce the situation that is causing a problem?
cardCatalog.noteEn: El problema names the difficulty, es identifies it, and que introduces the situation that follows. A de phrase may be inserted after problema to say whose problem it is.

example.es: El problema es que no tenemos tiempo.
example.en: The problem is that we do not have time.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you make it explicit that two people do something to each other?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use el uno al otro for two masculine people or a mixed pair; change the endings when the people are feminine.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The expression literally pairs “the one” with “the other.” Use la una a la otra for two feminine people. It often appears with nos, se, or another small object word when the verb needs one.

example.es: Nos ayudamos el uno al otro.
example.en: We help each other.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What is the Spanish name for the quantum theory of light and electrically charged particles?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Electrodinámica is a feminine noun, so cuántica takes the feminine singular ending -a. This is the conventional technical name, often abbreviated QED in English.

example.es: La electrodinámica cuántica hace predicciones muy precisas.
example.en: Quantum electrodynamics makes very precise predictions.

cardCatalog.promptEs: elevar algo a una forma de arte
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes an activity to the level of an art form?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use elevar algo a una forma de arte.
cardCatalog.noteEn: This is often humorous or critical. It says someone does an activity with such intensity or skill that it resembles an art form.

example.es: Elevó la procrastinación a una forma de arte.
example.en: He turned procrastination into an art form.

cardCatalog.promptEs: empezar/comenzar por + primera cosa o acción
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you identify the first item or action in a sequence?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of empezar or comenzar, then por, then the first thing or action.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The verb changes for the person and time. After por, use a noun or an unchanged action verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This pattern means ‘start with’ or ‘start by.’

example.en: We will start by reviewing the data.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “at some point” without specifying when?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Algún comes before the masculine noun momento; the expression can refer to the past or future according to the verb.

example.en: We will see each other at some point.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is said or done as a joke rather than seriously?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en broma after the action.
cardCatalog.noteEn: En broma is a fixed expression meaning “as a joke” or “jokingly.” Its opposite is en serio, “seriously.”

example.en: I said it to you as a joke.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you introduce a contrasting fact or an alternative choice?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en cambio: “instead,” “on the other hand,” or “by contrast.”
cardCatalog.noteEn: En cambio compares what follows with what was just mentioned. It can introduce an alternative action or show that two facts differ. A comma often follows it when it begins the new contrast.

example.es: Ana fue en tren; Luis, en cambio, condujo.
example.en: Ana went by train; Luis, on the other hand, drove.

cardCatalog.answerEn: En cierta manera means “in a way” or “in a sense.”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Use this expression when a statement is only partly true or is true from one particular point of view. It signals that a qualification or explanation may follow.
cardCatalog.questionEn: How can you say that something is true only from one point of view?

example.es: En cierta manera, los dos tienen razón.
example.en: In a way, they are both right.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you describe something expressed in code or in deliberately indirect wording?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en clave after the thing, message, or way of speaking that is coded.
cardCatalog.noteEn: En clave is a conventional expression. Depending on context, English may say ‘in code,’ ‘coded,’ or put ‘code’ before a noun; clave does not name one particular physical key here.

example.en: The note arrived in code.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What expression introduces a final summary or conclusion?
cardCatalog.noteEn: This transition signals that the speaker or writer is finishing an argument and stating its main result. It is common in formal speech and writing.

example.en: In conclusion, we need another plan.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something may happen at any time?
cardCatalog.noteEn: En introduces a point in time, and cualquier before the singular noun momento leaves that point unrestricted.

example.en: You can call at any time.

cardCatalog.promptEs: en cuanto, seguido de una acción habitual
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that one repeated or habitual action happens as soon as another one does?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en cuanto before the ordinary present form of the action that sets the time.
cardCatalog.noteEn: En cuanto works as one time connector meaning 'as soon as.' For a repeated or habitual fact, the following verb uses an ordinary present form. For one awaited future event, Spanish normally uses a special form instead: en cuanto llegue means 'as soon as I arrive,' with llegue rather than llega.

example.es: El perro ladra en cuanto oye un ruido.
example.en: The dog barks as soon as it hears a noise.

cardCatalog.promptEs: en el momento en que + hecho
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you introduce something that happened at the exact moment another event occurred?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en el momento en que, then state the event.
cardCatalog.noteEn: En el momento en que acts as one time connector. En begins the time setting, el momento names the point, and en que links it to the event. The following verb changes normally for the person and time.

example.es: En el momento en que sonó el timbre, salimos.
example.en: The moment the bell rang, we left.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you introduce an overall view rather than one specific case?
cardCatalog.noteEn: It can appear at the beginning or end of a statement and means “in general” or “overall.”

example.es: La ciudad es tranquila en general.
example.en: The city is quiet overall.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that a service or activity is available online?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en línea after the noun or verb it describes.
cardCatalog.noteEn: En línea is the standard expression for being online or connected through a network. Línea stays singular and normally has no article in this expression.

example.en: The store is online.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After en lugar de, use a thing or the dictionary form of an action verb. That dictionary form is called the infinitive and usually ends in -ar, -er, or -ir.
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “instead of” before a thing or an action?

example.en: We walk instead of driving.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something happens sometimes or on some occasions?
cardCatalog.noteEn: This fixed expression marks something as occasional rather than constant. Both words stay unchanged, and the expression can appear at the start or later in the statement.

example.en: Sometimes, I work from home.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Use it to correct or qualify what someone may believe. It does not mean “currently”; Spanish normally uses actualmente for that meaning.
cardCatalog.questionEn: What expression means “actually” or “in fact” when correcting an impression?

example.es: Pensaba que era lunes, pero en realidad es martes.
example.en: I thought it was Monday, but it is actually Tuesday.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you introduce a strictly precise qualification?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en rigor for ‘strictly speaking’ or ‘properly speaking.’
cardCatalog.noteEn: En rigor is a fixed expression, not a word-for-word use of en and rigor. It often appears between commas before a correction or a more technically exact statement.

example.es: En rigor, aún no es oficial.
example.en: Strictly speaking, it is not official yet.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something happens right away?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en seguida, meaning “right away” or “immediately.”
cardCatalog.noteEn: En seguida is a fixed two-word time expression. The one-word spelling enseguida has the same meaning and is also standard.

example.en: The doctor will come right away.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you ask whether someone is really serious or whether something is actually true?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en serio to mean “seriously,” “really,” or “for real.”
cardCatalog.noteEn: En serio is a fixed expression. In a question, ¿En serio? often reacts with surprise or disbelief; in a statement, it can contrast sincerity with joking.

example.en: Are you really going to run tomorrow?

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something applies at every time and in every place?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en todo momento y lugar.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Todo distributes over both singular nouns: momento for time and lugar for place. Spanish can share todo across the coordinated pair instead of repeating it.

example.es: Debes llevar la tarjeta en todo momento y lugar.
example.en: You must carry the card at every time and place.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that an effort was unsuccessful or pointless?
cardCatalog.noteEn: En vano means the effort did not achieve its intended result, like English “in vain.”

example.en: I tried to convince him in vain.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What expression can mean “actually,” “really,” or “in truth”?
cardCatalog.noteEn: The two words work together to confirm something, correct an impression, or emphasize that it is true. The natural English choice depends on that conversational purpose.

example.en: Actually, I prefer to walk.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that one option replaces another?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Put en vez de before the alternative that was not chosen: ‘instead of.’
cardCatalog.noteEn: A noun, pronoun, or unchanged action verb can follow: en vez de café, en vez de eso, en vez de llamar. The three words en vez de stay together.

example.es: Usamos el tren en vez del coche.
example.en: We used the train instead of the car.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is happening live, in real time?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use en vivo after the activity, event, or medium.
cardCatalog.noteEn: En vivo is a fixed adverb-like expression. Vivo stays in this form even when the noun is feminine or plural; the phrase describes the activity as it happens rather than describing something as biologically alive.

example.en: We watch the concert live.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone meets, encounters, or runs into a person or thing?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of encontrarse, then con and the person or thing encountered.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontrarse includes a short word that matches the person doing the meeting: me encuentro, te encuentras, se encuentra, nos encontramos, or se encuentran. Con stays before the person or thing encountered. This differs from encontrarse en, which describes where something is located, and from encontrar without the matching short word, which commonly means “to find.”

example.es: Marta se encuentra con un amigo.
example.en: Marta runs into a friend.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is found or located somewhere?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of encontrarse, then en, then the place.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontrarse contains the small matching word se in the dictionary form. In a sentence, both parts match what is located: la tienda se encuentra and las tiendas se encuentran. En introduces the location. This use describes where something is; it does not mean that two people meet each other.

example.es: La biblioteca se encuentra en la plaza.
example.en: The library is located in the square.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone finds out about or learns something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of enterarse, then de, then state the information or subject learned.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” Enterarse is used with a short person marker: me entero, te enteras, se entera, nos enteramos, os enteráis, or se enteran. Keep de before the fact, news, event, or topic, even where English simply says find out.

example.es: Nos enteramos de la noticia ayer.
example.en: We found out about the news yesterday.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that text is written in parentheses?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Entre usually means ‘between,’ but this conventional expression describes words placed between an opening and a closing parenthesis. Paréntesis has the same written form for one parenthesis and for more than one.

example.en: Write the date in parentheses.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone chooses the wrong door, road, number, or similar option?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of equivocarse, then de, then the option chosen incorrectly.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The short marker changes with the person: me equivoqué, te equivocaste, se equivocó. De introduces what was wrong. This pattern often sounds more natural than translating “wrong” with an adjective.

example.en: I chose the wrong door.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you name a burst of energy from the Sun?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use erupción solar for “solar flare”; the plural is erupciones solares.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Erupción names the burst and solar identifies the Sun. In the plural, both words show the change: erupciones solares.

example.es: La sonda observó una erupción solar.
example.en: The probe observed a solar flare.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you restate or clarify an idea with ‘that is’ or ‘in other words’?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use es decir before the clarification.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Es decir is a fixed connector that reformulates what came before. It commonly appears between commas and does not change for person or time.

example.es: Llegará mañana, es decir, el martes.
example.en: She will arrive tomorrow, that is, Tuesday.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How can you introduce an explanation, excuse, or hesitant objection?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Start with es que, then give the explanation.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Es que often softens what comes next, especially when the speaker is explaining a problem or pushing back politely. The phrase functions as a unit; its meaning is not obtained by translating es and que separately.

example.es: No puedo ir; es que trabajo esta tarde.
example.en: I can't go; the thing is, I work this afternoon.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that doing something is an honor?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use es un honor, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as hablar, conocer, or recibir. Es can change when the time changes, but the action verb after honor stays in that dictionary form.

example.en: It is an honor to meet you.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What can you say when you suddenly recognize the right answer or explanation?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Say ¡Eso es! to mean “That's it!” or “Exactly!”
cardCatalog.noteEn: This short reaction confirms that the idea just mentioned is the answer. It is more idiomatic than translating eso and es separately in this use.

example.en: “The blue door?” “That's it!”

cardCatalog.questionEn: What is the usual Spanish expression for “tonight”?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Esta means “this” and uses its feminine singular form to match noche. Spanish normally uses this two-word time expression without a preposition.

example.en: We are having dinner together tonight.

cardCatalog.promptEs: estar a punto de + verbo en forma de diccionario
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that an action is just about to happen?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of estar, then a punto de, then the action verb in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Only estar changes for the person and time: estoy, estás, está, and so on. A punto de stays together, and the following action verb remains unchanged. The plus sign means ‘followed by.’

example.es: La película está a punto de empezar.
example.en: The film is about to start.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is backward, upside down, or the wrong way around?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by the fixed expression al revés.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estar changes to match the person or thing and the time: está al revés, estaban al revés. Al revés stays unchanged; its exact English wording depends on whether the problem is orientation, order, or direction.

example.en: The numbers are backward.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What can estar bueno or estar buena mean when it informally describes a person?
cardCatalog.answerEn: It can mean that the person is physically attractive or “hot.”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Use está bueno for a masculine singular person and está buena for a feminine singular person; other forms change for number and speaker. This informal use focuses on physical appearance and can sound objectifying, so guapo or guapa is often a more neutral compliment.

example.es: En la película dicen que el actor está muy bueno.
example.en: In the movie they say the actor is really hot.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you introduce something that a person is convinced is true?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of estar convencido, then de que, then the belief.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Convencido changes to match the person or group described.

example.en: We are convinced that it will work.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that a candidate or political team is actively campaigning?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by en campaña, optionally adding electoral.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time, while en campaña names the active campaign period. Electoral makes the election meaning explicit; without it, the surrounding political context can do that work.

example.en: The candidates are campaigning.

cardCatalog.promptEs: estar en plan + actitud o palabras aproximadas
cardCatalog.questionEn: How can colloquial Spanish frame someone's attitude, manner, or loose quotation?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of estar followed by en plan, then give the attitude or approximate words.
cardCatalog.noteEn: This informal expression is especially common in Spain. It can describe a mood or work much like conversational English 'be like' before an approximate quotation.

example.en: We were in a relaxed sort of mood.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that two people or things are synchronized or in sync?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by en sincronía.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The form of estar changes for the subject and time, while en sincronía stays fixed. The expression can describe timing, movement, plans, or ideas that match.

example.es: Los dos relojes están en sincronía.
example.en: The two clocks are in sync.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is focused on or aimed at a particular goal or audience?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of estar, then enfocado, enfocada, enfocados, or enfocadas, followed by a and the target.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estar changes for the person, thing, and time. Enfocado changes to match what is being described, and a introduces the aim, audience, or intended result. A describing adverb can go before enfocado, as in muy enfocado.

example.es: El proyecto está enfocado a reducir residuos.
example.en: The project is aimed at reducing waste.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Use estar equivocado or estar equivocada: “to be wrong” or “to be mistaken.”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses estar here because it describes the person’s state. Equivocado changes to match the person being described: equivocado for one male person, equivocada for one female person, and equivocados or equivocadas for groups.
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that a person is wrong or mistaken?

example.en: I think I am wrong.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say what material something is made from?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of estar, then hecho, hecha, hechos, or hechas to match the thing, then de and the material.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estar changes for the thing and the time: está or estaba, for example. Hecho is the completed-action form of hacer, ‘to make,’ and changes to hecha, hechos, or hechas to match the thing described. De introduces the material; the plus sign in the prompt means that the material comes next.

example.es: La mesa está hecha de metal.
example.en: The table is made of metal.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone is available or not busy at a particular time?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of estar followed by libre.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time: estoy libre, está libre, and so on. Libre stays the same for one man or woman and becomes libres for more than one person. Ser libre usually describes being free rather than availability in a schedule.

example.en: Clara is available on Friday.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is restricted to a particular amount or option?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use estar, then limitado or limitada to match the thing, then a before the limit.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Limitado changes to agree with the thing being described: limitado for a masculine singular noun and limitada for a feminine singular noun. Only estar changes for person and time; a introduces what the restriction allows.

example.es: La entrada está limitada a dos personas.
example.en: Entry is limited to two people.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is full of something else?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use estar, then lleno or llena, then de.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Change lleno to match the thing that is full: lleno for a masculine singular noun and llena for a feminine singular noun. The thing filling it follows de.

example.es: La caja está llena de libros.
example.en: The box is full of books.

cardCatalog.promptEs: estar pegado/pegada a alguien o algo
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is stuck to, pressed against, or extremely close to another thing?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of estar, then pegado, pegada, pegados, or pegadas, followed by a and the reference person or thing.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time. Pegado changes to match the person or thing being described. A introduces what it is attached or very close to. The expression can describe literal contact or, from context, unusually close proximity.

example.es: La mesa está pegada a la pared.
example.en: The table is right up against the wall.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone is worried about something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of estar, the matching form of preocupado, then por and the cause.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time. Preocupado changes its ending to match whom it describes: preocupado, preocupada, preocupados, or preocupadas. Por remains unchanged before the source of concern.

example.es: Lucía está preocupada por su perro.
example.en: Lucía is worried about her dog.

cardCatalog.promptEs: estar seguro/segura de + cosa o pregunta
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say what someone is sure or certain about?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of estar, seguro or segura, then de before what follows.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguro changes to match the person being described: seguro for masculine singular and segura for feminine singular. De is required before a noun, before que plus a statement, and before an embedded question such as de quién or de si.

example.es: Ana está segura de la respuesta.
example.en: Ana is sure of the answer.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that one thing is linked to another?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of estar, then vinculado changed to match the linked thing, then a before the related thing.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estar changes to match the linked person or thing and the time: está for one present item and están for several. Vinculada describes one feminine-noun item, vinculados several masculine or mixed items, and vinculadas several feminine-noun items. The linking word a stays unchanged, but it combines with el as al.

example.es: La cuenta está vinculada al teléfono.
example.en: The account is linked to the phone.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What is the usual Spanish expression for a thought experiment?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use experimento mental; the plural is experimentos mentales.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mental follows experimento and describes an imagined test carried out through reasoning rather than a physical experiment. It changes only for number: mental or mentales.

example.en: They proposed a simple thought experiment.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone is an expert in a subject or field?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of ser, experto or experta, and en before the field.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Experto changes to match the person: experto, experta, expertos, or expertas. The field can be a noun or an action used as a noun.

example.en: Ana is an expert in linguistics.

cardCatalog.promptEs: fin de semana / fines de semana
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “weekend” or “weekends”?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use fin de semana for one weekend and fines de semana for more than one.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The expression literally contains “end of week,” but it functions as the ordinary unit “weekend.” In the plural, fin changes to fines while semana remains singular: los fines de semana.

example.es: Visitamos a Ana los fines de semana.
example.en: We visit Ana on weekends.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “septic tank” in Spanish?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Fosa names the underground pit or tank, and séptica identifies its wastewater function. Séptica follows the noun and uses feminine singular -a to match fosa.

example.es: La fosa séptica está detrás de la casa.
example.en: The septic tank is behind the house.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What do you call the rule that scores candidate solutions in a genetic algorithm?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use función de aptitud for ‘fitness function.’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Función names the scoring rule, de links it to the technical noun aptitud, and the complete phrase names the function used to compare candidate solutions. Depending on the setup, a program may seek a higher fitness score or a lower cost.

example.es: La función de aptitud asigna una puntuación a cada solución.
example.en: The fitness function assigns a score to each solution.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “to gain time” or “to buy time”?
cardCatalog.answerEn: to gain time; to buy time
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ganar literally means to win or gain. With tiempo it conventionally means creating or obtaining extra time before a deadline or event.

example.es: Haz una pregunta para ganar tiempo.
example.en: Ask a question to buy time.

cardCatalog.promptEs: girar a la izquierda / a la derecha
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you tell someone to turn left or right?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of girar, then a la izquierda for left or a la derecha for right.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Only girar changes for the person and time. The directional part stays a la izquierda or a la derecha; the a is part of this standard navigation expression.

example.es: Gira a la derecha en la esquina.
example.en: Turn right at the corner.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you name a balloon filled with helium?
cardCatalog.noteEn: De links the balloon to the gas inside it. English usually places helium directly before balloon.

example.es: El globo de helio llegó al techo.
example.en: The helium balloon reached the ceiling.

cardCatalog.promptEs: algo se graba en la memoria o el recuerdo
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something becomes vividly fixed in someone's memory?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Say that the thing se graba en la memoria or se graba en el recuerdo.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Grabar literally means to record or engrave. In this expression, se plus a matching form of grabar presents an image, sound, or experience as becoming etched in memory. Change graba for the time: se grabó for a completed past event, or se grabará for a future one.

example.es: Su voz se grabó en mi memoria.
example.en: Her voice became etched in my memory.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you thank someone for doing something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Say gracias por, then put the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por introduces the reason for the thanks. The following action stays in the dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, even where English uses a verb ending in -ing.

example.en: Thank you for coming.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What does gripe porcina mean?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Gripe means flu. Porcina means related to pigs and takes its feminine singular form to match the feminine noun gripe.

example.es: El hospital confirmó un caso de gripe porcina.
example.en: The hospital confirmed a case of swine flu.

cardCatalog.promptEs: hay tiempo para + verbo en forma de diccionario
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that there is time available to do something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use hay tiempo para, then put the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hay says that something exists and does not change for one thing or several. Tiempo names the available time, and para introduces its use. The following action stays in its dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Other times can use había tiempo or habrá tiempo.

example.en: There is time to rest.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone talks to another person on the phone?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of hablar followed by por teléfono.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hablar changes for the person and time. Por teléfono stays together to name the communication channel; Spanish uses por here where natural English normally says ‘on the phone.’ Add con plus a person when you want to name the other participant.

example.es: Lucía habla por teléfono con su hermano.
example.en: Lucía talks with her brother on the phone.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something happened a long time ago?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use hace mucho after the completed event.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mucho supplies an unspecified long amount of elapsed time. For an exact duration, Spanish can instead use hace dos años or another stated period.

example.es: Ese tren dejó de funcionar hace mucho.
example.en: That train stopped operating long ago.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone shops or makes purchases?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of hacer followed by compras.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer changes for the person and time: hago compras, haces compras, hicimos compras. Compras remains plural and names the shopping activity or purchases.

example.en: We do our shopping on Saturdays.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that an action hurts or harms someone or something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of hacer with daño. Introduce a named affected person or thing with a, or mark the affected person with a small pronoun such as me, te, or le.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer daño works as a unit for causing physical or emotional harm. The affected person can appear after a, as in hace daño a Pablo, or in a small pronoun: me hizo daño (“it hurt me”) and hacerte daño (“to hurt you”). Hacer changes for person and time; daño stays unchanged.

example.es: Ese comentario le hizo daño a Pablo.
example.en: That comment hurt Pablo.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say to make money or make more money?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use hacer dinero; put más before dinero for ‘make more money.’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer normally means ‘to do’ or ‘to make.’ With dinero it describes earning or obtaining money.

example.es: Quiere hacer dinero con su negocio.
example.en: She wants to make money from her business.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “to exercise” or “to work out”?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish commonly builds this activity with hacer, “to do,” plus ejercicio. The expression covers physical exercise generally.

example.es: Hago ejercicio tres veces por semana.
example.en: I exercise three times a week.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is needed?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of hacer followed by falta; hacer agrees with what is needed.
cardCatalog.noteEn: For one needed thing, use hace falta. For several, use hacen falta. The needed item acts like the grammatical subject, so the form of hacer changes even though falta stays singular.

example.es: Hace falta una llave, pero hacen falta dos tornillos.
example.en: One key is needed, but two screws are needed.

cardCatalog.promptEs: hacer pensar en + persona o cosa
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something reminds someone of another person or thing?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use hacer, the person affected, pensar en, and then what comes to mind.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The form of hacer matches the thing causing the association. The person can appear as me, te, le, nos, or another object expression.

example.es: Esta canción me hace pensar en casa.
example.en: This song makes me think of home.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “to make noise” in Spanish?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacer followed by ruido.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish conventionally pairs hacer, “to make or do,” with ruido, “noise.” Hacer changes for the person and time: hago ruido, hacen ruido, hizo ruido.

example.en: The neighbors make a lot of noise.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “to cheat” in a game, test, or competition?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of hacer followed by trampa.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer changes for the person and time, while trampa normally stays singular in this expression. The phrase refers to breaking the rules for an unfair advantage.

example.es: Nadie hizo trampa en el examen.
example.en: Nobody cheated on the test.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone works a scheduled shift?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of hacer followed by un turno or turnos.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer changes for the person and time. Turno names the scheduled period of work; an adjective can specify its type, as in turno nocturno or turno doble.

example.es: Marta hace el turno de noche.
example.en: Marta works the night shift.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that three people have sex together?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use hacer un trío, changing hacer for the people and time.
cardCatalog.noteEn: This is a fixed expression: hacer is not translated literally as ‘make.’ Hacer changes, as in hacemos for ‘we do’ or hicieron for ‘they did,’ while un trío stays unchanged.

example.en: They decided to have a threesome.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “to ask a question”?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses hacer, literally “to do” or “to make,” with pregunta. Change hacer for the person and time, and change pregunta to preguntas when more than one is asked.

example.en: I want to ask a question.

cardCatalog.promptEs: hacer una foto · hacerle una foto a alguien/algo
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use hacer una foto; to name what is photographed, use hacerle una foto a alguien or algo.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer normally means “to make” or “to do,” but in this expression it corresponds to English “take.” Le and the words after a point to the person or thing in the photo. Tomar una foto is common in many other regions.
cardCatalog.questionEn: In Spain, how do you say “to take a photo” or “to take a photo of someone”?

example.es: Vamos a hacerle una foto al perro.
example.en: We are going to take a photo of the dog.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that people cuddle or exchange affectionate caresses with each other?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacerse followed by arrumacos.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacerse arrumacos is a conventional expression for mutual affectionate touching. In the dictionary form, se is attached to hacer. With a stated subject, the matching short word usually stands before the changed verb: nos hacemos arrumacos or se hacen arrumacos.

example.es: La pareja se hace arrumacos en el sofá.
example.en: The couple cuddles on the sofa.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets older or grows up?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacerse followed by mayor.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacerse is the unchanged dictionary form. The short word and hacer change with the person: me hago mayor, te haces mayor, se hace mayor. Mayor stays singular for one person and becomes mayores for more than one.

example.en: Ana is getting older.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets or takes a test, especially a medical or screening test?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of hacerse followed by una prueba or the specific test name.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The short pronoun changes with the person tested: me hago, te haces, se hace, nos hacemos. With another changed verb before it, hacer can stay in its unchanged form with the pronoun attached: debemos hacernos una prueba.

example.es: Clara se hizo una prueba médica.
example.en: Clara got a medical test.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that movement, direction, or progress goes backward?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacia supplies the direction and atrás points toward the back or reverse. The phrase can describe physical movement or an abstract process.

example.en: The video is going backward.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that a container or place is full all the way to the top?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use hasta arriba to mean filled to the top or completely full.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hasta gives the endpoint and arriba supplies the upper limit. With a container it can be literal; with a place such as a bus or bar, it can also mean packed or completely full.

example.es: La caja está llena hasta arriba.
example.en: The box is full to the top.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you limit a statement to what you currently know?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use hasta donde yo sé to mean “as far as I know.”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hasta sets a boundary, donde marks where that boundary lies, and yo sé states whose knowledge is limited. The subject word can change or be omitted: hasta donde sabemos means “as far as we know,” and hasta donde sé keeps the same meaning without yo.

example.es: Hasta donde yo sé, Ana llega mañana.
example.en: As far as I know, Ana arrives tomorrow.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone's blood runs cold from fear?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of helarse with la sangre, and use me, te, le, nos, os, or les to mark the person who feels the fear.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Helar literally means “to freeze.” Se makes it helarse, where the blood itself goes cold, and the person marker identifies whose reaction it is. The form of helar changes for the time; sangre is singular, so the verb is singular.

example.es: Al oír el grito, se me heló la sangre.
example.en: When I heard the scream, my blood ran cold.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that one thing is identical to another?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of idéntico followed by a and the comparison.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Idéntico changes to match the first thing: idéntico, idéntica, idénticos, idénticas. The a remains before the comparison. Before el, a and el combine as al: idéntico al original.

example.es: La llave nueva es idéntica a la vieja.
example.en: The new key is identical to the old one.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is like another person or thing in the same way?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use igual que before the person or thing being used for comparison.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The connector means “just like” or “the same as.” Igual stays unchanged in this connector, and que introduces the reference point for the comparison.

example.en: Marta cooks just like Ana.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone pictures themself doing an action?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use me, te, se, nos, or os with a form of imaginar, then give the pictured action in its -ando or -iendo form.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The small word changes with the person: me imagino, te imaginas, se imagina, and so on. The next verb names the pictured action with an ending such as -ando for caminar or -iendo for vivir; only imaginar changes for the person and time.

example.es: Me imagino viviendo junto al mar.
example.en: I imagine myself living by the sea.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that one person or organization informs someone of something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of informar, then a + the recipient, and de + the information or event.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The a-part answers who receives the information. The de-part answers what that person is informed of. The order may move in a question, but both links keep the same roles.

example.es: La agencia informó a Marta del incidente.
example.en: The agency informed Marta of the incident.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you name the person, system, or thing that someone interacts with?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of interactuar, then con, then name the other participant.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Interactuar changes for the person and time. Con is the required link to the other person or thing involved; English also normally uses 'with.'

example.es: Los clientes interactúan con la aplicación.
example.en: The customers interact with the application.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What is the Spanish term for compound interest?
cardCatalog.noteEn: The phrase names interest that is added to the balance before future interest is calculated. Interés is masculine, so compuesto uses masculine singular -o.

example.es: El interés compuesto aumenta el saldo poco a poco.
example.en: Compound interest increases the balance little by little.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone understands one thing as having a particular meaning?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of interpretar, name the first item, add como, then name the meaning assigned to it.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The form of interpretar changes for the person and time, but como stays unchanged and has no written accent. Each algo in the prompt stands in for an item: the first is what is being interpreted, and the second is the reading or category assigned to it.

example.es: Interpretaron el silencio como una respuesta.
example.en: They interpreted the silence as an answer.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone invites a person to an event or treats them to food or a drink?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use invitar for the invitation, identify the invited person, then use a before the event, activity, food, or drink.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Alguien means the person invited and algo means what they are invited to; they are placeholders, not words that must appear literally. A name often has a before it: invito a Marta. An object pronoun can replace the person: te invito. The second a introduces the invitation or treat.

example.en: I will treat you to a coffee.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do speakers in Spain commonly say that someone goes to get or fetch something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of ir, then a por, then the thing being fetched.
cardCatalog.noteEn: In this Spain usage, both a and por stay before the object: voy a por, fue a por, iremos a por. This is not the ir a plus action-verb pattern for “going to do” something. Speakers elsewhere often say ir por or ir a buscar instead.

example.en: I am going to get the keys.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that a person, group, or schedule is running late or falling behind?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of ir followed by atrasado, atrasada, atrasados, or atrasadas.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here ir describes how something is progressing rather than physical movement. Ir changes for the person and time. Atrasado changes its ending to match who or what is behind: va atrasada for one feminine subject and van atrasados for a masculine or mixed plural group.

example.en: The project is running behind schedule.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone goes out partying?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of ir, then de marcha.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ir changes for the person and time: voy, vas, vamos, fueron, and so on. De marcha stays together and refers to going out for lively nightlife or partying, not to marching somewhere.

example.en: We are going out partying on Saturday.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone or a team is currently in first place?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of ir followed by primero or primera to match the person or team being ranked.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ir changes for the person and time. Primero changes to primera for a feminine singular person or thing, and plural rankings use primeros or primeras. The expression states a current position, not physical movement.

example.en: Our team is in first place.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone goes or comes for a visit?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of ir or venir followed by de visita.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Only ir or venir changes for the person and time. The fixed words de visita identify the purpose as visiting, and natural English usually supplies “for a visit.”

example.en: Our friends are coming for a visit.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say to go home or return home?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use ir or volver, then a casa, normally without an article before casa.
cardCatalog.noteEn: When casa means one's home as a destination, Spanish commonly leaves out la: ir a casa and volver a casa. The motion verb changes for the person and time; a casa remains unchanged.

example.en: Marta returns home early.

cardCatalog.promptEs: irle algo a alguien, con sentido de gustos
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something suits someone or is their kind of thing?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Put me, te, le, nos, os, or les before a form of ir that matches the thing that suits or appeals.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The short word identifies the person whose taste is described. The form of ir matches the thing that appeals, not that person: va for one thing and van for several things in the present; another time frame can use forms such as fue or fueron. Os identifies more than one person addressed informally in Spain. This preference use is especially common in informal Spanish in Spain.

example.en: Quiet films are my kind of thing.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone likes excitement, energetic action, or a bit of trouble?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching short person word with ir, followed by la marcha; you can put the word a before the person to name who enjoys it.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person: me va la marcha means that I like excitement, while le va la marcha says that he, she, or formal 'you' does. La marcha is singular, so the usual verb form is va. To identify the person explicitly, put the word a before that person, as in a Marta le va la marcha.

example.es: A Marta le va la marcha.
example.en: Marta likes excitement.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How can you say that a period of time passes or comes to an end?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the period of time as the subject of irse: se va for one period, or se van for several.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Irse often describes someone leaving. With a day, season, year, or other period as its subject, it figuratively describes time passing or ending. The verb matches a singular or plural period: se va el día, se van los meses. Past forms include se fue and se fueron.

example.en: Winter came to an end.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone leaves for or goes off to a destination?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of irse, then a and the destination: me voy a…, se va a…, or nos vamos a….
cardCatalog.noteEn: The short word before ir changes with the person: me, te, se, nos, os, or se. Plain ir focuses on going somewhere; irse often highlights leaving the current place. The destination may include an article, as in a la playa or a las islas.

example.en: We are leaving for the beach.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you refer to sexual play, including activity that builds arousal before intercourse?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use juego sexual for sexual play; depending on context, it can refer to foreplay.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Juego sexual is broader than English “foreplay”: it can name different kinds of consensual sexual activity, so the surrounding context determines whether “foreplay” is the best English meaning.

example.es: Hablaron de sus preferencias para el juego sexual.
example.en: They talked about their preferences for sexual play.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you name the game that someone plays?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of jugar, then a, then the game.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Jugar changes for the player and time. A links it to the game. If the game has masculine article el, a + el must contract to al: jugar al tenis. With an indefinite article, keep a un or a una.

example.es: Marta juega a un juego de cartas y Luis juega al tenis.
example.en: Marta plays a card game and Luis plays tennis.

cardCatalog.promptEs: jugar con + control, herramienta o idea
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone experiments or plays around with a control, tool, or idea?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of jugar followed by con and name what is being tried in different ways.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Jugar changes for the person and time, while con stays before the thing being adjusted or explored. In this use, jugar does not mean playing a game.

example.en: We are playing around with the design.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you warn that someone is toying with or taking risks with something serious?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of jugar followed by con and the risky thing.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Jugar con literally means to play with. With danger, feelings, power, or another serious matter, it means to toy with it, handle it carelessly, or take a risk. Jugar changes for the person and time; con stays unchanged.

example.en: The company is playing with fire.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that one person or thing is next to another?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use junto a before the person or thing that is beside it.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Junto a is a fixed location expression meaning “next to” or “beside,” so junto stays unchanged inside it: la farmacia está junto a la estación. The adjective junto, junta, juntos, or juntas is a different construction, as in Ana y Marta están juntas.

example.es: La farmacia está junto a la estación.
example.en: The pharmacy is next to the station.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is included together with another item?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use junto con, followed by the additional person or thing.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Junto con stays together as a connector. It can often be translated as ‘together with’ or simply ‘along with.’

example.es: Mandó el informe junto con las fotos.
example.en: She sent the report along with the photos.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you refer to most members of a group?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use la mayoría de, followed by the group.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The following noun phrase names the complete group from which the majority is taken.

example.es: La mayoría de los trenes llegó a tiempo.
example.en: Most of the trains arrived on time.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How can razón introduce why something happened?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use razón por la que, meaning “reason why.”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Razón is normally accompanied by a determiner or description, as in la razón or una razón. With a plural reason, use razones por las que. Spanish literally builds “reason for which,” while natural English normally says “reason why.”

example.es: Esa es la razón por la que salí temprano.
example.en: That is the reason why I left early.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say ‘last week’ when referring to the most recent completed week?
cardCatalog.noteEn: The article la and the adjective pasada both match the feminine noun semana. Spanish normally places pasada after the time noun in this expression.

example.es: Fuimos al museo la semana pasada.
example.en: We went to the museum last week.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone gives another person a look?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of lanzar and una mirada, with a short person word such as le to mark who receives the look.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lanzar changes for the person and time. The short word identifies who receives the look: me for me, te for you, le for him or her, nos for us, os for you all in Spain, and les for them. A named recipient can follow a, as in le lanza una mirada a Luis.

example.es: Marta le lanza una mirada a Luis.
example.en: Marta gives Luis a look.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone plunges or rushes into doing an action?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of lanzarse, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The small marker changes with the person: me lanzo, te lanzas, se lanza, nos lanzamos. The action after a stays in the dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The construction can suggest energetic action or action begun too quickly.

example.es: Se lanzaron a construir una solución.
example.en: They rushed into building a solution.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “programming language”?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Say lenguaje de programación; use lenguajes de programación for more than one.
cardCatalog.noteEn: De programación identifies the field or purpose of the language. Only lenguaje changes to mark the plural.

example.es: Python es un lenguaje de programación.
example.en: Python is a programming language.

cardCatalog.questionEn: In informal Spanish from Spain, how can you say that someone makes out or hooks up with another person?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of liarse, usually followed by con and the other person.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The short marker changes with the person: me lío, te lías, se lía, nos liamos. In this colloquial sense, the expression is about a romantic or sexual encounter. In other contexts, liarse can instead mean to get tangled, confused, or involved in a mess.

example.es: Se lió con alguien en la fiesta.
example.en: They hooked up with someone at the party.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “hardcover book” in Spanish?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish builds the description literally as a book “of hard cover.” De links the book to its cover type, and dura agrees with the feminine noun tapa.

example.es: Compré un libro de tapa dura.
example.en: I bought a hardcover book.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What common Spanish phrase means a textbook?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use libro de texto; use libros de texto for more than one.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Libro is the main noun and carries the plural ending. De texto classifies the book's use and stays unchanged in the plural.

example.es: Necesito un libro de texto nuevo.
example.en: I need a new textbook.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “command line”?
cardCatalog.noteEn: This is the conventional computing term for a text interface where a person types commands instead of choosing controls in a graphical interface. Línea stays singular, while comandos is normally plural.

example.es: Abro el programa desde la línea de comandos.
example.en: I open the program from the command line.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say “timeline” in Spanish?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del is the required contraction of de + el inside this fixed expression.

example.es: Dibujamos una línea del tiempo de la historia.
example.en: We drew a timeline of history.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What is the ordinary Spanish expression for an electric power line?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use línea eléctrica for a line that carries or supplies electricity.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Línea names the physical route or cable system, and eléctrica follows it to say what kind of line it is. Eléctrica changes to match the feminine singular noun línea.

example.es: La tormenta dañó la línea eléctrica.
example.en: The storm damaged the power line.

cardCatalog.promptEs: llamar a alguien + nombre o apodo
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use llamar a alguien followed by the name or nickname: “to call someone…”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here llamar means “to call someone by a name,” not “to telephone.” Small words such as lo, la, or—in much of Spain—le can stand for the person being named. The name or nickname follows llamar.
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say what name or nickname people use for someone?

example.en: People call Elena “Nena.”

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone knocks on a door?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of llamar followed by a la puerta.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llamar usually means “to call,” but llamar a la puerta is the conventional expression for knocking on a door. Only llamar changes for the person and time; a la puerta stays unchanged unless a different door is named.

example.en: Marta knocked on the door.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something reaches a destination?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of llegar, then a, then name the destination.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llegar changes for the person and time, while a remains before the endpoint. A plus el contracts to al; a plus la, los, or las stays separate.

example.es: La carta llegó a su destino.
example.en: The letter reached its destination.

cardCatalog.promptEs: llegar a ser + identidad o estado
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you describe someone or something eventually becoming a new identity or state?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use llegar a ser followed by the new identity or state.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Only llegar changes for the person and time; a and ser stay unchanged. Ser alone names an identity or characteristic, while llegar a ser presents it as the eventual result of a change.

example.es: Con los años, llegó a ser médico.
example.en: Over the years, he became a doctor.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone carries out or conducts a plan, test, or activity?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of llevar followed by the fixed words a cabo.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Only llevar changes for the person and time. A cabo remains fixed, and the activity being conducted follows afterward. The expression is not about physically carrying an object.

example.es: El laboratorio llevó a cabo dos pruebas.
example.en: The laboratory carried out two tests.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone carries or has an object on their person?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of llevar, name the object, and add encima.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Only llevar changes for the person and time. The object may come between llevar and encima, or encima may appear first when the object follows. Here encima means ‘with oneself,’ not physically ‘on top.’

example.en: I have my passport on me.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone has an item of clothing on?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of llevar followed by puesto, puesta, puestos, or puestas and the clothing item.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llevar changes for the wearer and time. Puesto changes to match the clothing noun in gender and number: lleva puesto un abrigo, lleva puestas unas botas.

example.en: Ana is wearing a hat.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone keeps a journal or diary?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of llevar with diario.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llevar changes to show who keeps the journal and when. In this collocation it means ‘to keep’ or ‘maintain,’ not to carry the journal physically.

example.es: Marta lleva un diario de viaje.
example.en: Marta keeps a travel journal.

cardCatalog.promptEs: lo de + tema, persona o momento
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you refer informally to “the thing about” a topic or to what happened at a certain time?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use lo de followed by the topic, person, or time reference.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Neutral lo leaves the event or matter unnamed, while de identifies it indirectly. The listener must recover the specific event or subject from context.

example.es: Tenemos que hablar de lo de ayer.
example.en: We have to talk about what happened yesterday.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something should be as fast, simple, close, or otherwise extreme as possible?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use lo más, then the description, then posible.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lo and posible stay fixed around the description being pushed to its greatest practical degree. The middle word can describe a quality or manner, as in lo más claro posible or lo más pronto posible.

example.en: Explain it as clearly as possible.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you refer to “the best thing” or “the best part” without naming a noun?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Neutral lo turns mejor into an abstract idea. The phrase does not refer to a masculine noun; it means whatever aspect is best.

example.en: The best thing is to rest.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone does something as well as they can?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use lo mejor que followed by a form of poder that matches the person and time.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” Lo and mejor stay fixed. Poder changes: puedo for “I can,” puedes for “you can,” and podemos for “we can.”

example.en: We cook as well as we can.

cardCatalog.promptEs: lo que pasa es que + explicación
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you introduce the real issue or explanation with ‘the thing is that…’?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use lo que pasa es que, followed by the explanation.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The expression frames what follows as the point the speaker wants to clarify. The words in the frame stay in this order; the explanation after que has its own verb changed for its subject and time.

example.es: Lo que pasa es que hoy no puedo.
example.en: The thing is that I cannot today.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How can you concede or dismissively accept whatever another person says?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lo que refers to “whatever” is said, tú names one familiar listener for emphasis, and digas is the special form used in this open-ended concession. Tone can make the response sincere or dismissive.

example.es: De acuerdo, lo que tú digas.
example.en: All right, whatever you say.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How does a group or organization say “we're sorry” in Spanish?
cardCatalog.noteEn: This is the plural counterpart of lo siento. Lo stays fixed, while siento changes to sentimos because the speakers are saying “we feel.” Learn the two words together as an apology rather than translating them literally.

example.en: We're sorry for the confusion.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Use this fixed expression for an apology or when reacting sympathetically to bad news. Learn it as a complete expression instead of translating lo and siento separately.
cardCatalog.questionEn: What is the standard way to say “I'm sorry” when apologizing or expressing sympathy?

example.en: I'm sorry. It was a mistake.

cardCatalog.promptEs: luchar contra + obstáculo, fuerza o adversario
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone fights or struggles against an obstacle, force, or opponent?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of luchar, then contra, then name what is being opposed.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Luchar changes for the person and time. Contra stays unchanged and introduces the opposing person, thing, condition, or force.

example.en: We struggle against the wind.

cardCatalog.promptEs: luchar por + causa, persona u objetivo
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone fights for or works hard in support of a cause or goal?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of luchar, then por, then name the cause, person, or goal.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por introduces what the effort supports or seeks to defend. If the goal is an action, luchar por can instead be followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.es: Luchan por la libertad de expresión.
example.en: They fight for freedom of expression.

cardCatalog.promptEs: luchar por + verbo en forma de diccionario
cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone struggles or strives to do something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of luchar, then por, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Luchar changes for the person and time, while por stays fixed and the goal action keeps its dictionary form.

example.en: We strive to improve.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What common exclamation can express surprise, shock, or amazement?
cardCatalog.noteEn: The words literally mean “my mother,” but speakers often use the complete expression as a reaction without referring to their mother. Tone and context determine whether it sounds alarmed, impressed, or overwhelmed.

example.en: Goodness, what a storm!

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you exclaim “Damn it!” when something has gone wrong?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use ¡maldita sea! as a fixed expression of anger or frustration.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The words literally resemble “damned be it,” but Spanish speakers use the pair as one exclamation. Sea is a special form of ser used here in a wish-like reaction. The expression can sound strong, so use it with care.

example.en: Damn it! I missed the bus.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that people have or carry on a conversation?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of mantener with conversación, or conversaciones for more than one.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mantener literally often means to keep or maintain, but with conversación it describes having or carrying on the exchange. Mantener changes with the person and time; for example, yo mantengo and estamos manteniendo.

example.en: We have a calm conversation.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What is the usual Spanish name for a machine used in the voting process?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use máquina de votación; for more than one, use máquinas de votación.
cardCatalog.noteEn: De links the machine to its function. Máquina changes to máquinas for the plural, while votación remains singular because it names the type of machine.

example.es: El colegio instaló dos máquinas de votación.
example.en: The school installed two voting machines.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What is the usual Spanish expression for a machine that travels through time?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. The expression keeps del tiempo after máquina; Spanish does not normally build this noun pair by placing tiempo directly before máquina.

example.es: La novela incluye una máquina del tiempo.
example.en: The novel includes a time machine.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is farther away or beyond a point?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use más allá; add de before a named reference point.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Más allá works as a fixed place expression. It can stand alone for “farther away,” or appear as más allá de followed by the place, limit, or idea that is exceeded.

example.es: El pueblo está más allá de la colina.
example.en: The town is beyond the hill.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How can you say that a number, time, or description is approximate?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use más o menos before or after the approximate information.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The literal pieces are ‘more or less,’ but together they often work like ‘roughly,’ ‘about,’ or ‘approximately.’

example.es: El viaje dura más o menos dos horas.
example.en: The trip takes about two hours.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something makes a person laugh extremely hard?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a form of matar, then de risa, and identify the person who laughs.
cardCatalog.noteEn: This is an exaggerated fixed expression: matar literally means “to kill,” but matar de risa means to make someone laugh very hard. The person can appear as me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, or las, or after the personal a.

example.es: Ese vídeo nos mató de risa.
example.en: That video made us laugh so hard.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you refer to material used for building?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use material de construcción for ‘construction material.’
cardCatalog.noteEn: This established combination uses de to link material to construcción, the activity of building. English places ‘construction’ directly before ‘material,’ while Spanish keeps the nouns joined by de.

example.en: We need durable construction material.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you politely say that someone would like to do something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person, then gustaría, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cardCatalog.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The short word identifies who has the wish: me gustaría means “I would like,” te gustaría means “you would like,” os gustaría means “you all would like” in Spain, and le gustaría can mean “he, she, or formal you would like.” Gustaría stays singular because the following activity is treated as the thing that would be pleasing.

example.en: I would like to learn Italian.

cardCatalog.promptEs: ¿me lo dices o me lo cuentas?
cardCatalog.questionEn: What colloquial expression says that you already know or have experienced what someone has just told you?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use ¿me lo dices o me lo cuentas? It works like ‘tell me about it’ and can sound ironic or slightly brusque.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Although decir and contar can both mean ‘to tell,’ this fixed question does not ask the listener to choose between them. It signals that the information is already familiar to the speaker; tone can also add disbelief or irritation.

example.es: —Los lunes son agotadores. —¿Me lo dices o me lo cuentas?
example.en: —Mondays are exhausting. —Tell me about it!

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say approximately or exactly half a dozen of something?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use media docena de, then name what is counted.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Media agrees with the feminine noun docena and means half. Docena stays singular here, and de introduces the counted thing; only the later noun normally changes for plural meaning.

example.en: We bought half a dozen eggs.

cardCatalog.questionEn: What expression names the middle stage of adult life?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use la mediana edad for “middle age.”
cardCatalog.noteEn: This is an established life-stage expression. It differs from la mediana de las edades, which would refer to the statistical middle value of a set of ages.

example.es: Cambió de profesión en la mediana edad.
example.en: She changed careers in middle age.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is worth the time or effort?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use a matching form of merecer followed by la pena.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Merecer changes for the person, thing, or time, while la pena stays fixed. An action worth doing can follow in its unchanged dictionary form: merece la pena esperar.

example.es: Merece la pena visitar el museo.
example.en: The museum is worth visiting.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone deserves something, using the common pattern with me, te, se, nos, or os?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Put the matching small pronoun before a form of merecer that matches the person and time, then name the deserved thing.
cardCatalog.noteEn: For example, te mereces is used with tú and se merece with él, ella, or usted. The thing deserved can follow the verb or be understood from context.

example.en: You all deserve a vacation.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets or draws another person into a situation?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use meter a alguien en algo, changing meter for the person and time.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Meter literally means “to put.” A introduces the person affected, and en introduces the situation. With a problem, conflict, or activity, the whole pattern can mean to get or drag someone into it.

example.es: No metas a Leo en el problema.
example.en: Don't drag Leo into the problem.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets into trouble?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use the matching form of meterse followed by en problemas.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Meter changes for the person and time, and a matching small marker accompanies it: me meto, te metes, se mete, nos metemos, os metéis, or se meten. Before another changed verb, meter can stay in its unchanged dictionary form ending in -er, and the marker may move before that earlier verb: me puedo meter. The expression can mean entering a difficult situation or attracting punishment.

example.en: I do not want to get into trouble.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you contrast two facts with “whereas” or “while”?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use mientras que before the contrasting fact.
cardCatalog.noteEn: This use compares two different situations. It is different from plain mientras when that word only means that two actions happen at the same time.

example.es: Ella madruga, mientras que yo trabajo de noche.
example.en: She gets up early, whereas I work at night.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How does Spanish express thousands of millions of something—what English commonly calls billions?
cardCatalog.answerEn: Use miles de millones de, followed by the thing being counted.
cardCatalog.noteEn: Miles and millones stay plural, and de appears both between them and before the counted noun. In standard Spanish numbering, mil millones is one thousand million; English commonly calls that one billion.

example.es: La galaxia contiene miles de millones de estrellas.
example.en: The galaxy contains billions of stars.

cardCatalog.questionEn: How do you say that something is tracked or changes minute by minute?
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can repeat a unit with a between the two copies to describe gradual or repeated progress: minuto a minuto, día a día, paso a paso. The repeated noun normally stays singular.

example.es: Seguimos el partido minuto a minuto.
example.en: We followed the match minute by minute.
