cardCatalog.noteEn: Acostumbré is a completed-past form used by the speaker. With me before it and a after it, acostumbrarse a means to become familiar or comfortable with something through repeated experience.

example.en: I got used to the noise.

cardCatalog.noteEn: El actinio is the radioactive chemical element actinium, symbol Ac.

example.es: El actinio es un elemento radiactivo.
example.en: Actinium is a radioactive element.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish actual means current, not usually English ‘actual.’

example.en: The current state is stable.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Actualidad refers to what is current now. It does not mean the English word ‘actuality.’

example.es: El gráfico llega hasta la actualidad.
example.en: The graph reaches the present day.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Actúas comes from actuar. The ending -as identifies one person addressed informally, and the written accent keeps the stress on ú.

example.en: You act very calmly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a diplomatic context, acuerdos can name formal agreements between governments.

example.en: The accords set the border.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Adecuada is the feminine singular form of adecuado. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular person or thing.

example.en: It is the right tool.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Adecuados ends in -os because it describes a masculine plural noun. The other matching forms are adecuado, adecuada, and adecuadas.

example.en: They are suitable places for children.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Adelante can grant permission or challenge someone to continue. It does not literally describe forward movement in this conversational use.

example.en: Go ahead, ask your question.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Adicción usually names an addiction or dependence. It can also point to the quality that makes an activity very hard to stop, which English can call “addictiveness.”

example.en: The game can cause addiction.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Adjunto can mean ‘attached.’ Used as a noun in email, an adjunto is a file included with the message.

example.en: I opened the message attachments.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Admin is an informal shortened form of administrador or administradora, especially common in computing and online communities.

example.es: Ella es la admin del servidor.
example.en: She is the server administrator.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Admite is the present form of admitir for one person or thing. A following que clause states what is acknowledged.

example.es: El autor admite que se equivocó.
example.en: The author admits that he was wrong.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Adoptar can mean taking up a technology, practice, method, or policy, as well as legally adopting a person.

example.es: La oficina decidió adoptar el nuevo sistema.
example.en: The office decided to adopt the new system.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Adorable has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: It is an adorable dog.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Adulación is exaggerated praise used to please or influence someone.

example.es: No se dejó convencer por la adulación.
example.en: He was not persuaded by flattery.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Adultos can name adult men or a mixed group of adults. The feminine plural is adultas.

example.en: The activity is for adults.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I noticed; I became aware of
cardCatalog.noteEn: Advertí is a completed-past form of advertir. Advertir can mean either “to notice” or “to warn”; this card teaches the notice sense.

example.en: I noticed the error too late.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aerodinámica describes something connected with the movement of air around objects. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular noun such as resistencia.

example.en: They studied the aerodynamic force.

cardCatalog.answerEn: aerospace; relating to flight and space
cardCatalog.noteEn: Aeroespacial describes something involving flight through Earth's atmosphere or outer space. The same singular form can describe a masculine or feminine noun.

example.en: The aerospace project is ambitious.

cardCatalog.answerEn: does it affect; does it make a difference
cardCatalog.noteEn: Afecta is a present form of afectar. In a question, it asks whether something changes the result or matters in some way. English adds ‘does’ before the subject, while the Spanish verb form stays afecta.

example.en: Does that affect the result?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Afectado describes a masculine singular person or thing that experiences the effect of a problem or event.

example.en: The affected system is disconnected.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Afectan is the present form used with a plural subject.

example.en: The changes affect the schedule.

cardCatalog.answerEn: affect (special form for an intended or uncertain result)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Afecte is a form of afectar used when the effect is presented as a goal, possibility, wish, or other non-established result. The ordinary one-thing form afecta changes its final -a to -e.

example.es: Espero que el ruido no afecte al bebé.
example.en: I hope the noise does not affect the baby.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Afirma is a present form of afirmar for one person, document, theory, or other singular source. It introduces something presented as true.

example.es: El informe afirma que el método funciona.
example.en: The report states that the method works.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Afirmar can mean stating something confidently as true. It does not by itself say whether the claim is correct.

example.es: No basta con afirmar que funciona.
example.en: It is not enough to claim that it works.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Afirme is the present subjunctive form of afirmar for one person. After cuando, it presents a future claim whose occurrence is not yet a fact.

example.es: Escucha cuando ella afirme algo distinto.
example.en: Listen when she claims something different.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Afortunados can be a masculine or mixed plural adjective or a noun for fortunate people.

example.en: The lucky ones received tickets.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here agotadas describes a supply of addresses that has all been used, not tired people.

example.en: The tickets are sold out.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Agradecidos describes more than one male person or a mixed group. A feminine plural group would be agradecidas.

example.en: We are grateful for your help.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For a policy or limit, agresivo can mean forceful or stringent rather than physically violent.

example.en: The plan includes aggressive targets.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Agridulce literally combines agrio, “sour,” and dulce, “sweet,” and can describe mixed happy and sad feelings.

example.en: The farewell left bittersweet memories.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With se, agrieta describes one thing developing cracks.

example.es: El barro se agrieta al secarse.
example.en: The mud cracks as it dries.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses plural aguas when naming a body, supply, or category of water. Aguas residuales is the standard plural expression for wastewater.

example.en: The plant treats wastewater.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For sound, agudo means high in pitch, opposed to grave, “low-pitched.” In other contexts it can mean sharp or acute.

example.es: El silbato produce un sonido agudo.
example.en: The whistle produces a high-pitched sound.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For a remark or analysis, agudo describes quick, penetrating intelligence. In other settings it can instead describe a high-pitched sound or a sharp point.

example.en: She made a perceptive comment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Águila is a feminine noun. Because its first stressed sound is á-, singular Spanish normally says el águila rather than la águila; the plural returns to las águilas.

example.es: El águila vuela sobre el valle.
example.en: The eagle flies over the valley.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ah can signal recognition, surprise, or a challenge. In ¿Ah, sí?, the speaker questions what was just said, much like “Oh, really?”

example.en: “You wouldn't dare.” “Oh, really?”

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ah can be used as a brief questioning response when someone has not understood or expects an explanation.

example.en: “The meeting changed locations.” “Huh?”

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ah can show that the speaker has just understood, noticed, or recognized something. Its exact English equivalent depends on tone.

example.en: Oh, yes, now I remember.

cardCatalog.answerEn: arou—; the interrupted beginning of ahí in por ahí (“around”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: The printed speech cuts ahí off after ah because the speaker interrupts themself. The complete expression te veré por ahí can mean “I'll see you around.”

example.en: See you around.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ahí points to a place away from the speaker but normally not as distant as allí. The distinction varies by region and context.

example.en: Leave the box there.

cardCatalog.answerEn: hanged man; person executed by hanging
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ahorcado comes from ahorcar, “to hang by the neck.” As a noun it can name a person who has been hanged.

example.es: La leyenda habla de un ahorcado.
example.en: The legend tells of a hanged man.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ahorrará is the simple future form of ahorrar for one person or thing. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: The repair will save energy.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to save myself; to spare myself (time or effort)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ahorrarme joins me to ahorrar. With time, effort, or trouble after it, the form says that the speaker avoids spending or undergoing that amount.

example.es: Quiero ahorrarme una hora de espera.
example.en: I want to save myself an hour of waiting.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ajá is a short acknowledgment showing that someone is following or has understood what was said. Tone can also make it skeptical.

example.en: “We arrive at six.” “Uh-huh.”

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ajusta is the present form used with one other person or thing. With se and a, it describes that subject fitting, matching, or adapting to something.

example.es: La tapa se ajusta a la caja.
example.en: The lid fits the box.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In software or equipment, an ajuste is a setting that changes how something behaves or appears.

example.en: I changed the brightness setting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins an alarm cry naming the danger
cardCatalog.noteEn: In cries such as ¡al ladrón! or ¡al fuego!, al introduces the danger people should respond to.

example.en: Fire!

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; a + el before an animate direct object
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al combines a and el. Spanish can use this a before a definite animal, creature, or personified thing treated as animate.

example.en: The hero defeated the dragon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

example.en: I’m going to the market.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins al azar, ‘at random’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al is normally the combined form of a and el. In the fixed expression al azar, the two words work together to mean that no deliberate choice or pattern is used.

example.en: She took a card at random.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of al fin, “finally”
in the; part of al final (“in the end”)
no separate English word; part of al habla (‘speaking’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the fixed telephone formula al habla, al does not express ordinary movement ‘to the.’ The complete formula identifies the person currently speaking.

example.en: Mr. López? Speaking.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of al igual que (“just like”)
no separate English word; begins al menos, “at least”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al combines a and el, but the complete fixed expression al menos corresponds to “at least.”

example.en: We need at least one hour.

cardCatalog.answerEn: at the; begins al principio, ‘at the beginning’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. With principio it locates something at the beginning of a process or period.

example.en: At the beginning it was difficult.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of al respecto, “about it”
no separate English word; part of al revés (‘backward’ or ‘upside down’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al normally combines a and el, but al revés is learned as a fixed expression.

example.en: The photo is upside down.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a frequency expression, al combines a + el before a masculine time period: una vez al mes means ‘once per month.’

example.es: Voy al médico dos veces al año.
example.en: I go to the doctor twice a year.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; a + el before the named language
cardCatalog.noteEn: The printed al combines a and el before the specifically named language. Natural English simply names the language after “include.”

example.es: El grupo incluye al dialecto local.
example.en: The group includes the local dialect.

cardCatalog.answerEn: with; by means of the (a + el, introducing a method)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a and el. In some technical expressions, it introduces the tool or process used, as in al láser and al arco.

example.es: La pieza se cortó al láser.
example.en: The piece was laser-cut.

cardCatalog.answerEn: a + el before a specific person; often “the” or “to the” in English
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish contracts a + el to al. The personal a can mark a specific person who receives or is affected by an action; English may use “the,” “to the,” or no separate preposition, depending on the verb.

example.en: I see the teacher.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the one; a + el before the person affected
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al combines a and el. The a marks a person affected by the action, while el joins que to mean “the one who.”

example.en: I help the one who needs it.

cardCatalog.answerEn: on the; a + el before the phone being called
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al combines a and el. With llamar, Spanish can use it before the phone or number where a person is being contacted; natural English often says “on.”

example.en: I called him on his cell phone.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to the; a + el marking the end of a range
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al combines a and el. In a range, it introduces the ending endpoint when that endpoint uses the masculine article el.

example.es: La oficina abre del lunes al viernes.
example.en: The office opens from Monday to Friday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; combines a + el before what is feared after temerle
cardCatalog.noteEn: In temerle a algo, the required a combines with el to form al before a masculine singular target.

example.en: She is afraid of thunder.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; a + el before the opponent of vencer
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vencer normally takes a before the person or thing defeated. Al combines that a with el.

example.en: Our team beat the favorite.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ala is feminine, but singular el is used immediately before it because the word begins with a stressed a sound: el ala. The plural is las alas.

example.en: The left wing is damaged.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In informal speech in Spain, ¡ala! can show surprise or amazement. This is unrelated to the noun ala, “wing.”

example.en: Wow, what a tall building!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Alabando is the ongoing-action form of alabar.

example.es: Siguió alabando el trabajo del equipo.
example.en: She kept praising the team's work.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Alcanzar can mean physically to reach something or figuratively to attain a goal or state.

example.en: She wants to achieve her goal.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aleatorias describes several feminine things selected or arranged without a planned pattern. The -as ending matches a feminine plural noun such as diapositivas.

example.en: We choose three random questions.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Alegando is the -ando form of alegar. It can add the reason or explanation that someone gives for another action.

example.en: She canceled the meeting, citing tiredness.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Algo refers to an unspecified thing. In a question, natural English often uses ‘anything’; after en, en algo can mean ‘in any way.’

example.en: Do you need anything?

cardCatalog.answerEn: some; some day/time (before a masculine noun)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Alguno shortens to algún directly before a masculine singular noun: algún día, algún libro.

example.en: Some neighbor will have the key.

cardCatalog.answerEn: any (before a masculine singular noun in a question)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Algún is the shortened form of alguno used directly before a masculine singular noun. In a question, natural English often uses “any.”

example.en: Is there any problem?

cardCatalog.answerEn: some; any (as part of alguna vez)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Alguna is the feminine singular form of alguno. With vez, it helps form alguna vez. Questions and conditions often use it for “ever,” while positive statements can use it for “sometime.”

example.en: Have you ever been here?

cardCatalog.noteEn: With an imagined or uncertain possibility, alguna can have the natural English sense “any.” It is feminine because it describes a feminine noun, such as idea or manera.

example.en: Is there any way out?

cardCatalog.answerEn: any; at all (after a noun in a negative expression)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a negative idea such as sin, alguno can follow the noun and strengthens the absence: sin respuesta alguna means no answer at all. It agrees with the noun, so feminine respuesta takes alguna.

example.en: She left without any explanation.

cardCatalog.answerEn: any; at all (after a noun in a negative setting)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Alguno normally means some before a noun. After a noun and following a negative word such as sin, it strengthens the negative meaning.

example.en: She did it without any problem at all.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Alitas is the plural diminutive of alas, “wings.” On a menu it commonly refers to chicken wings.

example.en: The wings are spicy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Almacenadas is almacenar's completed-action form used as a description. Its -as ending matches more than one feminine item.

example.es: Las copias están almacenadas en otro equipo.
example.en: The copies are stored on another computer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Alquiló is a completed-past form of alquilar. The final accent marks the stressed last syllable.

example.en: He rented a bicycle yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a mi, tu, or su alrededor, alrededor refers to the surrounding area and natural English says ‘around me, you, him, her, or them.’

example.en: Look around you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Alta can describe a high amount or intensity rather than physical height.

example.es: La máquina funciona a alta presión.
example.en: The machine operates at high pressure.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Altavoces is the plural of altavoz, a device that produces sound.

example.es: Los altavoces están junto al televisor.
example.en: The speakers are next to the television.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a describing word, alternativa presents something as another possible choice. Its ending matches a feminine singular noun; for example, método alternativo uses the masculine form.

example.en: We are looking for an alternative route.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Amañó is the completed-past form of amañar used with él, ella, or formal usted. It suggests secretly arranging an event or result dishonestly.

example.en: The promoter rigged the result.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Amarillo changes its ending to match what it describes: amarillo, amarilla, amarillos, or amarillas.

example.en: The paper is yellow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses el Amazonas for the Amazon River. Cuenca del Amazonas therefore names the broad area drained by that river.

example.es: El Amazonas cruza una región enorme.
example.en: The Amazon crosses an enormous region.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Americana ordinarily means ‘American’ in the feminine singular. In Spain, the fixed name cinta americana refers to strong cloth-backed duct tape.

example.en: I need duct tape to fix it.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Amigo can identify a male friend or appear as the masculine dictionary form when discussing the word itself.

example.en: Pablo is a good friend.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Amplía is a present form of ampliar used with one thing. With se, it says that the thing becomes wider.

example.es: La zona se amplía cada año.
example.en: The area expands every year.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Amplié is the completed-past form of ampliar used for yo. The written accent keeps the final syllable stressed.

example.en: I expanded the garden.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to add to it; to give it an added feature
cardCatalog.noteEn: Añadir is the unchanged dictionary form, and le attaches to identify the thing receiving the addition.

example.es: Queremos añadirle una función al programa.
example.en: We want to add a feature to the program.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Análisis has the same written form in the singular and plural; the surrounding article or verb shows the number.

example.en: The analysis was brief.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Análisis keeps the same written form in singular and plural. A plural article or another plural word shows when more than one analysis is meant.

example.en: They published several analyses.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Analizar stays in its unchanged dictionary form, and las attaches to represent the feminine plural things being analyzed.

example.es: Necesito analizar las muestras; voy a analizarlas mañana.
example.en: I need to analyze the samples; I am going to analyze them tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: hey; wow; well, look at that
cardCatalog.noteEn: Anda literally comes from andar, “to walk,” but it is also a common conversational reaction in Spain. It can show surprise, encourage someone, or draw attention; tone supplies the exact feeling.

example.en: Oh, you came!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Anhelo is a strong, sustained wish rather than an ordinary momentary preference.

example.en: He felt a longing for freedom.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I root for; I cheer on
cardCatalog.noteEn: Animo is the present form of animar for the speaker. It has no written accent; ánimo with an accent is a noun or an encouraging exclamation.

example.es: Animo a mi equipo desde casa.
example.en: I cheer on my team from home.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ano without an accent or ñ is an anatomical word. Do not confuse it with año, ‘year,’ which has the distinct letter ñ.

example.en: The doctor examined the anus.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.en: We lived there for two years.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In health care, antecedentes are earlier conditions, diagnoses, or events that help a clinician assess the present situation.

example.en: The doctor reviewed my medical history.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An antena sends or receives radio signals, including television, mobile, and wireless-network signals.

example.es: La antena recibe una señal débil.
example.en: The antenna receives a weak signal.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Anterior can stand on its own when the omitted noun is already clear. The article la shows that the understood noun is feminine singular.

example.es: Esta página es más clara que la anterior.
example.en: This page is clearer than the previous one.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Anteriormente places something at an earlier time. It often introduces a contrast with what is true now.

example.en: Previously, I lived in another city.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a full event with its own verb, antes normally begins the connector antes de que.

example.en: Call me before you leave.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Used by itself, antes can point back to an earlier time rather than introducing a following event.

example.en: We used to live nearby.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a would-form such as besaría, antes can mean that the speaker would sooner choose that option.

example.es: Antes caminaría que tomar ese autobús.
example.en: I would rather walk than take that bus.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a noun, antiguo or antigua can mean the earlier or former version of something rather than something ancient.

example.en: She returned to her former routine.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Antiguas describes more than one feminine noun.

example.en: We visited some ancient ruins.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a noun, antiguo often means former or previous rather than physically old.

example.en: They rejected the former system.

cardCatalog.noteEn: El antimonio is the chemical element antimony, symbol Sb.

example.en: The alloy contains antimony.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An anuncio can be a notice that informs readers or an advertisement that promotes something.

example.es: Vi el anuncio en la página web.
example.en: I saw the notice on the website.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Anuncio can mean either a commercial advertisement or a public announcement. The surrounding words show which meaning is intended.

example.en: The radio broadcasts many advertisements.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Apagado describes a masculine singular device that is not operating. The ending changes to apagada for a feminine singular thing.

example.en: The phone is switched off.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all manage; get along (informal plural, mainly Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Apañarse is a conversational verb for managing, coping, or sorting things out. When two or more people are named together, it can ask how they manage together or whether they get along.

example.es: Los dos compañeros se apañan bien.
example.en: The two coworkers get along well.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aparcado is the completed-action form of aparcar, “to park.” It follows a form of haber in a completed-action construction.

example.es: He aparcado cerca de la estación.
example.en: I have parked near the station.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aparearse is a pronominal verb used for animals mating. Its small pronoun changes with the subject.

example.en: The birds return to mate.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aparente describes how something seems, which may differ from what it really is.

example.es: Su calma aparente ocultaba los nervios.
example.en: His apparent calm hid his nerves.

cardCatalog.answerEn: feels appealing; feels like; is up for
cardCatalog.noteEn: Apetece is the singular present form of apetecer. Spanish makes the desired thing the grammatical subject, while me, te, le, nos, os, or les identifies the person who wants it.

example.en: Do you feel like having a coffee?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aplazado describes something moved to a later time.

example.en: It was a postponed project.

cardCatalog.answerEn: applied; put to practical use (feminine singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the name or description of a field, aplicada contrasts practical use with more abstract theory. Use feminine singular aplicada with a feminine singular field name, such as física or lingüística.

example.es: El curso trata de lingüística aplicada.
example.en: The course is about applied linguistics.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Apocalipsis is masculine in Spanish: el apocalipsis.

example.en: The novel imagines an apocalypse.

cardCatalog.answerEn: settling lazily into an armchair; lounging
cardCatalog.noteEn: Apoltronándose comes from apoltronarse, a vivid verb for making oneself comfortable and inactive, as if sinking into an armchair.

example.es: Pasó la tarde apoltronándose frente al televisor.
example.en: He spent the afternoon lounging in front of the television.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Apreciar can mean valuing someone or recognizing and enjoying a quality in something.

example.en: I learned to appreciate silence.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aprobado is aprobar's completed-action form. After a present helper such as ha, it says that one person, group, or institution has formally accepted or authorized something.

example.es: El consejo ha aprobado el plan.
example.en: The council has approved the plan.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aproximadamente signals that a number or amount is not exact.

example.en: It will take approximately one hour.

cardCatalog.answerEn: fitness; quality score (in an optimization algorithm)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In a genetic algorithm, aptitud is the measured quality assigned to a candidate solution. It is a technical use related to how well that candidate meets the goal, not a person's ordinary talent.

example.es: El programa calcula la aptitud de cada solución.
example.en: The program calculates the fitness of each solution.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to stab you all; to stab both of you (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Apuñalar is the unchanged action verb ‘to stab.’ Attached os identifies several people addressed informally, and the two parts are written as one word.

example.es: En la obra, el villano amenaza con apuñalaros.
example.en: In the play, the villain threatens to stab you all.

cardCatalog.answerEn: are you joining; are you up for it (with te and a)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Apuntas is the present tú form of apuntar. In te apuntas a, the full verb apuntarse means to sign up, join in, or be willing to take part.

example.en: Are you joining the excursion?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Arañado is the completed-action form of arañar. With hemos, it says that “we” have scratched something.

example.en: We have scratched the table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The singular is arándano. The word keeps its written accent in the plural.

example.en: I put blueberries in the yogurt.

cardCatalog.answerEn: arbitrary; unrestricted by a fixed choice
cardCatalog.noteEn: Arbitrarios is masculine plural to match a masculine plural noun. It describes choices that are not limited to one predetermined case.

example.en: The program accepts arbitrary values.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Arcade (part of the band name Arcade Fire)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Archivo can mean a physical archive or a computer file. In computing, it is a named collection of stored data.

example.es: Guardé el informe en un archivo nuevo.
example.en: I saved the report in a new file.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In welding, arco is the bright electrical discharge that supplies intense heat. This is different from arco meaning a bow or a curved arch.

example.es: El arco eléctrico produce mucho calor.
example.en: The electric arc produces a great deal of heat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ardilla is a feminine noun for a squirrel, so it normally takes la or una.

example.en: The squirrel climbs the tree.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Área is feminine but normally uses el or un immediately before it in the singular because it begins with a stressed a sound. Other describing words remain feminine.

example.en: It is a large area.

cardCatalog.answerEn: argh!; a cry of distress or frustration
cardCatalog.noteEn: Argh represents a nonverbal cry in writing. Its spelling varies, but it signals pain, dread, frustration, or disgust rather than naming an action.

example.en: Argh! Not again.

cardCatalog.answerEn: argument; input supplied to a function
cardCatalog.noteEn: In mathematics and computing, an argumento is a value given to a function, not a disagreement between people.

example.en: The function receives two arguments.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Arma is grammatically feminine, but singular el arma and un arma are used because the word begins with a stressed a sound. Its adjectives remain feminine: un arma peligrosa.

example.en: They found an old weapon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Arma is feminine, but singular el arma uses el because arma begins with a stressed a sound. The plural returns to las armas.

example.en: They banned weapons.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I start driving; I start up (subjunctive form)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Arranque is a special form of arrancar used for a pending event after a connector such as antes de que. The spelling changes from c to qu so the hard k sound remains before e.

example.es: Avísame antes de que yo arranque.
example.en: Tell me before I start driving.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, arranque is the process of starting a computer and loading its operating system.

example.es: El arranque del ordenador fue lento.
example.en: The computer's startup was slow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they will devastate; they will sweep through
cardCatalog.noteEn: Arrasar can mean destroying or devastating a place as something moves through it.

example.en: The flames will devastate the forest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Arrastrarse means ‘to crawl’ or literally to drag oneself along. For an action in progress, arrastrar becomes arrastrando and the matching se is attached at the end. The written accent keeps the original stress: arrastrándose.

example.es: El gato está arrastrándose bajo la mesa.
example.en: The cat is crawling under the table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Arremolinan is the plural present form of arremolinar. It commonly appears as arremolinarse for things that gather and move around one another in a confused circular way.

example.es: Las nubes se arremolinan sobre la montaña.
example.en: The clouds swirl over the mountain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An articulación is the place where bones meet and movement can occur.

example.es: El frío le molesta en las articulaciones.
example.en: The cold bothers her joints.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In academic or technical contexts, un artículo can be a scholarly paper rather than a newspaper article or a grammatical article.

example.en: I read two scientific papers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In equipo de asalto, asalto classifies the team as one assembled for an attack or strike.

example.en: They prepared a strike team.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Asegurado is the completed-action form of asegurar. In a security context it can mean bringing a place under control or making it safe.

example.es: El equipo ha asegurado la entrada.
example.en: The team has secured the entrance.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a masculine singular noun, asesino can describe something designed or used to kill. As a noun, asesino can also mean a male killer.

example.es: La novela presenta un virus asesino.
example.en: The novel features a killer virus.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, asesino names a male killer or a person whose gender is not being specified. Asesina is the feminine form.

example.en: The police are looking for the killer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Together, aun así introduces a result that remains true despite the previous point.

example.en: It was raining; even so, we went out.

cardCatalog.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Asignada is the completed-action form of asignar used as a description. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular person or thing.

example.en: I have an assigned table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aspecto can describe what someone or something looks like.

example.es: El edificio tiene un aspecto antiguo.
example.en: The building has an old appearance.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For a goal or desired outcome, aspirar is followed by a. Aspirar can also literally mean to inhale or vacuum, but those senses use different surrounding words.

example.es: Aspira a dirigir su propio equipo.
example.en: She aspires to lead her own team.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Asteroide is masculine; its plural is asteroides.

example.en: The telescope detected several asteroids.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you assume; you accept as a starting point
cardCatalog.noteEn: Asumes is the present form of asumir used with one familiar listener. In reasoning, asumir can mean accepting an idea temporarily as a premise.

example.es: Asumes que el dato es correcto.
example.en: You assume that the fact is correct.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Asustada describes a feminine singular person or animal that feels fear. Masculine singular is asustado.

example.en: The girl is frightened.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Atizar is informal when it means striking someone or something.

example.en: You should not hit anyone.

cardCatalog.answerEn: binge; excessive amount done or consumed at once
cardCatalog.noteEn: Atracón can describe overeating, but it also extends to an excessive burst of another activity. It is masculine: un atracón.

example.es: Se dio un atracón de películas.
example.en: He went on a movie binge.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Atrapado can describe someone unable to leave a place or situation. The ending changes to match the person or thing described: atrapado, atrapada, atrapados, or atrapadas.

example.es: El coche quedó atrapado en la nieve.
example.en: The car got stuck in the snow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Atrasados is masculine plural because it describes a mixed or masculine group. A feminine group would be atrasadas, while one person or thing would use atrasado or atrasada.

example.en: The buses are running late.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Atravesó is the completed-past form of atravesar for one person or thing. It describes movement from one side of something to the other.

example.en: The runner crossed the park.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Atraviesa tells one familiar person to cross something from one side to the other.

example.en: Cross the bridge.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Audible has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns. The plural is audibles.

example.en: The signal is barely audible.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An audiófilo is a person strongly interested in high-quality sound reproduction and audio equipment. This masculine or mixed-group plural keeps the written accent.

example.en: The audiophiles compared the amplifiers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a form of haber, aumentado is aumentar’s completed-action form.

example.en: Production has increased.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In this contrast expression, aun is now commonly written without an accent, although the printed source uses aún.

example.en: It was late; even so, we continued.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In mystical claims, an aura is an invisible field said to surround a person or object. The ordinary word can also mean an atmosphere or impression.

example.es: La curandera afirmó que podía ver auras.
example.en: The healer claimed that she could see auras.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Autista has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: She is an autistic student.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Autoconecta is a present form used with one device or connection. With se, it describes that thing connecting without the user starting the connection manually.

example.en: The tablet connects automatically.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Autoestopista names a person who travels by getting free rides from passing vehicles. The same noun form can refer to a man or a woman.

example.es: El conductor recogió a una autoestopista.
example.en: The driver picked up a hitchhiker.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An autómata is a machine or a person imagined as moving without independent thought. The plural autómatas can refer to a mixed or masculine group.

example.es: La novela presenta a los trabajadores como autómatas.
example.en: The novel presents the workers as automatons.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Autopolinización is pollination using pollen from the same flower or plant.

example.es: La planta puede reproducirse por autopolinización.
example.en: The plant can reproduce by self-pollination.

cardCatalog.answerEn: he or she found out; discovered
cardCatalog.noteEn: Averiguó is a completed-past form of averiguar for one person or thing. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: She found out the truth yesterday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: warn; tell (a positive command to one familiar person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Avisa is the positive command form of avisar for one familiar listener. Avisar can mean to warn, notify, or let someone know.

example.en: Tell Marta tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Avisado is avisar's completed-action form, also called a past participle. It stays unchanged after the helper haber.

example.en: I had already warned you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Avisar means making someone aware beforehand or notifying them.

example.en: You should warn us before entering.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Aviso can be a warning about possible danger or a notice that gives information. The surrounding situation determines which English word fits.

example.es: El cartel contiene un aviso de peligro.
example.en: The sign contains a danger warning.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An axioma is a statement accepted as a starting point in a system of mathematics or logic. Axiomas is its plural form.

example.es: La demostración parte de dos axiomas.
example.en: The proof starts from two axioms.

cardCatalog.answerEn: oh; an exclamation of alarm or annoyance
help me (informal command to several people, used mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ayudad is the positive command for vosotros, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain. Me is attached to the end because the speaker is the person receiving the help.

example.en: Help me close the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ayudamos is the present form of ayudar used with nosotros or nosotras.

example.en: We help our neighbors.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ayudar is the unchanged dictionary form, and le means the formal listener here. Spanish attaches le to the end of an unchanged verb and writes ayudarle as one word.

example.en: I want to help you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ayudarme combines ayudar, “to help,” with me, which identifies the speaker as the person receiving help. The short word attaches to the unchanged verb ending in -ar.

example.en: Thank you for helping me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ayudarte joins ayudar, “to help,” to te, “you.” Spanish writes the two pieces as one word.

example.en: I want to help you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ayude is a present subjunctive form of ayudar. After wish-introducing que, it presents the helping as something hoped for.

example.en: May luck help you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Azar is chance or randomness. The fixed expression al azar describes a choice or action made without a deliberate pattern.

example.en: She took a card at random.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Azucaradas describes feminine plural things that contain sugar or have had sugar added.

example.en: I avoid sugary drinks.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Azul has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns; the plural is azules.

example.en: The sky looks blue.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Azulado describes something with a blue tint, not necessarily something fully blue.

example.es: El humo tiene un tono azulado.
example.en: The smoke has a bluish tone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bahía has a written accent to keep the í in a separate spoken syllable.

example.es: El puerto está en una bahía.
example.en: The port is in a bay.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In batería baja, baja describes the battery's remaining charge as low. It uses feminine singular -a to match batería.

example.es: El teléfono avisa de batería baja.
example.en: The phone warns of low battery.

cardCatalog.answerEn: go down; travel down (informal singular command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Baja tells one familiar person to move downward or along a descending route.

example.en: Go down this path.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bajar literally means to lower or go down. On websites and in informal technology language, it can mean to download a file; descargar is another common choice.

example.es: Puedes bajar el archivo desde la página.
example.en: You can download the file from the page.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Baja is the positive command for one informally addressed person. Te is attached because the verb is bajarse, and the written accent keeps the command's original stress.

example.en: Get off the bus here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here bajo is a describing word for a masculine singular level or setting. It is different from bajo meaning “under” and from bajo meaning “I lower.”

example.en: The brightness is very low.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bajo is the present ‘I’ form of bajar here. The same written form can also mean ‘low’ or ‘under’ in other contexts.

example.en: I lower the volume.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bam represents a loud, abrupt blow, collision, or impact in comics.

example.en: The door slammed shut: bam!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Banear is an informal internet verb formed from English “ban.” The ending te is attached to the unchanged -ar form and identifies informal singular you as the person banned.

example.es: El moderador puede banearte del foro.
example.en: The moderator can ban you from the forum.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Barato describes a masculine singular thing with a low price.

example.en: We bought an inexpensive watch.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Base combines with de datos to form the common technical term base de datos.

example.es: La base de datos está disponible.
example.en: The database is available.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Básicamente summarizes something by its main or essential point.

example.es: Los dos planes son básicamente iguales.
example.en: The two plans are basically the same.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After an action verb, bastante can strengthen the amount or degree of that action. This differs from bastante before a noun, where it can mean “enough.”

example.en: The trip lasted quite a while.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a describing word, bastante increases its degree and often means ‘quite,’ ‘fairly,’ or ‘pretty.’ It stays unchanged even when the following description changes for gender or number: bastante claro, bastante clara, bastante claros. This differs from bastante meaning ‘enough.’

example.en: The instructions are quite clear.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a verb or adjective, bastante can mean that the amount or degree is sufficient: no es bastante means “it is not enough.”

example.en: One hour is not enough.

cardCatalog.answerEn: terrible; rubbish; worthless (in an insulting comparison)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Basura literally means “trash.” In ser una basura de followed by a role, it harshly says that someone is very bad at that role.

example.en: I'm a terrible singer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it flaps (special form after dejan que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Bata comes from batir. Ordinary bate states that it flaps; after dejar que, bata presents the flapping as the action being allowed. The special form is called the subjunctive.

example.es: Deja que el pájaro bata las alas.
example.en: Let the bird flap its wings.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A bata is a loose garment worn over other clothes. In a laboratory or medical setting, it refers to a lab coat; in other settings the same noun can mean a gown or robe.

example.es: La científica se puso una bata blanca.
example.en: The scientist put on a white lab coat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bebé keeps its written accent on the final é. It can refer to a baby of any sex.

example.en: The baby is asleep.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bebí is the completed-past form of beber used by the speaker. The written accent marks the stressed final sound.

example.en: Yesterday I drank a lot of water.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bebidas is the feminine plural noun for things people drink.

example.en: They served cold drinks.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bello is an evaluative adjective. It changes to bella for a feminine singular noun and to bellos or bellas in the plural.

example.en: We saw a beautiful garden.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In business and economics, beneficios commonly means the money left as profit, not merely general advantages.

example.es: La compañía declaró beneficios este año.
example.en: The company reported profits this year.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I would kiss; he or she would kiss
cardCatalog.noteEn: Besaría is the would-form of besar. The surrounding context identifies its subject.

example.en: I would kiss my partner.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Beso can also be the noun “a kiss.” As a verb, beso is the present form used by a speaker to say “I kiss.”

example.es: Beso a mi pareja antes de salir.
example.en: I kiss my partner before leaving.

cardCatalog.noteEn: El beso is the noun. The same spelling beso without an article can also be the verb form meaning “I kiss.”

example.en: He gave her a kiss.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In software, una beta is a version released for testing before the finished release. Spanish commonly uses the feminine article la because versión, the understood noun, is feminine.

example.en: The beta is now available.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Used by itself after a result or answer, bien can show approval, like ‘good’ or ‘great.’ This differs from bien meaning ‘well’ or opening a response as ‘all right.’

example.en: ‘I’ve finished.’ ‘Good.’

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a judgment on an answer, choice, or response, bien can label it as correct. This differs from bien meaning “well” or opening a reply as “all right.”

example.en: The first answer is right.

cardCatalog.answerEn: well; completes pasarlo bien, ‘have a good time’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Bien completes the fixed expression pasarlo bien. Its meaning belongs to the whole enjoyment expression rather than an evaluation of how a task was performed.

example.es: Lo pasamos bien en la fiesta.
example.en: We had a good time at the party.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Besides meaning 'well,' bien can strengthen a description or completed result. Its natural English equivalent may be 'really,' 'thoroughly,' or another emphatic wording.

example.en: The door ended up firmly closed.

cardCatalog.answerEn: welcome (addressing a mixed or all-male group)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Bienvenidos is the masculine plural form of bienvenido. Use bienvenidas for an all-female group.

example.en: Welcome to our city.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Biiip imitates a sustained electronic tone. Spanish sound spellings vary, and extra i letters make the tone feel longer.

example.en: The device went beep.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Biip is sound-imitating writing. Its doubled i stretches the conventional bip to suggest a longer electronic tone.

example.en: The sensor went beep.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Billete can mean a ticket, banknote, or travel pass. With de lotería, it means a lottery ticket.

example.en: She bought two lottery tickets.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Standard Spanish uses the long scale: un billón is a million million, 10¹². English billion normally means 10⁹, which standard Spanish calls mil millones. English influence can produce nonstandard uses, so the surrounding source matters.

example.es: Un billón es un millón de millones.
example.en: One Spanish billón is a million million (10¹²).

cardCatalog.answerEn: binary; based on two possibilities (feminine singular)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Biología is the scientific study of living things.

example.es: La biología estudia los seres vivos.
example.en: Biology studies living things.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Biólogos is the masculine or mixed-group plural for people who work in biology.

example.en: The biologists observed the cells.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A bit is the smallest ordinary unit of digital information and has one of two values, conventionally 0 or 1.

example.es: Ese bit cambia de cero a uno.
example.en: That bit changes from zero to one.

cardCatalog.answerEn: a penny; any money (in sin blanca)
cardCatalog.noteEn: A blanca was an old coin. In the fixed informal expression sin blanca, the word now contributes the idea of not having even the smallest amount of money.

example.en: I got home without a penny.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes the expression for rolling one's eyes
cardCatalog.noteEn: Blanco ordinarily means ‘white.’ In poner los ojos en blanco, it is a fixed part of the expression rather than a separate color description in natural English.

example.es: Él puso los ojos en blanco.
example.en: He rolled his eyes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In this context, the plural refers broadly to profanities. Blasfemia can more literally mean irreverent speech about something sacred.

example.en: I do not want to hear swear words.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Blogorayos humorously fuses blog with rayos, “rays,” as though blogs occupied a band of the electromagnetic spectrum.

example.en: The drawing invents blog rays.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Blog is a borrowed technology word used in Spanish; blogs is its common plural form.

example.en: I read several blogs every week.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In networking, a bloque is a group or range of addresses identified by one prefix.

example.es: Ese bloque contiene muchas direcciones de red.
example.en: That block contains many network addresses.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The -as ending matches a feminine plural noun.

example.en: The doors are blocked.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Boca names the mouth as a body part.

example.en: He closed his mouth.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bolsa usually means a bag. In scientific descriptions, a bolsa de aire is a bounded pocket or localized mass of air.

example.es: Hay bolsas de aire frío en el valle.
example.en: There are pockets of cold air in the valley.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bomba can also mean a pump. Here the plural refers specifically to explosive devices.

example.es: Los artificieros retiraron dos bombas antiguas.
example.en: The bomb squad removed two old bombs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bombilla is the common word in Spain for the replaceable electric bulb in a lamp.

example.en: The light bulb burned out.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bonita is the feminine form of bonito. Spanish can leave the noun unstated when it is already obvious, while the -a ending still points to one feminine thing.

example.en: —Do you like the table? —Yes, it is pretty.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bonito can come before a noun when the speaker presents a positive, often personal evaluation. Its ending changes to match the noun: bonita, bonitos, or bonitas.

example.en: It was a lovely gesture.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Used by itself as a reaction, bonito can approve something as pleasing or impressive rather than describe a specific masculine noun.

example.en: —Look at my drawing. —Nice.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bonitos ends in -os to describe a masculine plural noun. The other forms are bonito, bonita, and bonitas.

example.en: They bought some pretty glasses.

cardCatalog.answerEn: boom; the sound of an explosion
cardCatalog.noteEn: This comic keeps the internationally familiar English-style spelling BOOM as a printed sound effect. Spanish also commonly writes the sound as bum.

example.en: Boom! The box fell to the floor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Boop imitates a short rounded electronic tone rather than naming an object or action.

example.es: El robot respondió con un boop.
example.en: The robot answered with a boop.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Borrachos describes several men or a mixed group.

example.en: The guests were drunk.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to remove myself; to delete my account or entry
cardCatalog.noteEn: Borrarme combines borrar with me. In a service or list context, it can mean removing one's own account, registration, or entry rather than literally erasing one's body.

example.en: I decided to remove myself from the list.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A bosón is a category of subatomic particle. Spanish writes the singular with an accent, bosón, and the plural as bosones.

example.es: La física explicó qué es un bosón.
example.en: The physicist explained what a boson is.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bot is a technology loanword used in Spanish for an automated program that acts or communicates without continuous human control.

example.en: The site blocked a bot.

cardCatalog.answerEn: boots; completes ponerse las botas, ‘to make a killing’ here
cardCatalog.noteEn: Botas literally means boots. In ponerse las botas, it belongs to an informal fixed expression whose meaning comes from the phrase, not from footwear.

example.es: Con aquel encargo, se pusieron las botas.
example.en: They made a killing on that job.

cardCatalog.noteEn: It can be a physical button or an on-screen control.

example.en: Press the green button.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bovina describes a feminine singular noun and can literally mean related to cattle or figuratively suggest a dull, passive expression.

example.es: La figura tenía una expresión bovina.
example.en: The figure had a bovine expression.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Brillante has the same form for masculine and feminine singular nouns. Its plural is brillantes.

example.es: La luna está brillante esta noche.
example.en: The moon is bright tonight.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Brillante can describe a bright light or, figuratively, a very intelligent or impressive person. Its plural is brillantes for every gender.

example.en: They are brilliant researchers.

cardCatalog.answerEn: joke; completes en broma, “as a joke”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Broma means a joke. After en, the complete expression describes something done jokingly rather than seriously.

example.en: It was only a joke.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Broma is a humorous remark, trick, or prank; context distinguishes a spoken joke from an action played on someone.

example.en: It was an innocent joke.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bromeado is the completed-action form of bromear, ‘to joke.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have joked.’

example.en: We have joked about that.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Brutal can intensify something as extreme or severe; it need not describe physical violence.

example.en: There were massive delays.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bruum imitates a low, sustained rumbling or roaring sound. Its repeated vowel stretches the sound on the page.

example.en: The engine went “vroom.”

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bueno shortens to buen directly before a masculine singular noun.

example.en: It is a good book.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With estar, bueno or buena can informally describe a person as physically attractive. This use can sound objectifying, so it is not a neutral substitute for guapo or guapa in every setting.

example.es: Dice que esa actriz está muy buena.
example.en: He says that actress is really hot.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Buena has the feminine ending because it describes the feminine noun idea.

example.en: It is a good question.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Buena is the feminine singular form of bueno. It is used before or after a feminine singular noun, such as práctica or decisión.

example.en: That is a good decision.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins buenos días, a daytime greeting
cardCatalog.noteEn: Buenos is the masculine plural form of bueno, but buenos días is learned and used as one conventional greeting rather than assembled word by word.

example.en: Good morning, Ms. Ruiz.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the good ones; good people (masculine or mixed plural)
cardCatalog.noteEn: A plural adjective can stand alone when the omitted people or things are understood. Buenos can therefore label the good members of a masculine or mixed group.

example.es: Separaron a los buenos de los malos.
example.en: They separated the good ones from the bad ones.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the Buffyverse; the fictional universe of Buffy
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish fandom writing can add -verso to a name to refer to the shared fictional universe around it. This coined term behaves as a masculine noun after el.

example.es: El personaje aparece en el buffyverso.
example.en: The character appears in the Buffyverse.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bug is an English computing loanword often used informally in Spanish. Error and fallo are common Spanish alternatives; the plural bugs keeps the English spelling.

example.es: El programa todavía tiene varios bugs.
example.en: The program still has several bugs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A bujía creates the spark that ignites fuel in a petrol engine.

example.en: The mechanic checked the spark plug.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bujías is the plural of bujía.

example.en: The engine needs new spark plugs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bum is a written sound effect for an impact or explosion. It can represent a sudden blow, a heavy fall, or an explosive noise.

example.en: Thump! The box fell to the floor.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to make fun; to mock (with myself as the actor)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Burlarme combines burlar with attached me. In burlarse de, the attached pronoun marks the person doing the mocking, while de introduces the target.

example.en: I try not to make fun of anyone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Burlo is the present yo form used in me burlo de. Me marks the speaker as the actor in the pronominal expression, and de introduces the target.

example.es: No me burlo de sus preguntas.
example.en: I do not make fun of their questions.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we look for; we search for
cardCatalog.noteEn: Buscamos is the present form of buscar for a group that includes the speaker.

example.en: We are looking for a solution.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Buscar already includes the idea expressed by English ‘for.’ Spanish normally puts the sought item directly after buscar, without adding por.

example.en: I am looking for my keys.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to look it up; to search for it
cardCatalog.noteEn: Buscarlo combines buscar, “to look for or look up,” with lo, “it.” Lo attaches to the unchanged verb and points back to a masculine thing already mentioned.

example.es: Voy a buscarlo en el manual.
example.en: I am going to look it up in the manual.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to look for us; to search for us
cardCatalog.noteEn: Buscar is the unchanged action form, and nos is attached to its end to identify the speaker's group as the people sought.

example.en: They are going to look for us tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I search for; I look up
cardCatalog.noteEn: Busco is the present form of buscar used by the speaker. The spelling uses c before o.

example.en: I search for the answer online.

cardCatalog.answerEn: cancer, pronounced with an exaggerated long vowel
cardCatalog.noteEn: The standard word is cáncer. Extra a letters show that the stressed vowel is being drawn out for comic emphasis; the written accent stays on the first á.

example.en: The ordinary word is cancer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cable can name the physical wire, or the television and internet service delivered through a cable network.

example.es: El servicio de cable llega mañana.
example.en: The cable service arrives tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cable can name an electrical or signal-carrying wire, not only a television service.

example.en: I need a longer cable.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes llevar a cabo (“to carry out”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cabo has several meanings on its own, but after llevar a it completes the fixed expression for conducting or completing something.

example.es: El equipo llevó a cabo el plan.
example.en: The team carried out the plan.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, cadena is a sequence of characters or bits; outside computing it can mean a physical chain.

example.es: El programa lee una cadena de letras.
example.en: The program reads a string of letters.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In an organizational context, cadena describes a linked sequence of authority rather than a physical metal chain.

example.es: La orden bajó por toda la cadena.
example.en: The order moved down the whole chain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Caer can describe a number, level, score, or apparent ability decreasing.

example.es: La temperatura cae por la noche.
example.en: The temperature drops at night.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Caerse can describe a website, network, or service becoming unavailable.

example.es: Cuando se cae la red, esperamos.
example.en: When the network goes down, we wait.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Caen is the present form of caer for more than one thing. With se and network services, it describes connections failing or going down rather than objects literally falling.

example.es: A veces las llamadas se caen.
example.en: Sometimes the calls drop.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Caerse describes a person or thing losing balance or falling, without naming someone who makes it fall. The attached se changes with the person in changed verb forms: me caigo, te caes, se cae.

example.en: The child may fall.

cardCatalog.answerEn: screwed up; messed up (with la, vulgar)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cagado is the completed-action form of cagar. In the fixed expression cagarla, the literal meaning gives way to the informal vulgar sense of making a serious mistake.

example.en: I think we have screwed up.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Caída is the feminine singular form of caído. It can describe something that has fallen rather than naming the action itself.

example.en: We picked up a fallen branch.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Caído is the completed-action form of caer, ‘to fall.’

example.en: The glass has fallen.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I calculate (subjunctive form after espera que)

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a branch of mathematics, cálculo means calculus, the study of change and accumulation. In other settings, the same word can mean a calculation.

example.en: We are studying calculus this semester.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Calentado is the completed-action form of calentar used after haber.

example.es: El sol habrá calentado el agua.
example.en: The sun will have warmed the water.

cardCatalog.answerEn: calibration; careful adjustment to a standard

cardCatalog.noteEn: In technical contexts, calibre can name a tool or standard used to check a dimension or gap.

example.es: Comprueba el espacio con un calibre.
example.en: Check the gap with a gauge.

cardCatalog.answerEn: hot; very close to the target in a hot-and-cold game
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the game, caliente is not a report about temperature. It tells the searcher that the hidden object or chosen place is very near.

example.en: Hot! It is near your hand.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Calla tells one friend, relative, or other familiar person to stop talking. It comes from callar.

example.en: Be quiet for a moment, please.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Calor is masculine in standard Spanish: el calor. It can refer to thermal energy or the feeling of being hot.

example.en: Metal transmits heat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Calva describes a woman or feminine noun with no hair. The masculine form is calvo.

example.es: La actriz aparece calva en la escena.
example.en: The actress appears bald in the scene.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Camarero can refer to a man serving customers in a restaurant or bar. Camarera is the feminine form.

example.en: The waiter brings the drinks.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a form of haber, cambiado presents cambiar as completed. With a car part, it often means replaced.

example.es: He cambiado el filtro del coche.
example.en: I have replaced the car's filter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cambiar can mean altering something or replacing one item with another; the surrounding object supplies the exact sense.

example.en: I am going to replace the battery.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it will change; formal you will change
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cambiará keeps the whole dictionary form cambiar and adds -á for the future of one person or thing. Context identifies the subject.

example.en: The weather will change tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to change something closely connected to me; for example, to change my life
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cambiar is the unchanged dictionary form, and attached me marks the person affected. Spanish can then use the definite article with the affected person's body part or closely associated possession.

example.es: La noticia puede cambiarme la vida.
example.en: The news can change my life.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they change; flip (a bit, special purpose form)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ordinary cambian states that several things change something. Cambien is the special form used here because it remains inside the intended result introduced by para que.

example.es: Ajusta el sistema para que cambien el valor.
example.en: Adjust the system so that they change the value.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes en cambio, “instead” or “on the other hand”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cambio alone often means “change.” With en, it forms a fixed connector that introduces a contrast or alternative.

example.es: No fui en coche; en cambio, caminé.
example.en: I did not go by car; instead, I walked.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Caminando is the -ando action form of caminar, “to walk.” This form can add an action happening at the same time.

example.en: She came in walking.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Camino can be a physical path or, figuratively, a long process that leads to a result.

example.es: Fue un camino largo y difícil.
example.en: It was a long and difficult journey.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Camino is the present form of caminar used for yo. The same spelling can also be the noun camino, “path” or “way,” but that is a different sense.

example.en: I walk to the station.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Camiseta usually names a T-shirt or light casual shirt.

example.en: He is wearing a white T-shirt.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Campana normally means a bell. A roughly bell-shaped statistical curve is also called a campana in Spanish.

example.es: La curva tiene forma de campana.
example.en: The curve has a bell shape.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Campaña can name an organized effort. With electoral or in a political setting, it means an election campaign.

example.en: The election campaign starts in April.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A campaña is a coordinated series of actions toward a goal, such as an election, advertising, or fundraising campaign.

example.es: Organizan campañas para ayudar al barrio.
example.en: They organize campaigns to help the neighborhood.

cardCatalog.answerEn: field; work done on location rather than in an office
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a profession, de campo describes practical work carried out where events happen. English usually puts field before the profession instead.

example.es: Ella es una investigadora de campo.
example.en: She is a field researcher.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Campo can mean a physical field, but in an academic context it means an area of knowledge or study. Campos is its plural.

example.es: La historia y la química son campos distintos.
example.en: History and chemistry are different fields.

cardCatalog.answerEn: intensity or energy (in the informal expression dar caña)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Canadiense has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: She is a Canadian scientist.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In online chat, canal names a shared conversation space or channel, not a television station or waterway.

example.es: Nos vemos en el canal del grupo.
example.en: See you in the group's channel.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A canasta is a basket. In basketball, ¡Canasta! can announce that a shot has gone in and scored points.

example.en: The shot ended in a basket.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Software buttons often use the unchanged dictionary form cancelar as a neutral interface instruction.

example.es: Pulsa Cancelar para cerrar la ventana.
example.en: Press Cancel to close the window.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cancerígeno describes something capable of causing cancer. Its ending changes to agree with the noun.

example.en: They study possible carcinogenic effects.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cancerosas is the feminine plural form, used with a feminine plural noun.

example.en: The laboratory studies cancerous cells.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cansado is the completed-action form of cansar. With a form of haber and cansarse de, cansado helps say that someone has become tired of something.

example.en: I have gotten tired of the noise.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cansemos is a special “we” form of cansarse. It appears with nos, and de introduces what causes the tiredness. This form can appear inside a description of an unknown or desired person or thing.

example.es: Quiero un juego del que no nos cansemos.
example.en: I want a game that we don't get tired of.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Capacita is the present form of capacitar used with one third-person subject. It means giving someone the ability or qualification to do something.

example.es: El curso capacita a los técnicos.
example.en: The course trains the technicians.

cardCatalog.answerEn: tricky; designed to catch or mislead someone

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cápsula can be a small sealed container that protects equipment or material.

example.en: The capsule protects the instrument.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Capturado is the completed-action form of capturar. After a form of haber, it describes the completed act of capturing someone or something.

example.en: They have captured the fugitive.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In physics, carga is the electrical property described as positive or negative. This is distinct from a physical load or an explosive charge.

example.en: The particle has positive charge.

cardCatalog.answerEn: charge; a quantity of explosive material
cardCatalog.noteEn: As a technical noun, carga can mean an amount of explosive material. In other contexts it can mean a load, burden, or electrical charge.

example.es: El equipo retiró una carga explosiva.
example.en: The team removed an explosive charge.

cardCatalog.answerEn: load; demand on a computer system
cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, carga describes how much work the system is handling rather than a physical weight.

example.es: La carga del sistema es alta.
example.en: The system load is high.

cardCatalog.answerEn: takes out; beats up (as part of se carga a)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Carga normally relates to carrying or loading. With se and a person introduced by a, cargarse can informally mean to take that person out, which may range from defeating or beating them to killing them.

example.es: En la película, se carga a los enemigos.
example.en: In the movie, he takes out the enemies.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cariño literally relates to affection and can be used to address a loved one warmly.

example.en: Good morning, darling.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Carreras literally means races. After de in coche de carreras, it describes a car designed for racing.

example.es: Vieron un coche de carreras rojo.
example.en: They saw a red race car.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cartón names cardboard and can also refer to packaging made from it, such as a carton or box.

example.es: Guardó la leche en un cartón.
example.en: She kept the milk in a carton.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marriageable; considered old enough to marry (feminine)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Casadera is the feminine singular form of casadero. The word can sound traditional or old-fashioned because it describes someone in terms of suitability for marriage.

example.en: The expression “marriageable age” sounds traditional.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Casi goes before the word or action that comes close to being true but is not fully complete.

example.en: I have almost finished.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In physics, causality is the principle that an effect cannot occur before the cause that produces it.

example.es: La teoría debe respetar la causalidad.
example.en: The theory must respect causality.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes dar caza, 'to hunt down'
cardCatalog.noteEn: Caza means hunting by itself, but dar caza works as a fixed expression for pursuing and catching a target.

example.es: La policía da caza al ladrón.
example.en: The police hunt down the thief.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Caza can name the activity of hunting or a hunt itself.

example.en: Hunting is forbidden here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cazado is the completed-action form of cazar, “to hunt” or “to catch.” After habría it stays unchanged and helps describe an imagined past result.

example.es: El zorro habría cazado al conejo.
example.en: The fox would have caught the rabbit.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a battery, a celda is one electrochemical unit. The same word can mean other kinds of enclosed cells in different contexts.

example.en: The battery contains six cells.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Célebre has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: It is a famous novel.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Censurado is the completed-action form of censurar and can describe material that authorities have suppressed or hidden.

example.en: The passage was censored.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Centenario can describe something that has existed for a century. The masculine singular form ends in -o.

example.en: They visited a century-old building.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to center it; to base it around something
cardCatalog.noteEn: Centrarla combines centrar, “to center,” with la, “her” or “it” for a feminine thing. The object word attaches to the end because centrar is in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.es: Decidieron centrarla en una sola idea.
example.en: They decided to center it on one idea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cercano can describe physical nearness or a close emotional connection. It changes to cercana, cercanos, or cercanas to agree with the person or thing described.

example.es: Me siento cercano a mi familia.
example.en: I feel close to my family.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This card is for the animal, not pork as food.

example.es: El cerdo duerme en el establo.
example.en: The pig sleeps in the barn.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cerdo can name the animal or its meat. This card is for the food meaning.

example.en: I do not eat pork.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cerebral describes something related to the brain. Cerebrales is the plural for either masculine or feminine nouns.

example.en: The equipment measures brain signals.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cerebrito literally resembles “little brain,” but it is commonly a playful or mocking label for a very intellectual person. Tone decides whether it sounds affectionate or insulting.

example.es: Mi hermano es un cerebrito de las matemáticas.
example.en: My brother is a math brainiac.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cerebritos is the plural of cerebrito, a playful or mocking label for highly intellectual people rather than a literal reference to small brains.

example.en: The brainiacs solved the puzzle.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cerrada is the feminine singular completed-action form used as a description.

example.en: The door is closed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Chao is an informal farewell used across many Spanish-speaking regions.

example.en: Bye, see you tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Charla can be a talk or conversation. With entre, it can name a meeting or discussion between the people named.

example.es: Tuvimos una charla con la profesora.
example.en: We had a talk with the teacher.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Charla can mean a spoken presentation for an audience. That is distinct from its conversational sense, where it means an informal chat or discussion.

example.es: Marta dio una charla sobre astronomía.
example.en: Marta gave a talk about astronomy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Charla can be an informal conversation or a talk given to an audience. Here it means personal conversations.

example.en: We had several long conversations.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Charla can mean an informal conversation or a talk given to an audience. In the plural, charlas can refer to several presentations.

example.en: There will be two talks this afternoon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Chica can mean a girl or young woman. Mi chica often means “my girlfriend,” but context can also use it loosely for the woman who would be right for someone.

example.en: He met a friendly young woman.

cardCatalog.answerEn: guys; everyone (informal address to a group)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Chicos literally refers to boys or young men, but speakers can use it informally to get the attention of a male or mixed group, much like ‘guys’ in English.

example.en: Guys, come here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Chiste is a joke told for humor, often with a setup and a final punchline.

example.en: She told a short joke.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Chorra is an informal Spain description for something foolish, trivial, or unimpressive. It is the feminine singular form, used with a feminine naming word such as historia.

example.en: It was a really lame excuse.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Chupar literally means to suck. With fuel, electricity, or another resource, informal Spanish can use it for consuming a large amount.

example.en: That engine guzzles a lot of gasoline.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A ciclo is one repeated round in a process or machine.

example.en: The motor completes several cycles.
