cardCatalog.noteEn: Cielos literally means 'skies' or 'heavens.' Used alone as an exclamation, it expresses surprise or concern and is generally mild.

example.en: Good heavens, it is very late!

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, científica names a woman or girl who works in science. The matching masculine form is científico.

example.en: Ana wants to be a scientist.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Científico describes something related to science. Its ending changes to match the noun: científica, científicos, or científicas.

example.en: It is a scientific article.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Científicos ends in -os to agree with a masculine plural noun.

example.en: I read two scientific reports.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here científicos is a plural noun naming people who do science, not an adjective meaning “scientific.”

example.en: The scientists compared the results.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cierras comes from cerrar. In this present-time form, the stressed e in the middle changes to ie.

example.en: You close the door every night.

cardCatalog.answerEn: closing; close (as part of paréntesis de cierre)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cierre is a noun meaning a closing or close. After de, it can classify something by its closing function, as in paréntesis de cierre.

example.en: Look for the closing symbol.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Used as a brief response, cierto confirms that the preceding point is correct. This differs from cierto before a noun, where it can mean “a certain.”

example.en: —It's difficult. —True.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After es, cierto describes a statement or claim as true.

example.en: That is true.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, cifrado can name a method or system for encoding information. The verb cifrar means ‘to encrypt’ or ‘to encode.’

example.es: Este cifrado es fácil de romper.
example.en: This cipher is easy to break.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cima is the highest point of a mountain or, figuratively, the top position in a ranking.

example.es: Llegaron a la cima de la montaña.
example.en: They reached the summit of the mountain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cita can also mean an appointment or a quotation. In writing and research, it can name the reference that identifies a source supporting a claim.

example.es: El informe incluye una cita de una fuente fiable.
example.en: The report includes a citation from a reliable source.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cita can also mean an appointment or a quotation. Here citas are meetings between potential romantic partners.

example.en: They went on two dates.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a color, claro means a lighter shade.

example.en: I prefer light blue.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Clasificar can mean placing things in categories or arranging them by a ranking.

example.es: Van a clasificar los resultados de mejor a peor.
example.en: They are going to rank the results from best to worst.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Clavado is the completed-action form of clavar, “to drive, stick, or plunge something into something else.” With haber, it describes the completed action.

example.es: La rama se ha clavado en la tierra.
example.en: The branch has stuck into the ground.

cardCatalog.answerEn: code; coded form (as part of en clave)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Within en clave, clave refers to coded or deliberately indirect wording. Other contexts can use clave for a key, a password, or an important point.

example.en: They spoke in code.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In cryptography, a clave is data used for operations such as encryption or signature checking. A public key can be shared openly; it is not the same thing as a password.

example.es: Guardé una copia de mi clave pública.
example.en: I saved a copy of my public key.

cardCatalog.answerEn: key; keyword (as part of palabra clave)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish Scrabble uses unaccented vowel tiles even for words that carry a written accent in ordinary text, so the rack shows CLITORIS. Standard Spanish writes clítoris with an accent on the first í.

example.es: El clítoris forma parte de la anatomía genital.
example.en: The clitoris is part of genital anatomy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Coche commonly means “car” in Spain. Other Spanish-speaking regions may prefer carro or auto.

example.es: Hay muchos coches en la calle.
example.en: There are many cars in the street.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A códec is software or a method that encodes and decodes digital audio or video, often compressing it to use less data.

example.es: Este códec reduce el tamaño del audio.
example.en: This codec reduces the audio size.

cardCatalog.answerEn: was encoded; used to be encoded (with se)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Codificaba is an imperfect past form of codificar. With se before it, the thing being encoded is presented as the subject and the encoder is left unnamed.

example.es: El mensaje se codificaba en números.
example.en: The message was encoded as numbers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In mathematics and science, a coeficiente is a number that multiplies a quantity or describes a measurable relationship.

example.en: We calculated the coefficient of expansion.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In Spain, coger is ordinary for taking a bus, train, or plane. In parts of the Americas it can be vulgar, so tomar or agarrar may be preferred regionally.

example.es: Cogemos el tren a las ocho.
example.en: We take the train at eight.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you pick up; you answer (the phone, informal singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Coges is the present form of coger for one familiar listener. With el teléfono, it commonly means picking up or answering the phone in Spain.

example.en: You never answer the phone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cogí is the completed past form of coger for the speaker. Coger is ordinary for taking or picking something up in Spain, but it has a vulgar sexual meaning in parts of Latin America, where tomar or agarrar may be preferred.

example.es: Cogí un libro de la mesa.
example.en: I picked up a book from the table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cogido is the completed-action form of coger. With haber it forms a completed possibility such as podríamos haber cogido. In much of Latin America coger can sound sexual, but this source uses the ordinary Spain sense “take.”

example.en: We could have taken the train.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A cohete is a vehicle or projectile propelled by expelling gas at high speed.

example.en: The rocket lifted off at dawn.

cardCatalog.answerEn: holy shit!; damn! (vulgar exclamation, especially in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cojones literally names testicles, but by itself it can be a strong vulgar reaction to shock or surprise. It is much stronger than a neutral exclamation.

example.en: Damn, what a scare!

cardCatalog.answerEn: balls; testicles (very vulgar; part of an idiom for annoying someone)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cojones is a very vulgar body-part word. In tocar los cojones, it belongs to a fixed expression meaning to annoy, bother, or provoke someone; avoid it in polite settings.

example.es: La expresión tocar los cojones es muy vulgar.
example.en: The expression tocar los cojones is very vulgar.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Colarte joins colar with te. In the pronominal verb colarse, it means entering somewhere secretly or without permission.

example.es: No debes colarte en la fiesta.
example.en: You should not sneak into the party.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In teoría de colas, colas are mathematical waiting lines studied in systems where jobs or people wait for service.

example.es: La teoría de colas ayuda a modelar esperas.
example.en: Queueing theory helps model waiting times.

cardCatalog.answerEn: collection; a gathered set of related things
cardCatalog.noteEn: Colección is a feminine noun, so it uses una or la.

example.en: She started a coin collection.

cardCatalog.answerEn: collections; gathered sets of related things
cardCatalog.noteEn: This is the plural of colección.

example.en: The museum keeps several collections.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Colegio commonly means a primary or secondary school. It does not normally mean a university-level college.

example.es: Mi colegio está cerca de casa.
example.en: My school is close to home.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Colgando is the ongoing-action form of colgar, ‘to hang.’ For an action verb ending in -ar, this form normally replaces -ar with -ando; it can describe something that remains suspended or dangling.

example.en: The lamp remains hanging.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Colocaría is the conditional form of colocar for I, he, she, or formal you. In a list, it can mean “would rank.”

example.es: Yo la colocaría entre las mejores.
example.en: I would rank it among the best.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In biology, colonia can name a group of organisms living together. For ants, it includes the cooperating ants and their nest community.

example.en: The ant colony grew.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A comandante is the person in charge of a military unit or operation.

example.en: The commander gave the order.

cardCatalog.answerEn: command (an instruction given to a computer)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here comandos are military organizations with authority over forces, not instructions typed into a computer.

example.en: The commands coordinate several units.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Combinado describes one masculine thing made by bringing multiple elements or tests together.

example.en: It is a combined exercise.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, combustible is a substance burned to produce heat or energy. As a describing word, it can instead mean combustible or flammable.

example.en: The vehicle needs fuel.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to comment out; to disable a line of code by marking it as a comment
cardCatalog.noteEn: In programming, comentar can mean turning executable code into a comment so that the computer ignores it. This is more specific than ordinary comentar, ‘to comment on something.’

example.es: Voy a comentar esta línea mientras pruebo el programa.
example.en: I am going to comment out this line while I test the program.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comentario can be a written or spoken comment, including a short observation about current events.

example.en: She added a brief comment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comentarios can mean individual comments or ongoing spoken analysis and commentary about events.

example.es: Escuchamos sus comentarios sobre el partido.
example.en: We listened to her commentary on the match.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comentarios can label written feedback that customers leave about a purchase or seller.

example.es: Leí los comentarios de los compradores.
example.en: I read the buyers' reviews.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comenzó is comenzar's completed-past form for one person or thing. The written accent marks the stress on the final ó.

example.en: The movie began late.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comerciales is plural. The same form works with masculine and feminine plural nouns.

example.es: Estudian los usos comerciales del invento.
example.en: They study the commercial uses of the invention.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cometiste is the completed past form of cometer for one familiar person. Spanish commonly uses cometer with an error, crime, or other wrongful act.

example.en: You made a small mistake.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comido is the completed-action form of comer used after haber.

example.en: They had already eaten when I arrived.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comiendo is the ongoing-action form of comer, and se can emphasize consuming the item completely.

example.es: El niño está comiéndose una manzana.
example.en: The child is eating an apple.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a number or amount of time, como can show that the amount is approximate rather than exact.

example.en: We waited about twenty minutes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Como can mean “because” when it introduces the reason before the main point. If the reason follows the main point, porque is usually the more natural connector.

example.en: Since it is raining, we will go by bus.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.

example.en: She runs like her brother.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins como mínimo, “at least”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Como often means “as” or “like,” but in the fixed expression como mínimo it helps set a lower limit.

example.en: We need at least three chairs.

cardCatalog.answerEn: as; completes contar como, “to count as”
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a form of contar meaning to qualify, como introduces the category or description that applies. It has no written accent in this use.

example.en: The internship counts as experience.

cardCatalog.answerEn: how; the way that (after así es)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In así es como, como introduces the action or situation whose manner is being explained. It has no written accent because it is part of this statement pattern rather than an open question word.

example.en: That is how it works.

cardCatalog.answerEn: as; introduces the meaning assigned after interpretar
cardCatalog.noteEn: After interpretar, como introduces the reading, category, or meaning assigned to the first item. It has no written accent in this use.

example.es: Interpretaron la señal como una advertencia.
example.en: They interpreted the signal as a warning.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After words such as conocido, llamado, or descrito, unaccented como introduces the name, title, or label by which something is known.

example.es: Es conocido como el padre de la medicina.
example.en: He is known as the father of medicine.

cardCatalog.answerEn: as (in the role or capacity of)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the role, identity, or point of view from which someone speaks or acts. This is different from cómo with an accent, which asks “how.”

example.en: As a doctor, I recommend resting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: female roommate; female flatmate (in compañera de piso)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Compañera can mean a female companion or colleague. With de piso, it conventionally names a female person who shares the same apartment.

example.es: Mi compañera de piso cocina muy bien.
example.en: My roommate cooks very well.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Compañeras can mean companions or partners. For animals in a reproductive context, it can refer to mates.

example.es: Los pájaros buscan a sus compañeras.
example.en: The birds look for their mates.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Compañero can name someone who accompanies another person or shares an activity with them. Other contexts can make it mean a classmate or coworker instead.

example.es: Viajo con mi compañero de expedición.
example.en: I travel with my expedition partner.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With de trabajo, compañeros means people who work with someone.

example.es: Mis compañeros de trabajo almuerzan aquí.
example.en: My coworkers have lunch here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comparadas matches a feminine plural subject. Con introduces the reference used for comparison.

example.es: Son pequeñas comparadas con las otras.
example.en: They are small compared with the others.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to compile (convert source code into an executable form)

cardCatalog.noteEn: In pantalla completa, completa matches the feminine singular noun pantalla and says that the content uses the whole screen.

example.es: La presentación está a pantalla completa.
example.en: The presentation is full-screen.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Completo describes something that covers all the needed parts or the whole scope.

example.en: We need a full report.

cardCatalog.answerEn: complete; capable of general computation (in Turing-completo)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the technical expression Turing-completo, completo means that a system can in principle carry out any computation that a general-purpose computer can, given enough time and storage. Completo agrees with a masculine singular system.

example.en: That language is Turing-complete.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The ending -os makes completos match the masculine plural noun problemas. After NP-, it forms the technical description NP-completos.

example.en: These problems are NP-complete.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The ending -as matches a feminine plural noun such as formas.

example.en: They are complicated questions.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Complicado often means ‘complicated.’ When it describes an experience or situation, it can instead mean awkward, difficult, or uncomfortable.

example.en: The meeting was awkward.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Compramos has the same spelling for present ‘we buy’ and completed-past ‘we bought.’ Time words and the surrounding story show which reading is intended.

example.en: Yesterday we bought a table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comprando is the -ando form of comprar. With a form of estar, it presents buying as an action in progress.

example.en: I am buying a book.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Compraría keeps the dictionary form comprar and adds -ía. Without an explicit subject, the same form can also mean ‘he, she, or you would buy’; context identifies the person.

example.en: I would buy that book.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Compras is the plural of compra. In hacer compras, it refers to shopping or making purchases.

example.es: Hicimos las compras por la mañana.
example.en: We did the shopping in the morning.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Compromiso can mean a commitment. In a disagreement or negotiation, it can instead mean a middle position accepted between competing proposals.

example.es: Buscamos un compromiso entre las dos propuestas.
example.en: We are looking for a compromise between the two proposals.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comprueba is the positive command of comprobar for one friend, peer, or other familiar listener.

example.en: Check the address again.

cardCatalog.answerEn: compound (interest added back before later interest is calculated)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Interés compuesto adds each period's interest to the balance, so later interest is calculated on both the starting amount and earlier interest.

example.es: El ahorro crece con interés compuesto.
example.en: The savings grow with compound interest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Computadora is common in much of Latin America. Ordenador is a common alternative in Spain.

example.en: The computer is on.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comunes is plural and has the same form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: They are common mistakes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comunicaciones can refer collectively to the systems or channels used to exchange messages and information.

example.en: The storm damaged the communications systems.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Comunicada is the feminine singular completed-action form of comunicar. It can describe feminine information or news that is conveyed.

example.en: The decision will be communicated tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; links concordar to what matches
cardCatalog.noteEn: Concordar uses con before the person, statement, or thing that agrees or matches. English may translate concordar con simply as ‘to match.’

example.es: La copia no concuerda con el original.
example.en: The copy does not match the original.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After conectar, con can introduce the system or service at the other end of the connection.

example.es: La aplicación conecta con el servidor.
example.en: The application connects to the server.

cardCatalog.answerEn: with; introduces the second thing in a mix-up
cardCatalog.noteEn: The pattern is confundir X con Y: to confuse or mistake X for Y.

example.es: Confundí su abrigo con el mío.
example.en: I mistook her coat for mine.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With a network or connection, Spanish con can describe the service someone is using. Natural English may use 'on' instead of the usual literal translation 'with.'

example.es: Trabajo con la red de la oficina.
example.en: I work using the office network.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In contar con, con introduces the person, thing, or resource someone relies on or expects.

example.en: You can count on us.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; links cumplir to a requirement or standard
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cumplir con introduces the rule, promise, requirement, or standard that is met. English often uses ‘meet’ directly with no word for con.

example.es: El producto cumple con los requisitos.
example.en: The product meets the requirements.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; required before who or what is encountered
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish keeps con in encontrarse con alguien or algo. Natural English normally says “meet someone” or “encounter something” without a separate word for con.

example.en: I ran into Julia.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins con vida, ‘alive’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Con vida describes a person or animal as still living, often after danger or rescue.

example.en: They found the hiker alive.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Con remains unchanged in the expression junto con.

example.es: Envió la carta junto con una foto.
example.en: She sent the letter together with a photo.

cardCatalog.answerEn: with; required before what someone interacts with
cardCatalog.noteEn: Interactuar normally uses con before the person, system, or thing involved in the interaction.

example.en: We interact with other teams.

cardCatalog.answerEn: with; introduces what someone experiments with
cardCatalog.noteEn: In jugar con, con introduces the control, tool, or idea being tried in different ways.

example.en: Experiment with the lighting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: by; when you say (introducing the wording being explained)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After querer decir, con can introduce the exact word or expression whose meaning is being asked about.

example.en: What do you mean by “urgent”?

cardCatalog.answerEn: to; with (introducing the destination of a phone transfer)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After pasar in a telephone context, con introduces the person or department that the caller is put through to.

example.en: They put me through to reception.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces the person, thing, or option tried after probar
cardCatalog.noteEn: In probar con, con marks the chosen possibility that someone will try to see whether it works. English normally says “try” directly before that option, without a separate word for con.

example.en: Let's try another plan.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to; required after relación before what is connected
cardCatalog.noteEn: In tener relación con or sin relación con, con introduces what something is or is not connected to.

example.es: El cambio no tiene relación con el precio.
example.en: The change is not related to the price.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to; with (required after relacionado or relacionada)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses relacionado con where English usually says ‘related to.’

example.es: La noticia está relacionada con el clima.
example.en: The news is related to the climate.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Con can introduce the tool, format, or style used to produce something. Natural English may use “in” or “using” rather than a literal “with.”

example.es: Imprimieron el aviso con un tipo sencillo.
example.en: They printed the notice in a simple typeface.

cardCatalog.answerEn: with; required after verse before the other person
cardCatalog.noteEn: Verse con introduces the person someone meets, sees, or dates. Con stays the same for every person and time.

example.es: Marta se ve con Luis los viernes.
example.en: Marta sees Luis on Fridays.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conciso describes something that expresses what is needed without unnecessary words.

example.es: El informe es claro y conciso.
example.en: The report is clear and concise.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conclusión has a written accent on the final ó.

example.en: The conclusion is brief.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Concreto can mean physically concrete, but it often means specific or clearly identified. Concretos matches multiple masculine nouns.

example.en: We need specific examples.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Condimentos is the plural of condimento, a seasoning or table condiment added to food.

example.es: Hay varios condimentos en la mesa.
example.en: There are several condiments on the table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conduce is the present form of conducir for he, she, or formal singular you.

example.en: Ana drives to work.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conducir is the unchanged dictionary form. It can name the activity of driving without identifying who performs it.

example.en: I prefer to drive during the day.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here conductor is a material or object through which electric current can flow, not a person driving a vehicle.

example.es: El cobre es un buen conductor.
example.en: Copper is a good conductor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A conducto is an enclosed channel through which air, liquid, cables, or another material can pass. Conductos is plural.

example.es: El aire circula por los conductos.
example.en: The air circulates through the ducts.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conduje is the completed-past form of conducir used by the speaker.

example.en: Yesterday I drove to the coast.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conectada describes a female person or feminine thing that has a network connection. The -a ending matches that feminine referent.

example.en: Marta is online now.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conectar can describe establishing a technical link between systems.

example.es: No puedo conectar el ordenador con la red.
example.en: I cannot connect the computer to the network.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to connect them; to hook them up
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conectarles joins the unchanged action conectar to les, which identifies several people receiving the connection or service.

example.es: Van a conectarles el teléfono mañana.
example.en: They are going to hook up their telephone tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to connect; to get ourselves connected
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conectarnos joins the unchanged action conectar to nos. Here nos refers to the people who connect themselves to a network.

example.es: Vamos a conectarnos a la red.
example.en: We are going to connect to the network.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conectarte combines conectar in its unchanged -ar form with te, which identifies informal singular you. Conectarse a Internet commonly means to connect or go online.

example.en: You can log on from home.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With me before it, conecté is the completed-past form of conectarse for the speaker: me conecté means “I connected” or “I logged in.”

example.en: I connected to the server.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conecte is the command for one person addressed as usted, and lo stands for the masculine item being connected. Lo attaches to the command, and the written accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: Connect it to the screen.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conectémonos combines a group command with nos. The final s of conectemos drops before nos, and an accent is written to preserve the stress.

example.en: Let's connect to the meeting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to put together; draw up; formulate
cardCatalog.noteEn: Confeccionar often means to make something by assembling its parts. With un plan, it means to draw up or formulate a plan.

example.en: The team drew up a list.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Confiar uses en before the person or thing trusted.

example.en: You trust your team.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I confuse; I mistake one thing for another
cardCatalog.noteEn: Use con before the second thing in confundo X con Y.

example.es: A veces confundo la sal con el azúcar.
example.en: Sometimes I mistake salt for sugar.

cardCatalog.answerEn: conjecture; a mathematical claim not yet proved
cardCatalog.noteEn: A conjetura is a statement believed to be true but not yet proved. Outside mathematics it can also mean a reasoned guess.

example.es: La investigadora estudia una conjetura sobre números primos.
example.en: The researcher studies a conjecture about prime numbers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Connoisseur is a borrowed noun for someone with refined knowledge and judgment in a field.

example.en: He is a coffee connoisseur.

cardCatalog.answerEn: knows; is familiar with (a fact or subject)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conocer often means being acquainted with a person, place, subject, or item of knowledge. It contrasts with saber used for knowing that a statement is true.

example.en: She knows the subject well.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they know; they are familiar with
you will meet; you will get to know
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conocerás is the future form of conocer for one familiar person. With people not yet known, conocer often means to meet or become acquainted with them, not merely to know a fact.

example.en: You will meet my friends tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to meet you; to get to know you
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conocerte combines conocer, “to meet or get to know,” with te, the informal singular word for “you.” Te attaches to the unchanged dictionary form conocer.

example.en: I want to get to know you better.

cardCatalog.answerEn: do you know; are you familiar with
you meet; you get to know
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conocer can mean to know or be familiar with a person, place, or thing. When it describes the start of that familiarity, it means to meet or get to know. Conoces is the informal singular “you” form.

example.es: Mañana conoces a la nueva directora.
example.en: Tomorrow you meet the new director.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I knew; I was familiar with
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conocía is a past form of conocer. It presents knowing or familiarity as a past state, rather than the moment when someone first found something out.

example.en: I did not know that song.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conocida is the feminine singular form of conocido. It can match a feminine noun such as empresa in the expression antes conocida como.

example.en: She is a well-known author.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we know; we are familiar with (subjunctive form)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conozcamos is a special “we” form of conocer. It can appear in a description of a person, place, or thing being sought rather than one whose identity and characteristics are already established as fact.

example.en: Let's look for a place that we know.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I meet; I get to know

cardCatalog.noteEn: Consciente has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns; its plural is conscientes.

example.en: I am aware of the problem.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Consecuencias are the results or effects that follow an action or decision.

example.es: Pensaron en las consecuencias de la decisión.
example.en: They thought about the consequences of the decision.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conseguido is the completed-action form of conseguir. With has and a que-clause, it asks whether the listener has managed to bring about another result.

example.en: Have you managed to get it to work?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conseguido is the completed-action form of conseguir. After he, it says that the speaker has succeeded in obtaining a stated thing.

example.en: I have obtained a ticket.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to obtain; to work out; to achieve
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conseguir can mean obtaining a result through effort, not only physically getting an object.

example.en: We want to reach an agreement.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to get it; to obtain it
cardCatalog.noteEn: Conseguir is the unchanged dictionary form ‘to get.’ La is attached to its end and replaces one feminine thing.

example.en: I want to get it today.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Consejo is countable in Spanish: un consejo is one piece of advice and consejos is advice or several tips.

example.en: I need some advice.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Consejos is grammatically plural in Spanish even when natural English simply uses the uncountable word “advice.”

example.en: Your advice is useful.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here considerable describes something notably large rather than merely worthy of consideration.

example.es: El arreglo requiere una cantidad considerable.
example.en: The repair requires a substantial amount.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Considerar means examining an idea, choice, or consequence before deciding.

example.en: We should consider the alternatives.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I manage to; I succeed in
cardCatalog.noteEn: Consigo is an irregular first-person present form of conseguir. Before an unchanged action verb, it means that the speaker succeeds in doing that action; before que, it can introduce a result carried out by someone or something else.

example.en: I manage to open the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Consiguieron is a completed-past form of conseguir for a plural subject. Before an infinitive it says that they managed to do something.

example.en: They managed to open the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Consiste is a present form of consistir. Spanish normally follows it with en before the defining activity or components.

example.es: El trabajo consiste en comparar datos.
example.en: The work consists of comparing data.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here consola is an electronic device for playing video games.

example.es: La consola está conectada al televisor.
example.en: The game console is connected to the television.

cardCatalog.answerEn: constitution; a game statistic for physical toughness
cardCatalog.noteEn: In role-playing games, constitución is the translated name of a character attribute, not a political constitution.

example.en: My character has a high constitution score.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Constitucional has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: It is a constitutional reform.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Construyó presents one completed past act by he, she, or formal you. Its written accent distinguishes it from construyo, ‘I build.’

example.en: The team built a prototype.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we were counting on; we had expected
cardCatalog.noteEn: Contábamos is a past form of contar for ‘we.’ With con, contar means to count on, rely on, or include someone or something in one's expectations—not to count numbers. The -ábamos ending presents that earlier expectation as background.

example.en: We were counting on more time.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Contando is the ongoing-action form of contar, “to count.”

example.en: She is counting the coins.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to time; to count how long
cardCatalog.noteEn: Contar often means “to count” or “to tell.” When it is followed by cuánto tardar, it can mean measuring or timing how long something takes.

example.es: La profesora va a contar cuánto tardan en ordenar las tarjetas.
example.en: The teacher is going to time how long they take to sort the cards.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Conté is a completed-past form of contar for the speaker. Contar can mean either “to count” or “to tell”; the surrounding context decides which sense applies.

example.en: I counted the pages yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Contenía is a past form of contener. It often describes what something held or had inside over a stretch of past time, rather than a single momentary action.

example.en: The box contained old documents.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish combines con and ti into the special single word contigo.

example.en: I want to talk with you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Continúa tells one familiar person to continue. The written accent keeps the stress on ú.

example.en: Continue along this street.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Continuo describes something that keeps recurring or carries on. This adjective is written without an accent; continuó with an accent would be a past verb form.

example.en: The continual noise is annoying.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Contra can mark the surface or situation that someone or something is thrown or pushed against.

example.es: La ola lanzó la barca contra las rocas.
example.en: The wave threw the boat against the rocks.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a verb such as luchar, contra introduces the person, obstacle, or force being opposed.

example.en: They swam against the current.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Contra can introduce the danger that a barrier, medicine, or precaution is meant to stop.

example.es: Esta crema protege contra el sol.
example.en: This cream protects against the sun.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Contraataca is the present form of contraatacar for one person or thing.

example.en: The team strikes back quickly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Contradictorios describes masculine plural things whose claims cannot all be true together. Its -os ending matches a masculine plural noun.

example.en: The reports are contradictory.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Contratado is the completed-action form of contratar, “to hire.” After a form of haber such as ha, it stays unchanged.

example.es: La empresa ha contratado a Julia.
example.en: The company has hired Julia.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Controlan is a present-time form of controlar used with ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

example.en: They control the temperature.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Controlar is the unchanged dictionary form. For machinery or devices, it means directing how they work.

example.es: El mando sirve para controlar el motor.
example.en: The controller is used to operate the motor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Convence is the positive command used with one person addressed informally as tú. It is also the ordinary present form for él, ella, or usted; context distinguishes them.

example.en: Convince Luis with evidence.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Convencerían keeps the full dictionary form convencer and adds -ían, which supplies the ‘would’ meaning for a plural subject.

example.en: That evidence would convince the jury.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Convencidos describes a masculine or mixed plural group that firmly believes something.

example.en: They are convinced that it will work.

cardCatalog.answerEn: convention; an agreed rule or standard
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here convención means an agreed way of naming or handling something, not an organized gathering.

example.en: The convention uses positive numbers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here convención means an organized event or gathering. The same word can also mean an agreed practice or rule, which is a different sense.

example.es: La ciudad recibe varias convenciones cada año.
example.en: The city hosts several conventions each year.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Convertido is the completed-action form of convertir. After a form of haber and with se, it forms expressions such as se ha convertido en, ‘has become’ or ‘has turned into.’

example.es: El edificio se ha convertido en museo.
example.en: The building has become a museum.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you will become; you will turn into
cardCatalog.noteEn: Convertirás is the future form used for one familiar listener; with te and en it expresses becoming.

example.es: Con práctica, te convertirás en experta.
example.en: With practice, you will become an expert.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Convertirse is the verb's unchanged dictionary form with se attached. A changing form such as se convierte matches the person or thing that changes; en normally introduces the result.

example.es: La oruga puede convertirse en mariposa.
example.en: The caterpillar can turn into a butterfly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Convirtiendo is the ongoing -iendo form of convertir. The attached se makes convirtiéndose part of convertirse, and en introduces the resulting identity or form.

example.es: La nube está convirtiéndose en lluvia.
example.en: The cloud is turning into rain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Copa can name a stemmed glass or the alcoholic drink served in one. Invitar a una copa commonly means to buy someone a drink.

example.es: Tomaron una copa después del trabajo.
example.en: They had a drink after work.

cardCatalog.answerEn: copy; a particular copy of a book or other work
cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, copia can mean one physical or digital instance of a written, recorded, or visual work.

example.es: Tengo una copia de la novela.
example.en: I have a copy of the novel.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here copia names the process of duplicating data, rather than one particular copy of an item.

example.es: La copia de datos tardó una hora.
example.en: Copying the data took an hour.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Copiarse combines copiar with se. After poder, this se can leave the doer unnamed and present the bits as the things that can be copied.

example.en: The files can be copied quickly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Corre is the present form of correr for one person, animal, or thing.

example.es: El perro corre por el parque.
example.en: The dog runs through the park.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Correcaminos is the Spanish name for the roadrunner bird. With el and a capital letter, El Correcaminos is also the Spanish name of the fast cartoon character pursued by Wile E. Coyote.

example.en: A roadrunner crossed the trail.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Correcta agrees with a feminine singular noun.

example.en: That is the correct measurement.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a social comparison, correcto can mean appropriate or acceptable rather than factually correct.

example.es: Fue la respuesta correcta para la ocasión.
example.en: It was the appropriate response for the occasion.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This sense of correo is the physical postal service used for letters and parcels. Correo electrónico or email identifies electronic mail when the distinction matters.

example.en: The letter arrived by mail.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Corriendo is the ongoing-action form of correr. It ends in -iendo and stays unchanged after estado.

example.es: Han estado corriendo por el parque.
example.en: They have been running through the park.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Correr usually describes running on foot, but in technology it can describe operating software, a process, or a server.

example.en: We are running a test.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In an electrical setting, corriente is the flow of electric charge and can also refer generally to supplied electrical power. Elsewhere corriente can mean “current,” “ordinary,” or a flowing stream.

example.es: Corta la corriente antes de reparar el cable.
example.en: Cut the power before repairing the cable.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cortado is the completed-action form of cortar. With a service, signal, or communication link, it means that the connection has been interrupted.

example.es: Han cortado la conexión durante la reparación.
example.en: They have cut off the connection during the repair.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we cut off; we discontinue; we cut off (completed past)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cortamos is the nosotros form of cortar in both the present and the completed past. With a service, supply, cable, or connection, cortar can mean stopping or disconnecting it rather than literally slicing it; context shows the time intended.

example.es: Ayer cortamos el servicio durante una hora.
example.en: Yesterday we cut off the service for an hour.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to break up; to end a romantic relationship
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cortar literally means to cut. With a romantic relationship understood, it commonly means to break up or end the relationship.

example.en: They decided to break up after talking.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cosechar literally means gathering a crop and can extend to harvesting organs in medical language.

example.en: They harvest the grapes in September.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cosechar normally means gathering a crop. It can also be used grimly for collecting organs or figuratively for obtaining results.

example.es: Van a cosechar las uvas mañana.
example.en: They are going to harvest the grapes tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cósmico describes something related to the cosmos or outer space. The ending changes to match the noun.

example.en: The detector records cosmic rays.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Costes is especially common in Spain. Many other regions use costos for the same meaning.

example.en: We have to reduce costs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Costó is a completed-past form of costar. With me, te, le, nos, os, or les, it can describe how difficult something was for that person rather than its price.

example.en: It was hard for us to finish on time.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In mathematics and computer science, a cota is a value or growth rate that a quantity cannot pass in a specified direction.

example.es: Buscamos una cota para el error.
example.en: We are looking for a bound on the error.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Crea is the present form of crear used with one third-person subject or as a familiar positive command.

example.en: The program creates a file.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Crece is a present form of crecer used with one person or thing.

example.en: The city grows quickly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Crecer is the unchanged dictionary form. With hair as its subject, it describes the hair becoming longer.

example.es: Voy a dejar crecer la barba.
example.en: I am going to grow out my beard.

cardCatalog.answerEn: grown up; matured (after a form of haber)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After he, has, ha, or another form of haber, crecido presents growing or maturing as something that has happened.

example.en: The children have grown a lot.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Creía is a background-past form of creer. It presents a belief or opinion that was held over a stretch of past time rather than a single completed act of believing.

example.es: De niño, creía que la Luna era pequeña.
example.en: As a child, I thought the Moon was small.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cretácico names the geological period roughly 145 to 66 million years ago.

example.es: El clima cretácico era muy cálido.
example.en: The Cretaceous climate was very warm.

cardCatalog.answerEn: thinking of himself as; considering himself
cardCatalog.noteEn: Creyéndose comes from the pronominal verb creerse. Creyendo is creer in its -iendo action form, and se is attached for the person being described. A description normally follows.

example.en: Luis left thinking himself invincible.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The written form crisis is the same in singular and plural; nearby words reveal the number.

example.en: The two crises ended quickly.

cardCatalog.answerEn: crystal; a crystal used in mystical claims
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here cristal names the mineral object associated with claims about ‘crystal energy,’ not ordinary window glass. Spanish often makes the relationship explicit with de, as in energía de los cristales.

example.en: The shop sells decorative crystals.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cristal can mean glass as a material or one pane or panel of glass. Cristales is plural.

example.es: Cambiaron los cristales de las ventanas.
example.en: They replaced the window panes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Crítica can name the activity or field of analyzing and evaluating art, literature, or ideas.

example.en: She studies film criticism.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For roads, cruce is the place where routes cross.

example.es: Gira a la derecha en el cruce.
example.en: Turn right at the intersection.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cruzada is the completed-action form of cruzar used to describe one feminine item. In breeding, cruzar means to combine one variety with another.

example.es: Es una rosa cruzada con otra variedad.
example.en: It is a rose crossed with another variety.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cruzado is the completed-action form of cruzar. After a form of haber, it reports a completed crossing and does not change to match the item that was crossed.

example.es: El equipo ha cruzado dos variedades.
example.en: The team has crossed two varieties.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cruzando is the ongoing-action form of cruzar. Regular -ar verbs replace -ar with -ando for this form.

example.es: Veo a Pablo cruzando la plaza.
example.en: I see Pablo crossing the square.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuadro can mean a square, chart, frame, or painting. In genetics, cuadro de Punnett is the Spanish name for a Punnett square.

example.es: La clase dibujó un cuadro de Punnett.
example.en: The class drew a Punnett square.

cardCatalog.answerEn: what; which one (asking for an identity or value)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before es or son, cuál often asks the listener to identify the answer or value. Natural English frequently uses “what” even though cuál is related to “which.”

example.en: What is the answer?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cualquiera can stand alone for any one person or thing in a stated group.

example.es: Puedes elegir cualquiera de estas rutas.
example.en: You can choose any one of these routes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuándo has an accent when it asks, directly or indirectly, at what time something happens.

example.en: When does the class start?

cardCatalog.answerEn: when (printed without the normally required accent)
cardCatalog.noteEn: The strip prints cuando, but standard Spanish writes cuándo here because it introduces an embedded question about when something happens. The written accent remains even though the question sits inside a larger question.

example.en: Do you know when the movie starts?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuánto changes to match the thing being counted: cuánto, cuánta, cuántos, or cuántas. It keeps its written accent in both direct and embedded questions or exclamations.

example.en: I don't know how many letters arrived.

cardCatalog.answerEn: quantum; relating to quantum physics (feminine singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuántica describes a feminine singular noun in the context of quantum physics. The masculine singular form is cuántico.

example.en: They study quantum physics.

cardCatalog.answerEn: quantum; relating to quantum physics (masculine singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuántico describes phenomena governed by quantum physics, especially at atomic and subatomic scales. Its ending changes to cuántica with a feminine singular noun.

example.en: They study a quantum system.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the (as part of cuanto más, “the more”)
no separate English word; completes en cuanto, 'as soon as'

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuántos carries a written accent in a direct or indirect question and changes to cuántas before a feminine plural noun.

example.en: How many books are left?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuarto can also mean “fourth” or “quarter.” When it names a part of a home, it means a room and often specifically a bedroom.

example.en: My room is upstairs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cúbicas is feminine plural to match micras.

example.es: La muestra ocupa cinco micras cúbicas.
example.en: The sample occupies five cubic micrometres.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuchador is a playful blend of cuchara and tenedor for a utensil that combines features of both.

example.es: Llevé un cuchador para el picnic.
example.en: I brought a spork for the picnic.

cardCatalog.answerEn: hang up (an informal command to one person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuelga is the tú command of colgar. With a telephone understood or stated, it tells one familiar person to end the call.

example.en: Hang up when the call ends.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuello names the body part between the head and torso.

example.es: Lleva una bufanda en el cuello.
example.en: She wears a scarf around her neck.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A cuenca is the land area whose water drains into the same river or body of water.

example.es: El río recoge agua de toda la cuenca.
example.en: The river collects water from the whole basin.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes darse cuenta, “to realize”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuenta can mean an account, bill, or calculation. In darse cuenta, it is part of a fixed expression and is not translated separately.

example.es: Ella se dio cuenta muy tarde.
example.en: She realized very late.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes salir a cuenta, “to be worthwhile”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuenta can mean an account or a bill elsewhere. In salir a cuenta, the whole expression evaluates whether something is advantageous or good value.

example.es: El billete de ida y vuelta sale a cuenta.
example.en: The round-trip ticket is good value.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In the fixed expression tener en cuenta, cuenta helps express considering or remembering a relevant fact.

example.en: Keep the schedule in mind.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Contar can mean to count, but it also means to tell or recount information or a story. Cuentas is the present form for tú.

example.en: Will you tell me what happened?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuente is a special form of contar used when the idea is doubted or not presented as a fact. In contar como, contar means to qualify as something rather than to count numbers or tell a story; the ordinary present form is cuenta.

example.es: Dudo que eso cuente como ayuda.
example.en: I doubt that counts as help.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they tell; they recount (special form in a desired result)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuenten is a special form of contar. It appears after para que when the telling is the desired or prevented result.

example.es: Habla bajo para que no cuenten el secreto.
example.en: Speak quietly so that they do not tell the secret.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuerpos is the plural of cuerpo, “body.” In a context involving death, it can refer specifically to dead bodies or corpses.

example.en: The police found two bodies.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In physics, a cuerpo can be an object with mass, such as a planet or star, rather than a human body.

example.en: The two bodies attract each other.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Costar can describe difficulty rather than price. In cuesta followed by an action verb, the action is hard to do.

example.en: It is hard to admit a mistake.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, cuesta is a sloping stretch of ground. It is different from cuesta meaning ‘it costs’ or ‘it is difficult.’

example.es: La cuesta termina junto al parque.
example.en: The hill ends beside the park.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to question; to ask oneself about
cardCatalog.noteEn: The ending -se points the questioning back toward the person doing it. Cuestionarse algo means to question something for oneself rather than simply asking another person a question.

example.en: She began to question her decisions.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a warning by itself, cuidado means “careful” or “watch out.”

example.en: Watch out for the ice!

cardCatalog.answerEn: to care for; to look after
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuidar can be followed by de when it means taking responsibility for a person, animal, or thing.

example.es: Voy a cuidar de las plantas.
example.en: I am going to take care of the plants.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cumplen is a plural form of cumplir. With con, it says that several things meet a rule, requirement, or standard.

example.es: Las páginas cumplen con la norma.
example.en: The pages meet the standard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cumplió is a completed-past form of cumplir. Before a number of años, it states the age someone reached.

example.en: Marta turned ten.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Curadas is the feminine plural completed-action form of curar when it describes the resulting state of feminine plural things.

example.en: The injuries are already healed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Curioso can describe something as strange or noteworthy, not only a person who wants to know more.

example.en: It is an odd case.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to work; to get to work (informal, especially in Spain)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cutre is informal and dismissive. It describes something as shabby, low-quality, or embarrassingly cheap.

example.en: They bought some crappy chairs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cuyas links a feminine plural possession to the person or thing mentioned before it. It agrees with the possessed noun, not the owner.

example.es: Conocí a una autora cuyas novelas admiro.
example.en: I met an author whose novels I admire.

cardCatalog.answerEn: doesn't matter (as part of da igual)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Da is a present form of dar. With a feeling such as miedo, English normally uses “causes,” “makes ... feel,” or a verb such as “scares.”

example.en: The darkness scares me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Da is a present form of dar for one person or thing, or for formal singular you. With ponencia, dar means to give or deliver a formal talk.

example.es: La profesora da una ponencia mañana.
example.en: The professor is giving a talk tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Da is the present form of dar used with one other person or thing. In technical contexts, dar acceso means ‘to grant access.’

example.es: La tarjeta da acceso al edificio.
example.en: The card grants access to the building.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dar can describe light striking or falling on a place.

example.es: La luz da en la pared.
example.en: The light falls on the wall.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Da is the present form of dar used with one other person or thing. In dar la seguridad de que, it means to give or provide assurance about what follows.

example.es: El informe nos da la seguridad de que funciona.
example.en: The report assures us that it works.

cardCatalog.answerEn: realized; noticed (as part of me he dado cuenta)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dado is the completed-action form of dar, normally ‘given.’ Inside darse cuenta, the whole expression means ‘to realize’ or ‘to notice,’ so dado is not translated as ‘given.’

example.es: Me he dado cuenta del error.
example.en: I have noticed the mistake.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dados is the masculine plural form of dado when it introduces several facts or circumstances to be considered.

example.en: Given the prices, we will buy less.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Daltónicos describes more than one male or mixed-gender person who has color-vision deficiency.

example.en: My brothers are color-blind.

cardCatalog.noteEn: El daltonismo is reduced ability to distinguish certain colors. Different forms affect different color pairs.

example.es: El test detecta algunos tipos de daltonismo.
example.en: The test detects some types of color blindness.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dame joins da, the positive command of dar for one familiar listener, with me for the recipient. Positive commands attach short words such as me to the end.

example.en: Give me a minute.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The letter ñ is part of the word: dañar. It is the unchanged dictionary form after puede.

example.es: El agua puede dañar el teléfono.
example.en: Water can damage the phone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Danzante can describe a person or thing that dances.

example.en: We saw dancing figures.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to cause; to give (in dar problemas)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dar usually means “to give.” In dar problemas, English naturally uses “cause” or “create” instead.

example.en: That part can cause problems.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to give; here part of dar caña (“go hard; turn up the intensity”)
to give way; to make way (with paso a)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dar normally means to give. In dar paso a, it forms the conventional expression for allowing someone or something to follow or replace what came before.

example.es: La lluvia da paso al sol.
example.en: The rain gives way to sunshine.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dará is the future form of dar used with one person or thing.

example.en: Ana will give you the key.

cardCatalog.answerEn: will realize (as part of se dará cuenta)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dará is the future form of dar. With se and cuenta, it belongs to the fixed expression for realizing rather than meaning that someone will give something.

example.en: She will realize tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to do; to be into an activity (with a)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the colloquial pattern darle a una actividad, darle means to do that activity, practice it, or spend time on it. The attached le is part of the expression rather than a separately named recipient.

example.en: Alicia is into chess.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to give him, her, it, or them; to give something to a recipient
cardCatalog.noteEn: Darle joins dar, the dictionary form meaning “to give,” to le, a small recipient word. Depending on context, le can point to a man, woman, thing, or singular collective. The recipient may also be named later with a, as in darle el libro a Marta.

example.es: Voy a darle la llave a Marta.
example.en: I am going to give Marta the key.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to press; to click (a control, followed by a)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Darle normally combines dar, 'to give,' with le. In the conversational pattern darle a un botón or darle a una opción, it means to press, click, or activate that control.

example.es: Voy a darle al botón azul.
example.en: I am going to press the blue button.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to realize; to notice (as part of darme cuenta)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Darme joins the unchanged dictionary form dar, normally ‘to give,’ to me. In darme cuenta, the two words form the fixed expression ‘to realize’ or ‘to notice’; me identifies the speaker as the person who realizes something.

example.es: Tardé en darme cuenta del error.
example.en: It took me a while to notice the error.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to realize; to notice (as part of darse cuenta)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Darse combines the dictionary form dar with se attached. It does not mean ‘to give oneself’ here: darse cuenta is the complete fixed expression for realizing or noticing something.

example.es: Marta puede darse cuenta del error.
example.en: Marta can notice the error.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Darte combines dar, the verb's unchanged dictionary form meaning “to give,” with te, meaning “to you.” The two parts are written as one word.

example.en: I want to thank you.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; the verb part of te das cuenta, ‘you realize’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Das normally means ‘you give.’ Inside darse cuenta, it combines with the matching small pronoun and cuenta to express realizing or noticing.

example.en: Do you notice the change?

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; supplies the verb in dar caza, 'to hunt down'
cardCatalog.noteEn: Das is dar's present form for one familiar listener. In dar caza, dar is not translated literally as give.

example.en: You hunt down the fugitive.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dato can introduce a stated fact or statistic, as well as mean an individual piece of data.

example.en: I have an interesting fact.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; this de is an accidental duplicate
cardCatalog.noteEn: An accidental written repetition of de does not add meaning: one copy is redundant. This kind of editing error should be removed in normal Spanish.

example.es: El borrador decía «de de Madrid»; debe decir «de Madrid».
example.en: The draft said ‘de de Madrid’; it should say ‘de Madrid.’

cardCatalog.answerEn: before; required after antes when a noun follows
cardCatalog.noteEn: Antes de comes before a noun or an unchanged action verb. The two Spanish words often correspond to the single English word “before.”

example.en: I arrived before dinner.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a number or other quantity, Spanish uses más de for “more than.” This de is different from más que, which commonly compares one person, thing, or action with another.

example.en: There are more than twenty people.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links parar to the action that stops
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish requires de between a form of parar and the following action verb. English does not translate this linking word separately.

example.en: We stop running.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; or no separate English word, linking an amount to what it measures
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a quantity expression, de introduces the substance or thing being measured. English uses “of” in expressions such as a lot of or the amount of, but may leave de untranslated in others, such as un poco de agua, “a little water.”

example.en: I want a little water.

cardCatalog.answerEn: aged; no separate English word before an age
cardCatalog.noteEn: De can introduce a person's age or the numerical value of an age measure. English often turns de plus the number into “aged ...” or simply states the number without a separate word for de.

example.es: Es una persona de veinte años.
example.en: They are a twenty-year-old person.

cardCatalog.answerEn: often no separate English word; introduces what the assurance is about
cardCatalog.noteEn: After seguridad, de can introduce the content being guaranteed. When a complete claim follows, Spanish uses de que even though natural English often uses only ‘that.’

example.es: Tengo la seguridad de que volverá.
example.en: I am certain that she will return.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; introduces the activity or thing involved in a binge
cardCatalog.noteEn: After atracón, de introduces what was consumed or done excessively. An action can follow in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.es: Nos dimos un atracón de ver películas.
example.en: We binged on watching movies.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links basura to the role being insulted
cardCatalog.noteEn: In una basura de followed by a role, de connects the harsh judgment to that role. Natural English normally uses an adjective such as “terrible” instead of translating de.

example.en: He is a terrible boss.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; required after burlarse before the target
cardCatalog.noteEn: Burlarse uses de before the person or thing being mocked. Natural English normally expresses the whole pattern as ‘make fun of’ or ‘mock.’

example.es: No te burles de tu hermano.
example.en: Do not make fun of your brother.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to; of (linking capacidad to an action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After capacidad, de introduces the action that someone or something is capable of doing. English usually uses ‘to’ before that action.

example.en: She has the ability to adapt.

cardCatalog.answerEn: gives; causes (special form for a sought scary thing)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dé is a form of dar. The accent distinguishes it from the preposition de. Here the speaker asks about an unspecified story that might cause more fear, so dar appears in this special subjunctive form.

example.es: Busco una película que dé miedo.
example.en: I am looking for a movie that is scary.

cardCatalog.noteEn: De plus a noun phrase can describe what kind of thing something is or a characteristic it has. English may use “with,” “having,” or a compound adjective.

example.es: Buscan una casa de gran tamaño.
example.en: They are looking for a large house.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; links consciente to what someone is aware of
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses consciente de before the fact, issue, or situation that a person knows about. A following que can introduce a complete fact.

example.es: Soy consciente de que falta tiempo.
example.en: I am aware that time is short.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; no separate English word before que after convencido
cardCatalog.noteEn: Convencido requires de before a noun or before que plus the belief.

example.en: I am convinced that she will come.

cardCatalog.answerEn: by; from (identifying the creator or source)
cardCatalog.noteEn: De can connect a work, statement, or piece of commentary to the person who created or supplied it. Natural English often uses “by” rather than literal “of.”

example.en: I read an article by Marta.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When cuidar means looking after someone or something, de introduces the person or thing receiving care.

example.en: She takes care of her dog.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces what is realized after darse cuenta
cardCatalog.noteEn: After darse cuenta, de introduces the fact or thing that becomes clear. Before a full statement, Spanish normally uses de que.

example.es: Se dio cuenta de que era tarde.
example.en: She realized that it was late.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks an inference after deber
cardCatalog.noteEn: In deber de plus an action verb, de helps mark a guess or conclusion about what is likely true.

example.en: She must be tired.

cardCatalog.answerEn: on; required after depender before what decides the result
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish keeps de after depender. English usually expresses the same link with ‘on,’ as in depende del precio.

example.en: It depends on the weather.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; links a donor to what is donated
cardCatalog.noteEn: After donante, de introduces the thing that the person donates: donante de sangre, donante de órganos, or donante de médula.

example.en: They are looking for a blood donor.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces how long something lasts
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can put de and an amount of time after a noun to describe its duration. English often puts the time before the noun instead: una película de dos horas becomes “a two-hour movie.”

example.es: Vimos una película de dos horas.
example.en: We watched a two-hour movie.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; links something to an earlier time
cardCatalog.noteEn: De antes describes something as being from before or earlier.

example.en: I prefer the earlier version.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After echar in the sense of forcing someone to leave, de introduces the place the person must leave.

example.en: They threw him out of the office.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; required after enterarse before the information
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses enterarse de before the fact, news, or subject learned. The de remains even when natural English uses only find out.

example.en: She found out about the change.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; no separate word before a hoped-for event
cardCatalog.noteEn: Esperanza normally uses de before a noun and de que before a full statement about what is hoped for.

example.es: Tengo la esperanza de que vuelva.
example.en: I hope that she returns.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links tener to the quality being asked about
cardCatalog.noteEn: In ¿qué tiene de bueno, malo o especial?, de connects tener to the quality under evaluation. Natural English usually uses “about it” instead of translating de alone.

example.en: What is special about this place?

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; introducing what the evidence proves
cardCatalog.noteEn: After prueba, de can introduce the content supported by the evidence. When a whole statement follows, Spanish uses de que.

example.es: Hay pruebas de que el plan funciona.
example.en: There is evidence that the plan works.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces the period after a finales de
cardCatalog.noteEn: In a finales de, de connects the expression to the period whose late part is meant. English normally folds the whole expression into “in late…” rather than translating de separately.

example.en: We will return in late May.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes a pesar de, ‘despite’
cardCatalog.noteEn: De completes a pesar de and links the connector to the situation, thing, or action that did not prevent the result.

example.es: Salimos a pesar de la lluvia.
example.en: We went out despite the rain.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links acabar to a just-completed action
cardCatalog.noteEn: In acabar de plus an unchanged action verb, de is required even though natural English does not translate it separately.

example.en: We have just eaten.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links antes to the following action
cardCatalog.noteEn: Keep de after antes when the next action stays in its unchanged dictionary form: antes de salir. English expresses the sequence with 'before' and does not translate de separately.

example.es: Lávate las manos antes de comer.
example.en: Wash your hands before eating.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of antes de que (“before”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is a required middle piece when antes introduces a full event with que. Translate antes de que as one connector.

example.en: Let's return before it gets dark.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Cerca normally uses de before the nearby person, place, or thing.

example.es: La estación está cerca de casa.
example.en: The station is near home.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links cómo to the degree being asked about
cardCatalog.noteEn: This de is the fixed middle piece of cómo de, a construction especially common in Spain for asking how strongly a description applies.

example.en: How big is the box?

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de alguna manera, “somehow”
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is fixed in de alguna manera. Translate the three words together as “somehow” or “in some way,” rather than translating de on its own.

example.es: De alguna manera, encontró la salida.
example.en: Somehow, she found the exit.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links a noun to arriba, ‘above’ or ‘upper’
cardCatalog.noteEn: De arriba can identify the person or thing located above another reference point. Natural English may use “above,” “upstairs,” or put “upper” before the noun.

example.es: La ventana de arriba está abierta.
example.en: The upstairs window is open.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of de cabeza (“headfirst”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the fixed movement expression de cabeza, de introduces the body part that leads. The two words work together rather than using de in its ordinary “of” sense.

example.en: The child fell headfirst.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de cerca, “up close”
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is fixed before cerca when describing a close viewing distance.

example.en: I want to see it up close.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de hecho, ‘in fact’
no separate English word; begins de lo más before a description
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is the first fixed piece of de lo más, an expression that raises the degree of the description that follows.

example.es: La visita fue de lo más agradable.
example.en: The visit was extremely pleasant.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de mala muerte
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is fixed inside de mala muerte, a description meaning seedy, shabby, or disreputable.

example.es: Entraron en un bar de mala muerte.
example.en: They entered a seedy bar.

cardCatalog.noteEn: De is fixed with media in the statistical expression de media. Its meaning comes from the complete expression rather than the usual possession or origin senses.

example.en: Ten messages arrive on average.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; first part of de momento, ‘for now’
cardCatalog.noteEn: De combines with momento in the fixed time expression de momento. Its meaning comes from the whole expression rather than from the usual possession or origin uses of de.

example.en: For now, there are no changes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de nuevo, ‘again’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Inside de nuevo, de is a fixed part of the expression rather than the ordinary word ‘of’ or ‘from.’

example.en: I am going to try again.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de pronto, 'suddenly'
cardCatalog.noteEn: Keep de and pronto together in the fixed expression de pronto. English translates the pair as one word, 'suddenly.'

example.es: De pronto, se apagó la luz.
example.en: Suddenly, the light went out.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de sobra
cardCatalog.noteEn: De combines with sobra to form de sobra, which says there is more than enough.

example.en: We have more than enough food.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de verdad, “real or genuine”
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a noun, de verdad can distinguish a genuine example from something that only resembles it or bears the name.

example.en: I need a real vacation.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de vez en cuando, “from time to time”
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is the first fixed piece of the four-word expression de vez en cuando.

example.en: I cook from time to time.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; fixed link in ir/venir de visita
cardCatalog.noteEn: In ir de visita or venir de visita, de connects the movement verb to visita. Natural English usually translates the whole expression as going or coming for a visit.

example.en: My aunt and uncle are coming for a visit.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of de vuelta a (“back to”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: De often means “of” or “from,” but de vuelta is a fixed way to express being or going back. Translate the whole expression rather than assigning de its usual meaning here.

example.en: We are going back home.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links dejar to the activity being stopped
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is required between a form of dejar and the following action in the common pattern dejar de hacer algo, ‘to stop doing something.’

example.en: We stopped talking.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes dentro de, “in”
cardCatalog.noteEn: When dentro de introduces a future delay, translate the two words together as “in.”

example.es: La película empieza dentro de diez minutos.
example.en: The movie starts in ten minutes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of después de todo
cardCatalog.noteEn: De links después and todo inside the fixed expression después de todo.

example.en: After all, we can wait.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes detrás de, “behind”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Use de after detrás and before the reference point. The two words work together as detrás de.

example.es: La mochila está detrás de mí.
example.en: The backpack is behind me.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes en lugar de, ‘instead of’
cardCatalog.noteEn: De completes en lugar de and connects it to the alternative thing or action that follows.

example.es: Usó agua en lugar de leche.
example.en: She used water instead of milk.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes en vez de, ‘instead of’
cardCatalog.noteEn: De finishes the connector en vez de and comes directly before the alternative that is not chosen.

example.es: Escribió un correo en vez de llamar.
example.en: She wrote an email instead of calling.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links es hora to the action whose time has come
cardCatalog.noteEn: After es hora, use de before an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: It is time to leave.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es hora de que
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is the required link between hora and que when the following group of words has its own action and names who should act.

example.es: Es hora de que Marta vuelva.
example.en: It is time for Marta to return.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links estar a punto to the imminent action
cardCatalog.noteEn: In estar a punto de, de is required immediately before the action verb in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form.

example.en: I am about to call.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links fin and semana in “weekend”
cardCatalog.noteEn: De remains between fin or fines and semana in the fixed expression for “weekend” or “weekends.”

example.en: I work on the weekend.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links ir to marcha in ir de marcha
cardCatalog.noteEn: The de is required in the fixed expression ir de marcha, which means to go out partying. Translating de by itself would hide how the expression works.

example.en: We are going out partying on Friday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links matar to risa in matar de risa
cardCatalog.noteEn: The de is required by the fixed expression matar de risa, which means to make someone laugh very hard.

example.es: La historia nos mató de risa.
example.en: The story made us laugh really hard.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links pagado to sí mismo
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is required inside the fixed description pagado de sí mismo. Translate the expression as a unit rather than assigning de its ordinary meaning of of or from.

example.es: Está muy pagada de sí misma.
example.en: She is very full of herself.
