cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of pasar de página
cardCatalog.noteEn: The preposition de links pasar to página in the expression pasar de página.

example.es: Es hora de pasar de página.
example.en: It is time to turn the page and move on.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes por encima de
cardCatalog.noteEn: De is required before the point, object, or limit that something is above.

example.es: La cifra está por encima de cien.
example.en: The figure is above one hundred.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes se trata de, “it is about”
cardCatalog.noteEn: The fixed expression requires de before the topic or action. English includes its meaning in “about” rather than translating de as a separate word.

example.en: It is about listening.

cardCatalog.answerEn: by; required after seguido before what follows
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses de after seguido, seguida, seguidos, or seguidas to introduce the next event or thing.

example.en: A pause followed by music.

cardCatalog.answerEn: give; apply (a special form of dar)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dé is a form of dar, ‘to give.’ It appears when the surrounding words present the giving as wanted, rejected, uncertain, or reacted to rather than simply stating it as a fact; the accent distinguishes it from de, ‘of’ or ‘from.’

example.es: Espero que Ana dé una respuesta.
example.en: I hope Ana gives an answer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; about (introduces what someone is informed of)
cardCatalog.noteEn: With informar, de can introduce the event, fact, or subject being reported.

example.en: She informed us of the problem.

cardCatalog.answerEn: about; from (as part of lo de)
by; at (identifying someone by a place)
cardCatalog.noteEn: A phrase with de can identify a person by the place associated with them. Context makes the relation spatial rather than ownership.

example.es: Habla con el hombre de la entrada.
example.en: Talk to the man by the entrance.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links manera to the result it would make possible
cardCatalog.noteEn: In una manera de que..., de joins “a way” to a clause describing what that way would allow.

example.es: Buscamos una manera de que todos participen.
example.en: We are looking for a way for everyone to participate.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in (as part of de forma, in a … way)
of; made of or from (introducing a material)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After an object or an expression such as ser de or estar hecho de, de introduces the material that composes it.

example.en: The door is made of metal.

cardCatalog.noteEn: De can join an invention, theorem, or named object to the person whose name it bears. English may instead use an adjective based on that name.

example.en: We study Newton's laws.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces what someone has no idea about
cardCatalog.noteEn: After no tener ni idea or the shorter ni idea, de introduces the fact or question that is unknown. English normally places who, what, or whether directly after no idea.

example.es: No tengo ni idea de quién llamó.
example.en: I have no idea who called.

cardCatalog.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Bajarse uses de before the vehicle, surface, or place someone leaves. English often translates this de as “off” or “out of.”

example.en: She got off the train.

cardCatalog.answerEn: belonging to; often expressed with ’s in English
cardCatalog.noteEn: De can connect a thing to its owner. Spanish says el libro de Ana where English can say ‘Ana’s book.’

example.en: It is Luis's computer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in; packaged as (linking a product to its container)
cardCatalog.noteEn: De can link a product to a noun that identifies its packaging. It does not say that the product itself is made from that packaging material.

example.es: La tienda vende cerveza de lata.
example.en: The shop sells canned beer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; links a model or approach to its field
cardCatalog.noteEn: After words such as modelo, método, or paradigma, de can introduce the activity or field to which that approach belongs. English may use ‘for,’ ‘to,’ or a noun placed before another noun.

example.es: Probamos un nuevo paradigma de enseñanza.
example.en: We tried a new teaching paradigm.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links parar to the action that stops
of; links one member to a larger group
cardCatalog.noteEn: After uno or una, de introduces the group that the one member belongs to.

example.en: He is one of my neighbors.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; links ‘some’ to the larger group
cardCatalog.noteEn: After algunos or algunas, de introduces the group from which the smaller set is chosen. Spanish normally keeps the matching article before that group: algunos de los, algunas de las.

example.es: Algunas de las ventanas están abiertas.
example.en: Some of the windows are open.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links más to the time already passed
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses más de before the stated time; English can express the whole combination with “past.”

example.en: It is already past noon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Plagado de introduces what something is filled, covered, or overrun with.

example.es: El texto está plagado de errores.
example.en: The text is riddled with errors.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; connects probabilidad to a following que clause
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish says probabilidad de que before a full possible outcome. Natural English usually says “probability that,” absorbing de rather than translating it as a separate “of.”

example.es: Hay poca probabilidad de que nieve.
example.en: There is little chance that it will snow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; links probabilidad to the possible action
cardCatalog.noteEn: After probabilidad, de can introduce an action in its unchanged dictionary form: la probabilidad de ganar.

example.es: La probabilidad de llegar a tiempo es baja.
example.en: The chance of arriving on time is low.

cardCatalog.answerEn: from; required after proceder for an origin
cardCatalog.noteEn: When proceder means to come or originate, de introduces the source.

example.en: The word comes from Latin.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; links a quality or effect to what has or causes it
cardCatalog.noteEn: De can connect a quality, feature, or effect to the thing it comes from. English usually keeps “of” or uses a possessive form.

example.es: Me sorprende la fuerza de este viento.
example.en: This wind's force surprises me.

cardCatalog.answerEn: that; about the fact that (after queja)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After queja, de can introduce the content of the complaint. English often uses ‘that’ rather than translating de separately.

example.es: Hubo quejas de que faltaba información.
example.en: There were complaints that information was missing.

cardCatalog.answerEn: from; marks the start of a range
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the paired pattern de ... a ..., de introduces the starting point and a introduces the endpoint.

example.es: Ordena las notas de la mejor a la peor.
example.en: Order the grades from best to worst.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins a ratio stated with de ... a ...
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can frame odds or a ratio with de before the first quantity and a before the second.

example.es: Las probabilidades son de dos a uno.
example.en: The odds are two to one.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to atrás to describe it as the back or rear one
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can put de atrás after an object to identify the one positioned at the back. Natural English usually puts “back” before the noun.

example.en: We use the back door.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; introduces what a search or pursuit seeks
cardCatalog.noteEn: After búsqueda, Spanish uses de before the person, thing, or goal being sought. Natural English usually says “search for,” so the preposition changes between the two languages.

example.es: Continúa la búsqueda de una respuesta.
example.en: The search for an answer continues.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links results to their search source
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can put de between resultados and the service or source that produced them. English often places the service name directly before “results.”

example.en: The search-engine results changed.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links a hole or problem to the field of security
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses de in compounds such as agujero de seguridad and problema de seguridad. English normally puts ‘security’ directly before the other noun.

example.en: They found a security problem.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; links seguro to what someone is sure about
cardCatalog.noteEn: The adjective seguro normally takes de before the thing, fact, or question that follows. English often omits a separate preposition before a who, what, or whether clause.

example.en: I am sure that he will come.

cardCatalog.answerEn: on; belonging to (linking content to a sign or notice)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can use de to connect a message or wording to the sign that contains it. Natural English often says that the message is ‘on’ the sign.

example.es: El mensaje del cartel es muy claro.
example.en: The message on the sign is very clear.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links señales to the evidence that follows
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses de before que after señal or señales when the following clause states what the sign indicates. English normally expresses the combination as ‘a sign that...’ without a separate word for de.

example.es: Es una señal de que funciona.
example.en: It is a sign that it works.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in; among (introducing what ‘best’ or ‘worst’ is compared across)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a highest-or-lowest description such as el mejor or el peor, de can introduce the full group or time range being compared.

example.es: Es la mejor canción de la década.
example.en: It is the best song of the decade.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; links support or help to the system it covers
to; in being, after tener suerte
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tener suerte uses de before the action or circumstance that is fortunate.

example.en: I am lucky to live here.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes a través de, “through”
in; within (a stated period of time)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After un momento, de can introduce the larger stretch of time in which that moment falls. Natural English often uses “in” rather than a literal “of.”

example.es: Ocurrió en algún momento de la última semana.
example.en: It happened sometime in the last week.

cardCatalog.answerEn: who; the kind that (introducing a typical action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: The second de in de los de or de las de introduces the action that characterizes that type of person.

example.es: Soy de los de caminar al trabajo.
example.en: I am one of those people who walk to work.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”

example.en: I bought a history book.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; among (introducing a type or group)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In de los de or de las de, this first de places someone among a recognizable type of people.

example.es: Pablo es de los de llegar pronto.
example.en: Pablo is one of those people who arrive early.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; a required verb complement
cardCatalog.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs require de before their complement or a following infinitive. English often absorbs this de into the verb’s translation: dejar de means “to stop doing,” while disfrutar de means “to enjoy.”

example.en: I stopped smoking.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links equivocarse to the wrong choice
cardCatalog.noteEn: After equivocarse, de introduces what was chosen incorrectly: equivocarse de puerta means to choose the wrong door.

example.en: I took the wrong train.

cardCatalog.answerEn: behind; down (after an amount and por)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por debajo can describe a lower position. After an amount in a game or comparison, debajo gives the idea of being that amount behind or down.

example.es: El equipo va un gol por debajo.
example.en: The team is one goal behind.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With se, debate is a present form of debatirse used for one third-person subject. Here it describes effort and difficulty, not a verbal debate.

example.es: El nadador se debate contra la corriente.
example.en: The swimmer struggles against the current.

cardCatalog.answerEn: must; is probably (an inference, not an obligation)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Debe is a form of deber. In deber de followed by an unchanged action verb, it presents a conclusion or likely guess rather than saying that someone has a duty.

example.en: He must be busy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Debemos is the present “we” form of deber. Before an unchanged action verb, it expresses advice or obligation.

example.en: We should leave soon.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they must; they are required to
cardCatalog.noteEn: Deben is a present form of deber used with a plural subject. A following action verb stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: They must leave now.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Deberíamos is the “we” form of deber used for advice or what ought to happen. The -ríamos ending adds the “would/should” viewpoint: deber becomes deberíamos.

example.en: We should talk tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Deberían is a softened recommendation form of deber for a plural subject. It is followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: They should speak with her.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Deberías is the advice form of deber for one familiar listener. It softens the statement into a recommendation rather than saying what the listener absolutely must do.

example.en: You should drink water.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Debes is a form of deber for informal singular “you.” In deber de followed by an action verb, it expresses an inference about what is probably true rather than a duty.

example.en: You must be busy.

cardCatalog.answerEn: due; because of (as part of debido a)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Debido joins a to form the connector debido a, which introduces a cause.

example.es: El partido se canceló debido a la lluvia.
example.en: The game was canceled because of the rain.

cardCatalog.answerEn: he must have; he probably did
cardCatalog.noteEn: With de and an action verb, debió presents a conclusion about what was probably true in the past, not a duty someone had to perform.

example.en: He must have missed the train.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I must; I conclude (making an inference)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before haber and a completed-action form, debo can express a strong conclusion about the past rather than a duty. Context distinguishes this from debo followed by an ordinary action, which commonly states an obligation.

example.es: Debo haber dejado la llave dentro.
example.en: I must have left the key inside.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Debo is the present form of deber used by the speaker. A following action stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: I must call Ana.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they said; they used to say
cardCatalog.noteEn: Decían is an imperfect-past form for repeated, ongoing, or background speech by more than one person.

example.en: Many people used to say it was impossible.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Decidí is the completed-past form of decidir used for yo. It can be followed directly by an unchanged action verb.

example.en: I decided to wait.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Decidido is the completed-action form of decidir. After ha, it says that one person or thing has made a decision that matters now.

example.en: Marta has decided to stay.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to tell them; to say to them
cardCatalog.noteEn: Decirles joins decir, the dictionary form meaning “to say” or “to tell,” to les, which identifies more than one recipient. The information or instruction being told can follow after que.

example.en: I want to tell them to arrive early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Decir is the unchanged action form. In this sense, se stands for “to her,” and lo stands for the thing told. Both attach to the end, and the written accent keeps the original stress. In another context, se could instead refer to him, formal you, or them.

example.en: I have to tell it to her tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In literary theory, deconstrucción is an approach that examines tensions, assumptions, and unstable contrasts within a text.

example.es: El ensayo aplica la deconstrucción al texto.
example.en: The essay applies deconstruction to the text.

cardCatalog.answerEn: devote time to it or them (informal command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dedica is the affirmative tú command of dedicar, and attached le represents the target receiving the time or attention.

example.en: Devote an hour to the project.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to devote themselves; to engage in
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dedicarse is a verb used with a short marker that changes with the person: me dedico, te dedicas, se dedica, nos dedicamos, se dedican. It normally takes a before the activity.

example.en: They devote themselves to music.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dedo can mean either a finger or a toe. The surrounding context or the addition del pie makes the body part clear.

example.es: Me hice daño en un dedo del pie.
example.en: I hurt one of my toes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In an academic setting, defensa can name the formal presentation and questioning in which a student defends a thesis.

example.en: Her defense will be on Friday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Defensa can name the protection of a country and the government department responsible for it.

example.es: El ministerio coordina la defensa nacional.
example.en: The ministry coordinates national defense.

cardCatalog.answerEn: degenerate; deteriorate; turn into something worse
cardCatalog.noteEn: Degeneran is the present plural form of degenerar. With en, it names the undesirable result that situations turn into.

example.en: The meetings degenerate into arguments.

cardCatalog.answerEn: deterio—; visibly truncated beginning of degrada
cardCatalog.noteEn: Degra is not a complete ordinary verb form. It is the printed beginning of degrada, “it deteriorates,” cut off after degra and a hyphen without a visible continuation.

example.en: The text ends at “it deterio—.”

cardCatalog.noteEn: With se, degradan describes several things losing quality or condition over time.

example.es: Algunos materiales se degradan con la luz.
example.en: Some materials degrade in light.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Deja is a present form of dejar used with one person or thing that permits an action. A short word such as me, te, nos, or les can identify who is allowed to act.

example.en: The permit lets us enter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Deja can also mean ‘lets’ or ‘allows.’ Here it is a form of dejar meaning that a material leaves something behind on a surface.

example.es: La tiza deja polvo en la mesa.
example.en: The chalk leaves dust on the table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Deja is the positive command for one person addressed informally. Before que and another action, it asks that person to allow the action.

example.en: Let Pablo answer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Deja is the positive command for tú from dejar. In dejar de followed by an action verb, it tells one person to stop that action rather than to leave something behind.

example.en: Stop shouting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: stop (doing); command to several people informally, mainly in Spain
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dejad is the positive command form of dejar for vosotros or vosotras. When it is followed by de and another action, it tells the group to stop that activity.

example.en: Stop shouting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: left behind; given up (after a form of haber)
cardCatalog.noteEn: With a following thing, dejar can mean to leave that thing behind or give it up. Dejando de + action is a different construction meaning ‘stopping’ the action.

example.en: I have given up that habit.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all let; you all allow (informal, mainly Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dejáis is the present form of dejar used with vosotros or vosotras. In this use, the person being allowed acts next.

example.en: Are you all letting the children enter?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Déjame joins the affirmative command deja, “let,” to me, which marks the person receiving permission. The accent keeps the original stress after the pronoun is attached.

example.en: Let me think.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to leave; to keep (something in a state)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dejar can mean not changing something, especially when the following words describe the state in which it remains.

example.es: Voy a dejar la puerta abierta.
example.en: I'm going to leave the door open.

cardCatalog.answerEn: that she stop; she would stop (after a preference)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here dejara is the special form of dejar used for an action the speaker wants another person to take. Ordinary deja changes to dejara after preferiría que.

example.es: Preferiría que Marta dejara la puerta abierta.
example.en: I would prefer Marta to leave the door open.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dejarán is the future form used for they. With an object and en paz, it means that they will stop bothering that person.

example.en: They will leave us alone tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dejarán is the plural future form of dejar. Before de plus an unchanged action verb, it means that several people will stop doing that action.

example.en: Soon they will stop calling.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to let my ... grow; marks me as the person whose appearance changes
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dejarme combines dejar with me. Before crecer plus hair or another body feature, me identifies whose appearance changes; natural English usually expresses that relationship with “my.”

example.es: Voy a dejarme crecer la barba.
example.en: I am going to grow out my beard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In dejar de followed by an unchanged action verb, dejaste says that one person addressed informally stopped doing that activity.

example.en: You stopped calling.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Deje is a special form of dejar used after conseguir que because the stopping is a result someone is trying to bring about. Ordinary deja changes to deje.

example.en: I want it to stop raining.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here dejé is the completed-past form of dejar in dejar de followed by an action, the pattern for stopping that activity. Without de, dejé commonly means “I left” or “I left something in a state.”

example.en: I stopped running.

cardCatalog.answerEn: stop; leave (command form for a familiar group)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dejéis is the form used when telling more than one familiar person not to do something. In dejar de plus another action, dejar means to stop that action.

example.en: Do not stop practicing.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I am leaving; I am ending a romantic relationship
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dejo is the present form of dejar used by the speaker. Dejar can mean leaving a thing somewhere; with a romantic partner as the person affected, it can mean ending the relationship.

example.en: Today I am leaving my partner.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I stop; I quit (with de + action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In dejar de followed by a verb's unchanged dictionary form, dejo means that the speaker stops doing that action.

example.es: Dejo de trabajar a las seis.
example.en: I stop working at six.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Del is the required contraction of de + el. It can mean “of the” or “from the,” depending on context.

example.en: I’m coming from the market.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of the; combines de + el before nuestro (“ours”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish always contracts de + el to del. Here el introduces a masculine possessive form that replaces an already named noun, so del nuestro can contribute the meaning “of ours.”

example.es: El motor de tu coche es más potente que el del nuestro.
example.en: Your car's engine is more powerful than ours.

cardCatalog.answerEn: than what; combines de + el in an amount comparison
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before que and a complete second action, del can refer back to a masculine singular amount or thing being compared. El matches that earlier noun, as in más tiempo del que necesitamos (“more time than we need”).

example.es: Compró más pan del que podía comer.
example.en: He bought more bread than he could eat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de + el. After depender, de introduces the factor that determines the result.

example.en: The date depends on the weather.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of the; introduces the period after a finales
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. In a finales del mes, it connects a finales to the masculine period mes; natural English usually renders the complete expression as ‘late in the month’ or ‘at the end of the month.’

example.en: We will return late in the summer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins del revés, ‘upside down’ or ‘inside out’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del is the contraction of de + el, but in del revés the two words function together as a fixed orientation expression.

example.en: The drawing is upside down.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of línea del tiempo, “timeline”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. It is the required middle word in línea del tiempo.

example.es: Añadieron una fecha a la línea del tiempo.
example.en: They added a date to the timeline.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of máquina del tiempo (‘time machine’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. Spanish keeps it between máquina and tiempo in the conventional expression máquina del tiempo.

example.en: The time machine disappeared.

cardCatalog.answerEn: from the (de + el, identifying a source or location)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. When something comes from a place or side, de can mean “from.”

example.en: I hear music from the other room.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Del is the required single-word contraction of de followed by el. Before a century, it dates an object or event to that period.

example.es: Es una casa del siglo XX.
example.en: It is a house from the twentieth century.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. Here de marks a time or period as the source something comes from, rather than showing ownership.

example.en: We received a letter from the past.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks what is being changed after hacer
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. In hacer de algo otra cosa, de introduces the thing that is made into a new role, state, or result.

example.en: They turned the garage into a workshop.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in the; de + el identifying something by its location
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After an object, it can identify which one by naming the room or place associated with it, where natural English often says “in” or puts the location before the object name.

example.en: We use the table on the patio.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cardCatalog.answerEn: from the; de + el marking the start of a range
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. In a range, it introduces the starting endpoint when that endpoint uses the masculine article el.

example.es: La oficina abre del lunes al viernes.
example.en: The office opens from Monday to Friday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After a quantity such as interés, it can introduce the rate used to measure that quantity.

example.es: El préstamo tiene un interés del cinco por ciento.
example.en: The loan has an interest rate of five percent.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; de + el links a worker to a service
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can use de after a job title to identify the service or area involved. Del combines de and el; English often places that service directly before the job title.

example.en: I called the telephone technician.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in the; introduces the group used for a ‘most’ or ‘least’ comparison
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After a description with más or menos that picks out an extreme, it can introduce the larger group being compared. Natural English often uses ‘in the’ rather than translating de literally as ‘of.’

example.es: Es el edificio más alto del barrio.
example.en: It is the tallest building in the neighborhood.

cardCatalog.answerEn: about the (de + el, introducing a topic)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Del combines de and el. After an expression that introduces a subject of discussion, de can mean “about,” so del introduces a masculine topic.

example.en: We talked about the new project.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A delta is the landform where a river divides into channels near its mouth. The same word can name the Greek letter delta.

example.es: El río forma un delta junto al mar.
example.en: The river forms a delta by the sea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Demolió is the completed-past form of demoler used with él, ella, or formal usted.

example.es: La empresa demolió el edificio vacío.
example.en: The company demolished the empty building.

cardCatalog.answerEn: on earth; the hell (informal question emphasis)
to show or prove to someone
cardCatalog.noteEn: Demostrar means ‘to show’ or ‘to prove.’ The attached le marks the person receiving the proof; careful standard Spanish normally uses les when more than one receiver is meant.

example.es: Voy a demostrarle el resultado a Ana.
example.en: I am going to show Ana the result.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to prove it; to demonstrate it
cardCatalog.noteEn: Demostrar means to prove or demonstrate, and attached lo replaces a masculine thing or a whole previously mentioned idea.

example.es: Dice que puede demostrarlo con datos.
example.en: She says she can prove it with data.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate literal meaning here; supplies the force in que le den
cardCatalog.noteEn: Den is a special command-like form of dar, “to give.” In this idiom, translating dar literally would hide the dismissive meaning. The rejected target may be stated after a or left understood.

example.en: To hell with the plan!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dentro de followed by a length of time looks forward from now: dentro de una semana means “in a week.”

example.en: I will return in an hour.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After hacia, dentro gives the direction hacia dentro, “inward.”

example.es: La puerta se abre hacia dentro.
example.en: The door opens inward.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A departamento can be a division within an organization. In some countries it can also mean an apartment or an administrative region.

example.es: Envía el formulario al departamento correcto.
example.en: Send the form to the correct department.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Depresivo can describe a depressive tendency or a gloomy quality. Deprimido is more usual for saying that someone feels depressed at a particular moment.

example.es: La novela tiene un tono depresivo.
example.en: The novel has a gloomy tone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In tener derecho a, derecho is something a person is allowed or entitled to do. This is distinct from derecho as the direction ‘right’ or as the field of law.

example.en: Everyone has the right to rest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Derivado can literally describe something taken from another source. When it judges a work or idea, it can suggest that the thing is not very original.

example.es: El diseño parece derivado de otro.
example.en: The design seems derived from another one.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Derribada comes from derribar, ‘to knock down.’ Its -ada ending is used because the thing described is feminine singular, as in la pared; with fue, it says that the thing was brought down.

example.en: The wall was knocked down yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Derribadas comes from derribar, ‘to knock down’ or ‘overturn.’ Its -adas ending matches more than one feminine thing.

example.en: The barriers were left knocked down.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Derritiendo is the -iendo action form of derretir, “to melt.” The attached lo means “it,” and the written accent preserves the original stress when that extra syllable is added.

example.en: The heat is melting it.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Derrocó is a completed-past form for one person, group, or state.

example.en: The revolt overthrew the dictator.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Des is a special form of dar for one familiar listener. It appears after expressions of wanting, requesting, doubt, or possibility when the giving is not stated as a fact.

example.es: Quiero que me des una respuesta.
example.en: I want you to give me an answer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Desafía is a present-time form of desafiar for one person or thing.

example.es: La nueva prueba desafía esa teoría.
example.en: The new evidence challenges that theory.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The ending -emos added to desaparecer marks a future action by “we.”

example.en: We will disappear before dawn.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Desaparecieron presents the disappearance as a completed event in the past. It is the ellos/ellas form of desaparecer.

example.es: Las huellas desaparecieron con la lluvia.
example.en: The tracks disappeared in the rain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Desarrolla is the present form used with one project or situation. With se, it describes that subject unfolding over time.

example.en: The story develops slowly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Desarrollando is the ongoing-action form of desarrollar. It describes a process that is currently being created or improved.

example.en: We are developing an application.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they rest; they are at rest

cardCatalog.noteEn: Descanso can mean a rest or break. In a sports context, el descanso commonly names the interval between the two parts of a game.

example.en: They talked during halftime.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, descargar means transferring a file or data onto your device. In other contexts it can mean unloading or discharging.

example.en: I am going to download the report.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The prefix des- reverses compensado here: the parts no longer look balanced or well matched.

example.en: The drawing ended up looking unbalanced.

cardCatalog.answerEn: strangers; people one does not know
cardCatalog.noteEn: Desconocidos can describe unknown people or things. Used by itself for people, it is a plural noun meaning strangers; the masculine plural form can refer to a mixed group.

example.en: I do not usually talk to strangers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Descubierto is the irregular completed-action form of descubrir, “to discover”; Spanish does not use the expected form descubrido. In a passive description it changes to match what was discovered: descubierto, descubierta, descubiertos, or descubiertas.

example.es: La isla fue descubierta por una exploradora.
example.en: The island was discovered by an explorer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: discovered; found (completed-action form used after haber)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Descubierto is the irregular completed-action form of descubrir. After a form of haber, it stays unchanged: he descubierto, han descubierto, and so on.

example.en: They have discovered a new error.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of desde luego (“of course”)
since; from the time when (with que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Desde marks a starting point. Followed by que and a full event, it means that the event supplies the point from which a later period is measured.

example.es: Vivo aquí desde que terminé los estudios.
example.en: I have lived here since I finished my studies.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Desde marks the point when a period begins. Before a question word such as cuándo, it asks for that starting point.

example.en: I have worked here since January.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a form of estar, deseando can show strong eagerness for the action that follows.

example.en: We are eager to travel.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Desesperadamente describes how an action is done. It is formed from the feminine singular describing form desesperada plus -mente.

example.en: He was desperately looking for the keys.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Desgraciadamente introduces information that the speaker regards as regrettable or unfortunate.

example.en: Unfortunately, the train has already left.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you take apart; you undo (one familiar person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Deshaces is the informal singular present form of deshacer. The verb combines des-, which often reverses an action, with hacer, 'to make or do.'

example.en: You undo the knot carefully.

cardCatalog.answerEn: uninformed; based on poor information (masculine singular)
naked (feminine singular; describing an implied woman)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Desnuda is feminine singular. Here it describes the understood woman rather than the plural word fotos, so English expresses the relationship differently.

example.es: La modelo aparece desnuda en el cuadro.
example.en: The model appears naked in the painting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to undress; to take my clothes off
cardCatalog.noteEn: Desnudar stays in its unchanged dictionary form and attached me marks that the speaker performs the action on themself.

example.es: Voy a desnudarme antes de ducharme.
example.en: I am going to undress before showering.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Despertador comes from despertar, “to wake up.” As a noun it names a device that wakes someone.

example.es: El despertador suena a las siete.
example.en: The alarm clock rings at seven.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Despertarme combines despertar with me. The me marks the speaker as the person who wakes up; English normally expresses the same idea with “wake up.”

example.en: I want to wake up early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Desperté is the completed-past form of despertar used for yo. When it describes waking up rather than waking someone else, Spanish normally uses it with me: me desperté.

example.en: I woke up early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Despiadadamente is built from despiadada, “ruthless,” plus -mente. It describes how an action or focus is pursued.

example.en: The company competed ruthlessly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Despertarse means to wake up. Despiertas is the present form for one informal listener, and te marks that listener as the person waking.

example.en: You wake up very early.

cardCatalog.answerEn: wake up (special form in a negative informal command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Despiertes is the special tú form used after no to tell one familiar person not to wake up. Despertarse uses te with that person, so the complete command places te before the verb: no te despiertes.

example.en: Do not wake up yet.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Despierto can be a form of despertar, “I wake up,” or a describing word meaning “awake.” When it describes a masculine singular person, its feminine form is despierta.

example.en: I am still awake at midnight.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Desplegarían is the conditional form for plural things. With se, it describes events that would develop or play out under an imagined condition.

example.en: Several changes would then unfold.

cardCatalog.answerEn: after all (as part of después de todo)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Después begins the fixed expression después de todo, which adds a conclusion or correction after considering the circumstances.

example.en: After all, you were right.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Detalle names one small, specific part of a larger whole.

example.en: I remember every detail.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Detén is the command form of detener used with one familiar person. It takes a written accent.

example.en: Stop the car here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Detener stays in its unchanged -er form and le is attached to represent a male person. This use of le for a singular male person is common and accepted in Spain; detenerlo is also widely used.

example.es: Mandaron a dos agentes para detenerle.
example.en: They sent two officers to stop him.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a form of haber, detenido is detenerse’s completed-action form here.

example.en: The machines have stopped.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Determinado is determinar's completed-action form. After estar, it describes a result that has been set by some rule, cause, or factor, and its ending matches the thing described.

example.es: El precio está determinado por la demanda.
example.en: The price is determined by demand.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Detrás is followed by de before the person or thing used as the reference point.

example.es: El jardín está detrás de la casa.
example.en: The garden is behind the house.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Devastado is the completed-action form of devastar.

example.es: El incendio había devastado el bosque.
example.en: The fire had devastated the forest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Devolverá is the future form used with él, ella, or formal usted.

example.en: Marta will return the book tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: realized; noticed (as part of me di cuenta)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Di is dar's completed-past form for the speaker. With me and cuenta, it forms me di cuenta, not the literal meaning gave.

example.en: I noticed the mistake.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Diabetes is normally a feminine noun in Spanish: la diabetes.

example.en: Diabetes requires medical care.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Diagrama is masculine despite its -a ending: el diagrama. Many Spanish nouns ending in -ma and derived from Greek follow this pattern.

example.en: The diagram shows three steps.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Diagramas is plural. Although it ends in -a, diagrama is masculine: el diagrama and los diagramas.

example.en: The diagrams explain the process.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, diálogo or cuadro de diálogo is a small on-screen window that asks for information or reports status. This differs from diálogo meaning spoken conversation.

example.en: The dialog box shows the progress.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Diapositiva can name one image or page shown as part of a presentation. The plural diapositivas refers to several such slides.

example.en: The presentation has ten slides.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Diaria is the feminine singular form of diario because it describes a feminine singular noun.

example.es: Caminar forma parte de mi rutina diaria.
example.en: Walking is part of my daily routine.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes buenos días, a daytime greeting
cardCatalog.noteEn: Días ordinarily means ‘days.’ In buenos días, the plural form is part of the standard greeting used in the morning and, in some places, into the early afternoon.

example.en: Good morning, Ms. Ruiz.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dibujada is the feminine singular completed-action form of dibujar used as a description.

example.es: Vimos una figura dibujada a mano.
example.en: We saw a figure drawn by hand.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dice is a present form of decir used with one person or thing. A report, text, or analysis can be the thing that “says” or indicates information.

example.es: El informe dice que todo está bien.
example.en: The report says that everything is fine.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dicho is the irregular completed-action form of decir, “to say.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “said.”

example.en: I have told the truth.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Diciendo is the -iendo form of decir used for an activity in progress, and le is attached to identify the recipient. The written accent keeps the original stress after le is added. In other contexts, le can mean “to her” or polite “to you.”

example.es: Siguió diciéndole la verdad a Pablo.
example.en: She kept telling Pablo the truth.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dieciocho is written as one word and does not carry a written accent.

example.en: The course has eighteen students.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dieciséis is written as one word and carries a written accent on the final e sound.

example.en: There are sixteen chairs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The opposite is fácil, ‘easy.’ Difícil keeps its written accent in the singular.

example.en: The question is difficult.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they tell you; people may tell you
cardCatalog.noteEn: After por mucho que, digan is a form of decir that leaves the amount or identity of what people say open. It is also the form used for a formal or plural command in other settings.

example.es: Por mucho que digan, mantendré mi decisión.
example.en: No matter what they say, I will keep my decision.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you say (in a dismissive or conceding response)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Digas is a special form of decir for one familiar listener. Fixed responses such as lo que tú digas use it to concede or dismiss whatever the other person says.

example.en: Fine, whatever you say.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Digitales is plural and has the same form with masculine and feminine plural nouns.

example.en: We keep digital copies.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Digno describes a masculine singular person or thing. Use digna for a feminine singular person or thing.

example.en: He maintained a dignified silence.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dije is the completed-past form of decir for the speaker.

example.en: I told the truth yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dijiste is decir's completed-past form for one person addressed informally. Its stem changes from dec- to dij-.

example.en: You told the truth.

cardCatalog.answerEn: tell him/her; say to him/her (informal singular command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dile joins the command di, from decir, to le, which marks the person receiving the message.

example.en: Tell Marta to come.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dinero is the general word for money rather than a particular coin, bill, or currency.

example.en: We are saving money for the trip.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dios names God, but said by itself it can also react to surprise, excitement, frustration, or strong nostalgia. The tone decides whether natural English keeps ‘God’ or uses an exclamation such as ‘man.’

example.en: Man, it's been so long!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dirección can mean direction, management, or an address. With postal, it is the address used for mail.

example.es: Confirma tu dirección antes del envío.
example.en: Confirm your address before shipment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Direcciones can mean addresses or directions. With names and phone numbers, it refers to contact or location addresses.

example.es: Guardaron las direcciones de los clientes.
example.en: They saved the clients' addresses.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Diría is the conditional form of decir for I, he, she, or formal you.

example.en: I would say that it is enough.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dirigir can mean sending movement or traffic toward a destination.

example.es: Van a dirigir el tráfico hacia el puente.
example.en: They are going to direct traffic toward the bridge.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computer language, disco refers to a storage disk or drive rather than a music record or a dance club.

example.es: El archivo está en el disco.
example.en: The file is on the disk.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Discos is plural. In computing, disco duro is the conventional name for a hard disk or hard drive.

example.es: El servidor tiene dos discos duros.
example.en: The server has two hard drives.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you excuse; you pardon (addressing a group)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Disculpan is a present form of disculpar used with ustedes, the usual plural ‘you’ throughout Latin America and a formal plural ‘you’ in Spain. In si me disculpan, it makes a polite request for the listeners' brief patience.

example.en: Will you excuse me for a moment?

cardCatalog.answerEn: please excuse me; bear with me (formal)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Disculpe is a polite command to one person, and me means “me.” In a positive command, Spanish attaches me to the end and writes discúlpeme as one word; the accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: Excuse me, can you repeat that?

cardCatalog.noteEn: The final accented -é marks a completed past action by the speaker.

example.en: I designed this table.

cardCatalog.answerEn: he or she designed; formal you designed
cardCatalog.noteEn: The final accented -ó marks a completed past action by one person. Context identifies whether the subject is he, she, or formal you.

example.en: Ana designed the bridge.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In engineering, disipación describes unwanted energy, especially heat, being spread out and removed from a system.

example.es: El ventilador mejora la disipación de calor.
example.en: The fan improves heat dissipation.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dispara tells one person addressed informally to fire a weapon or shoot. The same form can mean “he, she, or formal you fires” in a statement.

example.en: Aim and fire.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After mecanismo, disparador describes a mechanism that triggers or fires something. Used as a masculine noun with el, disparador can itself mean ‘trigger.’

example.es: El temporizador activa el mecanismo disparador.
example.en: The timer activates the triggering mechanism.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they shoot at; they fire at
cardCatalog.noteEn: Disparan is a present form of disparar for they or you plural. A short object word can identify the target.

example.en: The guards fire into the air.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to shoot at him, her, or it
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dispararle joins disparar with singular le, which marks one target. Use dispararles when that target is plural; a following phrase beginning with a can name the target explicitly.

example.en: You must not shoot at the animal.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Disparatado describes an idea or claim that is unreasonable or makes little sense. It changes to disparatada, disparatados, or disparatadas to match what it describes.

example.en: That rumor seems absurd.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dispositivo names a piece of equipment made for a particular purpose.

example.en: The device measures the temperature.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dispositivos is the masculine plural of dispositivo, a device or piece of equipment designed for a purpose.

example.en: Turn off the electronic devices.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dispuesto changes to dispuesta, dispuestos, or dispuestas to match the person or group being described. A following a can introduce the action that person is willing to do.

example.en: Luis is willing to wait.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you got; you gave yourself (in darse un golpe)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Diste is a completed-past form of dar for one familiar listener. With te and un golpe, it says that the listener bumped or hurt themself.

example.es: Te diste un golpe en la rodilla.
example.en: You bumped your knee.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Distinguir means recognizing the difference between people, things, or ideas.

example.es: No puedo distinguir las dos voces.
example.en: I cannot tell the two voices apart.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Distro is informal technical shorthand for distribución, especially a packaged version of an operating system such as a Linux distribution.

example.es: Probé una distro diferente de Linux.
example.en: I tried a different Linux distribution.

cardCatalog.answerEn: having fun; enjoying yourselves (addressing several people informally)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Divertiros is the form of divertirse, ‘to have fun,’ used for an informally addressed group in Spain: the attached se changes to os. After dejar de, English naturally uses ‘having fun’ for this activity.

example.en: You all can have fun here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Divides is the familiar singular present form of dividir. A preceding lo can stand for the number being divided.

example.en: You divide the total by four.

cardCatalog.answerEn: double; twice as long or large
cardCatalog.noteEn: Dobles is plural because it describes more than one turno.

example.en: They worked two double shifts.

cardCatalog.answerEn: hurt; ached (the completed-action form used after ha)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dominas is the ordinary present form of dominar for one familiar person.

example.en: You master the technique well.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Donatello; the name of a Renaissance sculptor and a Ninja Turtle

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dónde carries a written accent when it directly or indirectly asks about a location. In a direct question, Spanish also uses the opening question mark ¿.

example.en: Where is the station?

cardCatalog.answerEn: where; as far as (in hasta donde)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After hasta, donde identifies the figurative boundary reached by someone's knowledge. It has no written accent because it is not asking a question.

example.en: As far as we know, everything works.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dónde keeps its written accent in an indirect question: the location is being asked about even though the words do not stand alone as a direct question.

example.en: I don't know where Ana lives.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Donde has no written accent here because it links back to the available ideas and arguments rather than asking a direct or indirect question.

example.en: There are several options to choose from.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Donnas (part of the band name The Donnas)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Donut is a common borrowed food word in Spanish; dónut is also written with an accent in edited Spanish.

example.en: I bought a chocolate doughnut.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dormido comes from dormir, “to sleep.” As a description of a person or animal, it means that the subject is asleep; dormida is used for a feminine singular subject.

example.en: The child is asleep.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I realize (as part of me doy cuenta)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Doy normally means “I give.” In the expression darse cuenta, the matching form of dar combines with cuenta to mean “to realize” or “to notice.”

example.en: I realize the mistake.

cardCatalog.answerEn: DROP (SQL command that deletes an object)
dual; using two systems (in arranque dual)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, arranque dual is a setup that lets one machine start either of two installed operating systems.

example.en: The laptop has dual boot.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Duele is used when one thing causes pain. The person feeling it is marked with me, te, le, nos, os, or les.

example.en: My back hurts.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Duerme is the present form of dormir used with one person or thing. Spanish treats gente, 'people,' as grammatically singular, so gente goes with duerme rather than duermen.

example.es: La gente duerme poco en verano.
example.en: People sleep little in summer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I fall asleep (when used with me)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Duermo alone normally means “I sleep.” Me duermo uses the same verb form with me to describe the change from awake to asleep.

example.en: I fall asleep early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dulce can describe affectionate words or gestures as “sweet,” not only the taste of food.

example.en: It was a very sweet gesture.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Dura is a form of durar, which describes how long something continues. It is unrelated to dura meaning “hard” when used as an adjective.

example.en: The movie lasts two hours.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Durante introduces a period of time. Natural English often uses ‘for’ before a measured duration, such as an hour, but ‘during’ before a named event or period, such as the meeting.

example.en: We waited for an hour.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a duras penas, “barely”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Duras is not translated separately inside the fixed expression a duras penas.

example.es: A duras penas llegó a tiempo.
example.en: He barely arrived on time.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Durmiendo is the -iendo action form of dormir, 'to sleep.' Dormirse means to fall asleep, so te estás durmiendo presents that change as happening now.

example.en: The child is falling asleep.

cardCatalog.answerEn: hard (as part of disco duro, “hard drive”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Duro usually means physically hard. In the conventional computer term disco duro, the two words together mean a hard disk or hard drive.

example.es: El portátil tiene un disco duro nuevo.
example.en: The laptop has a new hard drive.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After trabajar, duro describes the intensity of the work: trabajar duro means to work hard.

example.en: We work hard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here duro describes a material that resists pressure. In other contexts it can describe something difficult or someone acting harshly.

example.en: The ground is hard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Duros is masculine plural to match discos in the computing term discos duros.

example.en: They replaced the hard drives.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish commonly keeps the international abbreviation DVD and adds a written plural s in informal use.

example.es: Guardó los DVDs en una caja.
example.en: She kept the DVDs in a box.

cardCatalog.answerEn: and (used instead of y before an i sound)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish changes y to e before a following word that begins with the vowel sound i, which makes the two words easier to distinguish in speech.

example.en: We invited parents and children.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ebook is an English loan used in Spanish for a book read on an electronic device. The printed plural ebooks adds -s.

example.en: I read e-books on the train.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I'll take, as part of echar un vistazo
cardCatalog.noteEn: Echar has many meanings, including “to throw” or “to put.” In echar un vistazo, it forms the conventional expression “to take a look.” The ending -é marks a future action by “I.”

example.en: I'll take a look at the report.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to step aside; to move myself out of the way (with a un lado)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Echarme combines the unchanged verb echar with me. In echarme a un lado, the full expression means that the speaker steps aside or gets out of the way.

example.es: Voy a echarme a un lado.
example.en: I am going to step aside.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you start off (in echas a correr)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Echo is the present form of echar for the speaker. Echar has many meanings; before an approximate age, time, or amount, it can mean “to estimate.” Echo has no h, unlike hecho, “done” or “made.”

example.en: I estimate that person to be about thirty.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Echó is a completed-past form of echar. With a person and de plus a place, echar means forcing that person to leave the place.

example.es: El casero lo echó del piso.
example.en: The landlord threw him out of the apartment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Editando is editar's ongoing-action form ending in -ando. A preceding form of estar may be understood from a nearby coordinated action.

example.en: I am editing the document.

cardCatalog.noteEn: EEUU abbreviates Estados Unidos. The repeated E and U show that both words are plural; formal writing often adds periods and a space as EE. UU.

example.es: La empresa vende sus productos en EEUU.
example.en: The company sells its products in the US.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Eficiencia is the ability to achieve a result while avoiding unnecessary waste of time, energy, or resources.

example.es: El cambio mejora la eficiencia del sistema.
example.en: The change improves the system's efficiency.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Placed after a comment, eh can turn it into a casual request for the listener to agree. This differs from hesitation eh, meaning ‘uh,’ or an attention-getting ‘hey.’

example.en: It is cold, isn't it?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Eh can show that the speaker is surprised or did not understand what was just said.

example.en: Huh? I didn't hear you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Eh can fill a pause while a speaker thinks or reacts. Its tone and punctuation determine whether it sounds hesitant, surprised, or attention-getting.

example.en: Um... I need to think about it.

cardCatalog.answerEn: huh?; eh? (a skeptical or surprised echo)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Eh can repeat or react to what was just said. The questioning tone can show surprise, doubt, or mild skepticism rather than hesitation.

example.en: You're leaving tomorrow, huh?

cardCatalog.answerEn: they run; they execute (software or files)

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, ejecutar means making a program or set of instructions run. It has other senses, including carrying out a plan.

example.en: I am going to run the program.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ejem represents the sound of clearing one's throat, often to attract attention or pointedly interrupt.

example.en: Ahem, I'm still here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ejes is the plural of eje. In a graph, the axes are the reference lines along which values or categories are positioned.

example.es: Los ejes del gráfico muestran tiempo y distancia.
example.en: The graph's axes show time and distance.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; article before the name of a command
cardCatalog.noteEn: A masculine noun such as comando can remain understood before its specific name, while el still appears. Natural English often gives the command name directly without “the.”

example.en: Use the Save command.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; article used before a product or software name
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can put el before the name of software, a vehicle model, or another product when a masculine noun such as sistema or modelo is understood. English often uses the product name without an article.

example.en: She bought the red Toyota.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; article before a masculine technical name
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can keep el before the name of a masculine service, protocol, or technical system even when English uses the name by itself.

example.en: Wi-Fi stopped working.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the particular thing (as part of el qué, what exactly)
it (referring back to a masculine singular thing)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Él normally means “he” or “him,” but after a preposition it can also replace a masculine singular thing already named. English then uses “it.” Keep the accent to distinguish él from el, “the.”

example.es: El ruido es fuerte, pero me acostumbré a él.
example.en: The noise is loud, but I got used to it.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces a numbered service
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can use el before a number that names a masculine service or line. English often uses the number alone.

example.en: Is this 061?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can leave out a masculine noun that is already understood and keep el before the words that distinguish it. English often supplies “the one.”

example.en: I prefer the blue one.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the; English often uses a possessive because le already marks the affected owner
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can use le for the affected owner and an ordinary article before that person's item or service. English often uses a possessive word instead. El matches a masculine singular item, not the owner's gender.

example.es: Le cancelaron el servicio a Laura.
example.en: They canceled Laura's service.

cardCatalog.answerEn: my here; Spanish uses el because me already marks the affected owner
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses the definite article before an owned item when a short word such as me, te, or le already identifies the affected owner. English commonly uses a possessive instead.

example.en: They broke my phone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The written accent distinguishes the pronoun él from the article el, which means “the.”

example.en: The book is for him.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the masculine article inside el que (‘which’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a linking word such as en, el que can refer back to one masculine thing. El matches that earlier thing, while que introduces the added information.

example.es: Ese es el libro en el que aparece la foto.
example.en: That is the book in which the photo appears.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When no noun is written before el que, el identifies one unnamed masculine person or thing and que introduces what defines it. This differs from ordinary el before a noun and from a use after a linking word, such as en el que, ‘in which.’

example.es: Él es el que organiza las reuniones.
example.en: He is the one who organizes the meetings.

cardCatalog.answerEn: on (before one particular day of the week)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish normally uses el before a singular weekday where English uses “on”: el martes means “on Tuesday.” No extra en is needed.

example.en: The store opens on Friday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In this comic, elección means a choice or decision rather than a political election.

example.en: It is a difficult choice.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here the plural elecciones means choices or decisions.

example.en: We make small choices every day.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Electoral has one form for masculine and feminine singular nouns: proceso electoral and campaña electoral.

example.en: The election debate begins.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Eléctrica is the feminine singular form of eléctrico and matches a feminine singular noun.

example.en: The electric current is weak.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Electrodos are conductors through which electric current enters or leaves a material or device.

example.en: The electrodes are separated.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Electromagnético describes something involving linked electric and magnetic effects. Its ending changes to electromagnética with a feminine noun.

example.en: We study the electromagnetic field.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Elegido is the describing form made from elegir, “to choose.” With an article, el elegido or la elegida can name the person who was chosen.

example.en: She was the chosen one.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This is the unchanged dictionary form ending in -ir.

example.en: You can choose an option.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I would choose; he or she would choose
cardCatalog.noteEn: Elegiría keeps the full dictionary form elegir and adds -ía. This form presents the choice as dependent on an imagined condition or situation.

example.en: I would choose the blue option.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a one-word reaction, elemental says that a conclusion is basic or easy to deduce.

example.en: The answer is elementary.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Elvish; relating to elves or an elf language
cardCatalog.noteEn: Élfico can describe something associated with fantasy elves. Used after en, it can name an Elvish language.

example.es: La inscripción está escrita en élfico.
example.en: The inscription is written in Elvish.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a preposition such as con, ella corresponds to her. As a sentence subject, it means she.

example.en: I spoke with her yesterday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it (referring to a feminine thing after a preposition)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a preposition such as en, con, or de, ella can refer back to a feminine singular thing as well as to a woman. English normally uses “it” for the thing.

example.es: La caja está vacía; no hay nada en ella.
example.en: The box is empty; there is nothing in it.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ella is the feminine singular subject pronoun. Spanish often leaves subject pronouns unstated, but ella can be included for clarity or emphasis.

example.en: She lives here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ellas is the feminine plural stressed pronoun. After a preposition it can mean ‘them.’

example.en: I spoke with them yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ello is a small neutral reference word that can point back to an idea, event, or task rather than to a masculine or feminine object. It is more common in formal writing and in fixed expressions such as ponerse a ello.

example.en: We will talk about it tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: them (masculine or mixed group, after a preposition)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ellos usually means ‘they,’ but after a preposition such as con, para, or sin, English uses ‘them.’

example.en: I am going with them.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here ellos is the subject that performs the following action.

example.en: They can enter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Embarazada describes a pregnant woman or another feminine subject. Embarazado is the matching masculine form in contexts where it applies.

example.es: La prueba indica que no está embarazada.
example.en: The test indicates that she is not pregnant.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sin embargo (“however”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In sin embargo, embargo does not contribute a separate English word. The two Spanish words work together as the connector “however” or “nevertheless.”

example.es: Es difícil; sin embargo, es posible.
example.en: It is difficult; however, it is possible.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Embusteros is masculine or mixed plural. The feminine plural form is embusteras.

example.en: Do not believe those liars.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Emite is a form of emitir for one person or thing. It is used for giving off light, heat, sound, radiation, or a signal.

example.en: The lamp gives off little light.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Empecé is the completed-past form of empezar used for yo. The spelling changes from z to c before é so the consonant sound stays the same.

example.en: I started reading yesterday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they make it worse; they worsen
cardCatalog.noteEn: Empeoran is a plural present form of empeorar. With lo before it, lo stands for the situation being made worse.

example.en: Those changes make it worse.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Empezado is the completed-action form of empezar, “to start.” It follows a form of haber in expressions such as han empezado, “they have started.”

example.en: The class has started.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Empezamos is the present form of empezar used for nosotros or nosotras, “we.”

example.en: We start with the first question.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Empezando presents empezar as an action in progress. Before por, it can introduce the first item in a sequence.

example.es: Estoy empezando por la tarea corta.
example.en: I am starting with the short task.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Empezaste is empezar's completed-past form for one familiar person addressed as tú. When an action follows, Spanish places a before that action verb's unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: You started reading yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Empiezas is empezar's present form for one familiar listener.

example.en: You start working tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Empiezo is the present form of empezar for the speaker. The e changes to ie in this stressed form: empezar becomes empiezo.

example.es: Empiezo a trabajar a las nueve.
example.en: I start working at nine.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Empresa is a feminine noun for a company or business organization.

example.es: La empresa abrió una oficina pequeña.
example.en: The company opened a small office.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Empuña is a form of empuñar for one person. It commonly describes holding and using a weapon or tool by its handle.

example.en: The guard wields a spear.

cardCatalog.answerEn: at (with a time period such as night)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a part of the day, en can place an event within that period. Natural English often uses “at” with night where Spanish uses en; usage varies, and por la noche is also very common.

example.en: We read at night.

cardCatalog.answerEn: on; engaged in (as part of estar en campaña)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses en between estar and campaña to describe being actively engaged in a campaign. Natural English often says “campaigning” or “on the campaign trail.”

example.en: The party is campaigning.

cardCatalog.answerEn: into; introduces the result after convertirse
cardCatalog.noteEn: After convertirse, en links the changing person or thing to what it becomes. Keep en even though English may simply use become before a noun.

example.es: El agua se convierte en hielo.
example.en: Water turns into ice.

cardCatalog.answerEn: into; required after colarse before a place
cardCatalog.noteEn: Use en after colarse to introduce the place entered secretly.

example.en: He sneaked into the building.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in; within (the time taken to finish)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a duration, en can state how much time an action took to complete.

example.es: Terminé el informe en dos horas.
example.en: I finished the report in two hours.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in; required after confianza before the person or thing trusted
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses confianza en to introduce the person or thing in whom confidence or trust is placed.

example.en: I have confidence in Clara.

cardCatalog.answerEn: of; introduces what something consists of
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses consistir en before the activity or components. English normally uses “consist of.”

example.es: La prueba consiste en ordenar las piezas.
example.en: The test consists of arranging the pieces.

cardCatalog.answerEn: into; introduces the result after degenerar
cardCatalog.noteEn: Degenerar en presents what a situation deteriorates or turns into.

example.es: La charla degeneró en una pelea.
example.en: The conversation degenerated into a fight.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in; in any way, as part of en algo
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a verb about changing or affecting something, en algo can ask whether there is any effect or difference at all.

example.en: Did the plan change in any way?

cardCatalog.answerEn: to; required before the action after primero or primera
cardCatalog.noteEn: When primero or primera identifies who does something before everyone else, en links it to the unchanged action verb.

example.en: She was the first to answer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of de vez en cuando, “from time to time”
cardCatalog.noteEn: En is a required middle piece of the fixed expression de vez en cuando.

example.en: We go out from time to time.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links dejar to paz in dejar en paz
cardCatalog.noteEn: En is required inside the expression dejar a alguien en paz, meaning to leave someone alone or stop bothering them.

example.en: Leave the dog alone.

cardCatalog.answerEn: at; begins en algún momento, “at some point”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here en introduces an indefinite point in time rather than a physical location.

example.en: We will discuss it at some point.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en broma, “as a joke”
cardCatalog.noteEn: En combines with broma to make the fixed expression en broma. Translating en by itself as “in” would be unnatural here.

example.en: I said it as a joke.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en cambio, “instead” or “on the other hand”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Learn en and cambio together. The expression contrasts the next choice or fact with what came before.

example.es: No fui en coche; en cambio, caminé.
example.en: I did not go by car; instead, I walked.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; begins en clave, ‘coded’ or ‘in code’
cardCatalog.noteEn: En belongs to the conventional expression en clave. English may translate the expression with ‘in code’ or use ‘code’ directly before a noun.

example.es: El mensaje está escrito en clave.
example.en: The message is written in code.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en cuanto, 'as soon as'
no separate English word; begins en general, “in general”
cardCatalog.noteEn: The two words form a fixed expression about an overall view.

example.en: In general, I prefer walking.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en línea (“online”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: The two words en línea work together as the standard expression for something online or connected through a network. In this use, en is not translated on its own.

example.en: The course is online.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en lugar de, ‘instead of’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Inside en lugar de, en is a fixed part of the expression rather than an independently translated location word.

example.es: Tomé té en lugar de café.
example.en: I had tea instead of coffee.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en ocasiones (‘sometimes’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: En ocasiones is a fixed time expression meaning that something happens on some occasions rather than always.

example.en: Sometimes, we eat dinner out.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en realidad (“actually”)
no separate English word; begins en rigor (‘strictly speaking’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: En and rigor form a fixed expression used to make a precise qualification. Translating en by itself would hide the expression's meaning.

example.en: Strictly speaking, it is not required.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en seguida, “right away”
cardCatalog.noteEn: En and seguida work together as the time expression en seguida.

example.en: I will call you right away.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en serio (“seriously”)
at; fixed opening of en todo momento y lugar
cardCatalog.noteEn: En introduces the time-and-place expression en todo momento y lugar, ‘at every time and place.’

example.es: La norma se aplica en todo momento y lugar.
example.en: The rule applies at every time and place.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en verdad
cardCatalog.noteEn: En combines with verdad to form an expression meaning “actually,” “really,” or “in truth.”

example.en: Actually, I did not know.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en vez de, ‘instead of’
cardCatalog.noteEn: En belongs to the fixed three-word connector en vez de. Learn the connector as a unit rather than translating en as ordinary ‘in.’

example.es: Tomé té en vez de café.
example.en: I had tea instead of coffee.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en vivo, 'live' or 'in real time'
in (fixed part of estar en plan)
cardCatalog.noteEn: En belongs to the colloquial expression estar en plan. The expression presents someone's attitude, mode, or approximate words.

example.en: She was in an optimistic sort of mood.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of poner los ojos en blanco
cardCatalog.noteEn: En links ojos to blanco inside the fixed expression for rolling one's eyes. Translate the complete expression rather than this en on its own.

example.es: No pongas los ojos en blanco.
example.en: Don't roll your eyes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; fixed part of tener en cuenta
cardCatalog.noteEn: En links tener to cuenta in the fixed expression tener en cuenta, ‘to keep in mind’ or ‘to take into account.’

example.en: We take the price into account.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a time span, en can measure how long from now it will be until a future event occurs. In another context, en plus a time span can instead say how long an activity takes to complete.

example.es: El tren llegará en diez minutos.
example.en: The train will arrive in ten minutes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; required after insistir before the claim
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses insistir en before the topic or claim someone keeps pressing. When a full statement follows, the sequence is insistir en que.

example.en: I insist that it is true.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in; required after interesado before the activity
in; required after interesarse before the activity
using; in (a keyboard layout or system)
