cardCatalog.noteEn: With the name of a keyboard layout, en identifies the system being used. Natural English often says ‘using’ that layout.

example.en: She types using QWERTY.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses en before a website, app, or online service where something happens. English commonly uses “on” in the same setting.

example.es: Vi el anuncio en una página web.
example.en: I saw the advertisement on a website.

cardCatalog.answerEn: into; introduces what is entered after penetrar
cardCatalog.noteEn: Penetrar en presents a movement or reach into a place, material, subject, or person's inner world.

example.es: El agua penetró en la pared.
example.en: The water seeped into the wall.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pensar en means to think of or think about someone or something.

example.en: I think about my family.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces the proportion being described
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can use en before a percentage to state how much of something has a particular description. Natural English normally puts the percentage directly before that description, without a separate word for en.

example.es: El trabajo está terminado en un 80%.
example.en: The work is 80% complete.

cardCatalog.answerEn: from; at (introducing where a ban applies)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After estar vetado, en introduces the place, event, or setting where the ban applies. Natural English often uses ‘from’ or ‘at’ rather than the usual literal ‘in.’

example.en: He is banned from several stadiums.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links a time noun to que
cardCatalog.noteEn: In a connector such as el momento en que, en que works like “when” or “in which.”

example.es: Recuerdo el día en que llegó.
example.en: I remember the day when she arrived.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In game-like descriptions, a number followed by en can identify which statistic receives that increase or penalty, much like English '+2 to risk.'

example.en: The armor gives +1 to defense.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links tardar to the action that takes time
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tardar uses en before an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: She took an hour to reply.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a specific moment, en can correspond to English “at.”

example.en: He arrived at just the right moment.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links the time taken to the action
in; required after confiar before what is trusted

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a form of haber, encantado is the completed-action form of encantar. With an experiencer word such as me, it says that something has delighted that person.

example.en: I have loved your stories.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encantador describes a masculine singular person or thing. The feminine singular form is encantadora.

example.en: He is a charming neighbor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encender often means to turn on a light or device. With something combustible, it means to ignite or light it.

example.es: Una chispa puede encender el gas.
example.en: A spark can ignite the gas.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For a device, encendido means switched on or running. It is the describing form made from encender, “to turn on.”

example.en: The computer is on.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encerrado describes the resulting state of a masculine singular person or thing after being confined or shut inside.

example.es: El perro está encerrado en el patio.
example.en: The dog is shut in the yard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Enciende is the present form of encender for one person or thing. With se, encenderse describes a device or system starting up without naming whoever activates it.

example.en: The computer turns on.

cardCatalog.answerEn: above; over (as part of por encima de)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Encima refers to an upper position, but por encima de is the complete expression used before the reference point.

example.es: La lámpara está por encima de la mesa.
example.en: The lamp is above the table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After llevar, encima says that the object is being carried with the person, not merely located physically above something.

example.en: I always carry money on me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encima places something in the upper position. It can stand alone when the reference point is understood; encima de names that reference point explicitly.

example.en: Put the book on top.

cardCatalog.answerEn: found (feminine singular, in a status message)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontrada is the feminine singular result form of encontrar, ‘to find.’ A short status message can omit a full verb such as se ha and simply report encontrada before or after a feminine noun.

example.en: Solution found.

cardCatalog.answerEn: found (masculine plural, in a status message)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontrados is the masculine plural result form of encontrar, ‘to find.’ In a terse status message it agrees with a masculine or mixed plural noun even when the full expression se han encontrado is omitted.

example.en: Two documents found.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontramos is the present form of encontrar for nosotros. With nos before it, nos encontramos can mean 'we meet each other.'

example.en: We meet at the station.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontrará is the future form of encontrar for one person or thing.

example.en: Someone will find the box.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontrarlas combines encontrar, “to find,” with las, “them.” Las refers back to more than one feminine thing.

example.en: I hope to find them soon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontraron is the completed-past form of encontrar for they or formal plural you. The stem stays encontr- and the -aron ending marks an -ar verb's completed plural action.

example.en: They found the keys yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encuentra is the present form used for one third-person subject. With se before it and con after it, se encuentra con describes meeting or coming across someone or something.

example.en: Leo meets Marta.

cardCatalog.answerEn: find (an informal command to one person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Encuentra is the positive tú command of encontrar, used to tell one familiar person to find something or someone.

example.en: Find an empty chair.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encuentra is the singular present form of encontrar. With the matching se before it, encontrarse can describe where something exists or is located.

example.es: El museo se encuentra en el centro.
example.en: The museum is located downtown.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontrar can mean judging a person or thing to have a quality, not only locating something that was lost. A following describing word states that judgment.

example.en: I find this tool useful.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This is the present form of encontrar used with yo. It means locating something here, not considering it a certain way.

example.en: I cannot find my keys.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to become ill; to get sick

cardCatalog.noteEn: Enfocado describes something directed toward a subject, goal, or result. It changes to enfocada, enfocados, or enfocadas to match what is described.

example.es: El curso está enfocado a principiantes.
example.en: The course is aimed at beginners.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Enfocando is the ongoing-action form of enfocar, “to focus.” Los attaches to the end and means “them,” referring to masculine plural things.

example.es: Ajusta los rayos enfocándolos en un punto.
example.en: Adjust the rays by focusing them on one point.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Enfrente can describe the position directly opposite. Enfrente de adds the person or thing that serves as the reference point.

example.en: I sat across from Ana.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Enganchar literally involves hooking or attaching something. With equipment or a service, it can describe things hooked up or connected to it.

example.es: Las cámaras están enganchadas al sistema.
example.en: The cameras are hooked up to the system.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Engañoso describes something that gives a false or mistaken impression. Its ending changes to engañosa with a feminine singular noun.

example.en: The advertisement is misleading.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An enjambre is a large moving group, especially of insects or, by extension, tiny robots.

example.en: A swarm surrounded the hive.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Enmarca is the present form for one thing that surrounds or visually highlights another.

example.en: The window frames the landscape.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you show (one familiar person or thing)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Enseñas is the present form of enseñar used for tú, one familiar listener. Enseñar can mean either “to teach” or “to show”; the surrounding object decides which sense applies.

example.en: You show me a photo.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I show; I teach (special form after deja que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: The ordinary speaker form is enseño. After deja que asks to allow the action, enseño changes to enseñe, a form used for an allowed or requested action rather than a stated fact.

example.es: Deja que te enseñe el mapa.
example.en: Let me show you the map.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Entendemos is the present form of entender for “we.” With reciprocal nos, it describes understanding shared between the people in that “we.” Without nos, it can simply mean “we understand.”

example.en: We understand each other well.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Entender is the unchanged dictionary form. Its present forms change the stressed e to ie in most persons: entiendo, entiendes, entiende, and entienden.

example.en: I want to understand the problem.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to find out; to learn about something
cardCatalog.noteEn: Enterarme joins the dictionary form enterar with me. In this pronominal use, enterarse de means to become informed or find something out; it does not mean to put something inside.

example.en: I want to find out about the news.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Enteró is the completed-past form used with se for one person: se enteró. The information learned can follow de or be understood from context.

example.es: Carlos se enteró de la reunión.
example.en: Carlos found out about the meeting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you understand; do you understand? (informal singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Entiendes is the present tú form of entender. The stressed e changes to ie: entender becomes entiendes.

example.en: Do you understand this explanation?

cardCatalog.answerEn: I take it; I gather; I understand (an inference)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Entiendo que can introduce a conclusion drawn from what has just been said, much like English “I take it that...” It need not mean that the speaker has received an explanation.

example.en: I take it you are not coming today.

cardCatalog.answerEn: so; well then (opening or returning to a topic)
cardCatalog.noteEn: At the start of a conversation, entonces can introduce the subject the speaker wants to discuss. This discourse use differs from temporal entonces, “then,” although both can move a conversation forward.

example.en: So, shall we talk about the project?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Entrar literally means to enter. With a group or online space, it can describe joining or coming into that community.

example.es: Ana entra en el chat cada tarde.
example.en: Ana joins the chat every afternoon.

cardCatalog.answerEn: entered; come in (past participle of entrar)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Entrar often means ‘to enter’ or ‘to go in.’ With an object and an opening or available space, it can say that the object fits into that space.

example.es: Las cajas entran en el armario.
example.en: The boxes fit in the cupboard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After dividir, entre introduces the number used as the divisor: dividir doce entre tres means ‘divide twelve by three.’ This differs from the location meaning ‘between’ or ‘among.’

example.en: Divide twenty by five.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Entregado is the completed-action form of entregar. After a form of haber, it stays unchanged and can say that work, forms, or documents have been submitted.

example.en: I have submitted the report.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Entretenido can describe something that holds attention or is enjoyable. Its ending changes to match the noun.

example.en: They are short, entertaining games.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ent is Tolkien's name for one of these beings; Spanish uses ents as the plural.

example.es: Los ents parecen árboles que caminan.
example.en: The Ents look like walking trees.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Envejecen is the present-time form for more than one person or thing.

example.en: Some people age slowly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Enviado is the completed-action form of enviar. After han, it says that more than one person or thing has sent something or someone.

example.es: Han enviado el paquete esta mañana.
example.en: They sent the package this morning.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Enviamos can be present or completed past. A narrative of finished events gives it the completed-past reading.

example.en: Yesterday we sent two technicians.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Envió is a completed-past form of enviar, “to send.” The written accent distinguishes it from envío, which can mean “I send” or “shipment.”

example.en: Luis sent the letter yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Equipo can also mean equipment; here it names a group of people working together.

example.en: The team is looking for a solution.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Equivocada describes a feminine singular person or thing as mistaken or incorrect.

example.en: The answer is wrong.

cardCatalog.answerEn: make a mistake; choose the wrong one (informal command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Equivócate is a positive command to one familiar person. It combines equivoca with te and gains a written accent to preserve the spoken stress.

example.en: Make mistakes without fear.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Era is a past form of ser used for a background state, description, or ongoing past situation. This form is called the imperfect.

example.en: The house was small.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Error can describe a mistaken action, judgment, or result. In computing it can also mean an error or bug, but this card teaches the ordinary mistake sense.

example.en: It was an honest mistake.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With solar, erupción names a burst of energy from the Sun.

example.es: Una erupción solar alcanzó su punto máximo.
example.en: A solar flare reached its peak.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With solares, erupciones refers to bursts of energy from the Sun rather than volcanic eruptions.

example.es: Las erupciones solares pueden afectar los satélites.
example.en: Solar flares can affect satellites.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cardCatalog.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.

example.en: Chess is a game.

cardCatalog.answerEn: part of es decir: that is; in other words
cardCatalog.noteEn: Within the fixed linking expression es decir, es does not independently identify what something is; the two words work together as a clarifying connector.

example.es: No puedo ir, es decir, tendrás que conducir.
example.en: I cannot go; in other words, you will have to drive.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es que

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can begin an impersonal evaluation with es plus a describing word. English normally supplies an impersonal ‘it,’ but Spanish does not add a separate subject word.

example.en: It is strange that it is raining.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it is (in an impersonal time expression)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can use es without a separate subject word in expressions such as es hora, “it is time.” English supplies the impersonal word “it.”

example.en: It is time to leave.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is, in the reaction eso es: that's it
cardCatalog.noteEn: This form of ser combines with eso in a conventional reaction that recognizes the answer or realization.

example.en: “The blue key?” “That's it!”

cardCatalog.answerEn: you are; printed misspelling of está
cardCatalog.noteEn: The visible word omits the t from está but keeps the accent on á. The intended está is the form used with formal usted and helps form an ongoing action.

example.en: You are joking.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escasas describes a feminine plural group as limited in number or difficult to find.

example.en: Tickets are scarce.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escenario can mean a stage, but it also means an imagined or possible situation being considered.

example.en: We analyzed the worst-case scenario.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escondí is the speaker form of esconder for one completed action in the past. The ending -í identifies the speaker and carries a written accent.

example.es: Escondí la llave en un cajón.
example.en: I hid the key in a drawer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escribe is the present form of escribir for él, ella, or usted. The same written form can also be an informal command. In an action caption, it narrates what the person does.

example.en: Marta writes a note.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escriben is the present form of escribir used with ustedes. The same written form can also mean “they write”; the stated subject shows which meaning applies.

example.en: You all write every week.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escrita is the completed-action form of escribir and takes the feminine singular ending when it describes a feminine singular noun.

example.es: La nota está escrita a mano.
example.en: The note is written by hand.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escrito is the irregular completed-action form, also called the past participle, of escribir. After a form of haber, it helps express that writing as completed.

example.en: Ana has written a letter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escritura usually means writing. In a computing context, velocidad de escritura is the speed at which someone types.

example.es: Su escritura es más rápida con este teclado.
example.en: Her typing is faster with this keyboard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escucha is the positive command of escuchar for one friend, peer, or other familiar listener.

example.en: Listen carefully.

cardCatalog.answerEn: listen (command to several people, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Escuchad is the positive command form of escuchar for vosotros or vosotras. Most positive vosotros commands replace the dictionary form's final -r with -d: escuchar becomes escuchad.

example.en: Listen carefully, all of you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escuchado is the completed-action form of escuchar. It follows a form of haber: he escuchado, has escuchado, and so on.

example.en: I have never heard that song.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escuchando is the ongoing-action form of escuchar. It follows a form of estar to describe listening or hearing in progress.

example.en: They are hearing the news.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to listen to you; to hear you
cardCatalog.noteEn: Escuchar stays in its dictionary form and te attaches to represent one familiar listener.

example.en: On listening to you, I understood the problem.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escuchar goes directly before what is heard. Spanish does not add a separate word for the English “to” in “listen to.”

example.en: I listen to music at home.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Escuche tells one person addressed as usted to listen. The informal command to a friend would be escucha.

example.en: Listen to this explanation, please.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ese points to a masculine singular noun that is not presented as right next to the speaker. Feminine singular is esa.

example.en: I do not recognize that sound.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When ese appears without a following noun, it stands in for a masculine singular thing already visible or understood.

example.en: I prefer that one.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With se, esfuerza is the present form of esforzarse used for one third-person subject.

example.en: Tomás makes an effort every day.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Esnob can be a noun or an adjective for someone who displays supposedly superior taste.

example.en: His comment sounded snobbish.

cardCatalog.answerEn: that, in the reaction eso es: that's it
cardCatalog.noteEn: Eso normally points to an idea or thing as “that.” In the reaction eso es, it identifies an explanation or answer as the right one.

example.en: “The blue key?” “That's it!”

cardCatalog.noteEn: Esos points to masculine plural people or things that are not right beside the speaker. It changes to esas before feminine plural nouns.

example.en: Those books are new.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Espacial can also mean spatial in other contexts. After transbordador, it identifies a space shuttle.

example.en: They study space exploration.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Espantapájaros combines a form related to espantar, “to scare away,” with pájaros, “birds.” The compound has the same form in singular and plural.

example.es: Hay un espantapájaros en el campo.
example.en: There is a scarecrow in the field.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Espectro can mean a continuous range, especially a range of wavelengths or frequencies. In other settings it can also mean a ghost, but that is not the sense taught here.

example.es: La luz ocupa una parte del espectro.
example.en: Light occupies one part of the spectrum.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Esperaba is a past form of esperar that presents the expectation as an existing background state rather than as one completed event.

example.en: I was expecting that answer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: wait; a formal command to one person
cardCatalog.noteEn: Espere tells usted, the polite singular ‘you,’ to wait. With a regular verb ending in -ar, the polite command changes that ending to -e: esperar becomes espere. The informal command is espera.

example.en: Wait here, please.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Esperemos is a special nosotros form of esperar used to express a shared hope. A hoped-for event introduced by que follows in the subjunctive, the form used when that event is desired rather than stated as fact.

example.en: Let's hope she arrives soon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Esperar can mean either “to wait” or “to hope/expect.” When no hoped-for event or object follows, context can give it the simple meaning “to wait.”

example.en: I wait here.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you are (formal singular; a state or condition)

cardCatalog.noteEn: In está bien followed by an action, está introduces a general judgment. Spanish does not add a separate word for English “it.”

example.en: It is good to ask for help.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is; helps form an ongoing action
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before an action form ending in -ando or -iendo, está says that one other person or thing is doing that action now or around the time being discussed.

example.en: Marta is reading.

cardCatalog.answerEn: this one; this situation (standing without a following noun)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Esta can stand in for a feminine thing or situation that is already understood instead of appearing before a noun. Modern standard spelling normally leaves it without a written accent in this use.

example.en: I prefer this one.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estaba is a background-past form of estar. The subject can be I, he, she, or one formal you; here the unstated subject is the speaker.

example.en: I was tired after the trip.

cardCatalog.answerEn: was; forms an ongoing past action with an -ando or -iendo form
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estaba is a past form of estar for I, he, she, or one thing. Before an ongoing-action form such as parpadeando, it presents an action in progress in the past.

example.en: The light was flashing.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it was; used to be (a past state)
they were (in a state or condition)
you were (helper for an action in progress)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estabas is the informal-singular imperfect form of estar. Before an -ando or -iendo form, it presents what the listener was doing in the background.

example.en: You were reading when I called.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The -as ending matches more than one feminine thing being described.

example.en: The rules were established.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estableciendo is the ongoing-action form of establecer, ‘to establish.’ It ends in -iendo and is used here with a form of estar.

example.en: She is establishing a clear rule.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estableció is a completed-past form for one person, group, or institution.

example.es: El país estableció un nuevo sistema.
example.en: The country established a new system.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estado is the completed-action form of estar, the verb for being or being in a state. After a helper such as he, has, or ha, it supplies the idea “been” and does not change for the person.

example.en: I have been sick.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This is a condition or situation, not a political state.

example.es: Comprobamos el estado actual del sistema.
example.en: We check the current state of the system.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estadounidense can describe a person or thing from the United States. It has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns.

example.es: Una científica estadounidense dio la charla.
example.en: An American scientist gave the talk.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Una estafa is a dishonest scheme intended to take money, property, or some other benefit from someone.

example.es: El mensaje advierte sobre estafas por internet.
example.en: The message warns about online scams.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all are (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estáis is the present form of estar used with vosotros or vosotras when speaking informally to several people, mainly in Spain.

example.en: You all are at home.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we are (at a place or location)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estamos is the form of estar used with nosotros, ‘we.’ Use it for where a group is; somos instead gives an identity or defining description.

example.en: We have been here since early.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we are (helping to describe an action in progress)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estamos is the present form of estar for nosotros. Before a form ending in -ando or -iendo, it helps present an action as ongoing.

example.en: We are preparing dinner.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they are (in a place or state)
they are (helping to describe an action in progress)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here están is the plural form of estar used before an action ending in -ando or -iendo.

example.en: They are cooking.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they are (in a state or condition)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Están is the present form of estar for a plural subject. Estar commonly describes a current condition.

example.en: The children are calm.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish normally uses estar to say where a person or thing is. Estar is the verb's unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: I hope to be there tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to be (in a state or condition)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estar is the unchanged dictionary form used for states, conditions, and locations. After another conjugated verb, estar itself remains unchanged.

example.en: I want to be calm.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estarán is the third-person plural future form of estar.

example.en: Tomorrow they will be ready.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you must be; I suppose you are (a guess about now)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estarás has the form normally used for future 'you will be,' but Spanish can also use a future-shaped verb to make a tentative guess about the present. The context and questioning tone select that conjecture meaning.

example.en: You must be tired, I suppose?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estaré is the first-person future form of estar.

example.en: I will be at home tonight.

cardCatalog.answerEn: would be (helper before an ongoing action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estarían is the plural “would” form of estar. Before a form ending in -ando or -iendo, it helps describe what people or things would be doing.

example.en: At this time they would be working.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estarían keeps the full dictionary form estar and adds -ían. It can describe the later state of several people or things from a past point of view.

example.en: I thought they would be ready.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the East; a broad eastern geographic or cultural region
cardCatalog.noteEn: Este can name the compass direction or, by convention, a broad geographic or cultural region. The article el is used because the word is acting as a noun; context, not the article alone, selects the regional sense.

example.es: El libro compara el este con el oeste.
example.en: The book compares the East with the West.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Without a following noun, este can name the cardinal direction east; this is different from este meaning “this.”

example.es: El sol sale por el este.
example.en: The sun rises in the east.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is; am; are (special estar helper for an ongoing action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Esté is a subjunctive form of estar. Before an -ando or -iendo form, it helps present an ongoing action inside a pending, uncertain, or otherwise non-established situation.

example.en: Call me while I am traveling.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Este can stand without a following noun when the nearby masculine person or thing is clear. Before a noun, the same form simply means ‘this,’ as in este libro.

example.en: This is my neighbor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estimaron is the completed-past form of estimar for a plural subject.

example.en: They estimated the cost yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

example.en: This is difficult.

cardCatalog.answerEn: part of a todo esto: by the way; speaking of that
cardCatalog.noteEn: Inside this fixed transition, esto points back loosely to the topic before introducing a related thought.

example.en: By the way, what time is it?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses a form of estar, rather than ser, to say where someone or something is. Estoy is the form for the speaker.

example.en: I am at home.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I am (in a state or condition)

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a geography noun, estrecho names a narrow channel joining larger bodies of water. As an adjective, it can mean “narrow.”

example.en: The ship crossed the strait.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estrella can mean an astronomical star or a famous performer. The surrounding words determine the sense.

example.en: That star is very far away.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estrellarías is the conditional form used with te for the pronominal verb estrellarse, “to crash.” The ending -ías marks one familiar listener.

example.en: Without brakes, you would crash.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estrellas is the plural of estrella. It can name astronomical stars or star-shaped figures.

example.en: We saw many stars tonight.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estudiante can refer to a male or female student; the surrounding article or other context can show gender when it matters.

example.en: Ana is a chemistry student.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estudió is a completed-past form of estudiar. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: Rosa studied physics.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estudio can mean the act of studying, a research investigation, or a studio. A scientific or participant context points to the research meaning.

example.es: El hospital publicó un estudio nuevo.
example.en: The hospital published a new study.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estudios is the plural of estudio. In a scientific context it names research investigations rather than schoolwork or studios.

example.en: They compared several medical studies.

cardCatalog.answerEn: were; might be (a possibility form of estar)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Estuviera is a special past-looking form of estar used for past possibilities and for more distant or hypothetical ideas. After puede que, context can make it mean ‘might have been’ or a tentative ‘might be.’ The ordinary factual present form is está.

example.en: It might be good to wait.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Estuvo is a completed-past form of estar. With an evaluation such as bien or impresionante, it describes how an event or experience turned out.

example.en: The party was great.

cardCatalog.answerEn: aether; ether (an obsolete proposed medium for light)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In older physics, scientists proposed a substance called the luminiferous aether through which light would travel. Experiments and relativity made that idea unnecessary; this is different from the chemical substance ether.

example.es: En el siglo XIX, algunos científicos hablaban del éter.
example.en: In the nineteenth century, some scientists spoke about the aether.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Eternamente is formed from eterna plus -mente and describes how long an action can continue.

example.en: Nothing lasts forever.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Una eternidad often exaggerates how long something feels rather than literally claiming that it never ends.

example.en: The wait felt like an eternity.

cardCatalog.answerEn: labels; marks with a descriptive label
cardCatalog.noteEn: Etiqueta is a present form of etiquetar for one person or thing. On a graph, etiquetar los ejes means to state what each axis represents and often its units or scale.

example.es: La autora etiqueta cada eje del gráfico.
example.en: The author labels each axis of the graph.

cardCatalog.answerEn: labeled; marked with a label (feminine singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Etiquetada is the feminine singular completed-action form of etiquetar. As a describing word, it matches a feminine singular noun.

example.en: Follow the arrow labeled ‘exit.’

cardCatalog.noteEn: Etiquetadas is feminine plural. After las, it can stand for previously mentioned feminine plural things without repeating their noun: las etiquetadas means ‘the labeled ones.’

example.es: De las cajas, abre las etiquetadas ‘libros’.
example.en: Of the boxes, open the ones labeled ‘books.’

cardCatalog.noteEn: Evitando is evitar with the -ando ending, which presents the avoiding as accompanying another action.

example.es: Cruzó la plaza evitando la lluvia.
example.en: She crossed the square while avoiding the rain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Evitara is a past subjunctive form of evitar. It can describe a desired or not-yet-identified thing by the result it was supposed to achieve.

example.es: Buscaban una ruta que evitara el centro.
example.en: They were looking for a route that would avoid downtown.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to help it; to avoid it
cardCatalog.noteEn: Evitar means ‘to avoid,’ and lo, ‘it,’ is attached to the end. In no puedo evitarlo, natural English commonly says ‘I can't help it.’

example.en: I couldn't help it.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Exa- is placed before a unit to multiply it by one quintillion, or 10¹⁸.

example.en: Exa- represents a factor of 10¹⁸.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Exageras is the informal singular present form of exagerar.

example.en: I think you are exaggerating the problem.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Excelente can describe something of very high quality or stand alone as a positive reaction to news or a result.

example.en: ‘It is ready now.’ ‘Excellent!’

cardCatalog.noteEn: Excepcionalmente is built from the feminine form excepcional plus -mente and describes an unusually high degree or an exceptional manner.

example.en: The material is exceptionally light.

cardCatalog.noteEn: It describes questions or crises about existence, meaning, or purpose.

example.en: They debated existential questions.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Existió is a completed-past form of existir for one person or thing.

example.en: That bridge existed for centuries.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Exitosos describes several masculine or mixed-gender things.

example.en: They were successful projects.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Experimentar can mean to experience a feeling, condition, or situation directly; it need not mean conducting a scientific experiment.

example.en: We want to experience something new.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Explica is the present form of explicar for one person or thing. With a thing as its subject, it says that the thing provides the explanation.

example.en: That explains the delay.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Explicaba is a past form of explicar. Its -aba ending presents the explaining as part of the background or an ongoing past situation, without marking a separate completed endpoint.

example.en: The guide was explaining the map.

cardCatalog.answerEn: security exploit; a way to take advantage of a software flaw
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish computing language borrows the English noun exploit. It names code or a method that uses a vulnerability to make a system do something unintended.

example.en: The team fixed the exploit.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In this named logical principle, explosión refers to the result that any claim can be derived after a contradiction is accepted. In that technical sense it does not describe a physical blast.

example.es: La explosión es un resultado de la lógica clásica.
example.en: Explosion is a result in classical logic.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In storytelling, exposición is the information that introduces the situation, characters, or background before the main events.

example.es: La exposición presenta a los personajes.
example.en: The exposition introduces the characters.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Extiende is a present form of extender for él, ella, or usted, and it is also the positive command for informal singular tú. In this comic it labels the repeated action of the tape stretching outward.

example.es: La cinta se extiende dos metros.
example.en: The tape extends two meters.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With se, extinguió is a completed-past form of extinguirse for one species or thing.

example.es: Ese animal se extinguió hace mucho.
example.en: That animal became extinct long ago.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Extra usually stays unchanged after both masculine and feminine nouns: tiempo extra, puntuación extra, horas extra.

example.en: They gave us extra time.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With an article and no following noun, extraño can itself name a male stranger. This differs from the adjective extraño meaning “strange” or “weird.”

example.es: Un extraño llamó a la puerta.
example.en: A stranger knocked at the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Extraño can describe something as strange, but used as a noun for people it means strangers—people one does not know.

example.en: I don't talk to strangers.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to extrapolate; to extend a trend beyond the known data
cardCatalog.noteEn: Extrapolar means using an observed pattern to estimate what lies outside the observations already available.

example.es: No conviene extrapolar una tendencia a partir de dos datos.
example.en: It is unwise to extrapolate a trend from two data points.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fábrica is stressed on the first syllable, so the written accent is required. Fabrica without an accent is a verb form meaning ‘he, she, or it manufactures.’

example.en: The factory produces bicycles.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The opposite is difícil, ‘difficult.’ Fácil keeps its written accent in the singular.

example.en: The exercise is easy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Facilidad names ease or lack of difficulty. Con facilidad describes how something happens and is naturally translated as “easily.”

example.en: Ana learns languages easily.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Falla is a present form of fallar for he, she, or one thing. It describes a system or attempt that does not work as intended.

example.es: El programa falla con archivos grandes.
example.en: The program fails with large files.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For machines or components, fallar means to stop working correctly or fail.

example.es: Las baterías viejas fallan a menudo.
example.en: Old batteries often fail.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fallo can be an error, fault, or failure depending on context. With work such as a translation, the plural fallos names mistakes in the content.

example.en: The report contains several errors.

cardCatalog.answerEn: needed; necessary (as part of hacer falta)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Falta combines with a form of hacer to say that someone or something is needed. It stays singular in this expression even when hacen is plural.

example.en: Patience is needed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Falta is singular because the one missing thing controls the verb. For several missing things, Spanish uses faltan instead.

example.en: A page is missing.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a noun, familiar can mean ‘family’ or ‘family-related.’ It is a false friend here: it does not mean that the object looks familiar.

example.en: It is a family tradition.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Familiar can describe something connected with a family. It can also mean ‘familiar’ or name a relative in other settings, so context matters.

example.en: They organize family dinners on Sundays.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses the borrowed word fan for a devoted follower of a person, team, story, or cultural work. The plural can be fans.

example.en: She is a fan of that author.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fantabuloso is a playful blend shaped like fantástico plus fabuloso rather than a standard neutral word. It can convey exaggerated enthusiasm or delight.

example.en: He described the party as fantabulous.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fantasma ends in -a but is normally masculine when it names a ghost: el fantasma.

example.en: The castle has a ghost.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fantasma is grammatically masculine despite ending in -a: el fantasma, los fantasmas.

example.es: El cuento habla de dos fantasmas.
example.en: The story is about two ghosts.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fase is a feminine noun for one stage within a longer process, project, or relationship.

example.es: El proyecto entró en una fase nueva.
example.en: The project entered a new phase.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fastidiado is the completed-action form of fastidiar, ‘to annoy’ or ‘to bother.’ After a form of haber such as ha, it stays unchanged.

example.es: Ese ruido me ha fastidiado todo el día.
example.en: That noise has bothered me all day.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fastidies is the special form of fastidiar used after no to tell one familiar person not to bother or annoy someone. The complete exclamation no fastidies also has a common idiomatic use taught separately.

example.en: Do not bother your brother.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Favorito can stand without a repeated noun when the noun is already understood: mi favorito means “my favorite one.”

example.es: De todos los libros, este es mi favorito.
example.en: Of all the books, this one is my favorite.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fecha is the calendar date associated with an event or document.

example.es: Escribe la fecha en la primera línea.
example.en: Write the date on the first line.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Use ¡felicidades! to congratulate someone on good news or an achievement.

example.en: Congratulations on the prize!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Femenino is masculine singular here because it describes the masculine word nick.

example.en: She chose a feminine name.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Ferdinand (part of the band name Franz Ferdinand)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pheromones are chemical signals released by an organism that affect members of the same species.

example.en: Ants follow pheromones.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ferry is a borrowed noun used in Spanish for a boat that carries passengers or vehicles across water.

example.es: El ferry sale a las nueve.
example.en: The ferry leaves at nine.

cardCatalog.answerEn: a hiss or burst of radio static
cardCatalog.noteEn: Repeated f sounds imitate the hiss of a radio transmission. Spellings for sound effects can vary because they represent a noise rather than an ordinary spoken word.

example.en: The radio answered with a burst of static.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ffshhh is an extended written sound effect for liquid rushing through an outlet.

example.en: The pipe went “ffshhh” when it opened.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A fiasco is a conspicuous failure, especially one involving confusion, poor planning, or public embarrassment.

example.en: The launch was a fiasco.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Fibonacci (name associated with a famous number sequence)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Fibonacci is the conventional name of the sequence in which each later number is the sum of the two before it.

example.en: We are studying the Fibonacci sequence.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In Spain, fichero is a common word for a computer file. It can also mean a physical file or collection of records in other contexts.

example.es: Guarda el fichero en esta carpeta.
example.en: Save the file in this folder.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fijo describes something that stays set rather than changing.

example.es: El aparato mantiene un ritmo fijo.
example.en: The device keeps a fixed rhythm.

cardCatalog.answerEn: end; part of fin de semana, “weekend”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Fin literally means “end.” In the fixed expression fin de semana, the three words together name the weekend.

example.es: El fin de semana fue tranquilo.
example.en: The weekend was quiet.

cardCatalog.answerEn: late part; end (in a finales de)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Final means “end.” Its plural form finales is used in a finales de to locate something near the end of a month, year, decade, or other period.

example.es: La tienda abrió a finales de verano.
example.en: The store opened in late summer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: ends; part of fines de semana, “weekends”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Fines is the plural of fin. In fines de semana, only fin becomes plural; semana stays singular inside the established expression.

example.en: We rest on weekends.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fingiendo is the -iendo form of fingir and presents pretending as an activity in progress.

example.en: She is pretending to sleep.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Finjo is the present ‘I’ form of fingir, ‘to pretend.’ Its g changes to j before the ending -o.

example.en: I pretend to be busy.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Fire (part of the band name Arcade Fire)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Firmaron is firmar's completed-past form for more than one person.

example.en: The ministers signed the agreement.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Firmas is the plural of firma.

example.en: The document needs two signatures.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Firmé is the completed-past form of firmar used by the speaker. With a cryptographic public key, signing means digitally certifying the link between that key and an identity.

example.en: I signed the document this morning.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With mano, firme describes a hand that does not shake and can make precise movements.

example.es: Dibuja la línea con mano firme.
example.en: Draw the line with a steady hand.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When firme describes a voice or tone, it means controlled, confident, and not yielding. This is different from merely saying that a hand or object does not shake.

example.en: She answered in a firm voice.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Físico can describe something related to physics or the physical world. As a noun, físico can instead mean “physicist.”

example.en: They built a physical model.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Físico can be an adjective meaning “physical,” but here it is a noun for a person who works in physics.

example.en: The physicist studies light.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, físicos names people who work in physics. The same written form can be an adjective meaning “physical” when it describes a plural masculine noun.

example.en: The physicists compare the data.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Flash is the unchanged name of an older multimedia platform. In a phrase such as juegos Flash, it identifies the technology used to make or run the games.

example.es: El museo conserva una animación Flash.
example.en: The museum preserves a Flash animation.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Flash is a borrowed English noun commonly used in Spanish for a brief burst of light. This is different from Flash as the name of Adobe's former multimedia platform.

example.es: Vimos un flash en el cielo.
example.en: We saw a flash in the sky.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A fleco is literally a fringe or dangling edge. In work that is almost finished, plural flecos can figuratively mean small details still needing attention.

example.en: A few loose ends remain to be resolved.

cardCatalog.answerEn: floop; a long sliding or unrolling sound

cardCatalog.noteEn: Floosh is a written sound effect for water moving suddenly through a pipe or drain.

example.en: The water went “floosh” as it went down.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Flores is the plural of flor.

example.en: The garden has yellow flowers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Flotará is the future form of flotar for one person or thing.

example.es: La boya flotará hasta la costa.
example.en: The buoy will float to the coast.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fluida describes something that moves or works without interruptions. In de forma fluida, it matches the feminine noun forma while the full expression describes how an action happens.

example.es: La animación se reproduce de forma fluida.
example.en: The animation plays smoothly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Flujo can describe movement through a process. In diagrama de flujo, it refers to the routes that connect steps and decisions; this is broader than a stream of data or one program's control flow.

example.es: El diagrama muestra el flujo del trabajo.
example.en: The diagram shows the workflow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: flow; order in which a program runs
cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, flujo can describe the path and order that program instructions follow. This is distinct from a stream of data.

example.es: El bucle cambia el flujo del programa.
example.en: The loop changes the program's flow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fondo more often means “bottom,” “background,” or “fund.” As a figurative use influenced by English, it can also refer to a pool of available people.

example.es: La empresa eligió entre un fondo amplio de candidatos.
example.en: The company chose from a large pool of candidates.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fondo can mean a fund or reserve of money. In a financial context it can point to the resources or value someone has, rather than its more common physical meaning “bottom” or “background.”

example.en: The fund retains its resources.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fondo can mean a bottom or depth. In the fixed expression a fondo, that image becomes the idea of doing something thoroughly, fully, or all-out.

example.en: I know the subject thoroughly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fondos can mean money made available for a project or organization, not only physical bottoms or backgrounds.

example.en: The project needs more funding.

cardCatalog.answerEn: forged; shaped by heating and hammering (feminine singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Forjada is the feminine singular form used for something made by forging metal. With a form of ser, it can describe what was done to that thing.

example.es: La pieza fue forjada a mano.
example.en: The piece was forged by hand.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An opinión formada is a view that someone has already developed and settled on. Formada is feminine singular because it describes opinión.

example.es: Todavía no tengo una opinión formada.
example.en: I do not yet have a settled opinion.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In de formas followed by a description, formas means ways or manners of doing something.

example.en: They work in different ways.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Forzará is the future form of forzar for one person or thing. Spanish keeps the dictionary form forzar and adds the ending -á.

example.en: The change will force a decision.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fosa literally names a pit or cavity. In fosa séptica, the whole expression names a septic tank.

example.es: La casa usa una fosa séptica.
example.en: The house uses a septic tank.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A fotograma is one still image in a film, animation, or video sequence.

example.en: They analyzed every frame of the video.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A fotograma is one still image in a film, animation, or video sequence.

example.es: El vídeo tiene treinta fotogramas por segundo.
example.en: The video has thirty frames per second.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fracasado is the completed-action form of fracasar used after a form of haber.

example.en: The first attempt has failed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Francamente is an adverb formed from franca plus -mente.

example.en: Frankly, I do not agree.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Franz (part of the band name Franz Ferdinand)

cardCatalog.noteEn: For dialogue in a film or play, frase can refer to a spoken line.

example.es: Recuerdo una frase de la película.
example.en: I remember a line from the movie.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you frequent; you regularly visit or use
cardCatalog.noteEn: Frecuentar means to go to or use a place regularly. Frecuentas is the present form for informal singular you.

example.en: Do you frequent this library?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Freirá is the future form of freír for he, she, or formal you. With electronics, freír can figuratively mean to destroy or burn out the device.

example.es: El exceso de voltaje freirá el circuito.
example.en: The excess voltage will fry the circuit.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fresquita comes from fresca plus the affectionate or softening ending -ita. It is feminine singular because it describes agua, a feminine noun.

example.en: We drank nice cool water.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fría describes one feminine person or thing and carries a written accent on í.

example.en: The water is cold.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Frigorífico is a common word in Spain for a refrigerator. It keeps a written accent on rí.

example.es: La leche está en el frigorífico.
example.en: The milk is in the refrigerator.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Friki is an informal Spanish noun borrowed from English “freak.” The plural frikis can refer to enthusiasts with intense or specialized interests; tone determines whether it sounds affectionate or mocking.

example.es: Los frikis del cine conocen cada detalle.
example.en: The film geeks know every detail.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Friki is an informal Spanish description borrowed from English “freak.” It can be a noun for a geek or an adjective for geeky interests or people; here it describes a plural group.

example.en: We love geeky movies.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Frío is the masculine singular temperature adjective. After más with a definite comparison it can mean ‘coldest.’

example.es: Enero fue el mes más frío.
example.en: January was the coldest month.

cardCatalog.answerEn: cold; far from the target in a hot-and-cold game
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the guessing game, temperature words describe distance rather than actual heat. Frío tells the searcher that they are far from the hidden object or chosen place.

example.en: Cold! Look in another room.

cardCatalog.answerEn: was (a completed past instance of ser)
were; were the case, in an unreal condition
cardCatalog.noteEn: Fuera is a special form of ser used for a hypothetical situation. In si no fuera por..., it introduces something without which the result would be different. Do not confuse it with fuera meaning “outside.”

example.es: Si fuera fácil, todos lo harían.
example.en: If it were easy, everyone would do it.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they suited him; they were his kind of thing
cardCatalog.noteEn: Fueron is the completed-past plural form of ir. With me, te, le, nos, or les, ir can say that plural things suit or appeal to someone rather than that they physically go somewhere.

example.es: Nunca me fueron las fiestas grandes.
example.en: Big parties were never my thing.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fuerte has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns; its plural is fuertes.

example.en: We need a strong rope.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fui is the irregular completed-past form of ser used for yo. The same form can also be the completed past of ir, “I went”; context distinguishes them.

example.en: I was able to solve it.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Funcionado is the completed-action form of funcionar and follows a form of haber.

example.en: The plan has worked.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Funcionan is the present-time plural form of funcionar.

example.en: These machines work well.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Funcionara is a hypothetical past form of funcionar. After si, it presents something as imagined rather than stating that it really works.

example.es: Si el plan funcionara, ahorraríamos tiempo.
example.en: If the plan worked, we would save time.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Funcione comes from funcionar. After an expression of possibility such as puede que, ordinary funciona changes its final -a to -e because the result is not stated as certain.

example.en: It may work tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: furry; related to fans of anthropomorphic animal characters
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish commonly borrows the English word furry for this subculture. When it modifies an event or group, it is often left unchanged for gender and number.

example.es: Hay una convención furry este fin de semana.
example.en: There is a furry convention this weekend.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In most Spanish-speaking contexts fútbol refers to association football, called soccer in North American English.

example.en: We play soccer on Saturdays.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Fwoosh is a comic sound effect for a fast rush through air or water.

example.es: El objeto cayó con un fwoosh.
example.en: The object fell with a fwoosh.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gafas is normally used in the plural for eyeglasses, even when referring to one pair.

example.en: I need my glasses to read.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Galáctico describes something related to a galaxy. The feminine form is galáctica, and the plural forms are galácticos and galácticas.

example.en: They imagined a galactic journey.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gamma is the name of a Greek letter used in the scientific term rayos gamma. In that expression it identifies very high-frequency electromagnetic radiation.

example.en: The instrument detects gamma rays.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With tiempo, ganar means to obtain extra time before something happens.

example.es: La pausa nos permite ganar tiempo.
example.en: The pause lets us buy time.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gandulear is informal and describes spending time idly instead of working.

example.en: Today I want to laze around at home.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Carl Friedrich Gauss was a German mathematician. His name appears in terms connected with the normal distribution and its bell-shaped curve.

example.es: La campana de Gauss tiene dos colas.
example.en: The Gaussian bell curve has two tails.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Geek is an English borrowing used informally in Spanish for someone intensely interested in technology or another specialized subject. Friki is another common Spanish option.

example.es: Es un geek de la informática.
example.en: He is a computer geek.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The complete expression en general means “in general” or “overall.”

example.en: In general, the plan works.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Genética is the feminine singular adjective related to genes or heredity.

example.en: They study genetic diversity.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Genéticos describes masculine plural things as related to genes, inheritance, or a process modeled on biological evolution.

example.en: They study several genetic factors.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Geniales has one form for masculine and feminine plural subjects.

example.en: Both ideas are brilliant.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gilipollas is a strong informal insult widely associated with Spain. It can keep the same form for a man or a woman.

example.en: Don't be a jerk.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gilipolleces is a strongly informal and vulgar plural. The singular gilipollez can mean one stupid or nonsensical thing.

example.en: Stop talking bullshit.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gira tells one familiar person to turn. It comes from girar, “to turn.”

example.en: Turn here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Globo can name a small rubber balloon or a larger balloon used to rise through the air.

example.es: El globo ascendió sobre el campo.
example.en: The balloon rose over the field.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Glups imitates the sound of swallowing and is written as a reaction when someone suddenly feels afraid, worried, or embarrassed.

example.en: Gulp! I forgot the keys.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A golpe is a sudden impact. In darse un golpe, it commonly refers to bumping or hurting oneself.

example.es: Oí un golpe en la puerta.
example.en: I heard a knock at the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Golpeando is the action form of golpear ending in -ando. Used without a form of estar, it can explain the action used to accomplish something, much like English “by tapping.”

example.en: She tested the wall by tapping gently.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Golpear is the unchanged dictionary form ‘to hit,’ and attached te identifies the informal singular person being hit.

example.en: I do not want to hit you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gominola is a common word in Spain for a small chewy sweet. In this comic, the colored pieces correspond to jelly beans.

example.en: We bought a bag of gummy sweets.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gordo normally means fat or thick. In the body-part name dedo gordo, it identifies the big toe.

example.en: The big toe is swollen.

cardCatalog.answerEn: became etched; became fixed (in memory, with se)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Grabar literally means to record or engrave. In se grabó en la memoria or en el recuerdo, it describes an image or experience becoming firmly fixed in someone's memory.

example.es: La escena se grabó en su memoria.
example.en: The scene became etched in her memory.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Graciosas is the feminine plural form of gracioso, matching more than one feminine noun.

example.en: They are funny stories.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here gráfica is a visual display of data, not the feminine form of an adjective meaning ‘graphic.’

example.en: The chart shows the temperatures.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Grande shortens to gran directly before a singular noun. Before a person or work, gran often praises quality or importance rather than physical size.

example.en: Ana is a great doctor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Grande shortens to gran when it appears directly before a singular noun. With an amount such as a budget, gran describes large size.

example.es: El proyecto necesita un gran presupuesto.
example.en: The project needs a large budget.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Grande shortens to gran directly before a singular noun. Here it describes importance or significance rather than physical size.

example.en: We made a major decision.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The singular granada means ‘pomegranate’ here; in another context it can mean ‘grenade.’

example.en: Pomegranates have many seeds.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Grande has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: We saw a large circle.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gratis does not change for gender or number.

example.en: Admission is free.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gratuita is the feminine singular form because it describes a feminine singular thing such as muestra.

example.en: Admission is free.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In physics, gravedad is the force that attracts masses. In ordinary speech, the same word can also mean seriousness or severity.

example.es: La gravedad atrae los objetos hacia la Tierra.
example.en: Gravity pulls objects toward Earth.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Griegos describes masculine plural people or things associated with Greece or the Greek language.

example.en: We study several Greek symbols.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gritando is the ongoing-action form of gritar. When it appears on its own after another action, it can add how that action was happening.

example.en: He came in screaming.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In software, guardar means storing the current file or changes. Outside computing it can also mean keeping or putting something away.

example.en: Do not forget to save the document.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Guardia can name a person whose job is to protect or watch a place. The noun keeps the ending -a even when the person is male.

example.en: The guard watches the entrance.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Guau can express surprise or admiration. The same spelling can imitate a dog's bark in a different setting.

example.en: Wow, what a change!

cardCatalog.answerEn: cool; awesome (plural, informal, especially in Spain)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Guía can name a person who leads others or a written explanation that helps someone understand or do something. The surrounding context selects the sense.

example.en: I read a beginner's guide.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Guiará combines the unchanged verb guiar with the -á future ending for one person or thing.

example.en: The sign will guide you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Guiaría combines guiar with the -ía ending to describe what someone or something would do.

example.en: She would guide us well.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Guionista names someone who writes scripts for film, television, radio, or similar productions. The same ending is used for men and women; the article shows the gender when needed.

example.es: Las guionistas preparan una nueva serie.
example.en: The screenwriters are preparing a new series.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Guitar (part of the video-game title Guitar Hero)

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, a gusano is malicious code that can copy itself and spread from one system to another, often through a network.

example.es: Los gusanos se propagaron por la red.
example.en: The worms spread through the network.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I like; is pleasing to me
cardCatalog.noteEn: With me before it, gusta expresses that one thing or situation is pleasing to the speaker. The liked thing controls the verb: use gusta for one thing and gustan for more than one.

example.en: I like this book.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they like; is pleasing to them
cardCatalog.noteEn: Gusta remains singular when what is liked is one activity in its unchanged dictionary form, even when the people who like it are plural.

example.en: They like reading.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you like; is pleasing to you
are liked; appeal (used with plural liked things)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Gustan is plural because the things liked are plural. The person who likes them is identified separately by me, te, le, nos, os, or les.

example.en: I like these songs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Gustaría is gustar with the ending -ía. With a short word such as me, te, or le, it politely says who would like something: me gustaría means “I would like.”

example.en: I would like to rest.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you appeal; I like you (with me)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Gustas is the informal singular “you” form because the person being liked is the grammatical subject. Me identifies the speaker as the person who feels the liking.

example.en: I like you a lot.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all have (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Habéis is the present helper form of haber used with vosotros or vosotras. It comes before a completed-action form such as llegado or oído.

example.en: You all have arrived early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a verb such as debería, haber remains in its dictionary form and combines with a completed-action form such as llamado or comido. In this construction, haber is a helper rather than the hay construction meaning “there is.”

example.en: He could have called.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to have, with me attached for the speaker
cardCatalog.noteEn: Haberme combines the unchanged helper haber with me. A completed-action form follows it, and me belongs to that following action: haberme equivocado, haberme levantado, or haberme olvidado.

example.en: I may have become confused.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to have ... you (helper haber with te attached)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Haber is the unchanged helper used before a completed-action form. Te is attached to its end and marks informal singular 'you' as the person affected by the later action.

example.en: I should have called you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This past form of hay presents something as existing in a past setting. In this use, había stays singular even before a plural noun: había una silla and había dos sillas.

example.es: Había dos cartas en la mesa.
example.en: There were two letters on the table.

cardCatalog.answerEn: had (helper for an earlier completed action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a completed-action form such as escrito, había is a past form of the helper haber. It places one completed action before another point in the past.

example.en: I had already eaten when you called.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Había is the past form used to say that something existed or was present. In standard Spanish it stays singular even when the thing mentioned is plural.

example.es: Había tres sillas en la sala.
example.en: There were three chairs in the room.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Habitación usually means a room, especially a bedroom or hotel room. Habitaciones is the plural.

example.en: The house has four rooms.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hábitos are repeated behaviors or routines. The written accent remains in the plural.

example.es: Estudian los hábitos nocturnos de las aves.
example.en: They study the birds' nighttime habits.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Habla normally relates to speaking, but al habla is a fixed telephone response meaning that the requested person is the one speaking. Habla is not a command here.

example.en: —Ana Ruiz? —Speaking.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Habla is a feminine noun, but in the singular it uses el because its first a sound is stressed: el habla. It returns to las in the plural: las hablas.

example.es: El habla cambia de una región a otra.
example.en: Speech changes from one region to another.

cardCatalog.answerEn: talk; speak (command to several people, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hablad is the positive command for vosotros or vosotras, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain. It comes from hablar by replacing the final -r with -d.

example.en: Speak calmly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hablamos is the present form of hablar for nosotros. A time word or a clear sequence can give this present form an immediate future meaning.

example.es: Termina el informe y mañana hablamos.
example.en: Finish the report and we'll talk tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hablando is the -ando action form of hablar, “to speak.” This form can add an action happening at the same time.

example.en: He left while talking on the phone.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to speak to you all (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hablaros joins hablar, the unchanged dictionary form meaning ‘to speak,’ with os, the short word for several people addressed informally in Spain.

example.en: I want to speak to you all about an idea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hable is the polite command form of hablar for one person addressed as usted. Regular verbs ending in -ar replace that ending with -e in this command.

example.en: Speak more slowly, please.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hablo is the present form of hablar for yo. Spanish can use this simple present for an action happening now where English naturally uses ‘am talking.’

example.en: I am talking with Marta now.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Habrá is the future existence form of haber. It uses the irregular future stem habr- plus -á and stays singular even when what will exist is plural.

example.en: There will be more options tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: will have (helper for a completed future action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Habrá is the future form of the helper haber for one person or thing. Before a completed-action form such as terminado, it helps build “will have finished.”

example.en: Marta will have finished tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Habría followed by a completed-action form such as roto describes a past result that did not actually happen or was only imagined.

example.es: Sin el mapa, me habría perdido.
example.en: Without the map, I would have gotten lost.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Habríamos is the “we would have” form of the helper verb haber. It combines with a completed-action form such as visto.

example.en: We would have arrived earlier.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer usually means “to do” or “to make,” but hacer una pregunta is the normal expression for “to ask a question.”

example.en: She asks a question.

cardCatalog.answerEn: does; does so (replacing an earlier action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer normally means “to do” or “to make.” With lo, a form of hacer can stand in for a whole action already mentioned so that the speaker does not repeat that action.

example.es: A veces falla, pero cuando lo hace, avisa.
example.en: Sometimes it fails, but when it does, it gives a warning.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it has been; for (introducing elapsed time)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before an amount of time and que, hace measures how long a situation has continued. It is an impersonal form of hacer: it stays hace rather than changing to match a person.

example.es: Hace una semana que estudio aquí.
example.en: I have studied here for a week.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

example.en: I arrived two hours ago.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all do; you all make (informal plural, mainly Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacéis is the present-time form of hacer used with vosotros, the informal ‘you all’ used mainly in Spain. In most of Latin America, speakers normally use ustedes hacen instead.

example.en: You all do good work.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we become (as part of nos hacemos + description)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Nos hacemos uses a form of hacer with nos to describe a gradual or chosen change. The following word names the new state.

example.es: Con los años nos hacemos más pacientes.
example.en: Over the years we become more patient.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacen normally means ‘they make,’ but se hacen followed by a description can say that several things become or grow that way.

example.en: The nights grow cold.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacen is the plural present form of hacer. Before another action verb, it can mean that something causes a person to do or experience that action.

example.en: Those photos make me smile.

cardCatalog.answerEn: are (as part of hacen falta, are needed)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In hacer falta, hacer changes to agree with what is needed. Hacen is used when the needed people or things are plural.

example.en: Two chairs are needed.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to make; to cause (someone to do something)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer followed by que and a changed verb form can mean causing or making another person perform an action. This is a different sense from hacer meaning simply “to do.”

example.es: El ruido hizo que todos salieran.
example.en: The noise made everyone leave.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer can mean creating or producing a physical thing. This is distinct from its very common sense “to do.”

example.en: We are going to make a table.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to make; to turn into a new result
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer can describe causing a person or thing to become something new. The rest of the construction identifies what changes and the resulting role, state, or description.

example.es: La noticia hizo feliz a Marta.
example.en: The news made Marta happy.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to do; to perform or play (a tune)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer broadly means “to do” or “to make.” With a routine, imitation, version, or piece of music, it can mean doing or performing it; tocar is the more specific verb for playing an instrument.

example.es: El grupo hizo una versión acústica.
example.en: The band did an acoustic version.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer is the unchanged dictionary form ‘to do.’ Las is attached to its end and stands for feminine plural things already mentioned.

example.en: I prefer to do them tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to take a photo of it or them (in hacerle una foto)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacerle combines hacer with the indirect-object pronoun le. In hacerle una foto a algo or alguien, the full expression means “to take a photo of it or them.”

example.es: Quiero hacerle una foto al edificio.
example.en: I want to take a photo of the building.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to hurt me; to do harm to me (with daño supplied by context)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacerme joins the unchanged verb hacer to me, which marks the speaker as affected. When daño has already been named, hacerme can carry the sense of doing that harm to me without repeating daño.

example.en: You could not hurt me that much.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacérmelo joins hacer with me for the affected person and lo for the understood action or thing. The written accent keeps the original stress after both short words are attached.

example.en: The doctor can do it to me today.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to get ourselves; to take (a test) ourselves
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer is the unchanged action form and nos is attached to identify the speaker's group. With una prueba, hacerse commonly means to get or take a test.

example.es: Vamos a hacernos una prueba médica.
example.en: We are going to get a medical test.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to give each other; helps express mutual affection with arrumacos
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacer normally means ‘to do’ or ‘to make.’ Its attached se can show that two or more people exchange the action. In hacerse arrumacos, the whole expression describes affectionate cuddling or caressing.

example.en: The friends give each other gifts.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to become; to get (speaking to one familiar person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacerte joins hacer, the unchanged dictionary form, to te, the short word for the familiar person addressed. With an adjective after it, hacerse can mean “to become.”

example.en: You can become famous.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to hurt you; to cause you harm (with daño)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hacerte joins the unchanged verb hacer to te, which identifies one familiar person as affected. In hacerte daño, daño supplies the harm and the complete expression means to hurt you.

example.en: I do not want to hurt you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Haciendo is the -iendo form of hacer. Without a form of estar, it can describe how another action happens or what someone does at the same time.

example.en: We learn by asking questions.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Haciendo is the -iendo action form of hacer. It can name an activity happening during the time described.

example.es: Pasó la tarde haciendo una mesa.
example.en: He spent the afternoon making a table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Haciéndolo joins haciendo, the ongoing-action form of hacer, to lo, “it.” The written accent keeps the original stress in the same place after lo is attached.

example.en: Keep doing it that way.

cardCatalog.answerEn: becomes (special form of hacerse after an uncertain possibility)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Haga is a changed form of hacer. With se and a describing word, it belongs to hacerse, “to become.” After an expression of uncertainty or probability, Spanish often changes se hace to se haga.

example.es: Es posible que se haga famoso.
example.en: It is possible that he will become famous.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses hacer una foto where English uses “take a photo.” Hago is the yo form of hacer.

example.es: Le hago una foto al edificio.
example.en: I take a photo of the building.

cardCatalog.answerEn: haiku; a short Japanese poetic form
cardCatalog.noteEn: Haiku is used in Spanish for the Japanese poetic form. Here it names the poem type, not the Haiku operating system.

example.es: Escribió un haiku sobre la lluvia.
example.en: She wrote a haiku about the rain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hallado is the past participle of hallar. After a form of haber, it helps describe a completed action.

example.en: They have found a solution.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hará is the future form of hacer for one person or thing.

example.es: El cambio hará que trabajemos mejor.
example.en: The change will make us work better.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they will do; they will make
