cardCatalog.noteEn: Harán is the future form of hacer used with ellos or ellas. The same form can also mean “you all will do” with ustedes when the listeners are the subject.

example.en: They will do the work tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they will become (as part of se harán)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Harán is hacer's future form for more than one subject. With se and a description, hacerse means to become; hacer uses the irregular future stem har-.

example.es: Los días se harán más largos.
example.en: The days will become longer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: hardware; the physical parts of a computer or electronic system
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hardware is a standard technical borrowing in Spanish. It contrasts with software, the programs and instructions rather than the physical equipment.

example.es: El fallo está en el hardware.
example.en: The fault is in the hardware.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we would do; we would make
cardCatalog.noteEn: Haríamos is the conditional form of hacer for nosotros, or “we.” The conditional often describes what would happen in an imagined situation.

example.en: We would do it tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: getting fed up; becoming tired of it (the speaker)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hartarse means to become fed up. The -ando form presents that change as an ongoing action, and the attached me identifies the speaker.

example.en: I'm getting fed up with the noise.

cardCatalog.answerEn: fed up; sick and tired (masculine singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Harto describes someone who has had enough. It changes to harta, hartos, or hartas to match the person or people being described, and de can introduce what caused the frustration.

example.en: I am fed up with waiting.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a place, hasta marks the endpoint reached by movement. English often uses simply to, while as far as makes the endpoint emphasis explicit.

example.en: We walked to the station.

cardCatalog.answerEn: as far as (setting a limit on knowledge)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In hasta donde alguien sabe, hasta marks the boundary of that person's knowledge rather than a physical destination.

example.es: Hasta donde sé, la tienda abre hoy.
example.en: As far as I know, the store opens today.

cardCatalog.answerEn: one must; it is necessary (as part of hay que)
is; is located (inside a relative description)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hay normally means “there is” or “there are.” Inside a description with que, natural English can instead use “is,” as in la mesa que hay aquí, “the table that is here.”

example.es: La tienda que hay junto al banco cierra tarde.
example.en: The shop next to the bank closes late.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is up; is going on (as part of ¿qué hay?)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hay ordinarily means ‘there is’ or ‘there are.’ In the fixed casual question ¿Qué hay?, it helps ask ‘What's up?’ or ‘What's going on?’ rather than literally asking for an inventory.

example.en: —What's up? —Nothing new.

cardCatalog.answerEn: there is; there is to be (subjunctive form)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Haya is the special form related to hay, ‘there is’ or ‘there are.’ It appears when the existence of something is awaited, wanted, doubted, or otherwise not presented as an established fact.

example.en: I am waiting for there to be space.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all have (informal plural, in a non-factual or open-ended clause)
we have (special form before a completed action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hayamos is the we-form of haber used when the completed event is evaluated, desired, doubted, or otherwise not simply asserted as a fact. It combines with a completed-action form such as estado or llegado.

example.en: I'm glad we have finished.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Haz is the irregular positive command of hacer for one familiar person.

example.en: Make a list.

cardCatalog.answerEn: make me; give me (informal singular command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Haz is the irregular positive command of hacer for one person addressed informally. Me attaches to its end and identifies the speaker as the person receiving or benefiting from what is made.

example.en: Make me a list, please.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Haz is the irregular positive command of hacer for one familiar listener. Te is attached to its end and presents the result as being made or obtained for that listener.

example.en: Make yourself a cup of tea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hecha is the feminine singular form of hecho. With estar hecha de, it describes the material composing a feminine singular thing.

example.es: La caja está hecha de cartón.
example.en: The box is made of cardboard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hecho is the irregular completed-action form of hacer. With se and a form of haber, it helps form hacerse + description, meaning to become or grow into a new state. After haber, hecho does not change to match a feminine or plural subject.

example.es: El barrio se ha hecho famoso.
example.en: The neighborhood has become famous.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here hecho is the completed-action form of hacer in the pattern that makes someone do something.

example.es: La broma nos ha hecho reír.
example.en: The joke has made us laugh.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hecho is the irregular completed-action form of hacer, “to do” or “to make.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “done.”

example.en: I have already done the homework.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Standing alone, ¡hecho! announces that a task is complete. This differs from hecho after haber in he hecho, ‘I have done.’

example.en: Done! You can rest now.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Helio is the light chemical element used to make some balloons rise.

example.en: They filled the balloon with helium.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For connectors, hembra describes a socket that receives a plug. A repeated pair such as hembra-hembra says both ends are sockets.

example.en: This end is female.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For an animal, hembra identifies the female sex. It can follow the species noun and does not change for number in the same way as an ordinary adjective.

example.en: We saw two female wolves.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Herir can describe a physical wound or emotional hurt, especially with sentimientos (“feelings”).

example.en: I did not want to hurt her feelings.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Hero (part of the video-game title Guitar Hero)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Used as a masculine noun after un, híbrido can stand for an understood vehículo or coche híbrido.

example.en: They bought a small hybrid car.

cardCatalog.answerEn: hubris; excessive pride that invites a downfall
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hibris names overconfidence or arrogance, especially the kind that leads someone to overreach and suffer the consequences.

example.es: Su hibris le impidió escuchar las advertencias.
example.en: His hubris kept him from listening to the warnings.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hice is the completed-past form of hacer for the speaker.

example.en: I made dinner yesterday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: he would do; he did (special past form after para que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hiciera is a special past form of hacer used when a past action states the purpose or desired result of another past action. Ordinary hizo changes to hiciera after a frame such as para que.

example.es: Le escribí para que hiciera una copia.
example.en: I wrote to him so that he would make a copy.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I did (special past form used in “whatever I did”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hiciera is a special past form of hacer, “to do.” This form is called the imperfect subjunctive: it leaves possible past actions open rather than stating one as a fact. Repeating hiciera around lo que creates the reusable pattern hiciera lo que hiciera, “whatever I did.”

example.es: Hiciera lo que hiciera, el resultado era igual.
example.en: Whatever I did, the result was the same.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hicieron is the irregular completed-past form of hacer for a plural subject.

example.en: They asked several questions.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we had (as part of hacer un trío)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hicimos is hacer's completed-past form for ‘we.’ In hacer un trío, hacer is not the literal ‘make’ or ‘do’; the full expression means having a threesome.

example.es: Hicimos un trío con otra persona.
example.en: We had a threesome with another person.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hicimos is the completed-past ‘we’ form of hacer, ‘to do’ or ‘to make.’ Hacer changes its stem to hic- in this past tense, and hicimos has no written accent.

example.en: We made a table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hiela is a present form of helar. The e changes to ie in this form.

example.es: El lago se hiela en invierno.
example.en: The lake freezes in winter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hijos can mean sons, but the masculine plural also commonly refers to a group of children that includes a daughter.

example.es: Tienen un hijo y una hija: dos hijos en total.
example.en: They have a son and a daughter: two children in total.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hilo literally means ‘thread.’ Online, it names a connected discussion made of an opening post and its replies.

example.es: Leí todo el hilo del foro.
example.en: I read the whole forum thread.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hipster is an English loanword used in Spanish for a person linked to deliberately alternative tastes or style.

example.es: La revista describe un estilo hipster.
example.en: The magazine describes a hipster style.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hipster is a loanword used in Spanish for someone associated with deliberately alternative, fashionable, or non-mainstream tastes. The plural keeps the English-looking spelling hipsters.

example.es: Ese barrio atrae a muchos hipsters.
example.en: That neighborhood attracts many hipsters.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hissssss imitates a sustained hiss. Repeated s letters make the sound last longer on the page.

example.en: The snake went hiss.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Historiadores is a masculine or mixed-group plural for people who study and write about history.

example.en: The historians debated the date.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Históricos describes multiple masculine or mixed things connected with history.

example.en: We visited several historic places.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hobbit is a fantasy name used in Spanish; its plural is hobbits.

example.es: Los hobbits viven en la Comarca.
example.en: The hobbits live in the Shire.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hobby is an English loanword used in Spanish. A common Spanish alternative is afición or pasatiempo.

example.en: Photography is my hobby.

cardCatalog.noteEn: El hombre can refer collectively to humanity in older or literary language. La humanidad is a more explicitly inclusive choice in modern neutral prose.

example.es: La humanidad ha observado las estrellas durante siglos.
example.en: Humankind has observed the stars for centuries.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hombre usually names an adult male in this sense. It can also be used more broadly for humankind, which is a separate meaning.

example.en: That man is my neighbor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hora can name a length of sixty minutes as well as a clock time. A number before it makes the measured duration clear.

example.en: We waited for two hours.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After es, hora can identify the appropriate moment for an action rather than a clock hour.

example.en: It is time to begin.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Horribles has one form for masculine and feminine plural subjects.

example.en: Those noises are awful.

cardCatalog.answerEn: holy shit; damn (vulgar exclamation in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hostia has a religious literal origin, but as an exclamation in Spain it commonly expresses shock or alarm. It can sound vulgar or offensive, so it is unsuitable in formal settings.

example.en: Damn, what a scare!

cardCatalog.noteEn: House is an internationally used name for a style of electronic dance music.

example.en: The club plays house music.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hubiera is a special past form of haber. In a counterfactual result, it can combine with a completed-action form as an accepted alternative to habría: hubiera sido can mean “would have been.”

example.en: It would have been better to wait.

cardCatalog.answerEn: there were; there existed, in an unreal or wished-for situation
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hubiera is a special form of haber used when existence is imagined rather than presented as fact. After si, it often introduces a wish or an unreal condition.

example.en: If only there were a solution!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Hubo is the completed-past impersonal form of haber. It stays singular even when the thing mentioned afterward is plural.

example.en: There were two problems yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A huelga is a collective refusal to work, usually used to press for changes in pay or working conditions.

example.en: The workers are on strike.

cardCatalog.answerEn: human (a person, or a form of address)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Humano can be a noun for a human being as well as an adjective meaning ‘human.’ Used on its own while speaking to someone, it can address that person as ‘human.’

example.en: The robot greeted the human.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Huyen is huir's present form for a plural subject.

example.en: The animals flee from the fire.

cardCatalog.noteEn: IA is the Spanish abbreviation for inteligencia artificial. The initials appear in the opposite order from English because inteligencia comes before artificial.

example.en: AI analyzes the data.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we were going; we were planning (to do something)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Íbamos is a past form of ir. Before a and an unchanged action verb, it can present a plan viewed from the past, often one that was interrupted or not carried out.

example.en: We were going to call tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Idea ends in -a but is a feminine noun: una idea.

example.en: I have an idea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a technical problem, ideal describes components treated as perfectly matching a simplified model, without real-world imperfections.

example.en: The model uses idealized components.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Idéntica uses feminine singular -a to match a feminine noun and normally takes a before the thing used for comparison.

example.es: Esta copia es idéntica a la otra.
example.en: This copy is identical to the other one.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ignora is the affirmative command of ignorar for one familiar listener. The same spelling can also mean 'he, she, or it ignores,' so the surrounding instruction identifies the command.

example.en: Ignore that message.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ignoró is the completed-past form of ignorar for one person or thing. The written accent distinguishes this form from present-time ignoro, ‘I ignore.’

example.en: She ignored the warning.

cardCatalog.answerEn: doesn't matter (as part of da igual)
just like; the same as (with que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Igual normally means “equal” or “the same.” Followed by que and a comparison, it works as the common connector igual que, “just like” or “the same as.”

example.en: You sing just like Ana.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Igual can describe two or more experiences as the same.

example.en: The two versions sound the same.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Iluminadora describes something that makes an idea clearer or gives new understanding, not only something that produces physical light.

example.en: The talk was very enlightening.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Iluso can be a describing word or a noun for someone whose hopes or beliefs are unrealistic. The feminine form is ilusa.

example.es: Fui un iluso al creer esa promesa.
example.en: I was a fool to believe that promise.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Imaginar is the unchanged dictionary form “to imagine.” The attached lo means “it” and names what is being imagined.

example.en: I can't imagine it.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you imagine; you picture (yourself, with te)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Imaginas is the present form of imaginar for one informal listener. With te, it can introduce a scene in which that listener pictures themself doing something.

example.en: Can you imagine yourself living here?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Imbécil is a direct insult and can sound harsh. It is not a neutral description of a person.

example.en: Don't call him an idiot.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Imbécil can describe a person as very foolish and is normally insulting. The plural imbéciles carries a written accent.

example.en: Don't call them idiots.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For whole numbers, impar means odd: dividing it by two does not produce another whole number.

example.en: Nine is an odd number.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Imparable describes something that cannot be stopped. Its singular form is the same with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: The current seems unstoppable.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Imperio is a masculine noun, so a particular empire normally takes the article el.

example.en: The empire controlled several islands.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Impiden is the present form of impedir for a plural subject. A short word for the affected person normally comes before impiden, and the prevented action follows it.

example.en: The construction works prevent us from passing.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to implant in me; to put inside my body
cardCatalog.noteEn: Implantar is the unchanged dictionary form, and me attaches to identify the speaker as the person receiving the implant.

example.es: Van a implantarme un pequeño sensor.
example.en: They are going to implant a small sensor in me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Importan is plural because the things that matter are plural. Compare importa el detalle, “the detail matters,” with importan los detalles, “the details matter.”

example.en: The results matter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Importante has the same masculine and feminine singular form. The plural importantes ends in -es.

example.en: Several important matters remain.

cardCatalog.answerEn: would matter; mattered (a special past form after para que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Importar can mean to matter. Importara is a special past form used because the result after para que is blocked or not asserted as a fact. The ordinary background-past form would be importaba.

example.es: Era demasiado tarde para que importara.
example.en: It was too late for it to matter.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I matter; I am important to someone
cardCatalog.noteEn: Importo is the first-person singular form of importar in the sense of mattering.

example.es: Sé que importo a mis amigos.
example.en: I know that I matter to my friends.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Impresas is the completed-action form of imprimir used as a description. Its -as ending matches a feminine plural noun; masculine plural items would be impresos.

example.en: We kept the printed photos.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Impresiona is the present form used when one singular thing causes a strong reaction or makes an impression.

example.en: Her patience impresses me.

cardCatalog.answerEn: print (positive command to several people, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Replace imprimir's final -r with -d to make the vosotros command.

example.en: Print the form.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An impromptu is something said or done without preparation. Its plural is impromptus.

example.en: His improvised remarks surprised the audience.

cardCatalog.answerEn: improvised; made up on the spot
cardCatalog.noteEn: Improvisó is the completed-past form of improvisar for one person or thing.

example.en: The actress improvised an answer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: It refers to strong sudden desires or tendencies.

example.en: He controlled his urges to buy things.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inalcanzable has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns. Its plural is inalcanzables.

example.en: The goal seemed unattainable.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inamovible describes something that cannot be moved or shifted. Its singular form is the same with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: The rock seemed immovable.

cardCatalog.answerEn: becomes disabled; becomes unable to function (with se)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Incapacita is a present form of incapacitar. With se before it, the person or thing being described enters a disabled or nonfunctioning state rather than disabling something else.

example.es: El sistema se incapacita con el calor.
example.en: The system becomes unable to function in the heat.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they hit; strike (special purpose form after para que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Incidan comes from incidir. Ordinary inciden states that several things strike a surface; after para que, incidan presents that impact as the intended result. The special form is called the subjunctive.

example.es: Mueve el espejo para que los rayos incidan aquí.
example.en: Move the mirror so that the rays hit here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An incidente is an event or problem, especially one that is unusual or requires attention.

example.en: The technician documented the incident.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Incidentes is the plural of incidente.

example.en: The report lists several incidents.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Incluye is the present form of incluir used with one person, thing, group, or category.

example.en: The price includes breakfast.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Incluye tells one familiar listener to include something. The same written form can mean ‘he, she, or formal you includes’ in a statement; the advice context makes it a command here.

example.es: Incluye tu dirección en el formulario.
example.en: Include your address on the form.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Increíble has the same form for a masculine or feminine singular subject. Its plural is increíbles.

example.en: The view is amazing.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to set; to embed (a stone or decoration)

cardCatalog.noteEn: On a menu, individual says that an item is sized or intended for one person rather than for sharing.

example.en: We ordered two individual portions.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In electricity, inducir describes producing voltage or current through a changing magnetic field.

example.es: El imán puede inducir una corriente.
example.en: The magnet can induce a current.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inevitable has the same form with masculine and feminine singular nouns.

example.en: The change seems inevitable.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inextricable describes things connected so tightly that they cannot be separated or untangled.

example.en: The two problems are inextricable.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After cota, inferior identifies a minimum boundary rather than simply describing something as lower in physical position.

example.en: They proved a lower bound.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inferiores normally describes plural things as lower. With an article and no repeated noun, los inferiores means the lower masculine or mixed-group ones; context supplies the omitted noun.

example.es: Los cajones superiores están llenos; usa los inferiores.
example.en: The upper drawers are full; use the lower ones.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Infinita has a feminine ending because it describes the feminine noun malla.

example.en: Imagine an infinite line.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inflará is the future form of inflar for one person or thing.

example.en: The pump will inflate the balloon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Informa is a present-tense form of informar for él, ella, usted, or one named thing. The people who receive the information can follow with a.

example.es: La oficina informa a los clientes del retraso.
example.en: The office informs the clients of the delay.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here it describes plural feminine personas. Informático or informática can also name an IT professional.

example.es: Mis tías no son muy informáticas.
example.en: My aunts are not very computer-savvy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here informático describes an expert's technical field. As a noun, informático can also mean a male IT professional.

example.en: We need IT support.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ingredientes is the plural of ingrediente, one of the foods or materials combined in a recipe.

example.en: Mix all the ingredients.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Iniciado is the masculine singular completed-action form of iniciar. Used after a noun, it describes something that was started.

example.es: Es un proyecto iniciado en mayo.
example.en: It is a project started in May.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Insegura is feminine singular. Spanish describing words agree with the grammatical gender and number of what they describe.

example.en: Insecure people seek approval.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Insertando is insertar's ongoing-action form ending in -ando. It can follow a form of estar to describe an action in progress.

example.en: She is inserting an image.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to insist; to keep firmly claiming

cardCatalog.noteEn: Instaló is the completed-past form of instalar for one person or thing.

example.es: La técnica instaló el programa ayer.
example.en: The technician installed the program yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This feminine plural noun refers to steps that tell someone what to do.

example.es: Sigue las instrucciones de la pantalla.
example.en: Follow the instructions on the screen.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Insulina is a feminine noun for the hormone and medicine used to control blood sugar.

example.es: La insulina regula el azúcar en la sangre.
example.en: Insulin regulates blood sugar.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Intenta tells one person addressed informally to try something. The same written form can mean “he, she, or formal you tries” in a statement; context marks it as a command here.

example.en: Try to open the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Intenta is the affirmative command for one familiar person, and lo stands for the thing to try. Lo attaches to the command, and the written accent keeps the original stress: inténtalo.

example.en: Try it again.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Intentan is the present form of intentar for a plural subject.

example.en: They try to solve the problem.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Intentando is the -ando form of intentar. It presents the attempt as an action in progress or happening alongside another description.

example.en: He keeps trying to open the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Intentándolo joins lo, ‘it,’ to intentando, the -ando form of intentar. The written accent keeps the original stress after the extra syllable is attached.

example.en: Keep trying it a little longer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Intentar is the verb's unchanged dictionary form, meaning 'to try.' Lo is attached to its end and stands for the thing or action being tried.

example.en: You can try it tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Intentas is the present form of intentar for one familiar person. Follow it directly with an unchanged action verb to say what that person tries to do.

example.en: Are you trying to open the window?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Intenté is the completed-past form of intentar for the speaker.

example.en: I tried to call yesterday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you try; you attempt (special form after a recommendation)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Intentes is a changed form of intentar for one familiar person. It appears here because the action is recommended after será mejor que rather than stated as a fact.

example.en: It is better for you to try to rest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Interactuado is the completed-action form of interactuar. It follows a form of haber, such as he, to say that an interaction has happened.

example.en: I have interacted with the system.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Interactúe is a special form of interactuar used when the interaction is presented under a reaction, judgment, wish, or other non-statement frame rather than asserted on its own.

example.es: No importa que interactúe con otros sistemas.
example.en: It does not matter that it interacts with other systems.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In finance, interés is the extra money paid for borrowing or earned by saving or investing. The same Spanish word can mean personal interest in another context.

example.es: La cuenta paga interés cada mes.
example.en: The account pays interest each month.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An adjective can stand in for a noun that has just been mentioned. The surrounding article shows which omitted noun it describes.

example.es: Busco una película; quiero una interesante.
example.en: I am looking for a movie; I want an interesting one.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I became interested (with me: me interesé)

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, la interfaz is the set of controls and displays through which a person interacts with a program or device. Its plural is interfaces.

example.en: The interface has large buttons.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After yo, interior describes the private inner self rather than a physical interior space.

example.en: Seek inner calm.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, interior can mean the inside of something. Applied to a person, it can refer figuratively to private thoughts, feelings, or character.

example.es: Guardaba ese miedo en su interior.
example.en: She kept that fear inside herself.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Interpretada is the feminine singular completed-action form of interpretar.

example.es: La señal fue interpretada por el equipo.
example.en: The signal was interpreted by the team.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Interpretar can mean deciding what a sign, statement, or event means, or presenting it in a particular way.

example.es: No sé cómo interpretar la señal.
example.en: I do not know how to interpret the signal.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Interrumpí is the completed-past form of interrumpir for the speaker. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: I interrupted the meeting by mistake.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to introduce; to insert or embed
cardCatalog.noteEn: Introducir can mean putting something into a larger setting, not only introducing one person to another.

example.es: Introdujeron una regla nueva en el juego.
example.en: They introduced a new rule into the game.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inventado is the completed-action form of inventar. After he, it says that the speaker has invented something; inventado itself does not change for the speaker.

example.en: I have invented a game.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, invernadero is a structure kept warm for plants. It can also evoke extremely warm climate conditions.

example.en: The greenhouse retains heat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inversa describes a feminine singular thing whose order or direction is reversed. The masculine singular form is inverso.

example.en: They followed the reverse route.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Investiga is the present form of investigar used with one other person or thing, or as the informal singular command.

example.en: The team investigates the cause.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Investigad is the positive command used with informal plural vosotros in Spain. It comes from investigar by replacing the final -r with -d.

example.en: Investigate the problem carefully.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inviertes is used for one familiar listener who puts money into something with the aim of receiving a later return.

example.es: Si inviertes con cuidado, limitas el riesgo.
example.en: If you invest carefully, you limit the risk.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Invitado is the completed-action form of invitar, “to invite.” With a person and a before a drink or meal, invitar can also mean to treat that person or buy it for them.

example.es: Te he invitado a un café.
example.en: I have treated you to a coffee.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to go; to work or run
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ir normally means “to go.” In ir bien or ir mal, it describes how something works or is going: va bien means “it works” or “it’s going well.”

example.en: The app is working well.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ir normally means “to go.” With a matching small pronoun, as in me voy a ir or nos vamos a ir, it can express leaving.

example.en: We are going to leave early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ir is the unchanged dictionary form “to go.” Attaching te makes irte, the form of irse used when one familiar person leaves or goes away.

example.en: You can leave early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ja represents a short burst of laughter in writing.

example.en: Ha! That joke is good.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Jamás can mean “never” by itself. After nunca, it reinforces the negative and makes nunca jamás mean an emphatic “never ever”; the two negative words do not cancel each other in Spanish.

example.en: I will never ever say that.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Jamás is a strong way to say “never.” Like nunca, it can appear after a verb already negated with no, or before the verb without no.

example.en: I never forget a promise.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish writes laughter with repeated j sounds, such as ja, je, ji, jo, or ju. Je can suggest a restrained, knowing, or slightly awkward laugh.

example.en: Heh, what a coincidence.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Jedi; relating to the Jedi Order
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can use jedi as a noun or as an adjective after a noun; in adjective use, it describes something related to the Jedi Order.

example.es: El joven empezó su entrenamiento jedi.
example.en: The young man began his Jedi training.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Jett (part of the name Joan Jett)
ugh; darn (a mild frustrated reaction, especially in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Jo is a mild exclamation of annoyance, disappointment, or surprise. It does not literally name a sigh, even when it replaces a written sigh in a translation.

example.en: Ugh, not again!

cardCatalog.answerEn: Joan (part of the name Joan Jett)

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a reaction, joder can express anger, shock, pain, or frustration. It is common in informal speech in Spain but is strongly vulgar and unsuitable for polite situations.

example.en: Fuck, I have lost the keys!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Joven can be used on its own as a form of address rather than directly modifying a stated noun.

example.en: Excuse me, young person, can you help me?

cardCatalog.noteEn: A describing word such as joven can stand for people when the person-word is understood. Los jóvenes means young people as a group.

example.en: The young people organized the event.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Jugado is the completed-action form of jugar, “to play.” In the reaction bien jugado, the idea extends from games to any clever move or reply.

example.en: The match is well played.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Jugando is the -ando form of jugar. It can name a simultaneous action and is followed by a before the game being played.

example.es: Pasó la tarde jugando al dominó.
example.en: He spent the afternoon playing dominoes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Jugando is the form of jugar ending in -ando that presents play as ongoing. With danger, power, feelings, or another serious matter after con, it can mean toying with or handling it carelessly.

example.en: They are playing with fire.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With con and a tool, control, or idea, jugar can mean experimenting with it rather than playing a game.

example.es: Voy a jugar con los ajustes de color.
example.en: I am going to play around with the color settings.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Jugar means taking part in a game. It is commonly followed by a before the game or activity.

example.en: We are going to play chess.

cardCatalog.answerEn: next to; beside (as part of junto a)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Junto con introduces an additional person or thing included with the first one.

example.es: Escribe el nombre junto con la fecha.
example.en: Write the name together with the date.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A juramento is a solemn promise, including an oath of office or a promise made in court.

example.en: The president took the oath.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Justo describes a masculine singular person, choice, or result that is fair or morally right.

example.en: We are seeking a fair agreement.

cardCatalog.answerEn: kernel; core of an operating system
cardCatalog.noteEn: Kernel is a technical borrowing used in Spanish for the central software that manages hardware and basic system resources.

example.en: The kernel controls memory.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the (masculine plural; the letters spell los)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Hyphens between individual letters show a word being read out one letter at a time. Read l-o-s together as los.

example.en: C-A-S-A spells the word casa.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; the article used before nuestra (“ours”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: When a feminine noun has already been named, la can introduce a possessive form that means “the one belonging to us.” La matches the omitted feminine noun; natural English usually says only “ours.”

example.es: Su bicicleta es azul; la nuestra es roja.
example.en: Her bicycle is blue; ours is red.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the; used before my body part where English says “my”
cardCatalog.noteEn: When a sentence already identifies the affected person with me, Spanish normally uses el or la before that person's body part instead of mi. The same pattern can use te, le, nos, or les for other affected people.

example.en: My hand hurts.

cardCatalog.answerEn: your here; Spanish keeps “the” because te already marks the affected owner
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses an article before a body part when me, te, le, nos, or les already identifies whose body is affected.

example.en: Your hands get cold.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of a la larga
cardCatalog.noteEn: La is fixed between a and larga in the expression a la larga, ‘in the long run.’

example.es: A la larga, será más fácil.
example.en: In the long run, it will be easier.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; fixed part of cagarla, “to screw up”
cardCatalog.noteEn: The la in cagarla is fixed and does not point to a particular feminine person or thing. It moves before a conjugated verb or helper: la cagué and la he cagado.

example.es: La cagué al enviar el archivo.
example.en: I screwed up when I sent the file.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sobre la marcha (“as you go”)

cardCatalog.noteEn: When speaking formally to a woman, la can mean “you” as the direct object. The same form also commonly means “her.”

example.en: I’ll call you tomorrow, ma’am.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; Spanish uses la before a general abstract idea such as vida
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses el or la when discussing an idea in general, while English uses the bare noun without “the.” The article still matches the noun: la vida, la paciencia, el tiempo.

example.en: Patience is important.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can use el, la, los, or las before a description when an understood noun is left unstated. La refers to one feminine thing already clear from context.

example.es: De las dos lámparas, esta es la más alta.
example.en: Of the two lamps, this one is the tallest.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the; English often uses a possessive because le already marks the affected owner
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can use le for the affected owner and an ordinary article before that person's item. La matches a feminine singular item, not the owner's gender; natural English often uses “her” or “his” instead.

example.es: Le cerraron la cuenta a Marta.
example.en: They closed Marta's account.

cardCatalog.answerEn: my; literally the (when me already marks the affected owner)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses the definite article with a body part or close possession when an object pronoun already identifies the affected owner. Me supplies ‘my,’ so la still agrees with the feminine noun.

example.en: I washed my face.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the feminine article in la que; helps mean which, who, or whom
working; work (in días laborales, workdays or weekdays)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Laborales describes things connected with work. Días laborales are the days normally treated as workdays, in contrast with the weekend.

example.es: La oficina abre los días laborales.
example.en: The office opens on workdays.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lance is a special form of lanzar used when the throwing is presented as a pending, wished-for, feared, or otherwise non-asserted event.

example.es: Teme que yo lance la pelota.
example.en: He is afraid that I will throw the ball.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to rush into; to launch ourselves into
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lanzarnos combines the dictionary form lanzar with nos. In lanzarnos a hacer algo, it presents 'us' as plunging into an action, often too quickly or eagerly.

example.en: We should not rush into deciding.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lanzar usually means ‘to throw.’ With mirada, it forms the conventional expression for casting or giving someone a look.

example.en: I cast a glance at the clock.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lápiz is singular. Its plural is lápices, with c instead of z.

example.es: Necesito un lápiz para el examen.
example.en: I need a pencil for the exam.

cardCatalog.answerEn: long run; completes a la larga
cardCatalog.noteEn: Larga completes the fixed expression a la larga. Outside the expression, larga is the feminine form of largo, ‘long.’

example.en: In the long run, we will save money.

cardCatalog.answerEn: your here; Spanish uses “the” before body parts whose owner is already clear
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish commonly keeps the article before a body part and lets the surrounding pronoun or context identify the owner.

example.en: My legs hurt.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; used before plural clock hours
cardCatalog.noteEn: The understood word is horas, a feminine plural noun, so Spanish uses las before two o'clock and every later hour. One o'clock instead uses la: es la una.

example.es: La clase empieza a las nueve.
example.en: The class starts at nine.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a changed verb, las can replace a feminine plural noun that is already understood. Spanish puts this short object word before the verb: las guardé means “I stored them.”

example.es: Compré las llaves y las guardé.
example.en: I bought the keys and stored them.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; Spanish uses the article before a general feminine plural group
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often keeps las before a category discussed in general, where English may use a bare plural: las bicicletas, las herramientas.

example.en: Bicycles are practical.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Las can stand without a repeated feminine plural noun when the missing group is already understood.

example.en: I prefer the wooden ones.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the feminine plural article inside las que (‘which’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a preposition, las can join que to refer back to feminine plural things. Las matches those things; que itself does not change.

example.es: Son las salas en las que trabajamos.
example.en: They are the rooms that we work in.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Láser is a Spanish noun formed from an international acronym. Its written accent marks the first syllable, and the plural can be láseres.

example.es: El laboratorio usa un láser azul.
example.en: The laboratory uses a blue laser.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Latidos is the plural of latido. It most often names the beats of a heart, but it can also describe repeated throbs or pulses.

example.es: Oigo los latidos de mi corazón.
example.en: I can hear my heartbeat.

cardCatalog.answerEn: her; marks the person affected by a situation or result
cardCatalog.noteEn: Le can identify one person affected by what happens even when natural English does not use ‘to.’ A phrase beginning with a can make that person explicit: se le queda a Ana.

example.es: A Laura se le quedó esa sensación.
example.en: That feeling stayed with Laura.

cardCatalog.answerEn: may have no separate English word; marks the thing receiving the effect
cardCatalog.noteEn: Le can appear before a verb even when a later phrase beginning with a names the receiver explicitly. English normally states that receiver only once.

example.es: Le cambié la rueda al coche.
example.en: I changed the car's wheel.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks that person as the one who feels like something
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before apetecer, le identifies one person who has the desire. Natural English usually puts that person first and does not translate le as a separate word.

example.en: Leo feels like resting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: her; marks the person whose body part is affected
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often identifies the owner of a body part with me, te, le, nos, or les instead of putting a possessive word before the body part. A later a + person phrase can clarify who le refers to.

example.es: Le lavé las manos al niño.
example.en: I washed the child's hands.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; fixed part of que le den
cardCatalog.noteEn: Le is built into this colloquial dismissal. A rejected person or thing can follow with a, or the target can stay unstated when it is already clear. Natural English does not translate le separately.

example.en: To hell with the plan!

cardCatalog.noteEn: When addressing someone formally, le can mean “to you.” It is an indirect-object pronoun and normally appears before the conjugated verb.

example.en: I’ll write to you tomorrow, sir.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks the person whose preference or reaction is described
cardCatalog.noteEn: With gustar and similar preference expressions, le identifies the person experiencing the liking, appeal, or reaction. The thing that causes that reaction controls whether the verb is singular or plural, while le stays the same.

example.es: A Luis le gustan los trenes.
example.en: Luis likes trains.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Le usually marks an indirect object, such as a recipient (“to him”). With a masculine person, especially in Spain, le can also be used as the direct object (“him”); this accepted use is called leísmo.

example.es: Le di el libro a Pablo.
example.en: I gave Pablo the book.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks the person whose situation is being asked about
cardCatalog.noteEn: In ¿Cómo le va?, le points to one person addressed formally or one other person. English expresses that relationship through the subject of ‘How are you/is he/is she doing?’

example.en: How is Marta doing?

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks the person or thing that cares, or for whom something matters
cardCatalog.noteEn: The thing that matters controls the form of importar; le identifies the one who cares.

example.es: A Marta le importa el resultado.
example.en: Marta cares about the result.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to that person or group; marks who has the impression
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before parecer, le identifies one person, one thing, or a grammatically singular group that experiences the impression. English may express the same idea with “to” or by making that person the subject of “find.”

example.en: The idea seems useful to her.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks the person or thing in which a quality is perceived
cardCatalog.noteEn: In verle una cualidad a alguien o algo, le marks one person or thing and les marks more than one. It appears before a changed form of ver or attaches to ver in its unchanged dictionary form. Natural English usually expresses the same relation with ‘in.’

example.en: I see a future in the project.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you; marks the formal person who is allowed to do something
cardCatalog.noteEn: With permitir, le identifies one person affected by the permission. Here that person is the formally addressed listener; English normally places “you” directly before the allowed action.

example.en: The card will allow you to enter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here le points back to a thing and functions as an indirect-object pronoun with prestar atención. A fuller a + noun phrase can state what le refers to.

example.es: A esta cuestión le presto mucha atención.
example.en: I pay close attention to this issue.

cardCatalog.answerEn: her; to her (marks the female recipient)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Le identifies the person who receives a request or another action. The same Spanish form can also mean “to him” or formal “to you”; context identifies the person.

example.en: I asked Marta for water.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks the person or thing feared with temerle
cardCatalog.noteEn: In varieties that use temerle a, le appears with the verb and a introduces the feared target.

example.en: He is afraid of the dark.

cardCatalog.answerEn: at him; marks the target of the throw
cardCatalog.noteEn: With tirar una cosa a alguien, le can point to the person toward whom the object is thrown. A fuller phrase beginning with a can clarify that person.

example.es: Le tiré la pelota a Pablo.
example.en: I threw the ball to Pablo.

cardCatalog.answerEn: information leak; unauthorized release of information
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish technology and media writing sometimes borrows English leak informally. It is normally treated as a masculine noun: un leak, el leak.

example.es: El periodista investigó un leak de documentos.
example.en: The journalist investigated a leak of documents.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lechuga is the leafy vegetable lettuce.

example.en: He put lettuce in the salad.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lee is the positive command from leer used when telling one familiar person to read.

example.en: Read this message.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lees is the present form of leer for one familiar listener.

example.en: You read many books.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Legalmente is built from legal plus -mente. It describes what the law permits, requires, or recognizes.

example.en: Legally, the contract remains in force.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A legión was originally a large military unit. It can also describe a very numerous, organized, or devoted group.

example.es: Una legión de seguidores esperaba fuera.
example.en: A legion of followers was waiting outside.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Leibniz (the mathematician and philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Leído is the completed-action form of leer. It follows a form of haber in constructions such as he leído, “I have read.”

example.en: I have already read the message.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lejos describes distance. It normally appears without changing form and often follows de before the point of reference.

example.es: La estación está lejos de aquí.
example.en: The station is far from here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For the body-part sense, lengua means “tongue.” In a separate sense, lengua can mean “language.”

example.en: He bit his tongue.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In combinations such as ir lento, lento describes how an action or process runs. It stays masculine singular because it describes the action rather than a noun.

example.en: The program runs slowly.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Leonardo; the name of Leonardo da Vinci and a Ninja Turtle
them; marks several targets of dar caza
cardCatalog.noteEn: In dar caza a alguien, le or les can stand before dar for the person or people being pursued.

example.en: The guards hunt them down.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Some speakers use les for a masculine or mixed plural group as the direct object. More widely taught standard usage would normally use los here; les is standard when the people are indirect recipients.

example.es: A esos alumnos les vi ayer.
example.en: I saw those students yesterday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to them; marks the group that likes or dislikes something
cardCatalog.noteEn: With gustar, les identifies several people who experience the liking. It does not by itself mean “they.”

example.es: A mis amigos les gusta bailar.
example.en: My friends like dancing.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to them; marks them as the people receiving something
cardCatalog.noteEn: Les identifies more than one receiver. It normally appears before a verb that changes for the person and time, although it can attach to some unchanged verb forms and positive commands.

example.en: I send them a photo.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In tipo de letra, letra refers to the visual design used for written characters.

example.es: Elige un tipo de letra sencillo.
example.en: Choose a simple typeface.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Levantado describes a male person who is awake and no longer in bed. Its ending changes to levantada for a female person and to levantados or levantadas for a plural group.

example.en: Pablo is still up.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to get up; to rise (one informal listener)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Levantar means ‘to lift,’ while levantarse means to get oneself up. In levantarte, the dictionary form levantar has te attached to identify one familiar person as the person getting up.

example.en: You need to get up early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Leyendo is leer in its ongoing-action form ending in -iendo.

example.en: I am reading a book.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we made out; we hooked up (informal, especially in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Liar normally means to tangle or make a mess. The pronominal expression liarse con alguien can colloquially mean to make out or hook up with someone.

example.es: Se lió con alguien de la fiesta.
example.en: They hooked up with someone from the party.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With estar, libre can describe a person who has no commitment at a particular time. Libre has the same singular form for masculine and feminine people.

example.en: Marta is available on Saturday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: free; open for people to use or share
cardCatalog.noteEn: Libre emphasizes freedom or lack of restriction. It is different from gratis, which specifically means that something costs no money.

example.en: The project uses free and open-source software.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Libros is the masculine plural of libro.

example.en: These books are new.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Licenciatura names an undergraduate university qualification. The closest English label varies by education system.

example.en: She has a bachelor's degree in history.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ligero can describe something that has little weight. In other contexts it can also mean quick or slight.

example.en: I'm looking for a lightweight laptop.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A límite can be a boundary or the greatest allowed value. In technical descriptions, it often names the maximum a system supports.

example.es: El límite del sistema es de cien usuarios.
example.en: The system limit is one hundred users.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The singular is limón, with an accent; the plural limones does not keep that written accent.

example.en: I need three lemons.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I will clean; I will cleanse
cardCatalog.noteEn: The ending -é added to limpiar marks a future action by “I.” In a dramatic context, clean can carry the stronger sense “cleanse.”

example.en: I will clean the kitchen tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: line; part of línea de comandos (“command line”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, línea de comandos names a text interface where a person types instructions for the computer.

example.es: Escribo la orden en la línea de comandos.
example.en: I type the instruction on the command line.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Línea can be a visible stroke connecting points or shapes. This is distinct from línea meaning a phone connection, helpline, or the word inside en línea, ‘online.’

example.es: Traza una línea entre los dos cuadros.
example.en: Draw a line between the two boxes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Línea normally means “line,” but the complete expression en línea describes something available or happening online.

example.en: We made the reservation online.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here línea names the physical route that carries electrical power, not a drawn line or a line of text.

example.es: La línea lleva electricidad al pueblo.
example.en: The line carries electricity to the town.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Línea means a line. In línea del tiempo, the three words together name a timeline.

example.es: La línea del tiempo empieza en 1900.
example.en: The timeline begins in 1900.

cardCatalog.noteEn: On a diagram, líneas can refer to the drawn paths that trace people or things, rather than lines of written text.

example.es: Cada línea muestra una ruta distinta.
example.en: Each line shows a different route.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lingüística is the systematic study of language and how languages work.

example.en: She studies linguistics at university.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lista can mean “ready” in other contexts. When it describes a person as an ability, it means “smart” or “clever.”

example.en: Marta is very smart.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With estar, listo commonly means ready. It matches a masculine singular subject.

example.en: The team is ready.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When listo describes intelligence, it means smart or clever. The same written word can mean ready in a different context; lista is the feminine singular form.

example.en: Diego is very smart.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Literaria describes something related to literature and uses feminine singular -a with a noun such as crítica.

example.en: She published a literary magazine.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With se, llama is a form of llamarse used to state a person's or thing's name. Without se, llama can instead mean “calls.”

example.en: My dog is called Coco.

cardCatalog.answerEn: knock (on a door; informal singular command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llamar usually means “to call.” In llamar a la puerta, it means knocking so that someone answers.

example.es: Llama a la puerta antes de entrar.
example.en: Knock on the door before entering.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they are called; they are named
cardCatalog.noteEn: With se, llaman can state what several people or things are called. Llaman itself is the plural present form of llamar.

example.en: Those plants are called poppies.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Llamar often means “to call.” In the fixed expression llamar a la puerta, it means to knock on a door.

example.es: Voy a llamar a la puerta.
example.en: I am going to knock on the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Llamaremos keeps the full verb llamar and adds the -emos future ending for nosotros.

example.en: We will call you tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to call her; to phone her
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llamar is the unchanged dictionary form meaning “to call,” and la is attached to its end for a female person receiving the call.

example.en: I am going to call her this afternoon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Llamarte combines the unchanged verb llamar with te attached at the end. Te identifies one familiar person receiving the call.

example.en: I am going to call you tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: calls; phones (special form used for a caused action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After hacer que, Spanish uses a special verb form for the action being caused. Llama is the ordinary “calls” form; llame is the corresponding special form here.

example.en: I make Luis call today.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Llamemos is the nosotros command form of llamar used to propose a shared name or label.

example.es: Llamemos unidad solar a esta cantidad.
example.en: Let's call this quantity a solar unit.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Llega is a present form of llegar for one person or thing. Llegar takes a before the destination or endpoint.

example.es: El tren llega a la estación a las ocho.
example.en: The train reaches the station at eight.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Llegando is the -ando form of llegar. After a form of estar, it presents the arrival as an action in progress.

example.en: We are getting home.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to come to; eventually (in llegar a + action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llega usually means “to arrive.” Before a and another action verb, it can instead present something as an eventual result.

example.en: She eventually came to understand the idea.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to reach; to arrive at (a life stage)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llegar keeps its ordinary arrival sense when a following a phrase names an age or stage, as in llegar a adulto or llegar a los treinta.

example.es: Al llegar a adulta, se mudó.
example.en: When she reached adulthood, she moved.

cardCatalog.answerEn: arrives; comes (special form for a future event)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llegue is a form of llegar used after connectors such as cuando or para que when the arrival has not happened yet. The written u keeps the hard g sound before e.

example.en: I will call you when I arrive.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we reach; we arrive (an awaited-event form)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lleguemos is the special form used for we after expressions such as hasta que when the arrival is still in the future.

example.en: Wait until we arrive.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you arrive; you reach (special form for an event still ahead)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llegues is a present subjunctive form of llegar. After cuando, it presents the arrival as a future event that has not happened yet.

example.en: Call me when you arrive.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lleva is a singular present form of llevar. With encima, it means that someone has an object with them or on their person.

example.en: Marta has the keys on her.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lleva is the singular present form of llevar. With clothing or something worn on the body, llevar means ‘to wear’ rather than ‘to carry.’

example.en: He is wearing a blue jacket.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Llevado is the completed-action form of llevar. After ha and before a plus another verb, it says that something has led or prompted someone to do an action.

example.es: La duda me ha llevado a preguntar.
example.en: The doubt has led me to ask.

cardCatalog.answerEn: were wearing; had on (in an unreal condition)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llevara is a special -ra form of llevar used for an imagined condition. With puesto or puesta, it describes clothing that someone has on.

example.es: Si llevara abrigo, no tendría frío.
example.en: If I were wearing a coat, I would not be cold.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it took; it would take (in a past subjunctive form)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llevara is a past subjunctive form of llevar. In the time-taking construction, it describes the amount of time an activity required rather than carrying an object.

example.es: Dudaba que me llevara tanto tiempo.
example.en: I doubted that it would take me so long.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you have spent; you have been at (for a duration)
cardCatalog.noteEn: With a span of time, llevas says how long one familiar person has already spent on something.

example.es: Llevas una hora con ese informe.
example.en: You have been working on that report for an hour.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Llevar often means ‘to carry’ or ‘to wear,’ but with a journal, record, or account it can mean to keep or maintain it.

example.en: You keep a very clear record.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you are wearing; you have on
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llevar often means “to carry,” but with clothes or an accessory it means to wear or have that item on. Llevas addresses one familiar person.

example.en: You are wearing a blue jacket.

cardCatalog.answerEn: take with you (an informal command to one person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llévate is the positive tú command lleva with te attached. Llevarse can mean to take something away with oneself; the accent preserves the original stress.

example.en: Take a coat with you.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I carried out; I conducted (as part of llevar a cabo)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llevé is the completed past form for the speaker. In llevar a cabo, llevar does not mean physically carrying something; the whole expression means completing or conducting an activity.

example.en: I carried out the experiment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Llevar can mean ‘to take’ when talking about the time an activity requires. Lleve is a special subjunctive form used here after puede que because the duration is only a possibility; the ordinary statement form would be lleva.

example.en: It may take an hour.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it (in the fixed apology lo siento, I'm sorry)
how; marks the degree of a description in lo ... que
no separate English word; middle piece of de lo más
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lo is neutral here: it does not stand for a masculine object. Learn it as part of the fixed degree expression de lo más.

example.es: La visita fue de lo más agradable.
example.en: The visit was extremely pleasant.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins lo más... posible (“as... as possible”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lo stays unchanged in this degree expression. It works with más and posible around the description being maximized.

example.en: Make it as simple as possible.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes ponerlo fácil
cardCatalog.noteEn: In ponerlo fácil, lo stands for the situation being made easy. Natural English normally expresses this as “make it easy” without translating lo separately.

example.es: El profesor nos lo puso fácil.
example.en: The teacher made it easy for us.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the thing; what happened (as part of lo de)
no separate English word; helps lo que mean “how much”
cardCatalog.noteEn: In an emphatic lo que followed by a verb, lo does not mean “it” or “the thing.” Together with que, it points to the amount or intensity of the action.

example.en: You have no idea how much it rained!

cardCatalog.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cardCatalog.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cardCatalog.answerEn: “it” here, but this is nonstandard Spanish; standard Spanish would omit lo
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lo normally stands for the person or thing receiving an action; it does not name who or what performs that action. Spanish usually leaves an already understood performer unstated because the verb form carries it. A standard version would say abandona todo without lo.

example.es: La máquina falla y abandona la tarea.
example.en: The machine fails and abandons the task.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cardCatalog.answerEn: so; like one (standing in for a description or classification)
no separate English word; part of por lo que

cardCatalog.noteEn: Loca is the feminine singular form of loco. Applied to an adventure, idea, or entertainment, it can describe something wildly excessive or unrestrained rather than a medical condition.

example.en: It was a wild adventure.

cardCatalog.answerEn: speaker; here, a code talker who transmits messages

cardCatalog.noteEn: A logarithm answers what exponent is needed to produce a given number from a chosen base.

example.en: We study logarithms in mathematics.

cardCatalog.answerEn: your here; Spanish uses los before a body part whose owner is already clear
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses el, la, los, or las before a body part when the context already makes its owner clear. The verb or another short word can identify the owner. Los is used before a masculine plural body-part word, as in los brazos, where English may naturally say “your arms.”

example.en: You raise your arms.

cardCatalog.answerEn: our here; Spanish uses los before a body part whose owner is already clear
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses el, la, los, or las before a body part when the surrounding verb or context already identifies its owner. Natural English often supplies ‘my,’ ‘your,’ ‘our,’ or another possessive word instead.

example.en: We cross our arms.

cardCatalog.answerEn: your here; Spanish uses los before clothing whose wearer is clear
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses el, la, los, or las rather than a possessive before clothing when a verb or a short word such as me, te, or se already identifies the wearer. Los is the masculine plural form.

example.en: She put on her gloves.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; Spanish uses the article before a general group
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish normally uses los before a plural group discussed as a whole, as in los programadores. English often leaves “the” out and simply says “programmers” when making the same general statement.

example.en: Dogs need water.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a de phrase, los can stand on its own for an understood masculine or mixed plural group instead of introducing a stated noun.

example.es: Los de la oficina ya llegaron.
example.en: The people from the office have already arrived.

cardCatalog.answerEn: those; the ones (as part of los que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Los normally means “the” before a masculine plural noun. In los que followed by a description, the noun is left unstated and los identifies a masculine or mixed group: los que llegaron means “those who arrived.”

example.es: Conozco a los que viven aquí.
example.en: I know those who live here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lucecitas is the plural diminutive of luz. The ending -ecita adds the idea of smallness, and z changes to c before e.

example.es: Veo unas lucecitas en la ventana.
example.en: I see some little lights in the window.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Luchan is the present form of luchar for they or plural you. Besides a physical fight, luchar can describe making a determined effort toward a goal.

example.en: They struggle to finish on time.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I will fight; I will struggle
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lucharé keeps the full verb luchar and adds -é for a future action by the speaker.

example.en: I will fight for a fair solution.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of desde luego (“of course”)
no separate English word; middle of en lugar de, ‘instead of’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Lugar normally means ‘place,’ but inside en lugar de the three words form one expression that introduces an alternative.

example.es: Fuimos a pie en lugar de tomar el autobús.
example.en: We walked instead of taking the bus.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Luminosos describes masculine plural things that give off or reflect noticeable light.

example.en: We saw several illuminated signs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun for an animal, macho means a male.

example.en: No male came near.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Machos is the plural noun for male animals.

example.en: The males have dark plumage.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Madrugar means getting up very early, usually because the day or an obligation starts early.

example.en: Tomorrow we have to get up early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mágica describes one feminine singular noun. The written accent belongs on the first a.

example.en: They are looking for a magical solution.

cardCatalog.noteEn: It describes an action as happening by magic or as if by magic.

example.es: La puerta no se abre mágicamente.
example.en: The door does not open magically.

cardCatalog.answerEn: badly; poorly; wrong (describing how an action is done)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After an action, mal describes the way it is performed. Natural English may use ‘badly,’ ‘poorly,’ or ‘wrong’ depending on the action.

example.en: They fixed the door badly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After sentirse, mal can describe feeling physically unwell or emotionally bad about something.

example.es: Me siento mal por el error.
example.en: I feel bad about the mistake.

cardCatalog.answerEn: bad; badly (in ni tan mal, “not so bad”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mal supplies the negative evaluation in ni tan mal, a conversational way to say that something turned out reasonably well.

example.es: El resultado no fue perfecto, pero ni tan mal.
example.en: The result was not perfect, but not too bad.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After estar, mal can describe something as wrong, incorrect, or not as it should be. English uses the adjective ‘wrong,’ even though mal often works like an adverb in Spanish.

example.en: The date is wrong.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mala is the feminine singular form of malo. Here it labels the bad-tasting end of the vertical scale.

example.en: It was a bad idea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mala is part of the fixed expression de mala muerte rather than an ordinary adjective agreeing with the preceding noun.

example.es: Es un hotel de mala muerte.
example.en: It is a seedy hotel.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a noun, maldito can express strong anger or contempt. It is rude or emotionally charged.

example.en: Where is the damn report?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a masculine plural noun, malditos adds strong anger or contempt. It is rude or emotionally charged rather than a neutral description.

example.en: Those damn cables do not work.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In an electrical diagram, malla describes a gridlike network of connected branches rather than a piece of fabric.

example.es: La corriente pasa por una malla de resistencias.
example.en: The current passes through a grid of resistors.

cardCatalog.answerEn: bad at; not skilled at (masculine singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: With ser and para, malo describes a person as not skilled or comfortable with an activity or situation.

example.en: I am bad at remembering names.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Malo names the negative quality being evaluated. In ¿qué tiene de malo?, the complete question asks what is wrong or bad about something.

example.es: No veo nada malo en la idea.
example.en: I do not see anything wrong with the idea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Malo ordinarily means bad. In an informal boast or judgment about a person, especially after creerse, it can sarcastically suggest being tough, dangerous, or intimidating.

example.es: Se cree muy malo delante de sus amigos.
example.en: He thinks he is very tough in front of his friends.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the bad ones; bad people (masculine or mixed plural)
cardCatalog.noteEn: A plural adjective can stand alone when the omitted people or things are understood. Malos can therefore label the bad members of a masculine or mixed group.

example.es: En el cuento, los malos pierden al final.
example.en: In the story, the bad people lose in the end.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For food or ingredients, malo can mean spoiled or no longer fit to eat. Malos is masculine plural.

example.en: They threw away the spoiled tomatoes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mañana can be the noun ‘morning’ or the time word ‘tomorrow.’ An article or another determiner before it, as in una mañana, marks the noun meaning.

example.en: I work in the morning.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mandará is the future form of mandar for one person or thing. Mandar can mean to send an object or message.

example.es: Marta nos mandará la foto mañana.
example.en: Marta will send us the photo tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mandíbula is the lower or upper bony structure that holds the teeth.

example.en: Her jaw hurts.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mando can mean the authority to direct an organization or the position that holds that authority.

example.en: The colonel took command.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Besides meaning “to drive” in much of Latin America, manejar can mean managing or dealing with a person, problem, or situation.

example.en: She knows how to handle difficult situations.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mano is feminine despite ending in -o, so it takes una and feminine describing forms.

example.en: Raise your right hand.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to carry on; to have (a conversation)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mantener often means “to keep” or “to maintain.” With conversación, it describes having or carrying on the exchange.

example.es: Es fácil mantener una conversación con ella.
example.en: It is easy to carry on a conversation with her.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mantengo is the present form of mantener for the speaker. With a statement, opinion, or decision, it means continuing to support it rather than changing one's position.

example.en: I stand by what I wrote.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Manteniendo is mantener's ongoing-action form. With conversación, mantener can mean having, carrying on, or keeping a conversation going rather than physically maintaining something.

example.en: We are having a calm conversation.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Marcapasos has the same written form for one pacemaker and for several; the surrounding words show the number.

example.es: El marcapasos regula el ritmo del corazón.
example.en: The pacemaker regulates the heart's rhythm.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In the expression irle la marcha a alguien, la marcha means excitement, energetic action, or even a taste for trouble rather than a literal march.

example.es: A Sara le va la marcha.
example.en: Sara likes excitement.

cardCatalog.answerEn: progress; motion (in sobre la marcha, “as you go”)

cardCatalog.noteEn: In the fixed expression ir de marcha, marcha refers to lively nightlife or partying rather than a literal march or movement.

example.en: They went out partying last night.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Marengo names a very dark gray shade.

example.en: He is wearing a charcoal-gray suit.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A margarita is a cocktail commonly made with tequila, citrus juice, and orange liqueur. The same Spanish word also means “daisies,” but the bar context selects the drink meaning.

example.es: Pidieron dos margaritas en el bar.
example.en: They ordered two margaritas at the bar.

cardCatalog.answerEn: anymore; any longer (after a negative verb)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Más usually means ‘more.’ After no and a verb, it can instead reinforce that an action no longer happens, especially in Latin American usage.

example.en: I do not work there anymore.

cardCatalog.answerEn: more; an extra intensifier before mayores here
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mayor already means “older,” so neutral standard Spanish normally needs only mayores. Más mayor is sometimes heard when distinguishing degrees within adulthood, but it can sound redundant; this use simply emphasizes the older part of the group.

example.es: Mi hermana es mayor que yo.
example.en: My sister is older than me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Unaccented mas is an old-fashioned or literary alternative to pero. Do not confuse it with más, written with an accent, which means “more” or “most.”

example.en: I wanted to help, but I could not.

cardCatalog.answerEn: farther (as part of más allá, farther away)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Inside de lo más, más strengthens the following description. The whole expression is usually translated together rather than word by word.

example.es: El resultado es de lo más extraño.
example.en: The result is extremely strange.

cardCatalog.answerEn: most; part of lo más... posible (“as... as possible”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Más raises the degree of the description between lo and posible. The complete pattern is translated naturally with “as... as possible,” not word by word.

example.en: Leave as soon as possible.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins más o menos
cardCatalog.noteEn: Más, o, and menos combine as más o menos to mean ‘more or less,’ ‘roughly,’ or ‘approximately.’

example.es: Tarda más o menos una hora.
example.en: It takes roughly an hour.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no more than; only (as part of no ser más que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Más normally means “more.” Between a negative form of ser and que, it helps restrict something to the description that follows.

example.es: No fue más que un error.
example.en: It was nothing more than a mistake.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After nunca, más extends the negative into the future: nunca más means ‘never again.’

example.en: He never came back again.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes sin más, “just like that”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Más usually means “more,” but in the fixed expression sin más it suggests that nothing further is added: no extra thought, preparation, explanation, or ceremony.

example.en: He simply left without another word.

cardCatalog.answerEn: more; more people or things (with the noun understood)
