cardCatalog.noteEn: Más can stand without a following noun when the context already makes clear what ‘more’ refers to. The accent distinguishes más, ‘more,’ from mas, a literary word for ‘but.’

example.en: We need more like these.

cardCatalog.answerEn: past; later than (with a stated time)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Más normally means “more.” In a time expression such as es más de medianoche, it says the stated time has already passed.

example.en: It is past ten.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Más normally means “more.” After el, la, los, or las, it can instead mark the highest degree in a group: la más rápida means “the fastest one.”

example.en: Ana is the fastest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Matan is a present form of matar for a plural subject.

example.en: These substances kill the bacteria.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Matando is the -ando form of matar. It can add an action that happens at the same time as another action.

example.es: El veneno avanzó, matando a los insectos.
example.en: The poison spread, killing the insects.

cardCatalog.answerEn: making someone laugh very hard; literally “killing” (in matar de risa)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Matando normally means “killing.” In matar de risa, it is part of an idiom for causing intense laughter.

example.es: Ese cómico me está matando de risa.
example.en: That comedian is making me laugh so hard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Matarnos joins matar, “to kill,” to nos, the short word that marks the speaker's group as receiving the action.

example.en: That smoke could kill us.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Matar stays in its unchanged dictionary form, and te attaches to its end for the person affected.

example.en: That smoke could kill you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Maté is the speaker form of matar for one completed action in the past. The written accent on the final é is required for this past form.

example.en: Yesterday I killed a fly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The singular matemática can name mathematics as a field. The plural matemáticas is also very common for the subject or activity.

example.en: Mathematics studies patterns.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Materia can mean physical matter, but in education it means a subject or area of knowledge.

example.es: La física es su materia favorita.
example.en: Physics is her favorite subject.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here material names a physical substance used to make or build something, rather than a collection of equipment or supplies.

example.es: El vidrio es un material resistente.
example.en: Glass is a durable material.

cardCatalog.answerEn: supplies; equipment or material available for a task
cardCatalog.noteEn: Material can name a substance, but it can also collectively mean the supplies or equipment used for an activity.

example.es: Ya tenemos todo el material para el taller.
example.en: We already have all the supplies for the workshop.

cardCatalog.answerEn: morning; held in the morning (feminine singular)
to maximize; to make as large as possible

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mayonesa is the standard Spanish word for mayonnaise.

example.en: She added mayonnaise to the sandwich.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When it describes age, mayor means “older.” It has the same singular form for a man, woman, or thing.

example.en: I am older now.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mayor means “older” when comparing age; mayores is its plural form. The same form is used for a masculine, feminine, or mixed plural group.

example.en: My sisters are older.

cardCatalog.noteEn: La mayoría de introduces the larger part of a group.

example.es: La mayoría de los alumnos llegó temprano.
example.en: Most of the students arrived early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A mayorista sells large quantities to businesses rather than individual retail customers. After de in precios de mayorista, it describes wholesale-level prices.

example.es: La tienda compra la fruta a un mayorista.
example.en: The shop buys the fruit from a wholesaler.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks me as the affected person; English often expresses this as “my”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often uses me for the affected person and el or la before that person's body part. English usually uses a possessive word instead: me duele la mano means “my hand hurts.”

example.en: My hand hurts.

cardCatalog.answerEn: me (the speaker as the person allowed to act)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In a request such as deja que me siente, me belongs with the following action and identifies the speaker. Natural English likewise uses “me” after “let.”

example.en: Let me sit here.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; presents the reading as working through a specified text
cardCatalog.noteEn: With leer, me can add the sense that the speaker works through the stated text. It does not mean the speaker reads themself. The same completion pattern uses te, se, nos, os, or se for other people.

example.en: I read through the report last night.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for me; marks me as the person who finds something difficult
cardCatalog.noteEn: With costar in the sense “to be difficult,” me identifies the person who experiences the difficulty. Spanish makes the difficult task the grammatical subject.

example.en: It was hard for me to understand the question.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to me; marks the speaker as the person delighted
cardCatalog.noteEn: With encantar, me identifies who has the delighted reaction. The thing that causes the reaction controls whether the verb is singular or plural.

example.en: I love this song.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to me; marks the person who feels the pain
cardCatalog.noteEn: Doler is organized differently from English “hurt”: the painful thing controls the verb, while me, te, or le identifies who feels it.

example.en: My back hurts.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks me as the person who likes something
cardCatalog.noteEn: With gustar, Spanish presents the liked thing as pleasing to a person. Me identifies the speaker as that person; it does not become a separate English word when the natural translation uses “I.”

example.en: I like coffee.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With impedir, me identifies the person who is prevented from doing the following action. Spanish does not add a word corresponding to English ‘from.’

example.en: The noise prevents me from sleeping.

cardCatalog.answerEn: me; to me (the person who feels the impression)
cardCatalog.noteEn: With impresionar, me identifies the person who experiences the reaction. The thing that causes that reaction is expressed separately and controls whether the verb is singular or plural.

example.en: Your drawings impress me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With a form of ir, me can mark irse, which can mean “to leave” rather than simply “to go.”

example.en: I am going to leave soon.

cardCatalog.answerEn: from me; marks me as the person who loses the thing
cardCatalog.noteEn: With quitar, me identifies the speaker as the person something is taken away from. Natural English often uses “from me” or a possessive such as “my.”

example.en: They took my phone away.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cardCatalog.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

example.en: I complain about the noise.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for me; marks the person something is made easy or difficult for
cardCatalog.noteEn: With ponerlo fácil or ponerlo difícil, me identifies the speaker as the person who experiences the easier or harder situation.

example.en: They do not make it easy for me.

cardCatalog.answerEn: myself; marks the speaker in a reflexive verb
to me; marks me as the person who finds something a certain way
cardCatalog.noteEn: With resultar plus a description, me identifies the speaker as the person experiencing that judgment. Natural English often makes that person the subject: me resulta difícil is commonly expressed as “I find it difficult.”

example.en: I find the task simple.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to me; marks the person who experiences a taste
cardCatalog.noteEn: With saber in its taste sense, me identifies the speaker as the person to whom something tastes a certain way.

example.en: The tea tastes sweet to me.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to me; marks whose turn or responsibility it is
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before toca, me identifies the speaker as the person to whom the task falls.

example.en: It is my turn to pay.

cardCatalog.answerEn: me; marks the speaker as the person affected by the worry
cardCatalog.noteEn: With preocupar, me identifies the person who feels worried. The thing causing the worry is the grammatical subject.

example.en: The noise worries me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Media is the feminine noun for an average. In de media it describes a typical value across many cases.

example.es: La media es de ocho horas.
example.en: The average is eight hours.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Media agrees with the feminine noun hora. Medio is used before a masculine noun.

example.en: I waited half an hour.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With edad, mediana names the middle stage of adult life. This is different from the statistical mediana, the middle value in ordered data.

example.es: Llegó a la mediana edad con energía.
example.en: He reached middle age full of energy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In statistics, the mediana is the value in the middle after the values have been put in order. It is not necessarily the same as the average.

example.en: The median of 2, 5, and 9 is 5.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mediante introduces the means or method used to achieve something. It is followed by a noun or noun phrase.

example.en: We entered through a side door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With el, la, lo, los, or las, mejor usually means “best.” Without one of those words, it often means “better.”

example.en: This is the best option.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mejor compares one option with another. It does not change for gender: una solución mejor and un plan mejor both use mejor.

example.en: We need a better idea.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I'd better; it is better to
cardCatalog.noteEn: Placed before a present-time verb, mejor can introduce the course of action the speaker decides is wiser or safer.

example.en: I'd better leave now.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With a possessive such as nuestras, mejores picks out the best members of a plural group. Without that kind of determiner, the same form can also mean ‘better.’

example.en: They are our best ideas.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The fruit name melocotón can be used as a color label.

example.es: Pintaron la pared de color melocotón.
example.en: They painted the wall peach.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The singular is melocotón, with an accent; the plural melocotones does not keep that written accent.

example.en: I bought two peaches.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The singular is melón, with an accent; the plural melones does not keep that written accent.

example.en: The melons are ripe.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here memoria refers to computer storage used while an algorithm runs, not a person's ability to remember.

example.en: The program uses a lot of memory.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mencionado is the completed-action form of mencionar. After he, it says that the speaker has mentioned something.

example.en: I have mentioned the change.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Menor compares an amount, size, or degree. It has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.es: Esta opción tiene un coste menor.
example.en: This option has a lower cost.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of a menos que, “unless”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Menos is fixed between a and que in this connector.

example.en: We are leaving unless it snows.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Menos normally means “less” or “fewer.” With al, it forms the common expression al menos, “at least.”

example.en: There are at least two options.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes más o menos
cardCatalog.noteEn: Más, o, and menos combine as más o menos to mean ‘more or less,’ ‘roughly,’ or ‘approximately.’

example.es: Son más o menos veinte personas.
example.en: There are roughly twenty people.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Menstruación is a feminine noun: la menstruación.

example.es: La menstruación forma parte del ciclo menstrual.
example.en: Menstruation is part of the menstrual cycle.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mentalidad is feminine, so words that describe it use feminine forms such as nueva or obsesiva.

example.en: She has an open mindset.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes a menudo, ‘often’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Menudo has other uses on its own, but after a it forms the fixed frequency expression a menudo. Learn the two words together for ‘often.’

example.en: Clara comes often.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is worth (as part of merece la pena)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Merece is a form of merecer for one person or thing. The verb can mean “deserves” elsewhere; in merecer la pena, it says that something is worth the time or effort.

example.en: The trip is worth it.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Merecerte combines merecer, “to deserve,” with te, “you.” A short object word such as te can attach to the end of an unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.en: I hope to deserve you someday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mereces is the informal singular present form of merecer. In the common pronominal pattern, it appears as te mereces.

example.en: You deserve a clear answer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mesa names a table-like piece of furniture. English often calls a mesa used for working or studying a “desk,” even though Spanish keeps the ordinary word mesa.

example.es: Dejé el cuaderno sobre la mesa.
example.en: I left the notebook on the desk.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In geography, a meseta is a broad area of high, relatively flat land.

example.es: La ciudad está sobre una meseta.
example.en: The city is on a plateau.

cardCatalog.answerEn: meta-; about itself or a higher level of the same subject
cardCatalog.noteEn: The prefix meta- forms words for something that comments on, describes, or operates at a level above the original thing. It may be shown separately before a hyphen when its parts are being emphasized.

example.es: La novela incluye un metacomentario sobre su propia historia.
example.en: The novel includes meta-commentary about its own story.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Metástasis is the medical term for disease spreading from its original site to another part of the body.

example.en: The tests showed no metastasis.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here meter belongs to meterse en problemas. The small marker me appears earlier because another changed verb comes before meter.

example.en: I try not to get into trouble.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Meter describes placing something inside a container, space, or situation.

example.es: Mete la carta en el sobre.
example.en: Put the letter in the envelope.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Metes is the informal singular present form of meter.

example.es: Metes los libros en una caja.
example.en: You put the books in a box.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Metido is the completed-action form of meter. With a person and a situation introduced by en, it can describe getting or drawing that person into the situation.

example.es: Han metido a Leo en un problema.
example.en: They have gotten Leo into a problem.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Besides naming the unit “meter,” metro can refer to a tape measure in Spain. The surrounding object makes that meaning clear here.

example.es: Mide la mesa con un metro.
example.en: Measure the table with a tape measure.

cardCatalog.answerEn: me (after a preposition such as para)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses mí after most prepositions. The written accent distinguishes mí (“me”) from mi (“my”).

example.en: This gift is for me.

cardCatalog.answerEn: my; part of the exclamation madre mía
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mía is the feminine singular possessive form matching madre. In ¡Madre mía!, the whole expression is a reaction rather than a literal statement about one's mother.

example.en: Goodness, what a lot of noise!

cardCatalog.answerEn: Michelangelo; the name of a Renaissance artist and a Ninja Turtle

cardCatalog.noteEn: A micra is the everyday Spanish name for a micrometre, one millionth of a metre.

example.en: The layer measures two micrometres.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Microondas names microwave radiation. The same unchanged word can also mean a microwave oven, usually el microondas.

example.en: Microwaves heat the water.

cardCatalog.answerEn: awful; terrible (in ser una mierda, vulgar)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mierda literally means “shit.” In the vulgar judgment ser una mierda, it describes something as very bad, worthless, or deeply unpleasant rather than naming a literal substance.

example.en: The service is awful.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This informal written outburst repeats mierda without a space to show a rapid, panicked reaction. It is vulgar and belongs only in very informal contexts.

example.en: Shitshit, I lost the keys.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After haber, migrado is migrar’s completed-action form.

example.es: La empresa ha migrado al sistema nuevo.
example.en: The company has migrated to the new system.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Miles is the plural of mil when the number of thousands is not specified exactly.

example.en: Thousands of people arrived.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Millones is followed by de before the thing being counted.

example.en: There are millions of stars.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mimetiza is the singular present form of mimetizar.

example.es: El insecto mimetiza una hoja seca.
example.en: The insect mimics a dry leaf.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here mina is the place where minerals are extracted, not the explosive device.

example.en: The mine is closed.

cardCatalog.answerEn: look; listen; hey (to get someone's attention)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mira is the positive command form of mirar used with one familiar person. At the start of a comment, it often simply gets the listener's attention, like “look,” “listen,” or “hey,” without asking them to look at an object.

example.en: Listen, I have an idea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mirada can name the act or manner of looking, and it can also mean a way of viewing a topic.

example.es: El libro ofrece una mirada distinta al problema.
example.en: The book offers a different look at the problem.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mirado is the participle of mirar. With haber, it says that someone has looked at or checked something.

example.es: He mirado el registro esta mañana.
example.en: I checked the log this morning.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mirar already includes the idea expressed by English ‘at.’ Spanish normally puts the thing being watched directly after mirar, without adding a separate word for ‘at.’

example.en: I am looking at the screen.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I look; I check (special form after deja que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After deja que, the ordinary first-person form miro changes to mire because the action is being requested or allowed rather than stated as a fact.

example.en: Let me look at the map.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a noun, misma says that it is the identical one rather than a different one. It uses the feminine singular ending because it describes a feminine singular noun.

example.en: We take the same route.

cardCatalog.answerEn: right; this very moment (emphasis after ahora)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After ahora, mismo strengthens the time expression: ahora mismo means ‘right now.’ It does not mean ‘same’ in this use.

example.en: I need the answer right now.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a form such as mí, ti, or sí, mismo emphasizes that very person. Its ending changes to match: misma, mismos, or mismas.

example.en: Believe in yourself.

cardCatalog.answerEn: mmm; a sound of enjoyment or approval
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mmm represents a nonverbal reaction, often to something pleasant to taste, smell, or feel.

example.en: Mmm, this soup is tasty.

cardCatalog.answerEn: hmm; a sound of hesitation or thought
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mmm represents a pause while someone thinks, hesitates, or considers an idea.

example.en: Hmm... I am not sure.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mochila is the everyday word for a backpack. In el problema de la mochila, it supplies the Spanish name of the computer-science knapsack problem.

example.es: Guardé el libro en la mochila.
example.en: I put the book in the backpack.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Modernismo can name a modernist artistic or literary movement. Its exact dates and characteristics vary by field and country.

example.es: El museo dedica una sala al modernismo.
example.en: The museum devotes a room to modernism.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mola is an informal expression common in Spain for saying that something is cool or appealing.

example.en: That game is really cool.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Molestado is the completed-action form of molestar, ‘to bother’ or ‘to annoy.’ After ha, it stays unchanged even when the affected person changes.

example.en: The noise has bothered us.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Momento completes the fixed expression de momento. By itself, momento means ‘moment,’ but the two-word expression describes the present temporary situation.

example.en: For now, everything works.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Momentos is the plural of momento. It can refer to short stretches of time or particular occasions and situations.

example.en: We all have difficult moments.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Moneda can mean one coin, but it can also mean the currency or money system used by a country or community.

example.es: El euro es la moneda de varios países.
example.en: The euro is the currency of several countries.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Monitor is masculine: el monitor.

example.en: The monitor is on.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Montañas is the plural of montaña and keeps the letter ñ.

example.en: The mountains have snow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mordido is the completed-action form of morder. With ser it forms a passive description, and its ending changes to match the affected person or thing.

example.es: El pan fue mordido por el perro.
example.en: The bread was bitten by the dog.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Moribunda is the feminine singular form used for a living being near death.

example.en: They tried to save the dying plant.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Morirían keeps the dictionary form morir and adds -ían. This form is called the conditional; it can place an expected death later than an earlier past viewpoint, as English uses “would die.”

example.es: Pensaban que las plantas morirían sin agua.
example.en: They thought the plants would die without water.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, mortal means a human being viewed as someone who will eventually die. It can appear with an article, as in el mortal, or as a direct form of address without one.

example.es: Los mortales no viven para siempre.
example.en: Mortals do not live forever.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mostrando is the ongoing-action form of mostrar. Regular verbs ending in -ar replace -ar with -ando to make this form.

example.en: I am showing a photograph.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to appear; to show myself as being a certain way
cardCatalog.noteEn: Mostrarme joins mostrar with me. Before a describing word, mostrarse can mean presenting or showing oneself as having that quality, rather than displaying an object.

example.en: I prefer to appear calm.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Motivadoras uses feminine plural -as to match charlas.

example.en: We listened to some inspiring stories.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Motor can refer to the engine that powers a vehicle or machine.

example.en: The engine runs on petrol.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The written accent on í marks this completed past action by the speaker.

example.en: I moved the chair yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Moverse becomes moviendo for an action in progress, and se attaches to the end. The written accent keeps the word stressed in the same place: moviéndose.

example.es: Vimos al gato moviéndose bajo la mesa.
example.en: We saw the cat moving under the table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Móvil is the ordinary word for a cell phone in Spain. Many Latin American regions instead use celular.

example.es: Mi móvil está en la mochila.
example.en: My cell phone is in the backpack.

cardCatalog.answerEn: mobile; available through a mobile device or network
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here móvil is an adjective describing a kind of access, not the noun used in Spain for a cell phone. It has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: The app offers mobile access.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Móvil literally describes something that can move. In teléfonos móviles it distinguishes mobile or cell phones from fixed landlines.

example.en: Turn off the mobile phones.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here móviles stands by itself as the plural noun for mobile or cell phones, with teléfonos understood.

example.en: The new cell phones last longer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Movimientos is the plural of movimiento and can describe changes in position or a path followed over time.

example.es: La cámara sigue los movimientos del animal.
example.en: The camera follows the animal's movements.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After lo siento, mucho strengthens the apology. Natural English normally says “I'm very sorry” rather than translating mucho as a separate amount.

example.en: I am very sorry about the delay.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Put mucho before a comparison such as mejor or peor to make the difference stronger. Do not use muy in this pattern.

example.en: This option is much better.

cardCatalog.answerEn: much; however much (in por mucho que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Within por mucho que, mucho supplies the idea of an unrestricted amount or degree.

example.es: Por mucho que corra, llega tarde.
example.en: No matter how much he runs, he arrives late.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mucho can stand by itself when the kind of amount is already clear. It then means ‘much’ or ‘a lot’ without a following noun.

example.en: —How much rice is left? —A lot.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mucilaginoso literally means slimy or mucilaginous. In moho mucilaginoso it forms the conventional Spanish name for a slime mold.

example.en: We observed a slimy organism.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Nos mudamos is the completed-past form here. Mudarse means to change where one lives; nos is the matching short word used with we.

example.es: Nos mudamos a Sevilla el año pasado.
example.en: We moved to Seville last year.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mudarme joins mudar with me. The attached me identifies the speaker as the person changing homes.

example.en: I want to move soon.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you die (formal, subjunctive form after espero que)
no separate English word; completes de mala muerte
cardCatalog.noteEn: The full expression de mala muerte describes something as shabby or disreputable; it is not a literal reference to death.

example.es: Trabaja en un local de mala muerte.
example.en: He works in a shabby establishment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Used as a noun, muertos names people who are dead. Spanish can use an adjective with a plural article understood from context to refer to a group of people.

example.en: They remembered the dead.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With pixels, muertos means that the tiny screen elements no longer light or respond correctly, not that living beings have died.

example.es: La pantalla tiene dos píxeles muertos.
example.en: The screen has two dead pixels.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, muestra is a small part provided to represent or preview a larger thing. It is different from the verb muestra, ‘shows.’

example.en: I listened to a sample of the album.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Muestre is the formal command of mostrar, and me is attached because the speaker receives what is shown. The written accent in muéstreme keeps the original stress after me is added.

example.en: Show me your identification.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Mueve is the present form of mover for one person or thing. With se, it means that thing moves itself.

example.en: The robot moves slowly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Multiplicas is the familiar singular present form of multiplicar. A preceding lo can stand for the value being multiplied.

example.en: You multiply the result by two.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Muriendo is the irregular -iendo form of morir.

example.en: The plant is dying.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Murió is the completed past form of morir for one person or thing.

example.es: La planta murió durante el invierno.
example.en: The plant died during the winter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Murmurando is the -ando form of murmurar. It describes speaking very quietly or indistinctly while another action happens.

example.en: He left muttering a complaint.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Musical has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns; add -es for the plural.

example.en: It was a musical afternoon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Na is a very informal dismissive response. Nah is another common spelling; this comic prints na.

example.en: Nah, I'd rather stay here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Nacer is the dictionary form for coming into life. Spanish commonly uses al nacer for ‘at birth’ or ‘when born.’

example.es: El bebé pesó tres kilos al nacer.
example.en: The baby weighed three kilos at birth.

cardCatalog.answerEn: was born (special form after antes de que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Naciera is a past-looking subjunctive form of nacer. Antes de que uses this form because the birth is viewed as the later event relative to what happened before it.

example.es: La casa existía antes de que yo naciera.
example.en: The house existed before I was born.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.

example.en: I don’t see anything.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before de plus a thing or situation, nada can mean “none” or “nothing” out of that set. This use does not need a separate no before it when nada itself comes before the verb.

example.en: None of that matters.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a negative verb, nadie is commonly translated as “anyone.” Spanish uses negative concord, so no and nadie can appear together.

example.en: I don’t know anyone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ñam is a common Spanish sound for taking a bite or eating eagerly. Repeating it suggests repeated bites.

example.es: El niño miró el pastel y dijo: «¡Ñam!».
example.en: The child looked at the cake and said, “Yum!”

cardCatalog.noteEn: In Spain, a napolitana is a flaky rectangular pastry commonly filled with chocolate or cream.

example.en: She bought a chocolate-filled pastry.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a color word, naranja commonly stays unchanged for gender: una camisa naranja and un coche naranja.

example.en: The wall is orange.

cardCatalog.answerEn: birth rate; births in a population
cardCatalog.noteEn: Natalidad refers to births considered as a demographic measure. Tasa de natalidad is the standard expression for a birth rate.

example.en: The birth rate fell this year.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Natural has the same form with masculine and feminine singular nouns.

example.en: It is a natural reaction.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Navajo; relating to the Navajo people or language

cardCatalog.noteEn: Navegador can describe a navigator, but in computing it commonly means a web browser: the program used to open websites.

example.es: Abre el enlace en el navegador.
example.en: Open the link in the web browser.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Navegar can describe guiding a vessel through a route or difficult area, not only traveling by boat.

example.es: Es difícil navegar por este canal.
example.en: It is difficult to navigate this channel.

cardCatalog.answerEn: are needed; are required (with passive se)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Necesitan is a present plural form of necesitar. In se necesitan, the plural ending agrees with the people or things that are needed, while the person doing the needing is left unnamed.

example.en: Two signatures are needed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Necesite is a present subjunctive form of necesitar. The subjunctive is a special verb form used after puede que when the need is only a possibility.

example.en: He may need help.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we may need; we might need
cardCatalog.noteEn: Necesitemos is the special possibility form of necesitar for nosotros, 'we.' It appears after expressions such as puede que because the need is presented as possible rather than certain.

example.en: We may need more time.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Neec is a drawn-out comic sound for a heavy object or hinge creaking open.

example.en: The door creaked.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Negamos by itself usually means “we deny.” With nos before it and a before a following action, nos negamos a expresses that a group including the speaker refuses to do that action.

example.en: We refuse to lie.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Negativa ends in -a to match the feminine noun carga. In this physics context, it names one of the two conventional charge signs.

example.es: La carga de un electrón es negativa.
example.en: An electron's charge is negative.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In plan de negocio, de negocio classifies the plan as a business plan.

example.es: Prepararon un plan de negocio sencillo.
example.en: They prepared a simple business plan.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Nerd is an English loanword also used informally in Spanish for a highly intellectual or technically absorbed person. This printed plural keeps the English -s.

example.en: We are computer nerds.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Nervios can name the body's nerves. In other contexts, tener nervios or estar nervioso describes nervousness.

example.en: Nerves transmit signals.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no (as part of ni idea, “no idea”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ni normally adds a negative alternative or emphasis. In the short fixed reply ni idea, the whole expression means “no idea.”

example.en: I have no idea.

cardCatalog.answerEn: not even (as part of ni siquiera)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ni begins the fixed emphasis ni siquiera, which says that even a minimal or surprising possibility does not apply.

example.en: She did not even answer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: not; begins ni tan mal, “not so bad”
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the conversational expression ni tan mal, ni helps soften or reverse the negative evaluation rather than joining a list.

example.es: Llegamos tarde, pero ni tan mal.
example.en: We arrived late, but it was not too bad.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ni can add another rejected item after a negative, or begin a short emphatic rejection. It commonly has the force of “not even.”

example.en: He didn't call even once.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Repeated ni places each item inside the same negative choice: ni X ni Y. English commonly renders the pair as “neither X nor Y.”

example.es: No quiero ni té ni café.
example.en: I want neither tea nor coffee.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Nick is an informal English loan used in Spanish online communities for a nickname or username.

example.es: Uso otro nick en ese foro.
example.en: I use another username on that forum.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no; not any (before a masculine singular noun)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ningún is used directly before a masculine singular noun. When it comes after the verb, Spanish normally also keeps no before the verb: no tengo ningún problema.

example.en: We did not see any error.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ninguno can stand alone for an understood masculine item. After a negative verb, English often uses ‘any.’

example.en: I cannot find any of them.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Niños can refer specifically to boys or more generally to a group of children whose members are male or mixed. The surrounding context decides which meaning is intended.

example.es: Los niños juegan en el patio.
example.en: The children are playing in the yard.

cardCatalog.answerEn: level; a stage or rank in a game

cardCatalog.noteEn: This drawn-out sound effect represents hesitation or reluctant agreement. Repeated letters stretch the groan.

example.en: She answered with a reluctant groan.

cardCatalog.noteEn: No combines with solo to introduce the first part of the paired contrast no solo ... sino ....

example.es: No solo llamó, sino que vino.
example.en: She not only called, but also came.

cardCatalog.answerEn: non-; not a (before a category label)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a noun used as a label, no can divide people or things into a negative category, much like English non-. It remains a separate written word.

example.es: La entrada para no miembros está cerrada.
example.en: The entrance for non-members is closed.

cardCatalog.answerEn: right?; isn't that so? (at the end of a question)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a statement or assumption, ¿no? asks the listener to confirm it. English often uses a changing tag such as “right?”, “isn't it?”, or “don't you?”, but Spanish can use the same ¿no? after many different verbs.

example.en: You're coming tomorrow, right?

cardCatalog.answerEn: nodes; connection points in a network
cardCatalog.noteEn: In a circuit diagram, a node is a point where connected wires or components share the same electrical potential.

example.es: Los cables se unen en dos nodos.
example.en: The wires join at two nodes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Nombres is the plural of nombre. It can refer to personal names, labels, or the names assigned to things.

example.es: La lista contiene nombres y fechas.
example.en: The list contains names and dates.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here norma means the reference level treated as normal, not a rule that tells people what to do.

example.es: La temperatura está por debajo de la norma.
example.en: The temperature is below the norm.

cardCatalog.noteEn: It describes what happens in the usual or expected way.

example.en: I usually arrive early.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a verb such as salir or resultar, nos can identify the people for whom an outcome is advantageous, costly, easy, or difficult.

example.es: Nos resulta más barato viajar juntos.
example.en: It works out cheaper for us to travel together.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks us as the people who are missing or lacking something
cardCatalog.noteEn: With faltar, Spanish presents the absent thing as the subject and uses nos for the affected people. Nos falta tiempo therefore describes time as what is lacking for us.

example.en: We are missing a chair.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks a “we” verb that is used with nos
cardCatalog.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Nos marks the form for a group that includes the speaker. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

example.en: We complain about the noise.

cardCatalog.answerEn: each other; marks a shared action involving “us”
cardCatalog.noteEn: With a plural verb, nos can show that the speakers do the action to or with each other. Context distinguishes this reciprocal use from nos meaning simply “us.”

example.en: We hugged each other.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Noticias is grammatically plural in Spanish even when English uses the singular mass noun news.

example.es: Veo las noticias por la mañana.
example.en: I watch the news in the morning.

cardCatalog.answerEn: fame; how widely known someone or something is

cardCatalog.noteEn: Novedad names something new or unexpected; it can also appear sarcastically in an exclamation.

example.es: Esa noticia no es ninguna novedad.
example.en: That news is nothing new.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Noviazgo is the period or relationship in which people are a romantic couple before marriage.

example.en: Their relationship lasted two years.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Novios can mean boyfriends, a dating couple, or romantic partners depending on context.

example.es: Invitaron a sus novios a la fiesta.
example.en: They invited their partners to the party.

cardCatalog.noteEn: NP is an international computer-science abbreviation. It groups decision problems whose proposed solutions can be checked efficiently.

example.en: The problem belongs to NP.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Nuclear has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: They debated nuclear policy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Nuestro changes to nuestros before more than one masculine or mixed-gender thing. The ending matches what is owned, not the people who own it.

example.en: Our computers work well.

cardCatalog.answerEn: again; anew (as part of de nuevo)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Nuevo normally means ‘new.’ In the fixed expression de nuevo, the pair means ‘again’ or ‘anew.’

example.en: They started again.

cardCatalog.answerEn: ever (after a negative idea such as sin)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Nunca often means ‘never.’ When sin has already supplied the negative meaning, natural English commonly uses ‘ever’: sin mirar nunca atrás means ‘without ever looking back.’

example.en: He left without ever looking back.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Nunca usually means “never.” Inside a clause about what someone could possibly do, natural English can use “ever” because the negative or limiting force comes from the wider comparison.

example.es: Es más de lo que podría gastar nunca.
example.en: It is more than I could ever spend.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of más o menos
cardCatalog.noteEn: Más, o, and menos combine as más o menos to mean ‘more or less,’ ‘roughly,’ or ‘approximately.’

example.es: Llegarán más o menos a las ocho.
example.en: They will arrive at about eight.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With a reason introduced by a, obedecer can formally mean that something is caused by or explained by that reason, rather than literally obeying a person.

example.es: Los cambios obedecen a nuevas normas.
example.en: The changes are due to new rules.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Objeto can name a physical item or, in computing, a unit of data and behavior.

example.en: The program saves each object.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Obsesiva describes a feminine singular person or thing. The masculine singular form is obsesivo.

example.en: That concern seems obsessive.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Obtener follows the same stem change as tener in some forms: obtengo, obtienes, and so on.

example.en: I need to get a copy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Obtenidos reports a completed result and agrees with a masculine plural noun. Using obtener for people sounds deliberately cold and bureaucratic; it is more ordinary with things such as documents or results.

example.en: Documents obtained.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Octarino is the Spanish form used for octarine, the fictional color of magic in Terry Pratchett's Discworld stories. It is not a color in the real visible spectrum.

example.es: El mago describió una luz octarina.
example.en: The wizard described an octarine light.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With se and a short recipient word such as me or le, ocurre presents an idea as coming to someone rather than simply reporting that an event happens.

example.en: Another option occurs to her.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the West; a broad western geographic or cultural region
cardCatalog.noteEn: Oeste can name the compass direction or, by convention, a broad geographic or cultural region. The article el is used because the word is acting as a noun; context, not the article alone, selects the regional sense.

example.es: El texto habla de relaciones entre el este y el oeste.
example.en: The text discusses relations between the East and the West.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Oeste names the direction where the sun sets. This literal direction is distinct from el Oeste used as a broad cultural or geopolitical label.

example.es: El barco navega hacia el oeste.
example.en: The ship sails west.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Oh can express surprise or disappointment. Extra h letters in informal writing suggest that the sound is being drawn out; the spelling is flexible.

example.en: —The tickets are sold out. —Aw...

cardCatalog.noteEn: Writing extra letters stretches the spoken reaction. Here ohh shows pleased surprise at the measurement, rather than disappointment.

example.en: Ooh, how pretty!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ohhh represents an excited vocal reaction. Writers can lengthen the h to show that the sound is being held for longer.

example.en: Ooh, what a play!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Oído is the completed-action form of oír, ‘to hear.’ It keeps the written accent on í and stays unchanged after a form of haber.

example.en: I have never heard that song.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Oír means to perceive a sound. Its written accent keeps the two vowel sounds in separate syllables.

example.en: I can hear the music.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ola usually means a wave in water, but la ola also names the coordinated crowd movement called “the wave.”

example.es: El público empezó a hacer la ola.
example.en: The crowd started doing the wave.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Olifantes is the Spanish name for Tolkien's enormous elephant-like war animals.

example.en: The oliphaunts look like enormous elephants.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Olvida tells one friend, relative, or other familiar person to forget something. It comes from olvidar.

example.en: Forget that comment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Olvidado is the completed-action form of olvidar, “to forget.” It follows a form of haber in perfect constructions.

example.en: I have forgotten his name.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Olvida is the positive informal command for one listener, and lo attaches for the thing to forget. The written accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: If it does not work, forget it.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Olvidaría combines the dictionary form olvidar with the conditional ending -ía.

example.es: Sin una nota, olvidaría la cita.
example.en: Without a note, she would forget the appointment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ombligo means ‘navel.’ Ombliguismo figuratively criticizes excessive attention to oneself or one's own small circle.

example.es: El ensayo critica el ombliguismo del sector.
example.en: The essay criticizes the sector's navel-gazing.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Omisión literally names something left out. In por omisión, it refers to the option used when nothing else is specified.

example.es: El valor por omisión es cero.
example.en: The default value is zero.

cardCatalog.noteEn: An onda is a wave or repeating disturbance. Ondas is the plural and can describe electromagnetic, sound, water, or other waves.

example.es: Las ondas viajan por el agua.
example.en: The waves travel through the water.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ondea is a present-time form for one flag or other thing moving in waves.

example.es: La bandera ondea sobre el edificio.
example.en: The flag flies over the building.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Online is widely understood in Spanish technology contexts; en línea is the standard Spanish alternative.

example.en: The meeting will be online.

cardCatalog.answerEn: ooh (a sound of sudden interest or excitement)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ooh represents a drawn-out reaction rather than an ordinary dictionary noun or verb. Its tone can show delight, surprise, or sudden fascination.

example.en: Ooh, how interesting!

cardCatalog.answerEn: aww; ooh (a touched or charmed reaction)
cardCatalog.noteEn: The lengthened o represents an emotional reaction rather than an ordinary sentence word. This sense expresses being touched or charmed.

example.en: Aww, how lovely.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Opción is a feminine noun, so it uses una or la.

example.en: We have another option.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A sala de operaciones is an operating room used for surgery.

example.es: El hospital tiene dos salas de operaciones.
example.en: The hospital has two operating rooms.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Operando is the -ando form of operar. In a medical setting, operar means performing surgery on someone.

example.es: La cirujana está operando al paciente.
example.en: The surgeon is operating on the patient.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Una opinión is a belief or judgment rather than an established fact.

example.es: Ana explicó su opinión sobre el proyecto.
example.en: Ana explained her opinion about the project.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Optimista has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns; optimistas is plural.

example.en: They made optimistic calculations.

cardCatalog.answerEn: order; established social or political system
cardCatalog.noteEn: Orden is masculine when it means an arrangement, command, or established system.

example.es: El cambio alteró el orden político.
example.en: The change altered the political order.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ordenados describes several masculine or mixed items placed in an order. In a heading, that order can be a ranking by some criterion.

example.es: Los resultados están ordenados por fecha.
example.en: The results are ordered by date.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Orgullosa matches a feminine singular thing. With a verb of movement or appearance, English may express the same idea with an adverb such as proudly.

example.en: The winner walked proudly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Orquídeas is the plural of orquídea.

example.en: The orchids bloom in spring.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps apañáis refer to you all managing or getting along
cardCatalog.noteEn: Apañarse uses a matching small word: me, te, se, nos, os, or se. Os is the form for informal ‘you all,’ used mainly in Spain.

example.en: Do you all manage well together?

cardCatalog.answerEn: to you all; you all (informal plural, used mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Os is the short object form used with vosotros or vosotras. It identifies several informally addressed people as receiving or being affected by an action.

example.en: I am sending you all a photo.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Oscuridad is the noun related to oscuro, “dark.” It can describe absence of light or figurative obscurity.

example.es: No veo nada en la oscuridad.
example.en: I cannot see anything in the darkness.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Oscuro can describe low light literally. Applied to an idea or action, it can instead suggest something disturbing, sinister, or morally grim.

example.es: La historia tiene un final oscuro.
example.en: The story has a dark ending.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ostras is a mild informal exclamation of surprise. Its literal noun meaning is ‘oysters,’ but no oysters are meant in this reaction.

example.en: Wow, what a surprise!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Otorga is a form of otorgar for one person or thing. It is used for formally or figuratively giving a right, benefit, title, or power.

example.es: El permiso otorga acceso al edificio.
example.en: The permit grants access to the building.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Otras goes before a feminine plural noun. Spanish normally does not put un or una before otro or otra in this meaning.

example.en: We are looking for other answers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Oveja is grammatically feminine. The plural ovejas can refer to multiple sheep regardless of their sex.

example.en: The sheep crossed the field.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Paciente has the same written form for a male or female patient.

example.en: The patient is waiting for the doctor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Padres usually means ‘parents,’ but in a historical, genealogical, or religious setting it can refer to earlier generations or forefathers.

example.es: El relato recuerda a los padres de aquel pueblo.
example.en: The account remembers that people's forefathers.

cardCatalog.answerEn: smug; self-satisfied (in pagado de sí mismo)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pagado can literally mean paid, but pagado de sí mismo is a fixed description of a man who is excessively pleased with himself.

example.en: He seemed full of himself.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a computing context, páginas can refer to pages of technical documentation. A página man is a Unix-style reference page opened with the man command.

example.en: I consulted the manual pages.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Paisaje can describe the visible scenery of a place and also appears figuratively in compounds such as paisaje sonoro.

example.es: El paisaje cambia junto al mar.
example.en: The landscape changes by the sea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Palitos is a diminutive plural of palos. For food, it describes small stick-shaped pieces.

example.en: She cut the carrot into sticks.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Papel is masculine. In the game piedra, papel o tijeras, it names the paper option.

example.es: Elegí papel en la primera ronda.
example.en: I chose paper in the first round.

cardCatalog.answerEn: academic paper; research article (informal English borrowing)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish researchers sometimes use the borrowed English word paper informally. Artículo científico or trabajo de investigación are more fully Spanish alternatives.

example.en: They published a paper about energy.

cardCatalog.answerEn: academic papers; research articles (informal English borrowing)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish often prefers artículos or trabajos académicos. In academic conversation, the English borrowing paper is also used informally; its plural is papers.

example.en: She published two academic papers on astronomy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Papi is an affectionate, familiar way to address or refer to one's father.

example.en: Daddy, can I ask you a question?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Un par de before a plural noun commonly means “a couple of,” often an approximate small quantity rather than an exact matched pair.

example.en: I need a couple of minutes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For numbers, par means even. This is distinct from un par de, which means ‘a pair of’ or ‘a couple of.’

example.en: Twelve is an even number.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; introduces the topic or field that advice applies to
cardCatalog.noteEn: After consejo, guía, or recomendación, para can introduce the area or situation in which the advice is meant to be used.

example.es: Este consejo es para viajes largos.
example.en: This tip is for long trips.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After tener problemas, para can introduce the action that is difficult for someone. In natural English, tener problemas para dormir means “to have trouble sleeping,” not “to have problems in order to sleep.”

example.en: I have trouble concentrating.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Para can introduce the subject or case to which a statement applies.

example.es: La regla es válida para cualquier caso.
example.en: The rule is valid for any case.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; with (introducing what a talent applies to)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After don or talento, para introduces the subject, activity, or field in which the person is gifted.

example.en: She has a talent for music.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; at (a level or setting something is available for)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Para can introduce the level or setting that a resource supports. English may use “for” or, with a level, “at.”

example.es: No hay datos para ese nivel de detalle.
example.en: There is no data at that level of detail.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After tiempo, para introduces the action for which time is available. The action verb then stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: There is time to eat.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to; required after capacitar before the enabled action
cardCatalog.noteEn: Capacitar a alguien para hacer algo uses para before the action that the person becomes able or qualified to perform.

example.es: La práctica me capacita para responder.
example.en: The practice equips me to respond.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to; enough to (as part of como para)
for (enough or intended to cover a period of time)
to; enough for the following action
cardCatalog.noteEn: After suficiente, para introduces the action that the amount, ability, or age is enough to perform. The following action stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: There is enough light to read.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins para siempre, “forever”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Para and siempre form the fixed time expression para siempre. Here para does not introduce a purpose.

example.en: I want to live here forever.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Para can introduce the person, animal, or thing that something is meant for. This differs from para before an action verb, where it expresses a purpose such as “in order to.”

example.en: This gift is for Ana.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Para can introduce a period assigned to or covered by something, such as a reservation or pass. When simply describing how long an action continues, durante is often more natural.

example.es: La reserva es para toda la tarde.
example.en: The reservation is for the whole afternoon.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; required after preparar before what someone is prepared for
cardCatalog.noteEn: After preparar, para introduces the later situation, event, or action that the preparation is meant to handle.

example.en: We prepare for the interview.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; introduces the product that a price or rate applies to
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a word such as precio or tarifa, para can introduce the item or service whose price is being discussed.

example.es: Pedimos una tarifa para el servicio completo.
example.en: We asked for a rate for the complete service.

cardCatalog.answerEn: so that (before que and a desired result)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before que and a full event, para introduces the purpose of an action. Translate para que together as ‘so that’ or ‘in order that.’

example.es: Hablo despacio para que todos entiendan.
example.en: I speak slowly so that everyone understands.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for what purpose; what for (before qué)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In para qué, para asks about the goal or use of something. Qué keeps its written accent because it is asking a question.

example.en: What is this key for?

cardCatalog.noteEn: After resultados, para can introduce the words or expression whose results are being shown.

example.es: Hay diez resultados para esa frase.
example.en: There are ten results for that phrase.

cardCatalog.answerEn: at; with (introducing what someone is good or bad at)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After bueno or malo, para can introduce the activity or situation in which someone is skilled or unskilled.

example.en: She is good at languages.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; introduces what something is suitable for
cardCatalog.noteEn: After adecuado or a matching form such as adecuada or adecuados, para introduces the intended use, person, situation, or action.

example.es: Esta mesa es adecuada para niños.
example.en: This table is suitable for children.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; introduces what technical support covers or enables
cardCatalog.noteEn: After soporte, para can introduce a device, format, feature, or action that the system can work with.

example.es: La aplicación incluye soporte para exportar audio.
example.en: The application includes support for exporting audio.

cardCatalog.answerEn: before; until, after an amount of remaining time
cardCatalog.noteEn: After an expression such as queda tiempo, para que can introduce the later event that the remaining time leads up to. It does not express a desired purpose in this use.

example.es: Queda una hora para que empiece la película.
example.en: There is one hour left until the film starts.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; introduces a result blocked by being too much a certain way
cardCatalog.noteEn: After demasiado plus a description, para introduces the action or result that the excessive condition prevents. Use para que when that result has its own subject and verb.

example.es: Está demasiado lejos para que lo oiga.
example.en: He is too far away for me to hear him.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; corresponding to a word or meaning

cardCatalog.noteEn: Parad is the affirmative command for vosotros, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain. For an -ar verb such as parar, this command replaces final -r with -d.

example.en: Stop for a moment, everyone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A paradigma is a model or general way of understanding and approaching something. Despite its final -a, it is masculine: el paradigma.

example.en: That paradigm changed the research.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a form of haber, parado presents the stopping as completed.

example.en: The clock has stopped.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to stop; to make a stop

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pararnos combines parar with nos. It can describe us stopping our movement or pausing what we are doing.

example.en: We are going to stop for a moment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pararse uses the attached pronoun se. Before another action, pararse a means to stop what one is doing in order to perform that action.

example.es: Se paró a escuchar la música.
example.en: He stopped to listen to the music.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Paras is the present form of parar used for tú, one familiar listener. Before de and another action verb, it means that the listener stops doing that action.

example.en: You stop talking.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, a parche is a small software update intended to correct a defect or security weakness.

example.es: Instalaron un parche para corregir el fallo.
example.en: They installed a patch to fix the flaw.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Parecen is the plural present form of parecer. Before a noun it can describe resemblance, without saying that the things are literally identical.

example.en: Those clouds look like mountains.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pareja can name two people as a couple or one person's partner. This is the collective sense for the two people together.

example.en: Lucía and Marta are a couple.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pareja can mean one person's partner or a couple considered together. In a two-person interface label, it identifies the other partner.

example.en: My partner has arrived.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Parejas can mean romantic couples or matched pairs. In the test label it describes couples being tested together.

example.en: The game is for couples.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Paréntesis is written the same way in singular and plural. Context words reveal the number: un paréntesis is one parenthesis, while dos paréntesis is two parentheses.

example.en: The sentence contains two parentheses.

cardCatalog.answerEn: seems; looks (special form for a sought or unidentified thing)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Parezca is a form of parecer. It is used here because the speaker is looking for an option that has not yet been identified.

example.es: Busca un icono que parezca útil.
example.en: Look for an icon that seems useful.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Parezco is the yo form of parecer. With me and a, parecerse a means to resemble someone or something.

example.en: I look like my sister.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Parpadeando is the ongoing-action form of parpadear. It can describe eyes blinking or a light repeatedly switching on and off.

example.en: The screen keeps flashing.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In the formal expression por parte de, parte helps identify the person or group responsible for an action, judgment, or reaction.

example.es: Fue un error por parte del equipo.
example.en: It was a mistake on the team's part.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Parte can mean one portion of a whole. In money or ownership contexts, it can be the share that belongs to a person.

example.es: Cada socio recibió su parte de las ganancias.
example.en: Each partner received their share of the profits.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Parte can mean a physical part or, more broadly, a portion or area of a place or system.

example.es: Conozco varias partes de la ciudad.
example.en: I know several parts of the city.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A partida is one complete session of a board game, card game, or match. Partidas is the plural.

example.en: We played two games of chess.

cardCatalog.answerEn: spends (a period of time, with se)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasa is a present form of pasar. In se pasa plus a time period, it describes how someone spends that time.

example.en: He spends hours drawing.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasar has many meanings. When its subject is time, pasa means that time passes or goes by.

example.en: Time passes quickly.

cardCatalog.answerEn: turn; move on (an informal command to one person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasa is the tú command of pasar. Before de página, it tells one familiar person to turn the page or, figuratively, move on.

example.en: Turn the page carefully.

cardCatalog.answerEn: was passing through; used to pass (with por)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasaba is a background-past form of pasar. Followed by por and a place, it describes going through or by that place.

example.es: Pasaba por el centro cuando empezó a llover.
example.en: I was passing through downtown when it started to rain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a feminine time word such as semana, pasada identifies the most recent completed one. With a masculine time word, use pasado: el mes pasado.

example.en: She arrived last week.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasado is the completed-action form of pasar. With a form of haber and a duration, it says that an amount of time has gone by.

example.en: Three weeks have passed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasado is the completed-action form of pasar. In qué ha pasado, pasar means to happen rather than to move past a place.

example.en: What has happened here?

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a time expression, pasado or pasada identifies the immediately previous one. It matches the expression: el mes pasado, la semana pasada.

example.en: I traveled last month.

cardCatalog.answerEn: moved on; gone on to a new stage
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasado is the completed-action form of pasar. When pasar is followed by a, it can describe moving from one activity, topic, or stage to the next rather than physically passing by something.

example.es: El equipo ha pasado a otra tarea.
example.en: The team has moved on to another task.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasar often means “to pass,” but before a duration it can mean “to spend” that time. Pasan is the present form used for more than one person or thing.

example.es: Pasan dos horas en el parque.
example.en: They spend two hours in the park.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they pass; they go by (time periods)
cardCatalog.noteEn: When the subject is a plural span of time, pasar describes that time elapsing. Pasan is the present form used for a plural subject.

example.en: The years go by quickly.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to enter; to go beyond or past
cardCatalog.noteEn: On a notice, no pasar warns people not to enter or go beyond that point. Pasar has other meanings in other settings, including to pass something, to happen, and to spend time.

example.es: No podemos pasar por esa puerta.
example.en: We cannot go through that door.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to send; to pass (data through something)
to pass; to slip away (after dejar)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After dejar, pasar can describe allowing an opportunity, moment, or situation to go by instead of acting on it.

example.en: Don't let the opportunity pass.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasar often means “to pass,” but with an amount or period of time it can describe spending that time in an activity, place, or state.

example.en: I want to spend an hour reading.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to switch; to move (from one thing to another)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasar has several meanings. With de for a starting point and a for an endpoint, it describes changing from one option, stage, or system to another.

example.en: We switched from the train to the bus.

cardCatalog.answerEn: will be passed; will be transferred
to have it; in pasarlo bien, to have a good time
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasarlo combines pasar with attached lo. In the fixed expression pasarlo bien, the two words describe enjoying oneself rather than physically passing an object.

example.en: We want to have a good time.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to spend (a stretch of time), with me marking the speaker
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasarme combines the unchanged form pasar with me. In pasarse + time + activity, it describes filling that period with the activity.

example.es: Voy a pasarme la tarde leyendo.
example.en: I am going to spend the afternoon reading.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to pass her to me; put her on
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasármela combines pasar + me + la: pasar means “to pass,” me means “to me,” and la replaces a feminine person or thing. Object pronouns can attach to an infinitive.

example.en: The bottle is over there; can you pass it to me?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasaron is the completed-past they-form of pasar. With a recipient such as me and an object, pasar can mean to hand or give that object to someone.

example.en: They handed me a copy.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to pass to you; to hand to you
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasarte combines the unchanged dictionary form pasar with te, which identifies one familiar listener as the recipient.

example.en: I am going to pass you the report.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasas is the familiar singular present form of pasar. With a recipient word such as me and an object, it means passing or handing that object to the listener.

example.en: Could you pass me the water?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasar often means “to pass” or “to go by.” With a period or amount of time, it can instead describe how someone spends that time.

example.en: You spend two hours here.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you stop by; you come by
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasas is the present form of pasar for one familiar person. With por and a place, pasar can mean making a brief visit or coming through that place.

example.en: Are you stopping by my house this afternoon?

cardCatalog.answerEn: I spend; I may spend (a length of time)
cardCatalog.noteEn: With me, pase comes from pasarse and describes spending time in a state or activity. The ordinary present form paso changes to pase after a trigger such as aunque when the situation is treated as uncertain rather than stated as fact.

example.es: Aunque me pase una semana enfermo, terminaré el trabajo.
example.en: Even if I spend a week sick, I will finish the work.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I spent (time doing something, as part of me pasé)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasé is a completed past form of pasar. With me and a stated period, me pasé describes how long the speaker spent doing an activity; the activity can follow in a form ending in -ando or -iendo.

example.en: I spent an hour cleaning.

cardCatalog.answerEn: way; passage (as part of dar paso a)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Paso can mean a step or passage. Together with dar and a, it forms dar paso a, “to give way to” or “to make way for.”

example.es: La noche da paso al día.
example.en: Night gives way to day.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasar can mean spending time when it is followed by a period or amount of time. Paso is the present form for the speaker.

example.en: I spend an hour reading.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Patata is the usual word for “potato” in Spain. Papa is common in much of Latin America.

example.es: Añade una patata a la sopa.
example.en: Add a potato to the soup.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Paternidad can name the state of being a parent or the work and approach involved in raising children.

example.es: El curso trata sobre la paternidad.
example.en: The course is about parenting.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Patina tells one familiar person to skate. It is the positive tú command of patinar.

example.en: Skate carefully.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Patio can describe an outdoor area beside or enclosed by a house. In a school setting, the same word can mean playground or schoolyard.

example.es: Los niños juegan en el patio de la casa.
example.en: The children play in the yard of the house.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Patio can mean a courtyard or yard more generally. With de mi colegio, it refers to the school's outdoor play area.

example.es: Los niños juegan en el patio del colegio.
example.en: The children play in the school playground.

cardCatalog.answerEn: alone; in peace (inside dejar en paz)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Paz normally means peace. In dejar a alguien en paz, the full expression means leaving that person alone or no longer bothering them.

example.en: Please leave me alone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: At a restaurant, pedir is the ordinary verb for ordering food or drink. The same verb can mean asking for or requesting something elsewhere.

example.en: I am going to order the soup.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to ask you for; to request from you
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pedirte combines pedir, 'to ask for,' with te, which marks one familiar person as the person being asked. Te is attached because pedir is in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: I want to ask you for some advice.

cardCatalog.answerEn: stick it; attach it (command to several people, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pegad is the vosotros command of pegar. Lo means ‘it’ and attaches to the end.

example.en: Stick it on the wall.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pegado comes from pegar, “to stick.” With estar and a, it can describe someone or something pressed against or extremely close to another person or thing.

example.es: El armario está pegado a la pared.
example.en: The wardrobe is right up against the wall.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for us to indulge in; for us to go through (an excessive amount of something)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pegarnos is pegar with nos attached. In pegarse un atracón, it does not mean physically hitting; the whole expression means indulging in or doing far too much of something.

example.es: Decidimos pegarnos un atracón de series.
example.en: We decided to binge on TV series.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pelo usually refers to hair collectively and is masculine.

example.en: He has long hair.

cardCatalog.answerEn: effort; completes merecer la pena, “to be worth it”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pena can mean sorrow, pity, or a penalty elsewhere. In the fixed expression merecer la pena, the whole expression means that something is worth the time or effort.

example.en: It is worth waiting.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pena can name sorrow or distress. In una pena, it commonly expresses that something is unfortunate or disappointing.

example.es: Fue una pena perder el tren.
example.en: It was a shame to miss the train.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes a duras penas, “barely”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Penas literally relates to troubles or suffering, but the whole fixed expression a duras penas means with great difficulty or barely.

example.en: She could barely speak.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Penetrado is penetrar's completed-action form. It can describe entering something physically or, figuratively, reaching beneath the surface of a person's thoughts or feelings.

example.es: La luz ha penetrado en la habitación.
example.en: The light has entered the room.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Penetraste is the completed past form of penetrar for one familiar person. Penetrar en can describe entering a physical place or reaching into someone's private thoughts and feelings.

example.en: You entered the cave.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you thought; you were thinking (informal singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pensabas is the imperfect past form of pensar used for tú. The imperfect presents the thought as an ongoing past viewpoint or background assumption.

example.en: You thought it was Monday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: thought; considered (completed-action form used after haber)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pensado is the regular completed-action form of pensar. After he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han, it stays unchanged and helps describe a thought connected to the present.

example.en: I have thought about another option.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pensé is the completed-past form of pensar for the speaker. Before que, it introduces what the speaker thought.

example.en: I thought you were arriving tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With el, la, los, or las, peor normally means “worst.” Without an article it often means “worse.”

example.en: That was the worst option.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Percatado is percatarse's completed-action form. With se and a form of haber, it says that someone has noticed or realized something.

example.es: Los técnicos se han percatado del error.
example.en: The technicians have noticed the error.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to miss; to miss out on
cardCatalog.noteEn: With a matching me, te, or se marker, perderse algo means failing to experience an event or opportunity. With two verbs, that marker may appear before the first conjugated verb: no te quieres perder.

example.en: I don't want to miss the movie.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The ending -ás added to perder marks a future action by informal singular “you.”

example.en: You will lose the opportunity.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The ending -é added to perder marks a future action by “I.”

example.en: I will miss the train.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you were wasting; you used to waste
cardCatalog.noteEn: Perdías is an imperfect past form of perder. The -ías ending presents the wasted time as an ongoing or repeated past situation rather than one completed loss.

example.en: You used to waste time waiting.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With causa, perdida forms causa perdida, a situation no longer expected to succeed.

example.es: Todos creen que es una causa perdida.
example.en: Everyone thinks it is a lost cause.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Perdida describes a feminine person or thing that is lost. It can describe not knowing where one is or being unable to find one's way.

example.en: The hiker was still lost.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Perdiendo is the ongoing-action form of perder. After a form of estar, it presents the loss as in progress.

example.en: I am losing patience.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With a matching me, te, se, or nos marker, perderse can mean to miss an event or opportunity, not only to become lost.

example.en: You are missing the movie.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Perdona is the familiar singular command of perdonar, “to forgive.” It is commonly used to apologize or to get one person's attention.

example.en: Excuse me, do you have a minute?

cardCatalog.answerEn: excuse me; forgive me (said to several familiar people)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Perdonad is the positive command used in Spain when addressing more than one familiar listener. Me attaches to it and identifies the speaker asking to be excused.

example.en: Excuse me, I am late.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A periodo is a defined span or stage of time. Periodos is its plural form.

example.en: We compared two historical periods.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Permanecer emphasizes continuing in the same place, condition, or state.

example.en: The door must remain closed.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you will remain; you will stay

cardCatalog.noteEn: Permanente has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: They are looking for a permanent solution.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In poder permitirse algo, permitir is part of the expression for having enough money, time, or resources for something. This differs from permitir meaning to allow.

example.en: We cannot afford another expense.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Permitirá keeps the whole dictionary form permitir and adds -á for one future subject or formal listener.

example.es: El pase permitirá abrir la puerta.
example.en: The pass will allow the door to be opened.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all persevere; you all keep going
cardCatalog.noteEn: Perseveráis is the present form used with vosotros, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain.

example.en: If you all persevere, you will learn a lot.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Persiguen is a present form of perseguir for several doers. It can describe a physical chase, or figuratively describe memories, sounds, or worries that keep troubling someone.

example.en: Those memories haunt me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Personalizados describes masculine plural things adapted to a particular person, purpose, or preference.

example.en: We sell custom designs.
