cardCatalog.noteEn: It is the ability to notice and understand things clearly.

example.en: Her insight solved the problem.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Perspicaz has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: It was an insightful observation.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pertenezco is the present form of pertenecer used by the speaker. Pertenecer normally takes a before the group, category, or owner that something belongs to.

example.es: Pertenezco a un club de lectura.
example.en: I belong to a book club.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pesa is the present form of pesar used to state the weight of one thing.

example.en: The box weighs ten kilos.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of a pesar de, ‘despite’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pesar normally relates to weight or regret, but inside a pesar de the three words form one connector meaning ‘despite’ or ‘in spite of.’

example.es: Salimos a pesar de la lluvia.
example.en: We went out despite the rain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Peta- is placed before a unit to multiply it by one quadrillion, or 10¹⁵. For example, a petabyte is 10¹⁵ bytes in decimal SI usage.

example.en: Peta- represents a factor of 10¹⁵.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In informal Spanish, petardo can describe a person or thing that is a bore or a pain. As an adjective, its ending follows the noun it describes.

example.en: It was a pretty tiresome speech.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Photoshop is a product name retained in Spanish. Con Photoshop means that the software is the tool used for the edit.

example.en: She edited the photo with Photoshop.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The informal verb photoshopear is built from the product name Photoshop. Photoshopeado is its masculine singular completed-action form, used here as a description.

example.en: The background is Photoshopped.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pide is the present form of pedir used with one other person or thing. With passive se, se pide focuses on what is requested rather than who requests it.

example.en: A password is requested.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pedir is used when requesting a thing or action. Preguntar is normally used instead when asking a question.

example.en: You ask the waiter for the bill.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pidiendo is the ongoing-action form of pedir. The e in pedir changes to i before the -iendo ending: pedir becomes pidiendo.

example.en: She came in asking for help.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Piedra is feminine. In piedra, papel o tijeras, it names the rock option.

example.es: La piedra vence a las tijeras.
example.en: Rock beats scissors.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I lose; I may lose (special form used for a caused or uncertain action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pierda is a special form of perder. The surrounding words identify who loses something.

example.es: No quiero que pierda las llaves.
example.en: I do not want her to lose the keys.

cardCatalog.answerEn: miss out; miss it (in a negative informal command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In no te lo pierdas, ordinary pierdes changes to pierdas because the speaker is telling one familiar person not to miss something.

example.en: Don't miss the concert.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pierdo is the present yo form of perder. With oportunidad it means missing or losing an opportunity.

example.es: Pierdo una oportunidad si no voy.
example.en: I miss an opportunity if I do not go.

cardCatalog.answerEn: got; picked up (a car or other item)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pillado is the completed-action form of pillar. In informal Spain Spanish, pillar can mean to get, obtain, or pick up something; with has, it asks about an action connected to the present.

example.es: He pillado un coche de segunda mano.
example.en: I have picked up a second-hand car.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to get; to pick up (a signal or internet access, informal)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pillar has several informal meanings, especially in Spain. With a signal, coverage, or internet access, it can mean managing to get or pick it up.

example.en: I cannot pick up a signal here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pillemos is a “we” proposal form of pillar, an informal verb that can mean “to get” or “to grab.” The -emos ending turns pillar into a suggestion for the group.

example.en: Let's get a taxi.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In this fruit label, piña means ‘pineapple.’ It has other regional meanings in different contexts.

example.es: Cortaron dos piñas para el postre.
example.en: They cut two pineapples for dessert.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This sense names an artistic picture made with paint, not the paint material itself.

example.es: El museo compró una pintura antigua.
example.en: The museum bought an old painting.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In its material sense, pintura is the coating that can crack, not an individual painting or picture.

example.es: La pintura de la puerta se agrieta.
example.en: The paint on the door is cracking.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to step on; be stepped on

cardCatalog.noteEn: Piso can mean a floor or storey. In Spain it also commonly means an apartment or flat where someone lives.

example.en: We rented a small apartment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Píxeles is the plural of píxel, one tiny picture element in a digital image or screen.

example.en: The image has many pixels.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pizza is a borrowed food name pronounced naturally in Spanish.

example.en: We ordered a large pizza.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In laboratory language, placa can mean a shallow dish used to grow or observe cells. This is distinct from its everyday meanings such as plate, plaque, or sign.

example.es: La técnica coloca la muestra en una placa.
example.en: The technician places the sample in a dish.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Plagadas agrees with a feminine plural noun and is followed by de before what fills or overruns it.

example.es: Las calles están plagadas de baches.
example.en: The streets are riddled with potholes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: mode; like (fixed part of estar en plan)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In colloquial estar en plan, plan does not mean a literal plan. It helps frame an attitude, manner, or loose quotation.

example.en: He was like, 'It's no big deal.'

cardCatalog.noteEn: Planta can mean a plant, the sole of a foot, or a floor in a building. On an elevator sign or building directory, planta means a floor of a building.

example.es: La oficina está en la tercera planta.
example.en: The office is on the third floor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This is the living-organism sense of planta, not a floor of a building or an industrial facility.

example.en: The plant needs light.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In slime molds, plasmodios are the creeping, multinucleate stages of the organism.

example.es: Los plasmodios se desplazan hacia el alimento.
example.en: The plasmodia move toward food.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In this image, plátanos are bananas. Regional usage can distinguish or combine bananas and plantains differently.

example.en: She added two bananas to the smoothie.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Platillo is literally a small plate or saucer. Together with volante, it is the conventional Spanish term for a flying saucer.

example.es: La película muestra varios platillos volantes.
example.en: The film shows several flying saucers.

cardCatalog.answerEn: platter (the magnetic disk inside a drive)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Plato normally means a plate or dish. In computer hardware, a plato is one of the flat circular surfaces on which a hard drive stores data.

example.es: El disco tiene dos platos magnéticos.
example.en: The disk has two magnetic platters.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Plum is sound-imitating writing used for a sudden heavy impact or fall.

example.en: The box fell: thud!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish writes the astronomical name Plutón with an accent on the final syllable.

example.es: Plutón está más lejos del Sol que Neptuno.
example.en: Pluto is farther from the Sun than Neptune.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pluviosidad is a technical or formal word for how much rain a place receives over a period.

example.en: Rainfall increases in autumn.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a describing word, poco often says that a quality is present to an insufficient degree. Poco claro therefore means “not very clear,” while un poco claro would literally mean “a little clear.”

example.en: The sign is not very visible.

cardCatalog.answerEn: a short time; soon (inside dentro de poco)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After dentro de, poco names an unspecified short interval from now. The full phrase dentro de poco means ‘soon’ or ‘before long.’

example.en: I'll be back soon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pocos describes a small number of masculine plural things. Use pocas with a feminine plural noun.

example.en: Few days remain.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we can; we may (special form after a purpose or uncertainty)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Podamos is a present subjunctive form of poder for nosotros. A purpose introduced by para que calls for this special form because its result is intended rather than stated as a fact.

example.es: Habla despacio para que podamos entender.
example.en: Speak slowly so that we can understand.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all can; you all may (informal plural)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Podré is the future form of poder for the speaker. Poder uses the shortened future stem podr-, and the ending -é supplies both “I” and “will.”

example.en: Tomorrow I will be able to help you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Podría is a form of poder used for a possible or imagined option. Here the unspoken subject is yo, so it means “I could.” The same written form can also go with one other person or thing when context supplies that subject.

example.en: I could call tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Podría is a form of poder used for an imagined possibility. To make this form, poder changes to podr- and adds -ía. The same written form can mean “I could” or can go with one other person or thing; the stated subject shows which meaning applies.

example.en: The meeting could be brief.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we could (a possibility or tentative suggestion)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Podríamos is the “would/could” form of poder for “we.” Poder keeps its whole dictionary form and adds -íamos. It often makes a suggestion sound tentative rather than stating a firm plan.

example.en: We could leave early.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you could; you would be able to
cardCatalog.noteEn: Podrías is the conditional, or “would,” form of poder for one familiar person. Poder changes to the irregular stem podr- and adds -ías; the following action stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: You could come tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Polaca describes a feminine singular person or thing as Polish. The masculine singular form is polaco.

example.en: She bought a Polish magazine.

cardCatalog.answerEn: polymorphic; able to change form (masculine singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Polimórfico literally means ‘having many forms.’ Polymorphic malicious code changes its visible code pattern while preserving its behavior, which can make simple signature matching harder.

example.en: They analyzed a polymorphic program.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here polos means the geographic North and South Poles, not rods, magnets, or clothing.

example.es: Los polos reciben poca luz en invierno.
example.en: The poles receive little light in winter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pomelo is the usual word for grapefruit in Spain. Toronja is common in many parts of Latin America.

example.en: Grapefruits can be bitter.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I will put; I will set up
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pondré is the future form of poner for yo, 'I.' Poner changes its stem to pondr- before the future ending -é. With me and an item, context can suggest putting it on or getting oneself set up with it.

example.en: Tomorrow I will install a new lock.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I would put; I would place
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pondría is the conditional form of poner for the speaker. The ending -ía supplies the “would” meaning, while pondr- is the irregular conditional stem.

example.es: Yo pondría la mesa junto a la ventana.
example.en: I would put the table next to the window.

cardCatalog.answerEn: puts; subjects, as part of poner a prueba
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pone is a form of poner. In poner a prueba, the expression means to test someone or something.

example.es: El viaje pone a prueba su paciencia.
example.en: The trip tests her patience.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ponemos is the present form of poner for nosotros. With límites it means setting or imposing limits.

example.en: We set clear limits on the project.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A ponencia is a formal presentation, often at a conference or professional event.

example.es: La ponencia empieza a las diez.
example.en: The talk starts at ten.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Poner is an irregular verb whose first-person present form is pongo. Its dictionary form stays poner after words such as deber or poder.

example.es: Voy a poner el plato en la mesa.
example.en: I am going to put the plate on the table.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to get started; to get to work (on something)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ponerse is the dictionary form poner with se attached. In ponerse a ello, it describes turning one's attention to a matter and beginning work on it.

example.es: Tenemos tiempo para ponernos a trabajar.
example.en: We have time to get to work.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to make a killing; to profit greatly (in ponerse las botas)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ponerse normally means putting something on or entering a state. In the informal expression ponerse las botas, the whole phrase can mean profiting or enjoying something in abundance.

example.es: Los vendedores se pusieron las botas durante la feria.
example.en: The sellers made a killing during the fair.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pongámonos combines the group command pongamos with nos. The final s disappears before nos, and the written accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: Let's put on our coats.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they start; they get down to it (special form of poner)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pongan is a form of poner for more than one person. It is used here after an instruction rather than as a plain statement; ordinary ponen changes to pongan. With se and a following action, se pongan a means that they start that action.

example.es: Quiero que se pongan a estudiar.
example.en: I want them to start studying.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I put on; I start playing
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pongo is the irregular present form of poner for the speaker. With music or a recording, poner commonly means putting it on or starting it.

example.en: I put on music while I cook.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I roll (my eyes; in poner los ojos en blanco)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pongo is the present ‘I’ form of poner, normally ‘to put.’ In the complete expression poner los ojos en blanco, natural English uses ‘to roll one's eyes.’

example.es: Pongo los ojos en blanco sin querer.
example.en: I roll my eyes unintentionally.

cardCatalog.answerEn: made; used to make (someone feel a certain way)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ponía is a past form of poner used for a repeated or background past situation. With an affected person and a describing word, poner means to cause that person to enter the stated condition.

example.en: The wait used to make me impatient.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Poniendo is the -iendo form of poner. With se and a description, it belongs to ponerse and presents a change into a new state.

example.es: El cielo se va poniendo oscuro.
example.en: The sky is gradually getting dark.

cardCatalog.answerEn: pop; a sudden appearance sound effect
cardCatalog.noteEn: POP can imitate the abrupt sound of something appearing or opening. It is a sound effect, not the separate use of pop for a music genre.

example.en: Pop! The bubble disappeared.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In cultura popular, popular refers to entertainment, ideas, and references widely shared by the public.

example.en: It is a popular song.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After empezar or comenzar, por can introduce the first thing or action in an ordered process.

example.en: Let's start with the beginning.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a place in a sequence, por can mark an approximate position rather than a route or cause.

example.es: La explicación aparece por la página diez.
example.en: The explanation appears around page ten.

cardCatalog.answerEn: around; over (in por aquí, “around here” or “this way”)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Por can introduce what the participants hope to win, keep, or decide through a contest.

example.en: They played for the championship.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses por after atracción or sentir atracción to introduce the object of attraction, where English often uses to.

example.en: She feels an attraction to the sea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Por can identify the feature used to sort or organize things. In a heading, por causa means that the entries are grouped according to their cause.

example.en: We sort the books by topic.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Por can identify the channel used to communicate: por teléfono, por radio, or por videollamada. Natural English often uses ‘on,’ ‘by,’ or ‘over’ rather than translating por with one fixed word.

example.en: We talk by video call.

cardCatalog.answerEn: by; according to (introducing what determines a result)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After determinado or a similar description, por introduces the rule, cause, or factor that sets the result. English commonly uses “by.”

example.es: La fecha está determinada por el calendario.
example.en: The date is determined by the calendar.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Por can present a period as the span through which a situation lasts. This is different from para when para points toward a purpose or intended deadline.

example.en: They lived there for many years.

cardCatalog.answerEn: why?; for what reason? (with qué left understood)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the short echo ¿por?, the usual qué is omitted because the question being repeated is already clear.

example.en: “We have to leave.” “Why?”

cardCatalog.noteEn: Por can introduce the evidence or clue that lets someone know or recognize something.

example.en: I recognized him from his voice.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for (as part of vaya por Dios)
no separate English word; completes ir a por, “to go get”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por completes a por before the item being fetched in this common Spain construction.

example.en: She went to get the coat.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por casualidad
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por combines with casualidad to mean that something happened by chance.

example.en: We met by chance.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por encima de
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por, encima, and de work together to mean “above,” “over,” or “more than.”

example.es: Está por encima de la puerta.
example.en: It is above the door.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por mucho que
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por begins the concessive connector por mucho que, used to say that a result holds no matter how much something happens.

example.es: Por mucho que preguntes, no lo sé.
example.en: No matter how much you ask, I do not know.

cardCatalog.answerEn: by (as part of por omisión, “by default”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por begins the fixed expression por omisión, which describes what happens automatically when no other choice is made.

example.es: La respuesta por omisión es no.
example.en: The default answer is no.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; begins por primera vez, ‘for the first time’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por is fixed with primera vez in this time expression. Its meaning comes from the complete expression rather than a price, cause, path, or per-unit use.

example.en: We visited Granada for the first time.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por si, 'in case'
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por combines with unaccented si before a possible event to form por si.

example.es: Lleva agua por si hace calor.
example.en: Take water in case it is hot.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins por si acaso, ‘just in case’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por is fixed inside the three-word precaution expression por si acaso.

example.en: Take water just in case.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for (as part of por una vez, “for once”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por introduces the one exceptional occasion in the fixed expression por una vez.

example.en: For once, we arrived early.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes si no fuera por, if it weren't for
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the fixed counterfactual expression si no fuera por, por introduces the person or thing whose presence changes the result.

example.es: Si no fuera por Ana, llegaríamos tarde.
example.en: If it weren't for Ana, we would arrive late.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; introduces what a longing is directed toward
cardCatalog.noteEn: After anhelo, por can introduce the desired person, thing, or action.

example.en: Her longing to travel grew.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After multiplicar, por introduces the factor: multiplicar cuatro por tres means ‘multiply four by three.’

example.en: Multiply six by five.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; introduces what is paid for or what brings a consequence
cardCatalog.noteEn: After pagar, por can introduce either something bought or the reason for a figurative cost or punishment.

example.en: They paid for the tickets.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After pasar, por introduces the place someone passes through or stops by.

example.en: I’ll stop by the bank later.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a unit of time, por can distribute an amount across each unit, corresponding to English “per” or “a”: por día, por semana, por noche.

example.en: I read one hour per day.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Por can introduce the unit used to divide or distribute a quantity. The unit after por stays singular when it means “for each one.”

example.en: There are two books per student.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por ejemplo (“for example”)
no separate English word; part of por favor (“please”)
no separate English word; part of por parte de
no separate English word; part of por supuesto (“of course”)
for; required after preguntar before the person sought
cardCatalog.noteEn: Preguntar por alguien means asking to speak to, see, or locate that person.

example.en: Someone asked for you.

cardCatalog.answerEn: about; required after preocupado before the cause of concern
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish normally uses por after preocupado, preocupada, preocupados, or preocupadas to introduce what causes the worry.

example.en: We are worried about the exam.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of la razón por la que, “the reason why”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses por before la que to connect a stated reason with the following explanation. Natural English normally uses “why.”

example.es: Esa es la razón por la que vine.
example.en: That is the reason why I came.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Por can introduce the means or system through which something is controlled. Here the following abbreviation names remote control.

example.es: El juguete funciona por control remoto.
example.en: The toy works by remote control.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por lo que
no separate English word; works with por debajo after an amount
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a difference in points or another measured amount, por links that amount to debajo or encima. English usually expresses the whole combination as an amount behind, below, ahead, or above.

example.en: They are three points behind.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to; toward the goal of (after luchar)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After luchar, por can introduce the goal being pursued. When that goal is an action, natural English often uses “to” rather than translating por as “for.”

example.en: I strive to learn more.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for; in support of a cause
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a group, campaign, or movement, por can introduce the cause it supports.

example.es: Participan en una campaña por la igualdad.
example.en: They are taking part in a campaign for equality.

cardCatalog.answerEn: for (introducing what someone is thanked for)
through; along; down; via (a movement path)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Por can mark the path followed during movement. English may choose through, along, down, or via according to the route.

example.en: We went down the path.

cardCatalog.answerEn: through; around (in correr por la mente)
to; connects an urgency or rush to the action prompting it
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a noun such as urgencia or prisa, por can introduce the action someone is eager or pressed to complete. Natural English often uses ‘to’ instead of translating por as ‘for.’

example.en: There was a rush to finish.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Porcina describes something related to pigs. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular noun such as gripe.

example.es: La granja aplica controles de sanidad porcina.
example.en: The farm applies swine-health controls.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Porno is a common shortened form of pornografía.

example.en: The platform blocks pornographic content.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Portadas is the completed-action form of portar, “to carry,” changed to match a feminine plural subject. In a passive pattern such as eran portadas, it says that the action was done to those things.

example.es: Las cajas fueron portadas por dos personas.
example.en: The boxes were carried by two people.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun in computing, el portátil is a laptop. As an adjective, portátil means portable.

example.es: Mi portátil necesita una batería nueva.
example.en: My laptop needs a new battery.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With se, posa is the singular present form of posarse, used when an animal or object comes to rest on a surface.

example.es: El pájaro se posa en la rama.
example.en: The bird lands on the branch.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Posee is the present form of poseer for he, she, it, or formal you.

example.en: The company owns two buildings.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A posgrado is advanced study pursued after completing an initial university degree.

example.en: She is doing graduate studies in history.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Posmodernidad names the cultural and intellectual condition or period associated with postmodernism.

example.en: The essay analyzes postmodernity.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a noun, postal describes something belonging to or used by the mail service, such as una balanza postal or un código postal.

example.en: I need the postal code.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Postal (part of the band name Postal Service)

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a noun, potencial describes a capacity or effect that may become real but is not guaranteed.

example.en: It is a potential risk.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In mathematics, a potencia is the result of raising a number to an exponent. The plural is potencias.

example.es: Dos, cuatro y ocho son potencias de dos.
example.en: Two, four, and eight are powers of two.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Potente has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns. Potentes is its plural form.

example.en: We need powerful engines.

cardCatalog.answerEn: practice; recommended way of doing something
cardCatalog.noteEn: Práctica can mean repeated training, but in buena práctica it means a sound or recommended method used in a field.

example.es: Guardar copias es una buena práctica.
example.en: Keeping backups is a good practice.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Preferiría keeps the full verb preferir and adds -ía. This conditional form makes the preference sound less direct.

example.en: I would prefer to wait here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A prefijo is an element placed before a word or unit, such as re- or kilo-. Prefijos is the plural.

example.es: Kilo- y mega- son prefijos comunes.
example.en: Kilo- and mega- are common prefixes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pregunta tells one familiar person to ask. With por, it means asking to speak to or find someone.

example.en: Ask for the director.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pregunta is a feminine noun when it names a question. The same spelling can also be a command meaning ‘ask’; context distinguishes the two uses.

example.en: I have a question.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Preguntarle combines preguntar with attached le. The unchanged dictionary form names the action, while le identifies one person being asked.

example.en: You can ask the neighbor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pregunto normally means “I ask.” With me, the form me pregunto means that the speaker wonders or asks himself or herself a question.

example.en: I wonder whether Ana will come.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Premio can name something won or awarded, including a promotional prize.

example.en: The prize was a trip.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Preocupa is singular because one situation or idea causes the worry. The affected person appears separately as me, te, le, nos, os, or les.

example.en: The delay worries us.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Preocupados describes more than one masculine person or a mixed group. A feminine group uses preocupadas.

example.es: Mis vecinos están preocupados por el humo.
example.en: My neighbors are worried about the smoke.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Preocuparte combines preocupar with te, the matching marker for one familiar listener. The marker attaches to the end of the verb's dictionary form.

example.en: You do not have to worry.

cardCatalog.answerEn: worry (special form after no in a command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Preocupes is the form used when telling one familiar person not to worry. The positive command is preocúpate, but the negative pattern is no te preocupes.

example.en: Do not worry yet.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Prepara is a present form of preparar for one person or thing. A short word before it can identify the person being prepared.

example.es: El curso te prepara para el examen.
example.en: The course prepares you for the exam.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Preparando is the ongoing-action form of preparar. The attached me identifies the speaker as the person getting ready, and the written accent preserves the word's original stress.

example.en: I am getting ready for the trip.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Presentada is the feminine singular completed-action form of presentar. It can describe a feminine noun such as guía, idea, or propuesta.

example.en: The idea was presented yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Presentar can introduce a person to an audience or unveil something publicly.

example.es: Van a presentar el nuevo diseño.
example.en: They are going to unveil the new design.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a time label, el presente contrasts with el pasado, the past.

example.es: La gráfica llega hasta el presente.
example.en: The chart reaches the present.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Presidencial describes something related to a president. It has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns: discurso presidencial and campaña presidencial.

example.en: We watched the presidential debate.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to pay (as part of prestar atención)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Prestar normally means “to lend,” but prestar atención is a fixed expression meaning “to pay attention.”

example.en: Pay attention to the explanation.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Prestaras is the -ra form used for an imagined condition. In prestar atención, prestar means “to pay.”

example.en: If you paid attention, you would remember more.

cardCatalog.answerEn: pay (attention; special form in a negative informal command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Prestes comes from prestar. When telling one familiar person not to do something, ordinary prestas changes to no prestes. In prestar atención, prestar means “to pay” attention rather than “to lend.”

example.en: Do not pay attention to the rumor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Presupuesto is a plan for how much money is available and how it will be spent. It can also mean a price estimate or quote in another context.

example.es: El proyecto tiene un presupuesto pequeño.
example.en: The project has a small budget.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pretender usually means to intend, aim, or claim—not the English verb “pretend.” Pretendías presents one familiar person's intention as background in the past.

example.en: Did you intend to stay here?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Primero shortens to primer directly before a masculine singular noun: el primer libro. In other positions, use primero.

example.es: Es mi primer viaje a México.
example.en: It is my first trip to Mexico.

cardCatalog.answerEn: first; printed before a verb where standard Spanish would use primero
cardCatalog.noteEn: Primer is the shortened form of primero used before a masculine singular noun, as in el primer paso. Before an instruction verb such as pulse, standard Spanish uses primero instead. The comic visibly prints primer.

example.en: First, press the button.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Primeras matches a feminine plural noun.

example.en: They were the first visits.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Primero can describe the first step in an order. In a question about preparation, it can mean “first” or “beforehand.”

example.en: Read the instructions first.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After el, primero can stand on its own and refer back to the first previously mentioned masculine item; the name of that item does not need to be repeated.

example.es: Prefiero el primero de los dos planes.
example.en: I prefer the first of the two plans.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Primero can claim or state first position in an order or ranking. With a movement verb such as ir, it can describe the current leader: va primero means that a person or team is in first place.

example.es: Daniel va primero en la carrera.
example.en: Daniel is leading the race.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Principal identifies the most important or central one. It has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.

example.en: This is the main entrance.

cardCatalog.answerEn: beginning; start (as part of al principio)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Al principio places a state or event at the beginning of a process, story, or period.

example.en: I didn't understand at first.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In logic or another technical field, principio can name a basic rule or proposition. This differs from al principio, which refers to the beginning of something.

example.es: Es un principio básico de la lógica.
example.en: It is a basic principle of logic.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pringao is an informal, insulting spelling of pringado in which the d is dropped in speech. The feminine form is pringada.

example.en: Do not call him a loser.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Probablemente combines probable with -mente to describe a claim as likely rather than certain.

example.en: She will probably arrive late.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Probado is probar's completed-action form. After a form of haber, it asks or states whether an option has been tried.

example.en: Have you all tried another solution?

cardCatalog.answerEn: we try; we test an option
cardCatalog.noteEn: Probamos is a present form of probar for a group including the speaker. With con, it introduces a person, thing, or approach chosen to see whether it works.

example.en: We try another key.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Procede is a form of proceder for one thing. Proceder de identifies that thing's source or origin.

example.en: This coffee comes from Colombia.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, a procesador is the component that carries out instructions.

example.en: The processor runs the program.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, a procesador is the hardware that carries out program instructions. Procesadores is plural.

example.en: The server uses several processors.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Productividad measures how much useful work or output is produced with the available time and resources.

example.es: La nueva herramienta aumentó la productividad.
example.en: The new tool increased productivity.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Profundidad can be physical depth or the amount of complexity and richness in a subject.

example.en: The essay has a lot of depth.

cardCatalog.answerEn: deep; deeply (describing how an action is done)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Some Spanish describing words can also tell how an action is done. In this use profundo stays in its masculine singular form rather than changing to profundamente.

example.en: Breathe deeply.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Lo can turn profundo, “deep,” into the general idea of a deep or innermost part.

example.es: La luz no llega a lo profundo de la cueva.
example.en: The light does not reach the depths of the cave.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here programa is a planned set of activities or services, not a computer program.

example.es: La ciudad creó un programa de reciclaje.
example.en: The city created a recycling program.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Programé is the completed-past form of programar used for yo. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: I programmed a small tool.

cardCatalog.answerEn: go on; drag on; last longer
cardCatalog.noteEn: Prolongan is the present-time plural form of prolongar. With se before it, prolongarse describes several things continuing longer rather than someone deliberately extending them.

example.en: The meetings drag on too long.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pronto by itself often means 'soon.' In de pronto, the complete expression instead means 'suddenly.'

example.en: Suddenly, it began to rain.

cardCatalog.answerEn: say; utter (negative command to one familiar person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: For an ordinary statement to tú, pronunciar gives pronuncias. After no in a negative command to that same person, the ending changes to pronuncies.

example.en: Do not say his name.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Propia emphasizes that something belongs to the person already identified. It takes the feminine singular form when it describes a feminine singular noun.

example.en: Clara made her own decision.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When propuesta describes a feminine noun, it means “proposed.” As a noun on its own, propuesta can also mean “proposal.”

example.en: We will review the proposed date.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Propulsando is the -ando action form of propulsar. It adds an action happening alongside or as the result of the main action.

example.es: La hélice gira, propulsando el barco.
example.en: The propeller spins, propelling the boat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Protagonismo is the importance or attention given to someone or something as a central figure. Dar protagonismo means to give prominence or a leading role.

example.es: El informe da protagonismo a la seguridad.
example.en: The report gives prominence to safety.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Proteger is the unchanged dictionary form ‘to protect.’ Me attaches to its end and makes the speaker the person protected.

example.en: I use gloves to protect myself.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Provoca is a present form of provocar for one person or thing. Here provocar means to cause a result, not to taunt someone.

example.en: The button causes a sound.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Provocan is the present form of provocar for a plural subject. A nearby object word such as me or te identifies the person being provoked.

example.es: Esos mensajes provocan a los lectores.
example.en: Those messages provoke the readers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here provocar means to cause a result, not to taunt someone. Provocan is the present form for a plural subject.

example.en: These bacteria cause infections.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Provocando is the -ando action form of provocar. In this sense it means causing a result, not deliberately annoying someone.

example.en: The leak is causing problems.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Provocaría keeps the full verb provocar and adds -ía to describe a conditional result.

example.en: An error would cause another delay.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to cause something in someone; to give someone a condition
cardCatalog.noteEn: Provocarle combines provocar with attached le. The result or condition is named separately, while le identifies one person affected by it; a later phrase beginning with a can clarify that person.

example.es: El polvo puede provocarle tos a Luis.
example.en: The dust can give Luis a cough.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Proyecto can mean a planned piece of work or a proposal. Proyectos is the plural.

example.en: The team has several projects.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Prueba can mean a test, but it also means information or material that supports a claim.

example.es: Necesitamos una prueba de que ocurrió.
example.en: We need proof that it happened.

cardCatalog.answerEn: test; part of poner a prueba, to test
cardCatalog.noteEn: Prueba is “test,” and with poner a it forms the conventional expression poner a prueba.

example.es: La pregunta me pone a prueba.
example.en: The question tests me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Prueba can be a test, trial, or piece of evidence. After hacerse, it names a test someone undergoes.

example.en: The test was quick.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I am trying; I am testing
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pruebo is the first-person present form of probar. Spanish can use this ordinary present form for something the speaker is trying or testing right now when the context makes the timing clear.

example.en: I am trying the new program.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Psicología is the study of the mind, behavior, and mental processes.

example.es: La psicología estudia la conducta humana.
example.en: Psychology studies human behavior.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Psicólogos is the masculine or mixed-group plural for people who work in psychology.

example.en: Psychologists study behavior.

cardCatalog.answerEn: psychic; a person claimed to perceive thoughts or future events
cardCatalog.noteEn: Psíquico can describe supposed powers beyond ordinary senses or name a person who claims to have them. The -o form is masculine singular.

example.es: El supuesto psíquico predijo el resultado.
example.en: The supposed psychic predicted the result.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Puaj is a written reaction to something disgusting, unpleasant, or foul-smelling.

example.en: Yuck! The milk has gone bad.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pública is feminine singular because it describes the feminine noun clave.

example.en: The information is public.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Publicado is the masculine singular completed-action form of publicar. It can describe material made public online as well as in print.

example.en: The article was published yesterday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I was able to; I managed to
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pude is the irregular completed-past form of poder used for yo. Before an unchanged action verb, it often says that the speaker succeeded in doing that action.

example.en: I managed to finish the work.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I could; if I were able to
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pudiera is a hypothetical form of poder, “to be able to.” After si, it presents the ability as imagined rather than real.

example.es: Si pudiera elegir, viajaría en tren.
example.en: If I could choose, I would travel by train.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we could; we might be able to, in an imagined situation
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pudiéramos is a special form of poder used for a hypothetical possibility involving “we.” Compare podemos, “we can,” for a possibility presented as real now.

example.en: I wish we could stay.

cardCatalog.answerEn: could (expressing a possibility about the past)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pudo is a completed-past form of poder for one person or thing. Followed by haber and another completed-action form, it can evaluate what could have happened or been true.

example.en: It could have been a mistake.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pudo is a completed-past form of poder for one person or thing. In no se pudo plus an action, it says that completing that action was not possible.

example.es: No se pudo abrir el archivo.
example.en: The file could not be opened.

cardCatalog.answerEn: can (special form used when a possibility is not stated as a fact)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pueda is a special form of poder, the verb meaning “can.” Spanish can use it after que when a description is uncertain, sought, or denied rather than presented as a fact. The ordinary statement form puede changes to pueda.

example.es: Busco a alguien que pueda ayudar.
example.en: I am looking for someone who can help.

cardCatalog.answerEn: may; can (he, she, it, or formal you)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Puede is a present form of poder. Before another action verb, it can express either ability or a possibility; the surrounding sentence supplies the subject.

example.en: It may rain tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: can you; could you (formal or polite request)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In a question to one person addressed formally as usted, ¿puede + action? can make a polite request. Puede has the same written form used for he, she, or it.

example.en: Could you open the window?

cardCatalog.answerEn: may; might (as part of puede que)
they can; they are able to
you can; you are able to

cardCatalog.noteEn: Puedo is the form of poder for the speaker. In a question, it can ask whether an action is allowed rather than whether the speaker is capable of doing it.

example.en: May I use the bathroom?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Puerta can name a large defended gate as well as an ordinary door inside a building.

example.es: Cerraron la puerta de la fortaleza.
example.en: They closed the fortress gate.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Puerta usually means a door. At an airport, puerta also means the numbered gate through which passengers board a flight; puertas is the plural.

example.es: Las puertas de embarque están a la derecha.
example.en: The boarding gates are on the right.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing and electronics, a puerto is a physical or logical connection point. Elsewhere puerto can mean a harbor.

example.es: El portátil tiene un puerto libre.
example.en: The laptop has a free port.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pues often connects a conclusion or next step to what was just said. In conversation, it can work like English 'so,' 'then,' or a second 'well.'

example.en: Then we will continue with the plan.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Puesta follows a form of llevar to describe clothing being worn. It matches the clothing noun: puesto for masculine singular and puesta for feminine singular.

example.en: She is wearing a blue jacket.

cardCatalog.answerEn: connected; networked (feminine plural, with en red)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Puestas is the feminine plural completed-action form of poner, normally ‘to put.’ In poner algo en red, the expression means connecting devices so they form a network.

example.es: Las impresoras están puestas en red.
example.en: The printers are networked.

cardCatalog.answerEn: made it easy (completed-action form in ponerlo fácil)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Puesto is poner's irregular completed-action form. With a form of haber and ponerlo fácil or difícil, it describes how someone has made a situation.

example.en: They have made it difficult for us.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pulí is the completed-past form of pulir used for yo. It can describe making a surface smooth or refining details in a plan or piece of work.

example.en: I polished the details of the report.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pulsa is the present form of pulsar for él, ella, or usted. It can also be an informal command; in an action caption it reports what the person does.

example.en: She presses the red button.

cardCatalog.answerEn: press it; click it (informal singular command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pulsa tells one familiar person to press or click. Lo means ‘it’ and attaches at the end; the written accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: If you see the button, press it.

cardCatalog.answerEn: handful; a small bunch (with un ... de)
cardCatalog.noteEn: A puñado is literally the amount that fits in one hand. Un puñado de is also used figuratively for a modest group or amount.

example.en: I have a handful of ideas.

cardCatalog.answerEn: pointers (programming values that hold memory addresses)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In languages such as C, a pointer stores the address of data in memory. A bad pointer can make a program read or write an invalid location.

example.es: El programa usa punteros para acceder a la memoria.
example.en: The program uses pointers to access memory.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of estar a punto de
cardCatalog.noteEn: Punto usually means ‘point,’ but within estar a punto de it helps form the meaning ‘be about to.’

example.es: El tren está a punto de llegar.
example.en: The train is about to arrive.

cardCatalog.answerEn: point; one unit added to a game statistic

cardCatalog.noteEn: Puntos can mean small visible dots, mathematical points, score points, or periods in writing. Use the surrounding noun or description to choose the intended sense.

example.es: Hay tres puntos negros en la pantalla.
example.en: There are three black dots on the screen.

cardCatalog.answerEn: points in a score or numerical scale
cardCatalog.noteEn: Punto can mean a dot, a location, or a point in a score or measured scale. The plural puntos counts units on that scale, whether they are awarded in a game or used to state a measured score.

example.en: Our team has ten points.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they grade; they score, as a desired result
cardCatalog.noteEn: Puntúen is a special form of puntuar used after para que because the grading is the intended next action, not a fact already being reported. The plural ending leaves the graders unnamed.

example.es: Envío las pruebas para que las puntúen.
example.en: I send the tests so that they can be graded.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before an abstract noun, puro or pura can intensify it with the sense “sheer” or “nothing but.”

example.en: The news was pure joy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Pureza is the quality of being pure. It can be literal, or figurative when an idea is presented as abstract and free from practical complications.

example.es: El laboratorio mide la pureza del agua.
example.en: The laboratory measures the purity of the water.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Puros is the masculine plural form of puro. In a ranking of academic fields, it describes fields as more abstract or theoretical rather than more practical.

example.en: They are looking for pure materials.

cardCatalog.answerEn: became; got (as part of se puso + description)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Puso is the completed-past form of poner used when one other person or thing changed state. With se before it and a describing word after it, se puso presents a completed change into a new state.

example.en: The day became cold.

cardCatalog.answerEn: reset; set (something) to zero (with a cero)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Puso is a completed-past form of poner used with one doer. Poner has several meanings; with a cero, it means to return a counter, device, or value to zero.

example.es: El técnico puso el contador a cero.
example.en: The technician reset the counter to zero.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Puso is a past form of poner. In se puso a followed by an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form, the complete pattern means that someone started doing that action.

example.en: Marta started running.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a noun, puto can add strong anger or contempt rather than describing a literal property. It is offensive or very informal, so avoid it in polite settings.

example.en: Turn off that fucking noise!

cardCatalog.answerEn: pwned; thoroughly beaten or hacked (internet slang)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pwneado is a playful Spanish adaptation of the English internet slang pwned. The borrowed stem is treated like a Spanish verb and given the completed-action ending -eado; after han, it describes the completed defeat or compromise. It is informal and nonstandard.

example.es: Nos han pwneado en la partida.
example.en: They pwned us in the match.

cardCatalog.answerEn: wh—; the interrupted beginning of qué (“what”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: The speaker is cut off before finishing qué. The fragment is not a separate Spanish vocabulary word.

example.en: Wh... what did you say?

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes del que in an amount comparison
cardCatalog.noteEn: In más + noun + del que, que connects the amount named before del with the full action used as the other side of the comparison.

example.es: Hay más trabajo del que pensábamos.
example.en: There is more work than we thought.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; connects an elapsed period to a situation still continuing
cardCatalog.noteEn: In hace + amount of time + que + situation, que connects the measured time to what has continued through the present. Natural English usually expresses the connection with ‘for.’

example.en: It has been raining for three days.

cardCatalog.answerEn: since; no separate English word in a natural ‘a while ago’ translation
cardCatalog.noteEn: After hace and an amount of elapsed time, que can connect that time to the event being dated. English often restructures the idea rather than translating que by itself.

example.es: Hace un mes que hablé con Ana.
example.en: I spoke with Ana a month ago.

cardCatalog.answerEn: that; introduces what turns out to be true
cardCatalog.noteEn: After resulta, que opens the newly revealed statement. Learn resulta que together as ‘it turns out that.’

example.en: It turns out that you were right.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links an evaluation with the recommended action
cardCatalog.noteEn: After es, será, or sería mejor, que introduces the action judged preferable. Spanish then uses a specially changed verb form for that recommendation.

example.en: It will be better for us to leave early.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; completes cada vez que, “every time”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Inside cada vez que, que connects “every time” to the event that triggers the repeated result. It is written without an accent because it connects the two parts rather than asking a question.

example.en: Every time she calls, I smile.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links conseguir to an action by another actor
cardCatalog.noteEn: After conseguir, que introduces the action that the person or thing manages to bring about. English often expresses the same link with ‘get ... to’ rather than translating que as a separate word.

example.en: I manage to get Marta to come.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes the lo ... que degree pattern
no separate English word; links dejar to the allowed action
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a form of dejar meaning “let” or “allow,” que introduces the allowed action. The person doing that action may be stated after que or understood from the situation and the verb form.

example.en: We let Ana choose.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Qué keeps its written accent in a short echo question. The speaker repeats only the missing or unbelievable information instead of forming a longer question.

example.en: ‘I'm leaving tomorrow.’ ‘What?’

cardCatalog.answerEn: how (to what a degree, as in qué insoportable)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Qué before an adjective can express a strong degree, like English “how” in “how strange!” It keeps its written accent.

example.en: How beautiful the garden is!

cardCatalog.answerEn: what a; what (before a noun in an exclamation)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Qué keeps its accent when it introduces an exclamation such as ¡qué sorpresa!

example.en: What an idea!

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes a menos que, “unless”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Que completes the connector and introduces the possible exception.

example.es: Ven, a menos que estés ocupado.
example.en: Come unless you are busy.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes ahora que, “now that”
cardCatalog.noteEn: After ahora, que introduces the situation that is now true. It is written without an accent because it is a linking word, not the question word qué.

example.es: Ahora que estás aquí, podemos salir.
example.en: Now that you are here, we can leave.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes antes de que (“before”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Que completes the connector before a full event. The following verb uses a special pending-event form called the subjunctive.

example.en: Eat before they arrive.

cardCatalog.answerEn: that (fixed linker in claro que sí)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In claro que sí, que links claro to the emphatic sí. Learn the three words together as a common expression of confident agreement.

example.en: 'Will you come tomorrow?' 'Of course.'

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes desde que, “since”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Que lets desde introduce a whole event with its own verb. Learn the two words together as desde que when the starting point is an event rather than a date or place.

example.es: No lo veo desde que cambió de trabajo.
example.en: I have not seen him since he changed jobs.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes es hora de que before the action
cardCatalog.noteEn: Que completes the time-to-act expression before a group of words with its own action. The following verb uses a special form because the action is called for rather than reported as a fact.

example.es: Es hora de que Marta vuelva.
example.en: It is time for Marta to return.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es que
no separate English word; completes esperar a que before an awaited event
cardCatalog.noteEn: Que introduces the event being awaited after esperar a. English usually folds this link into ‘wait for’ rather than translating que separately.

example.es: Esperamos a que llegue el autobús.
example.en: We are waiting for the bus to arrive.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After igual, que introduces the person or thing used as the comparison. The two words form the connector igual que.

example.en: It is the same as the original.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word (part of nada que ver)
than; no separate word in the full expression “nothing but”
cardCatalog.noteEn: In no ser más que, que completes the restriction introduced by más. The form of ser changes for the person and time.

example.es: Eso no es más que una idea.
example.en: That is nothing but an idea.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes por mucho que
cardCatalog.noteEn: Que links por mucho to the action whose amount does not change the result.

example.es: Por mucho que insistas, diré que no.
example.en: No matter how much you insist, I will say no.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; opens que le den, a forceful dismissal
cardCatalog.noteEn: In this fixed expression, que introduces a wished-for dismissal rather than a statement meaning “that.” The rejected target can follow with a or stay unstated when the situation already makes it clear.

example.en: To hell with the plan!

cardCatalog.answerEn: how (as part of qué tal, “how about...?”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In qué tal, qué keeps its accent and joins tal to ask for an opinion or propose an option. Translate the two words together rather than assigning qué its ordinary “what” meaning by itself.

example.en: How about this table?

cardCatalog.answerEn: how (as part of asking qué tal about an experience)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Qué keeps its written accent inside the fixed question qué tal. When the question includes fue or ha ido, it asks how an event or experience went.

example.en: How did the meeting go?

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes solo que, ‘except that’
no separate English word; completes ya que, because or since
cardCatalog.noteEn: Que completes the fixed causal connector ya que and introduces the reason that follows.

example.es: Cerramos, ya que no había clientes.
example.en: We closed because there were no customers.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; it links hacer to the caused action
cardCatalog.noteEn: After hacer que, the later action uses its special caused-action form.

example.en: The music made them dance.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; links hay to the required action
no separate English word; completes the intensifying lo que, “how much”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Together with lo before a verb, que can help emphasize how much an action happens or how strong its effect is. This is different from lo que meaning “what” or “the thing that.”

example.en: You have no idea how much it rained!

cardCatalog.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to; no separate word (in no hay más que hablar)
to; links a noun to an action available or needing to be done
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a noun such as trabajo, algo, or nada, que can introduce an action in its unchanged dictionary form. Natural English often uses ‘to’ instead.

example.en: We have several tasks to finish.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes puede que (“may; might”)
no separate English word; completes para que, ‘so that’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Que completes the purpose connector para que before an event with its own person or thing carrying out the action.

example.es: Cierra la puerta para que no entre frío.
example.en: Close the door so that cold air does not come in.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces the action someone is told to do
cardCatalog.noteEn: After decir used to give an instruction, que links the instruction to the person receiving it. Natural English often uses “to” before the action instead of translating que as “that.”

example.en: I tell her to wait.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector
part of sí que, which strongly confirms what follows
cardCatalog.noteEn: In this pattern, que works with sí to add emphasis; it does not introduce an English “that” clause.

example.en: That really does help.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”
no separate English word; completes the time connector after para
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here que joins para to a full later event with its own changed verb.

example.es: Faltan dos días para que llegue Marta.
example.en: There are two days left until Marta arrives.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes para que before a separate blocked result
cardCatalog.noteEn: Que lets the result after para have its own subject and verb. In a demasiado... para que pattern, that result is presented as prevented or unreal rather than as a fact.

example.es: Era demasiado tarde para que saliéramos.
example.en: It was too late for us to leave.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Qué goes directly before a noun when asking which member or type is meant. It keeps the written accent in a direct question and in an embedded question inside a larger statement.

example.en: I do not know which route to choose.

cardCatalog.noteEn: At the start of a stand-alone wish, que introduces the hoped-for event and is followed by a special subjunctive verb form.

example.en: May you have good luck.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Queda is singular here because the question asks whether any one item remains.

example.en: Is there any bread left?

cardCatalog.answerEn: is left; ends up (in a resulting state)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here queda introduces the state that remains after something has been dealt with. The following completed-action form describes that result.

example.en: The door is left closed.

cardCatalog.answerEn: ended up; remained (completed form of quedarse)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Quedado is used with a form of haber to place quedarse in a completed time. A following word can name the resulting state or place.

example.en: I have ended up alone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With a short indirect word such as me, te, le, nos, or les, quedar can say what someone has left. The plural remaining thing controls quedan; one remaining thing uses queda.

example.en: You have two questions left.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With se, quedan is a present-time form of quedarse. It says that several people or things continue in, or end up in, the state named next.

example.en: The children stay still.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quedan is the plural present form of quedar when things remain. It does not require se in this sense.

example.en: Two tickets remain.

cardCatalog.answerEn: teasing; fooling (as part of quedarse con alguien)
to remain; to end up (in a state)
they will remain; they will stay
I will end up; I will remain (with me)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Quedaré is the future form for the speaker. With me and a describing word, it states the resulting or continuing condition.

example.en: I will remain calm.

cardCatalog.answerEn: were left; ended up (in a resulting state)
cardCatalog.noteEn: A form of quedar can introduce the state that remains after an event. The following completed-action form describes that state.

example.en: The doors were left closed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quédate joins the command queda to te because the verb is quedarse, “to stay.” The accent preserves the original stress.

example.en: Stay here.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I am left; I end up (with me)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Quedo is the present speaker form of quedar. In me quedo sin, it helps say that the speaker is left without something or runs out of it.

example.en: I run out of battery.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quejando is the -ando form used inside quejarse, “to complain.” Its matching marker appears separately before a conjugated helper: te estás quejando.

example.es: Siempre se está quejando del ruido.
example.en: He is always complaining about the noise.

cardCatalog.answerEn: burn; an informal command to one person
cardCatalog.noteEn: For the affirmative informal command of a regular -ar verb, use the same form as the ordinary él/ella present: quemar becomes quema.

example.en: Burn the letter.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Queremos is the present form of querer for nosotros or nosotras. A following action stays in its unchanged dictionary form: queremos salir.

example.en: We want to rest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Querer is the unchanged dictionary form. Before another unchanged action verb, it expresses wanting to do that action.

example.en: I want to open the window.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quería is a past-background form of querer. Before another action verb, it can describe an intended action that may not have happened.

example.en: I wanted to call you yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quería is a past form of querer used for a desire that existed at that past time. It does not say by itself whether the desire was fulfilled.

example.en: I wanted more time.

cardCatalog.answerEn: dear (addressing a mixed or all-male plural group)
cardCatalog.noteEn: At the start of a message, queridos warmly addresses the people named next. It is masculine plural because the addressed list is mixed or not limited to women.

example.en: Dear neighbors, thank you for coming.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you must mean; you presumably mean (formal)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Querría is a softened form of querer for the speaker. It can present a wish or request less directly than quiero, “I want.”

example.en: I would like a coffee, please.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Querríamos is a courteous form of querer, “to want.” It softens an order or request in much the same way as English “we would like.”

example.es: Querríamos una mesa junto a la ventana.
example.en: We would like a table by the window.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Unaccented quien refers back to a person in a statement. After a preposition such as a, natural English often uses “who” rather than formal “whom.”

example.es: La persona con quien trabajo es amable.
example.en: The person I work with is kind.

cardCatalog.answerEn: who? (plural; standard spelling in this question is quiénes)
cardCatalog.noteEn: The comic prints quienes without an accent. In a direct question, standard Spanish writes quiénes; it asks about more than one person.

example.en: Who is coming tomorrow?

cardCatalog.answerEn: you want (informal singular, with the choice left open)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Quieras is a form of querer used when the speaker treats the choice as open or not yet settled. The ordinary statement form is quieres; the e changes to ie in both forms, and quieras uses -as here.

example.en: Choose whatever you want.

cardCatalog.answerEn: do you want; would you like (formal singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Quiere is the present form used for usted, the formal singular “you.” The same written form can also mean “he or she wants”; context identifies the person.

example.en: Would you like to see the menu, sir?

cardCatalog.answerEn: one wants; people want (after impersonal se)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Quiere is third-person singular because impersonal se leaves the person unspecified.

example.es: Cuando se quiere aprender, hay que practicar.
example.en: When one wants to learn, one has to practice.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quiere is the present form of querer for one person or thing. Before another verb in its dictionary form, it expresses what that subject wants to do.

example.en: Marta wants to rest.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I love; I care deeply for (a person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Querer usually means “to want,” but when its object is a person it commonly expresses affection or love. Te quiero is often less intense than te amo, though usage varies.

example.en: I love you very much, Grandma.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quiero ordinarily means “I want.” In the conventional wedding response sí, quiero, it confirms that the speaker agrees to marry, so natural English uses “I do.”

example.es: En la ceremonia, Luis respondió: «Sí, quiero».
example.en: At the ceremony, Luis answered, “I do.”

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quietos is masculine plural because it describes more than one nanobot.

example.en: The children are still.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Química is the science of substances, their properties, and how they change.

example.en: We have a chemistry class.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, químicos names people who work in chemistry. The same form can mean “chemical” when it describes masculine plural things.

example.en: The chemists checked the reaction.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quisieron is a completed-past form of querer for ellos, ellas, or ustedes. In a negative sentence, no quisieron can mean that they did not want something or refused it.

example.en: They did not want the prize.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quitáis is the present form used with informal plural vosotros, common in Spain.

example.en: You all remove the boxes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to take away from him or her
cardCatalog.noteEn: Quitar means ‘to take away’ or ‘remove.’ The attached le identifies the person deprived of something; the thing being taken normally follows.

example.en: I want to take the toy away from him.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Quitaste is the completed past form of quitar for one familiar person. A short person word before it can identify who loses the thing.

example.en: You took the key away from him.

cardCatalog.answerEn: take off; remove from yourself (informal command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Quita is the positive command of quitar for one familiar listener. Te attaches to the end because the listener removes something from themself, and the written accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: Take off your coat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rabito adds the ending -ito to rabo. That ending often makes something sound small; with fruit, rabito can name the short stalk or stem.

example.es: Quitó el rabito de la fresa.
example.en: She removed the strawberry's little stem.

cardCatalog.answerEn: rationalizing; finding plausible reasons after the fact
cardCatalog.noteEn: Racionalizando is the -ando form of racionalizar. Here it names the activity at which the people are described as skilled.

example.en: He keeps rationalizing his decision.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Radiestesia is the claimed practice of finding hidden water, minerals, or other things with a rod, pendulum, or similar object.

example.en: The article examined dowsing.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Radio can mean the broadcast medium, a receiver, or a radio-frequency band. It is normally feminine when it refers to broadcasting: la radio.

example.es: Escucho las noticias en la radio.
example.en: I listen to the news on the radio.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Radioafición is the hobby of communicating by radio as a licensed amateur operator. It is written as one word even when a line break divides it in a label.

example.en: My grandfather practices amateur radio.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Raphael; the name of a Renaissance painter and a Ninja Turtle

cardCatalog.noteEn: Raptor can be used as a shortened dinosaur name; this sense does not refer to a bird of prey.

example.es: El raptor corre hacia la puerta.
example.en: The raptor runs toward the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Raro is normally an adjective meaning “strange.” Spanish sometimes leaves an adjective in its basic masculine singular form to describe how an action happens, much as an English adverb does.

example.en: The engine sounds strange.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rasca is the positive command of rascar for one familiar listener. It has the same written form as the ordinary present form used with él or ella.

example.en: Scratch the label carefully.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rascacielos is normally the noun for a skyscraper. Here it follows monstruo as an imaginative modifier, making the monster seem as tall as a skyscraper.

example.es: Un rascacielos domina el centro de la ciudad.
example.en: A skyscraper dominates the city center.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rastreado is the completed-action form of rastrear. After hemos, it describes a search carried out up to the present.

example.en: We have searched the area.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rastro is a mark or trail left behind that can be followed as evidence.

example.en: They found traces on the ground.

cardCatalog.answerEn: while; a short or unspecified period of time
cardCatalog.noteEn: Un rato refers to an imprecise stretch of time. Its length depends on the situation rather than on a fixed number of minutes.

example.en: We rest for a while.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ratón can name either the animal or a computer mouse. Words about clicking or a computer normally select the device meaning.

example.es: Muevo el cursor con el ratón.
example.en: I move the cursor with the mouse.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A rayo can be a ray or beam of radiation, a lightning bolt, or a sudden streak. The scientific labels here use the radiation sense.

example.en: The rays pass through the material.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Reaccionaron is the completed-past form of reaccionar used with ellos, ellas, or formal ustedes.

example.en: The neighbors reacted calmly.

cardCatalog.answerEn: actually; in fact (as part of en realidad)

cardCatalog.noteEn: A rebufo is the disturbed, often lower-drag flow behind a moving vehicle. Ir a rebufo means to follow closely in that wake and benefit from reduced air resistance.

example.es: El ciclista avanzó a rebufo del líder.
example.en: The cyclist rode in the leader's slipstream.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recarga tells one familiar person to load a page or resource again.

example.es: Recarga la página dentro de un minuto.
example.en: Reload the page in a minute.

cardCatalog.noteEn: For a website or app, recargar means loading the current page again. In other settings, the same verb can mean refilling or recharging something.

example.es: Recarga la página para ver los cambios.
example.en: Refresh the page to see the changes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recaudación is the act or result of collecting money, taxes, donations, or ticket revenue. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: The fundraising will help the hospital.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Said by itself after a message, recibido confirms that the message arrived and was understood. This conventional reply is comparable to English radio acknowledgments such as ‘roger’ or ‘copy.’

example.en: ‘Message sent.’ ‘Copy.’

cardCatalog.noteEn: Reconectó is the completed-past form of reconectar for one person or thing. The prefix re- adds the sense of connecting again.

example.en: The technician reconnected the cable.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Reconocimiento can be the act of identifying something. In technology, it names a system's ability to identify speech, faces, writing, or other input.

example.es: El teléfono tiene reconocimiento de voz.
example.en: The phone has voice recognition.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Reconstruí is the completed-past form of reconstruir used for yo. The written accent marks the stressed final sound.

example.en: I rebuilt the old table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish writes an accent in récord because the stress falls on the first syllable.

example.es: El atleta batió el récord mundial.
example.en: The athlete broke the world record.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recordando is the -ando form of recordar and presents the remembering as an action in progress or accompanying another action.

example.en: She walked while remembering the trip.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recordaré is the simple future form of recordar for yo.

example.en: I will remember your advice.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recordarnos joins nos, meaning “us,” to the unchanged dictionary form recordar.

example.en: Keep the photo to remember us.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recordé is a completed-past form used for a memory that came to the speaker at a particular moment.

example.en: Suddenly I remembered her name.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recorro is the present form of recorrer used for yo. It describes covering or moving along the length of a route, area, or sequence.

example.en: I go along the path every morning.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recortes often means reductions in spending, services, or resources. The singular is recorte.

example.en: The cuts affected the project.

cardCatalog.answerEn: do you remember?; you remember (formal singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Recuerda can be either an informal command, “remember,” or the ordinary present form for él, ella, or formal usted. A question addressed formally selects the present-tense “do you remember?” reading.

example.en: Ma'am, do you remember this place?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recuerda is the positive command of recordar for one familiar listener. Me attaches to the end, and the written accent keeps the original stress: recuerda + me becomes recuérdame.

example.en: Remind me about the appointment.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This is a present form of recordar. With no before it, no recuerdo means “I don't remember.”

example.en: I remember her name.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recuperación can mean getting an object back as well as returning to health or a previous condition.

example.es: La recuperación del equipo tardó dos días.
example.en: Retrieving the equipment took two days.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recuperado is the completed-action form of recuperar. With haber it says that a previous ability, level, or possession has been regained.

example.en: I have regained my previous pace.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recurren is the plural present form of recurrir. With a it describes turning to a measure or solution.

example.es: A veces recurren a métodos antiguos.
example.en: Sometimes they resort to old methods.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Recurso can be something available for solving a problem, including a last resort.

example.es: La negociación fue nuestro último recurso.
example.en: Negotiation was our last resort.
