cardCatalog.noteEn: Reduce is a present form of reducir used with él, ella, usted, or one singular thing. It takes the thing being made smaller as its object.

example.en: This measure reduces the noise.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Reduce is a present form of reducir used with one thing. With se, it describes that thing becoming smaller.

example.es: El ruido se reduce por la noche.
example.en: The noise decreases at night.

cardCatalog.answerEn: (if) I should rewrite; (if) I were ever to rewrite (rare, old-fashioned form)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Reescribiere is a future-subjunctive form of reescribir, “to rewrite.” This special -re form is nearly absent from everyday Spanish but still appears in old writing, legal language, and deliberate imitation of those styles.

example.es: Si alguien reescribiere el contrato, deberá avisarnos.
example.en: If anyone should rewrite the contract, they must notify us.

cardCatalog.answerEn: reference (in sistema de referencia, reference frame)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In physics, referencia helps name the coordinate viewpoint from which motion is measured.

example.es: Elegimos un sistema de referencia fijo.
example.en: We chose a fixed reference frame.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Referirse is the unchanged dictionary form of a pronominal verb. Its attached se changes to me, te, se, nos, os, or se when the verb changes for a subject.

example.es: Es difícil referirse a todos los casos.
example.en: It is difficult to refer to every case.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Te refieres addresses one familiar listener and identifies what that person is referring to or means.

example.es: No entiendo a qué te refieres.
example.en: I do not understand what you mean.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This is the visual sense of reflexión: an image produced when light bounces from a surface, not thoughts or careful consideration.

example.es: Veo dos reflexiones en el cristal.
example.en: I see two reflections in the glass.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to refresh; to reload (a page or inbox)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Refrescar can literally mean to cool or refresh something. In a computer context, it means reloading a page or checking it for updated content.

example.es: Refresca la página para ver los cambios.
example.en: Refresh the page to see the changes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Registrará is the future form of registrar for one person or thing.

example.en: The sensor will record every change.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Registro can name stored information that preserves what happened, not only the act of registering something.

example.es: El museo conserva un registro histórico.
example.en: The museum keeps a historical record.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rehenes is the plural of rehén, a person held so that another person or group will meet a demand.

example.en: The hostages came out safely.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The -as ending matches a feminine plural noun such as palabras.

example.es: Son preguntas relacionadas con el trabajo.
example.en: They are questions related to work.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Relacionado normally uses con before the other topic or thing.

example.es: El problema está relacionado con la red.
example.en: The problem is related to the network.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Religión is feminine; its plural is religiones.

example.en: She studies several ancient religions.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Reliquia can be an old object valued because of its history. With familiar, it refers to an object preserved and passed down in a family.

example.es: Este reloj es una reliquia familiar.
example.en: This watch is a family heirloom.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Remate can be the final touch that completes something. In a joke, it is the line that delivers the payoff.

example.es: El remate del chiste sorprendió a todos.
example.en: The punchline surprised everyone.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to come back; to recover from a deficit
cardCatalog.noteEn: In a game or competition, remontar means to overcome a disadvantage in the score or standings. Outside sports it can also describe overcoming another difficult situation.

example.es: El equipo logró remontar en la segunda parte.
example.en: The team managed to come back in the second half.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Remota is the feminine singular form of remoto and matches a feminine noun such as visión.

example.es: La señal viene de una estación remota.
example.en: The signal comes from a remote station.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Remotas normally means far away. With a device, it can describe operation or activation from a distance. Its -as ending matches a feminine plural noun.

example.en: They use remote cameras.

cardCatalog.answerEn: remote; usable over a network without physical access
cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, remoto describes access or an action performed from another machine or location through a network.

example.en: The server allows remote access.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, a renderizador turns data or code into the visible image or output shown to a user.

example.en: The renderer creates the image.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With a matching me, te, se, nos, or os marker, rendirse means to give up. Rendido is its completed-action form after haber.

example.en: I have not given up.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rendir becomes rendirse in this meaning. The short marker se attaches to the dictionary form.

example.en: He does not want to give up.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to rearrange; to put in a new order

cardCatalog.noteEn: In dar un repaso a algo, repaso means a review or careful examination rather than a physical pass by something.

example.es: Di un repaso a mis notas.
example.en: I reviewed my notes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Repetir changes e to i in some present forms, such as repito, but the unchanged dictionary form is repetir.

example.en: I am going to play the song again.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Repites is the familiar singular present form of repetir. The e in the dictionary form changes to i in this present form.

example.en: You repeat the step until you finish.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Reportado is the masculine singular participle of reportar. With a form of ser, it can describe something that is or will be reported.

example.en: The failure was reported yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Repostera can describe something connected with making cakes, pastries, and other sweets. Its feminine ending matches a feminine singular noun.

example.en: We visited a baking fair.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to play; to play back audio or video
cardCatalog.noteEn: With audio or video, reproducir means to play the media. In other settings it can mean to reproduce, copy, or recreate something.

example.es: Pulsa aquí para reproducir el vídeo.
example.en: Press here to play the video.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to reproduce; to recreate (a reported problem)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In software work, reproducir un fallo means to make the same failure happen again so it can be investigated. Reproducir also has ordinary meanings involving copying, playing media, and biological reproduction.

example.es: El equipo intentó reproducir el error.
example.en: The team tried to reproduce the error.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Repulsión literally means “repulsion” or strong disgust. A humorous label can extend it to socially creepy or repulsive behavior.

example.en: She felt disgust at the smell.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Requerida describes one feminine person or thing. The ending changes to match what is described: requerido is masculine singular, and requeridos or requeridas are plural.

example.en: The required authorization arrived today.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rescatado is the completed-action form of rescatar. After a form of haber, it describes a completed rescue.

example.en: They have rescued the hiker.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Residuales is plural to match aguas. Together, aguas residuales means wastewater.

example.en: They analyze the wastewater.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In motion through air, resistencia is the force that opposes the object's movement. Other contexts can use resistencia for resistance of different kinds.

example.es: El diseño disminuye la resistencia del aire.
example.en: The design reduces air resistance.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Electrical resistance measures how strongly a component or network opposes electric current.

example.en: We measure the circuit's resistance.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a circuit, resistencia can name either opposition to electric current or a component—a resistor—that provides it. The diagram makes the component sense prominent here.

example.en: We connect two resistors to the circuit.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Resistentes is plural to match the things that have this resistance.

example.es: Estas plantas son resistentes al frío.
example.en: These plants are resistant to cold.

cardCatalog.answerEn: resolution; the amount of pixel detail in an image or display
cardCatalog.noteEn: For a screen or image, resolución describes how much pixel detail it can show. In other contexts the same word can mean a solution or a formal decision.

example.en: The screen has high resolution.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Respondió is the third-person singular completed-past form of responder.

example.en: The director replied immediately.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Respuesta can be an answer to a question or a reply in a conversation or online discussion.

example.en: There is still no answer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: El resto names everything left after the already mentioned part has been separated out.

example.en: We will save the rest for tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Resuelta is the irregular completed-action form of resolver used here as a description. It changes to match the noun: resuelto, resuelta, resueltos, or resueltas.

example.en: The doubt was resolved.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Resuelto is the irregular completed-action form of resolver; it appears with haber in forms such as he resuelto.

example.en: I have already solved the problem.

cardCatalog.answerEn: seems; feels; is found to be (by someone)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Resulta is a present form of resultar for one thing. With me, te, le, nos, os, or les and a description, it says how that thing seems or feels to a person.

example.en: I find the exercise easy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Resulta que introduces information that has just been discovered, is surprising, or changes the listener's understanding.

example.es: Resulta que la tienda está cerrada.
example.en: It turns out that the store is closed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Resultaban is the imperfect past form of resultar used for a plural subject. With te, it describes how those things seemed or felt to one familiar person.

example.en: The instructions seemed clear to you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Resultado names an outcome. In an online search, it can mean one returned result or listing.

example.es: La búsqueda dio un solo resultado.
example.en: The search returned only one result.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Resultados are the outcomes or answers produced by a process, test, calculation, or search.

example.en: The search produced many results.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Retarme joins the verb's unchanged dictionary form retar, ‘to challenge,’ to me, which identifies the speaker as the person being challenged.

example.es: Lucía quiere retarme a una carrera.
example.en: Lucía wants to challenge me to a race.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Retirado is a completed-action form of retirar. With fue, it says that something was taken out of use in a completed past event.

example.es: El tren fue retirado del servicio.
example.en: The train was taken out of service.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Retocado is the masculine singular completed-action form of retocar, ‘to touch up’ or ‘to alter.’ In an image context it commonly means digitally edited.

example.en: The portrait looks retouched.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Retocados is the masculine plural completed-action form of retocar, ‘to touch up’ or ‘to alter.’ Here it describes several objects as digitally edited.

example.en: The portraits have been retouched.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Una retractación is a later statement taking back or disowning an earlier claim, instruction, or accusation.

example.en: The newspaper published a retraction.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Retrasa is the singular present form of retrasar.

example.en: The rain delays the departure.

cardCatalog.answerEn: retro; fashionable because it recalls the past
cardCatalog.noteEn: Retro describes a style, object, or idea that deliberately evokes an earlier time.

example.es: El café tiene una decoración retro.
example.en: The café has retro decor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Reunirse uses reúne for the positive command to one familiar person, and te is attached at the end because the action is joining or meeting with others. The written accent preserves the stress.

example.en: Meet up with us tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: backward; the wrong way around (as part of al revés)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the fixed expression al revés, revés says that the orientation, order, or direction is reversed.

example.en: He put the label on backward.

cardCatalog.answerEn: upside down; inside out (as part of del revés)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In del revés, revés marks an inverted or reversed orientation.

example.en: You are wearing your T-shirt inside out.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Reventar describes something bursting; with tires, English commonly says blow out.

example.es: Los globos revientan con el calor.
example.en: The balloons burst in the heat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Capitalized Los Reyes commonly refers to the Three Kings, or Magi. In Spain and other Spanish-speaking traditions, children may receive gifts from them around 6 January; their gift-bringing role is culturally comparable to Santa Claus.

example.es: Los Reyes traen regalos en enero.
example.en: The Three Kings bring gifts in January.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rica is the feminine singular form of rico when it describes how food tastes. Rico can also mean ‘rich’ in other contexts.

example.en: The soup is tasty.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rica matches the feminine singular noun gente even though gente refers to multiple people.

example.es: La gente rica vivía en ese barrio.
example.en: Rich people lived in that neighborhood.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; completes en rigor (‘strictly speaking’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Rigor by itself can mean strictness or rigor. In the fixed expression en rigor, the two words introduce a precise or technically exact statement.

example.en: Strictly speaking, one signature is missing.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I give up; I surrender (with me)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Rindo is a present form of rendir. With the matching short marker me, it forms rendirse, the usual verb for giving up or surrendering.

example.es: Me rindo después de tres intentos.
example.en: I give up after three attempts.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Riñones is the plural of riñón, one of the organs that filter waste from the blood.

example.es: Los riñones forman parte del sistema urinario.
example.en: The kidneys are part of the urinary system.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Río has a written accent to keep the í in a separate spoken syllable.

example.en: The river reaches the sea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ripeo is computing slang for a digital copy extracted from another recording or medium. Ripeos is plural.

example.es: Guardó varios ripeos de sus discos.
example.en: He saved several rips of his discs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Risa means laughter. In matar de risa it completes a fixed expression for making someone laugh intensely.

example.en: Her comment made me laugh.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Robótico describes something related to robots and matches a masculine singular noun.

example.en: They designed a robotic arm.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A roce is light contact or a brushing touch. The plural is roces.

example.es: Notó unos roces en la mano.
example.en: He noticed a few light touches on his hand.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rojas uses -as because it describes a feminine plural noun. The other matching forms are rojo, roja, and rojos.

example.en: There are two red flowers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rojo changes to match the noun it describes. Rojos is masculine plural; the other forms are rojo, roja, and rojas.

example.en: I bought two red notebooks.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rompo is the irregular present form of romper used with yo.

example.en: I break the seal carefully.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The color word rosa usually stays rosa in careful standard usage, but plural rosas is also widely used and is the form printed here.

example.en: They chose the pink flowers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rotos is the masculine plural form of roto. It matches a masculine plural noun describing things that have broken.

example.en: They removed the broken plates.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rozamiento is the resistive force between surfaces or through a medium; fricción is a common synonym.

example.en: Friction slows the box.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ruidoso comes from ruido, “noise,” and changes its ending to match the noun it describes.

example.en: The neighbors are noisy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Rumbo names the direction in which someone or something is traveling. With a, it commonly introduces the destination.

example.en: The ship changed course.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Runrún is Spanish onomatopoeia for a repeated low mechanical sound or murmur. Comics may print it without the written accent and in capitals as RUNRUN.

example.es: Se oía el runrún del motor.
example.en: The engine's low rumble could be heard.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sabe is the present form of saber for one person or thing. It expresses knowledge of information; before an infinitive it can instead mean ‘knows how to.’

example.es: Todo el mundo sabe la respuesta.
example.en: Everyone knows the answer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a dictionary-form verb, sabe says that one person or group has the knowledge or skill to do that action. Spanish does not add cómo in this pattern.

example.en: Marta knows how to swim.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When food or drink is the subject, saber describes its taste. Sabe is the present form for one thing; this is different from sabe meaning “knows.”

example.en: The soup tastes good.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you know? (addressing several people informally, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sabéis is the present form of saber used with vosotros or vosotras, the informal plural ‘you’ used mainly in Spain. As a brief question, ¿sabéis? can introduce a remark much like English ‘you know?’ or ‘you know what?’

example.en: You know what? I have an idea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Saben is a plural present form of saber. With a taste description, saber means “to taste,” not “to know.”

example.en: These apples taste tart.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A speaker can use ¿sabes? to introduce a thought or draw the listener's attention, without literally testing what the listener knows.

example.en: You know? I think you're right.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I knew; he, she, or formal you knew; used to know
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sabía is an imperfect past form of saber, “to know.” The imperfect presents knowledge as a state that was already true or ongoing, instead of as a single completed discovery. Context tells whether the subject is I, he, she, or formal you.

example.en: She knew the answer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: did you know; you knew (informal singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sabías is the imperfect past form of saber for tú. The imperfect presents knowledge as a state that existed at that past time; in ¿Sabías que...?, English commonly says ‘Did you know that...?’

example.en: Did you know that Ana lives here?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sabido is the completed-action form of saber. With a form of haber, it describes having learned or found out something.

example.en: How did you find out?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Saborear literally means to savor a flavor. It can also mean taking time to enjoy or appreciate an experience in detail.

example.en: I want to savor every moment.

cardCatalog.answerEn: might know; could know (a guess about what is true now)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sabrá is formed from saber's future stem sabr- and the singular ending -á. A future-looking form can also express uncertainty or a guess about the present, especially in a question, rather than knowledge at a later time.

example.en: What might Marta know about the problem?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sacado is the completed-action form of sacar. With a form of haber, it describes something that has been taken or pulled out.

example.es: Han sacado las cajas del coche.
example.en: They have taken the boxes out of the car.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sacando is sacar's ongoing-action form. With a physical object, sacar often means taking or pulling it out from where it was kept.

example.es: Está sacando un cuaderno de la mochila.
example.en: She is taking a notebook out of the backpack.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to get; to produce (a sound or pitch)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sacar often means “to take out.” With a sound, note, or tone, it can instead mean getting or producing that sound from an object or instrument.

example.es: Sacó un sonido claro de la flauta.
example.en: She got a clear sound from the flute.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they took; pulled (someone or something) out
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sacaron is a completed-past form of sacar used for more than one doer. Sacar often means moving someone or something from inside to outside.

example.en: They took the boxes out of the car.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sal is the irregular command form of salir for one familiar person.

example.en: Get out of the building.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sal is the feminine noun for salt. Do not confuse it with sal, the informal command of salir meaning ‘leave.’

example.en: The soup needs salt.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Salchicha is a feminine naming word, so descriptions of it use feminine forms such as polaca and inversa.

example.en: They heated a sausage.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sale is a form of salir. Depending on the setting, salir can mean to leave, to come out, or to appear. Here it describes something suddenly appearing.

example.es: De pronto sale un actor al escenario.
example.en: Suddenly, an actor appears onstage.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is worthwhile; works out as good value (as part of salir a cuenta)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sale normally comes from salir, “to go out,” but in salir a cuenta it describes whether a choice works out as worthwhile or good value.

example.es: El pase mensual sale a cuenta.
example.en: The monthly pass is worthwhile.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Salir often means to leave or go out. When the subject is a book, article, film, or similar work, sale can mean that it comes out or becomes available.

example.en: The article comes out tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Salir normally means “to leave” or “to go out,” but with a calculation or attempt it can describe the result that comes out.

example.en: The calculation comes out right.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Salir describes movement from inside to outside. English may choose ‘come out’ or ‘go out’ depending on the viewpoint.

example.es: El tren va a salir del túnel.
example.en: The train is going to come out of the tunnel.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to date; to go out with (in salir con)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Salir by itself usually means “to go out” or “to leave.” With con followed by a person, it can mean to date that person.

example.en: Marta is dating Elena.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to go out (socially or for entertainment)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Salir can mean simply leaving a place, but it also commonly means going out to socialize, eat, drink, dance, or enjoy entertainment.

example.en: We are going out tonight.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to go out; to go outside

cardCatalog.noteEn: The noun salmón is also used as a color label.

example.en: She bought a salmon-colored shirt.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Salvado is the past participle of salvar. After a form of haber, it helps describe a completed action.

example.en: We have saved the dog.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Salvar stays in its unchanged dictionary form, and te attaches to its end for the person being saved.

example.en: The life jacket can save you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The written accent keeps the stress on the first syllable.

example.en: She made a cheese sandwich.

cardCatalog.answerEn: sandwiches (printed without the standard Spanish accent)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Standard Spanish spelling is sándwiches, with an accent on the first a. This printed menu omits that accent, so the card preserves the exact surface form while showing the usual spelling here.

example.en: We ordered two sandwiches.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After costes, sanitarios means costs connected with healthcare. In other contexts, sanitario can refer to sanitation or a healthcare worker.

example.es: El informe compara los gastos sanitarios.
example.en: The report compares healthcare expenses.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sanos ends in -os to describe a masculine or mixed plural group. The singular forms are sano and sana.

example.en: The children are healthy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sartén names the shallow pan used for frying or cooking on a stove. It can be masculine or feminine depending on region; this occurrence uses feminine la.

example.en: Heat oil in the frying pan.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you satisfy; you fulfill (one familiar person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Satisfaces is the present form of satisfacer used with tú.

example.es: Con ese trabajo satisfaces tu curiosidad.
example.en: With that work, you satisfy your curiosity.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks ajustarse, “to fit or adapt”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ajustarse uses a short marker such as me, te, se, or nos when the subject itself fits or adapts. Without that marker, ajustar more often means adjusting something else.

example.es: El plan se ajusta al presupuesto.
example.en: The plan fits the budget.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks arremolinarse, “to swirl or churn”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Arremolinarse is normally used with me, te, se, nos, or os. With él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes, the matching small word is se.

example.es: Las hojas se arremolinan en la calle.
example.en: The leaves swirl in the street.

cardCatalog.answerEn: itself; marks autoconectarse, to connect automatically
cardCatalog.noteEn: Autoconectarse uses a matching small word for the thing that connects: me, te, se, nos, or os. Use se with one third-person thing that connects itself or connects automatically.

example.es: El teléfono se autoconecta a la red.
example.en: The phone connects to the network automatically.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sé is the irregular affirmative command of ser for one familiar listener. Its written accent distinguishes it from se.

example.en: Be patient with others.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of caerse when an online service, connection, or network goes down
cardCatalog.noteEn: With an online service, connection, or network, caerse means to go down or drop. Se stays before the changed form of caer: el servicio se cae for one service and las conexiones se caen for several connections.

example.es: La conexión se cae a menudo.
example.en: The connection drops often.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks cansarse, “to get tired”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Cansarse uses a small pronoun that changes with the person: me canso, te cansas, se cansa. Use se with él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

example.en: They get tired of waiting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks cargarse a, “to take out”
cardCatalog.noteEn: The informal Spanish verb cargarse uses a matching small word such as me, te, or se. Cargarse a someone can mean to kill, beat, eliminate, or ruin them, depending on context.

example.es: El villano se carga al guardia.
example.en: The villain takes out the guard.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks a change of state: turns off
cardCatalog.noteEn: With some verbs, se marks that something enters a new state rather than acting on another object. Apagarse means “to go out” or “to turn off.”

example.en: The light went out.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; with comen, it emphasizes eating someone up
cardCatalog.noteEn: Comer means 'to eat.' With a matching short word such as me, te, or se, comerse can emphasize eating something completely.

example.es: Los niños se comen el pastel.
example.en: The children eat up the cake.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps leerse mean “to read through”
cardCatalog.noteEn: With actions such as reading or eating, this small word can emphasize carrying the action through over a whole, clearly specified thing. Se is the form used with él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

example.en: Marta read through the report.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps comunicarse mean ‘to communicate’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Comunicarse uses a short marker that matches who communicates: me comunico, te comunicas, se comunica, nos comunicamos, os comunicáis, or se comunican. The marker stays directly before a normal changed form of comunicar.

example.en: We communicate by email.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; required with convertirse, ‘to become’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Convertir means to turn something into something else. Convertirse uses se when the named thing itself becomes or turns into the result.

example.es: El garaje se convirtió en una oficina.
example.en: The garage became an office.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of corresponderse con (“to match”)
no separate English word; marks darse cuenta, “to realize”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a changed form of dar, se marks that one other person or thing—or formal usted—is the one who realizes something in the expression darse cuenta.

example.es: Ella se dio cuenta del error.
example.en: She realized the mistake.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks debatirse (‘struggle’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Debatirse uses se as part of the verb when someone or something struggles against a difficulty. Se changes to me, te, nos, or os for other people.

example.es: La empresa se debate entre dos opciones.
example.en: The company struggles between two options.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps desarrollarse mean ‘to develop or progress’
cardCatalog.noteEn: With a project, plan, or situation as the subject, desarrollarse describes how it unfolds or progresses without naming an outside doer.

example.es: La reunión se desarrolla con calma.
example.en: The meeting is progressing calmly.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks that events unfold or play out
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the pronominal use desplegarse, events develop or play out. Se is part of that verb use; it does not mean a separate person or thing.

example.en: The story unfolds slowly.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks detenerse, “to stop”
cardCatalog.noteEn: With a form of detener, se shows that the people or things themselves come to a stop.

example.en: The train stopped.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks desconectarse, “to disconnect or log off”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Desconectarse uses se when the person or device leaves a connection. The form changes with the person: me desconecto, te desconectas, se desconecta.

example.es: Ana se desconectó de la llamada.
example.en: Ana disconnected from the call.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps encontrarse con mean ‘to meet’ or ‘encounter’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Encontrarse uses a short matching word such as me, te, se, nos, or os. Se is the form used with one third-person subject such as Ana or Mefistófeles.

example.es: Ana se encuentra con un vecino.
example.en: Ana runs into a neighbor.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps encontrarse mean ‘to be found’ or ‘to be located’
cardCatalog.noteEn: With this use of encontrarse, se matches the thing being located: se encuentra for one thing and se encuentran for more than one.

example.en: The station is located nearby.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of enterarse
cardCatalog.noteEn: Enterarse is a pronominal verb meaning to find out or learn some information. Se changes with the subject and stays beside the changed verb or attaches to an infinitive.

example.en: She found out yesterday.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks esforzarse (‘make an effort’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Esforzarse uses se as part of the verb. Se changes to me, te, nos, or os for other people.

example.en: She makes an effort to learn.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the small pronoun used with extinguirse
cardCatalog.noteEn: Extinguirse describes a species, fire, or activity dying out. The small pronoun is part of this use.

example.es: La especie se extinguió hace siglos.
example.en: The species died out centuries ago.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins se trata de, “it is about”
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the fixed expression se trata de, se helps make the statement impersonal: it describes the subject or point under discussion without naming a person who performs the action.

example.en: It is about choosing well.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps hacerse mean ‘to become’
cardCatalog.noteEn: With a describing word, hacerse can present a gradual or noticeable change in the subject's state.

example.es: Los días se hacen más largos.
example.en: The days are getting longer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks helarse, “to freeze” or “go cold”
cardCatalog.noteEn: The small word se turns helar, “to freeze something,” into helarse, where the subject itself freezes or goes cold.

example.en: The water freezes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: people; one; you in general (impersonal marker)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a third-person singular verb, se can leave the people doing the action unspecified.

example.en: People work a lot here.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to them/anyone; replaces le before lo
cardCatalog.noteEn: When le or les comes immediately before lo, la, los, or las, it changes to se. This se identifies the recipient; it is not reflexive.

example.es: Le doy el libro a Ana. → Se lo doy.
example.en: I give the book to Ana. → I give it to her.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; presents the thing as changing
cardCatalog.noteEn: With verbs such as reducir and ampliar, se lets Spanish describe a change without naming anyone who causes it. English often uses a simple verb such as “shrinks” or “widens.”

example.en: The stain shrinks.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; it forms irse, 'to leave' or 'to go away'
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ir means 'to go.' With a matching short word such as me, te, se, or nos, irse focuses on departure: se va means that someone or something leaves or goes away.

example.es: El último autobús se va a las once.
example.en: The last bus leaves at eleven.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps irse describe time passing or ending
cardCatalog.noteEn: Irse often means “to leave.” When its subject is a period of time, se helps give it the figurative sense of passing or coming to an end.

example.es: El día se va muy rápido.
example.en: The day goes by very quickly.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks llamarse, “to be called”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Llamarse uses a matching small word: me llamo, te llamas, se llama, nos llamamos, and so on. With he, she, formal you, or one named thing, use se.

example.en: Her name is Inés.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks moverse, “to move”
cardCatalog.noteEn: With mueve, se shows that the organism itself moves.

example.en: The shadow moves.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks the ‘come to mind’ use of ocurrir
cardCatalog.noteEn: In the pattern se me/te/le/nos/os/les ocurre, se is required before the short word naming the person who has the idea. It does not mean that the idea acts on itself.

example.en: A solution occurs to us.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps pasarse mean “to spend time”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Pasarse in the sense of spending a stretch of time uses a matching short word: me, te, se, nos, or os. Se is the form used with one third person.

example.en: She spends the afternoon reading.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks something as receiving a possible action; the doer is not named
cardCatalog.noteEn: With a form of poder and an unchanged action verb, se shifts attention away from the person doing the action and toward the thing that can receive it.

example.en: The door can be opened.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This se presents the action without naming who performs it. A following le can identify the person who receives or is affected by the action.

example.en: A message will be sent to you.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks an action whose doer is not named
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a third-person verb, se can focus on what happens rather than who does it. English often uses a passive form such as ‘is requested’ or ‘have been discovered.’

example.en: Several errors were found.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks percatarse, “to notice”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Percatarse uses a matching small word: me, te, se, nos, or os. Se is used with él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

example.en: They noticed the error.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks ponerse a, “to start doing”
cardCatalog.noteEn: In ponerse a, the small pronoun changes with the person: me pongo, te pones, se pone, nos ponemos, os ponéis, or se ponen. English normally expresses the full construction as “start” or “get down to.”

example.en: She starts cleaning.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; helps form ponerse, ‘to become’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ponerse uses me, te, se, nos, or os to match the person or thing that enters a new state. Se is the form used with one other person or thing, or with a group that does not include the speaker or listener.

example.en: The sky became dark.

cardCatalog.answerEn: the small pronoun used with posarse
cardCatalog.noteEn: Posarse is used when something lands or settles on a surface. The small pronoun changes with the subject: me poso, se posa, se posan.

example.es: La mariposa se posa en una hoja.
example.en: The butterfly lands on a leaf.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; makes prolongan mean ‘go on’ or ‘drag on’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Prolongarse uses a matching small marker with the person or thing that continues longer: me, te, se, nos, os, or se. Here se goes with a plural subject and makes the conversations themselves continue, without naming anyone who deliberately extends them.

example.en: The meeting dragged on.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks propagarse, “to spread”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Propagarse describes something spreading or traveling outward without naming an outside agent that spreads it. Se stays before the changed form of propagar.

example.es: El sonido se propaga por el aire.
example.en: Sound travels through the air.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks the idiom quedarse con alguien
no separate English word; marks quedarse, “to remain” or “stay”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Quedar and quedarse have several uses. With se here, the subject continues to be present rather than leaving.

example.en: The memory stays with me.

cardCatalog.answerEn: each other; marks an action exchanged by two or more subjects
no separate English word; makes romper mean that something breaks
cardCatalog.noteEn: With romper, se presents the named thing as becoming broken, without naming a person who breaks it. The form of romper still changes for the thing and time.

example.es: La taza se rompió al caer.
example.en: The cup broke when it fell.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks sentarse, ‘to sit down’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sentarse uses a matching short word: me, te, se, nos, or os. Use se with él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

example.es: Ella se sienta junto a la ventana.
example.en: She sits down by the window.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks sentirse, 'to feel'
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sentirse uses me, te, se, nos, or os to identify who or what has the experience: me siento, te sientes, se siente. English normally folds this small word into the meaning of 'feel.'

example.en: The fabric feels soft.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks sincronizarse, to synchronize
cardCatalog.noteEn: Se presents the program as becoming synchronized with something else rather than directly synchronizing an object.

example.en: The calendar synchronizes automatically.

cardCatalog.answerEn: one another; marks sucederse, ‘to follow one another’
cardCatalog.noteEn: With a plural subject, se suceden presents repeated events or items as following one another in sequence.

example.es: Los días se suceden sin pausa.
example.en: The days follow one another without pause.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks unirse, ‘to join’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Unirse is used with me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match who joins. Se goes before the changed verb when the people joining are ‘they’ or formal ‘you all.’

example.en: They join the group.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; presents the subject as undergoing an event without naming a doer
cardCatalog.noteEn: This use of se lets Spanish focus on what receives or undergoes the action. English may use a passive form or describe the result as happening on its own.

example.es: La imagen se grabó con claridad.
example.en: The image was recorded clearly.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks a change affecting them (part of volverse, “to become”)
be; no separate English word in maldita sea
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sea is a special form of ser used in wishes and reactions. In the fixed exclamation maldita sea, English normally translates the whole expression rather than this word separately.

example.es: Sea como sea, tenemos que salir.
example.en: Be that as it may, we have to leave.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is; may be (a possibility form of ser)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sea is a form of ser used when something is presented as uncertain, possible, desired, or otherwise not stated as a plain fact. For a straightforward statement, the corresponding form is es.

example.en: It may be true.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they are; may be (subjunctive form of ser)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sean is used for plural subjects when the speaker is not presenting their being as a plain fact, for example after doubt or a negative belief.

example.en: I do not think they are the same.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a government title, secretario names the official responsible for a department. It does not mean an office assistant in this context.

example.es: El secretario presentó el nuevo plan.
example.en: The secretary presented the new plan.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Secreto can be a noun, “a secret,” or an adjective meaning “secret.” Here it labels something that is not publicly disclosed.

example.en: The report is secret.

cardCatalog.answerEn: sector; fixed-size area of a disk
cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, a sector is one of the small fixed-size storage areas into which a disk is divided.

example.es: El disco tiene un sector dañado.
example.en: The disk has a damaged sector.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Secuestré is the completed-past form for the speaker. Its written accent keeps the stress on the final syllable.

example.es: En la película, el villano secuestró al científico.
example.en: In the film, the villain kidnapped the scientist.

cardCatalog.answerEn: segmentation fault; a program crash from invalid memory access
cardCatalog.noteEn: Segfault is an English computing abbreviation used as a masculine technical noun in this Spanish sentence.

example.es: El programa terminó con un segfault.
example.en: The program ended with a segmentation fault.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguía is an imperfect past form of seguir used for one subject. The imperfect presents the repeated row-to-row relationship as ongoing background rather than one completed event.

example.en: Each chapter followed the previous one.

cardCatalog.answerEn: right away; immediately (as part of en seguida)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In this fixed expression, seguida does not describe a feminine noun. The one-word spelling enseguida is also standard.

example.en: We will be right back.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguido is the completed-action form of seguir, ‘to follow.’ After a form of haber, it stays unchanged: he seguido, has seguido, han seguido.

example.en: You have followed the instructions.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguidos is the masculine plural form of seguido. It matches a masculine plural thing and uses de before what comes next.

example.en: Two days followed by rest.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we continue; we are still going
cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguimos is the present form of seguir for nosotros. It can describe continuing an action or remaining on a course.

example.en: We continue along the same road.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to follow; keep track of (events or news)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguir can mean to follow developing news, a campaign, a competition, or another continuing sequence of events—not only to move behind someone physically.

example.en: I follow the news every day.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to follow (a trail, line, or route)
I will continue; I will keep going
cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguiré adds the future ending -é to seguir, 'to continue.' Before an activity form ending in -ando or -iendo, it means that the speaker will keep doing that activity.

example.en: I will keep reading.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguir normally means “to continue.” Before a word describing a condition, it means to remain or still be in that condition. The ending -ía makes this an imagined “would” result.

example.es: Sin ayuda, la puerta seguiría cerrada.
example.en: Without help, the door would still be closed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Según introduces the source, standard, or evidence on which a statement is based.

example.en: According to the map, we are close.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This noun names one second of time. It is separate from segundo meaning ‘second’ in an ordered list.

example.en: Wait one second.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguramente often presents something as highly likely without making it completely certain.

example.en: She will probably arrive this afternoon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In this sense, seguridad is the confidence or reassurance given by a claim, not physical safety or computer security.

example.en: Her answer gave me confidence.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Seguro que is a common conversational opener for something the speaker strongly expects to be true. Seguro stays masculine singular in this use.

example.en: I'm sure Marta will arrive soon.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Seleccione politely tells one person addressed as usted to choose something. It is the formal command of seleccionar.

example.en: Select an option.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a food label, con semilla and sin semilla distinguish seeded and seedless varieties.

example.es: Esta fruta tiene una semilla grande.
example.en: This fruit has a large seed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Señal can name a posted sign, a transmitted signal, or evidence that points to a condition.

example.es: La fiebre puede ser una señal de infección.
example.en: A fever can be a sign of infection.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Señal can also mean a signal or indication. Here it is a physical sign carrying information on a wall.

example.es: La señal está junto a la puerta.
example.en: The sign is beside the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Señalados describes the masculine plural nodos and points to the ones marked in the diagram.

example.en: Compare the marked points.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here señales means clues or indications that suggest something is true, not road signs or posted notices.

example.es: Hay señales de que todo mejora.
example.en: There are signs that everything is improving.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Señal can be a physical sign that directs road users, not only a signal or indication.

example.en: Follow the road signs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here señales are physical or electronic signals sent from one place or time to another, not signs that serve as evidence.

example.es: La antena envía señales de radio.
example.en: The antenna sends radio signals.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sendos comes before a plural masculine noun and says that each previously named person or thing has one of that noun. The feminine form is sendas. It does not simply mean “two” or “both.”

example.es: Ana y Luis llevan sendas mochilas.
example.en: Ana and Luis each carry a backpack.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to sit down; to sit myself down
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sentar means “to seat.” With the matching small word me attached, sentarme normally means that the speaker sits down. The attached me does not need a separate English word.

example.en: I am going to sit down here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sentar is the verb's unchanged dictionary form. Te is attached to it to form sentarte, which focuses on the listener taking a seated position.

example.en: You can sit down here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sentí is the completed-past form of sentir for the speaker. The stem changes from sient- in siento to sent- in sentí.

example.en: I felt great joy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sentido is the irregular completed-action form of sentir. With a matching short word such as me and the helper haber, it describes how someone has felt.

example.es: Nunca me he sentido tan tranquilo.
example.en: I have never felt so calm.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In sin sentido, it describes something with no meaning or point.

example.en: The explanation makes sense.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sentimos normally means “we feel.” In the fixed expression lo sentimos, it is the plural apology used by a group or organization.

example.en: We're sorry for the delay.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to feel; to find oneself feeling
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sentirse is sentir with the pronominal ending se. It is followed by a description of someone's physical or emotional state.

example.es: Después del viaje, se sintió cansado.
example.en: After the trip, he felt tired.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Separación can mean the measured space between two parts.

example.es: Mide la separación entre las piezas.
example.en: Measure the gap between the parts.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Separada is the feminine singular form of separado. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular person or thing.

example.es: Una pieza está separada del resto.
example.en: One piece is separate from the rest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Séptica is the feminine singular form because it describes the feminine noun fosa.

example.en: They inspected the septic tank.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ser usually appears as the dictionary form “to be.” With an article, el ser can instead be a noun meaning a being, existence, or the self.

example.es: El ensayo reflexiona sobre el ser.
example.en: The essay reflects on being.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Será is the future form of ser for one person or thing.

example.en: Tomorrow will be another day.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it will be; it will come to (a plural amount)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Serán is the future form of ser used with a plural amount. Spanish can match ser to plural time units, as in serán dos días, while natural English may use singular ‘it’: ‘it will be two days.’

example.en: It will be a three-hour trip.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Serás is the simple-future form of ser for informal singular “you.” Spanish writes an accent on the final -ás.

example.en: You will be a good guide.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sería is the “would” form of ser, “to be.” Spanish keeps the full dictionary form ser and adds -ía.

example.en: It would be a good solution.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Serían is a conditional form of ser, 'to be.' The ending -ían marks a plural subject and can present a state that was still in the future from an earlier viewpoint.

example.en: I thought they would be kind.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Una serie de introduces a related group or succession of people, things, or events.

example.en: There was a series of problems.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In mathematics, serie can name an ordered sequence of values, although secuencia is also common and is more technically precise in some contexts.

example.es: La serie empieza con uno y uno.
example.en: The sequence begins with one and one.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here serie is a continuing television production made up of episodes, rather than a numerical sequence or a general group of things.

example.en: They started a new TV series.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Serie has the same spelling pattern as English “series,” but Spanish uses series as the plural form.

example.en: We watch two new series.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Service (part of the band name Postal Service)

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, a servidor is a computer or program that provides data or services to other computers.

example.es: Los servidores alojan la página web.
example.en: The servers host the website.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Shock is an English borrowing used unchanged as a masculine noun in Spanish: el shock. Choque, conmoción, or impresión may be preferred depending on the situation.

example.en: The initial shock passed quickly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: At the start of a statement, sí can acknowledge that a point is true before adding a contrast, often with pero. English may use “yes,” “admittedly,” or “granted” for this use.

example.es: Sí, es caro, pero dura muchos años.
example.en: Granted, it is expensive, but it lasts many years.

cardCatalog.answerEn: really does; indeed, as part of sí que
cardCatalog.noteEn: The accent distinguishes affirmative sí from conditional si, “if.” Before que and a changed verb, sí adds strong confirmation rather than answering a yes-or-no question by itself.

example.en: Ana really does work a lot.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a verb, stressed sí can contradict a negative idea and emphasize that the action really does happen. It keeps its written accent.

example.es: No corro mucho, pero sí camino cada día.
example.en: I do not run much, but I do walk every day.

cardCatalog.answerEn: but; after all (introduces an emphatic objection or reminder)
cardCatalog.noteEn: This is standard unaccented si at the start of an exclamation: it pushes back or reminds someone of an obvious fact. It is not accented sí, ‘yes,’ and it does not set a condition as in si llueve, ‘if it rains.’

example.en: But I already told you!

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes por si, 'in case'
cardCatalog.noteEn: Si remains unaccented in por si and introduces the uncertain event for which someone prepares.

example.es: Cierra la ventana por si llueve.
example.en: Close the window in case it rains.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; middle of por si acaso, ‘just in case’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Si remains unaccented inside por si acaso. The whole expression introduces a precaution for an uncertain possibility.

example.es: Trae una chaqueta por si acaso.
example.en: Bring a jacket just in case.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Si has no accent when it introduces the possibility after y. Together, ¿y si...? asks someone to consider what might happen.

example.en: What if we wait?

cardCatalog.answerEn: but; why, when…? (introducing a protest after pero)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Unaccented si does not always introduce an if-condition. After pero, it can open an objection by pointing to a fact the listener is overlooking: ¡Pero si ya lo sabes!

example.en: But the door is already open!

cardCatalog.answerEn: sí (‘yes’) or si (‘if’); Spanish Scrabble tiles omit the accent mark
cardCatalog.noteEn: Standard Spanish distinguishes sí, ‘yes,’ from si, ‘if.’ Spanish Scrabble uses unaccented vowel tiles even for words that carry a written accent in ordinary text, so the played SI can represent either spelling. Without a sentence, the board alone does not choose between them.

example.en: Yes, I will go if I can.

cardCatalog.answerEn: himself; herself; itself; themselves (after a preposition)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a preposition such as de, para, or por, stressed sí points back to a third-person subject. It has a written accent and often appears with mismo, misma, mismos, or mismas for emphasis.

example.es: Guardó el secreto para sí misma.
example.en: She kept the secret to herself.

cardCatalog.answerEn: really?; is that so? (asking for confirmation)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sí normally means ‘yes.’ Said as a short question, it can echo surprising information and ask the other person to confirm it.

example.en: ‘The exam is tomorrow.’ ‘Really?’

cardCatalog.answerEn: whether; if (introducing an indirect yes-or-no question)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Unaccented si can introduce a condition or an indirect yes-or-no question. In me pregunto si, English usually uses “whether.” Accented sí means “yes.”

example.en: I do not know whether it is open.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sido is the completed-action form of ser. It follows a form of haber: ha sido means “has been,” and haber sido means “to have been.”

example.en: It must have been difficult.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Siempre alone commonly means “always.” After para, the complete expression para siempre means “forever.”

example.en: She will keep the letter forever.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Siendo is the irregular ongoing-action form of ser, “to be.” It can follow a form of estar to describe current behavior.

example.en: You are being very kind.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you feel (special form for an event still ahead)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sientas is a present subjunctive form of sentir. After cuando, it presents the feeling as a future event that has not happened yet.

example.en: Rest when you feel pain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Siente is the present form used with one person or thing. Together with se, it can describe what an experience or object feels like.

example.en: The floor feels cold.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Se siente here comes from sentarse, ‘to sit down,’ not sentirse, ‘to feel.’ After wording that presents the sitting as still awaited, ordinary se sienta changes to the special form se siente.

example.es: Espero a que Luis se siente.
example.en: I am waiting for Luis to sit down.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I feel (in lo siento: I'm sorry)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Siento is the form of sentir used by the speaker. With me before it, me siento describes how the speaker feels or what the speaker feels like; this is different from lo siento, the fixed expression for “I'm sorry.”

example.en: I feel better today.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Significaban describes an ongoing or general meaning in the past.

example.en: Those signs meant danger.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here simpatía is fellow-feeling for someone in pain, not simply friendliness.

example.en: She showed sympathy for the family.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Simplificada is the completed-action form of simplificar used as a description. Its -a ending matches a feminine singular noun.

example.en: This is a simplified version.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins sin más, “just like that”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sin normally means “without,” but sin más functions as a fixed expression for doing something with no further thought, preparation, explanation, or ceremony.

example.en: You cannot just walk in like that.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sin embargo (“however”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sin normally means “without,” but sin embargo is one fixed connector. In that expression, translate the pair together rather than translating sin separately.

example.en: I wanted to go out; however, it was raining.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sincronice is the special form of sincronizar used after hacer que because synchronization is the result being caused. Ordinary sincroniza changes to sincronice.

example.es: Haz que el reloj se sincronice.
example.en: Make the clock synchronize.

cardCatalog.noteEn: La sinestesia is a condition in which stimulation of one sense or kind of thought consistently produces an additional experience, such as associating letters or numbers with colors.

example.es: Ella asocia sonidos con colores por su sinestesia.
example.en: She associates sounds with colors because of her synesthesia.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Siniestro can describe something threatening or disturbing. In insurance language it can instead mean a damaging incident or claim.

example.en: They heard some sinister noises.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After a negative statement, sino replaces the rejected option with a contrasting one.

example.en: I do not want to run, but rather to walk.

cardCatalog.answerEn: but also; introduces the added contrast after no solo
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sino introduces the second noun, description, or matching phrase after no solo. Before a full changed verb, Spanish commonly uses sino que.

example.es: No solo estudia física, sino química.
example.en: She studies not only physics, but also chemistry.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A sintetizador de voz is a speech synthesizer: software or hardware that produces spoken audio.

example.es: El sintetizador produce una voz artificial.
example.en: The synthesizer produces an artificial voice.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Síntoma is grammatically masculine despite ending in -a: el síntoma, los síntomas.

example.en: The symptoms disappeared.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes ni siquiera, ‘not even’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Siquiera completes ni siquiera. Learn the two words together for the common meaning ‘not even.’

example.es: No tengo ni siquiera un minuto.
example.en: I do not even have one minute.

cardCatalog.answerEn: more than enough; surplus (in de sobra)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sobra normally relates to something left over. In de sobra, it completes a fixed expression for an ample surplus.

example.en: There is plenty of time.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sobras are portions of prepared food left after a meal.

example.en: We saved the leftovers for tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sobre la marcha (“as you go”)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sobre can locate one thing above and supported by another. It has a separate common sense meaning ‘about.’

example.es: Las llaves están sobre la mesa.
example.en: The keys are on the table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sobre can introduce the geographical area across which something is measured or happens. This is different from sobre meaning ‘about’ a topic.

example.es: La tormenta avanza sobre la costa.
example.en: The storm moves over the coast.

cardCatalog.noteEn: El sobremesa is a shortened form of el ordenador de sobremesa. In other contexts, la sobremesa can instead mean the conversation and time spent at the table after a meal.

example.es: Uso un sobremesa en la oficina.
example.en: I use a desktop computer at the office.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you jolt; you start suddenly (with te)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sobresaltarse describes reacting with a sudden involuntary start because of surprise, fear, or a physical sensation. Te marks the informal listener.

example.en: You jolt at the noise.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Social has the same form with a masculine or feminine singular noun: un acto social, una regla social.

example.en: It is a social norm.

cardCatalog.answerEn: socialized; accustomed to social contact (masculine plural)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Socializados describes people or animals that have learned to interact comfortably with others.

example.en: The puppies are well socialized.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sociología is the study of societies, social relationships, and institutions.

example.en: She studies sociology at the university.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sociólogos is the masculine or mixed-group plural for people who work in sociology.

example.en: The sociologists analyzed the survey.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Socorro is a conventional emergency cry asking for immediate help.

example.en: Help! There is a fire!

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all are (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Sois is the present form of ser used with vosotros or vosotras, the informal way to address several people in Spain.

example.en: You all are very kind.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they used to; they would usually
cardCatalog.noteEn: Solían is soler's imperfect-past form for more than one person. It is followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: They used to walk together.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Solicitando is the -ando form of solicitar. It presents a formal request or application as an ongoing action.

example.en: I am applying for a scholarship.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Solicito is the present form of solicitar for yo, 'I.' Although it resembles English 'solicit,' its ordinary Spanish meaning is simply to request or apply for something.

example.en: I request a copy of the report.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When solo describes a masculine person's state, it means alone or lonely rather than “only.” The feminine form is sola.

example.es: Se sintió solo en la ciudad nueva.
example.en: He felt lonely in the new city.

cardCatalog.noteEn: After no, solo marks the first item in a contrast that later adds another item with sino.

example.es: No solo llamó, sino que vino.
example.en: She not only called, but also came.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The comic uses the formerly common accent in sólo. Current standard spelling normally writes solo without an accent when it means “only,” unless an accent is exceptionally needed to prevent genuine ambiguity.

example.en: I only need a minute.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Soltará is a future form of soltar. With se, it can describe something detaching or coming free without naming a person who releases it.

example.es: La pieza se soltará con el movimiento.
example.en: The piece will come loose with the movement.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Solteros is the masculine or mixed-group plural of soltero. With no following noun, it stands for the people themselves.

example.es: Hay muchos solteros en el grupo.
example.en: There are many single people in the group.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sombrero is the general Spanish word for a hat with a brim; it does not name only the Mexican style called a sombrero in English.

example.es: Dejó el sombrero junto a la puerta.
example.en: He left the hat beside the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sometidos comes from someter. Its -os ending matches a masculine or mixed plural group.

example.es: Los planes están sometidos a revisión.
example.en: The plans are subject to review.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I subject; I expose (something to a condition)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Someto is the present form of someter used with yo. The thing affected normally comes before a, and the test or condition comes after a.

example.en: I subject the sample to pressure.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we are (an identity or defining description)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Somos is the present form of ser used with nosotros or nosotras, “we.” Ser presents an identity, category, or defining description; estamos normally presents a state or location instead.

example.en: We are neighbors.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Son normally means 'they are,' but clock time uses son before every hour except one o'clock because the understood word horas is plural.

example.en: It is five o'clock.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Soñar is the verb's unchanged dictionary form, normally meaning “to dream.” When el appears before it, Spanish can treat the activity itself like a noun.

example.es: El soñar inspira a la artista.
example.en: Dreaming inspires the artist.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sonido can mean sound in general or a particular noise that can be heard.

example.en: I hear a strange sound.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sonoro describes something that produces or relates to sound. Sonoras agrees with the feminine plural noun ondas.

example.es: Las ondas sonoras llegan al micrófono.
example.en: The sound waves reach the microphone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sonoro describes something made of, relating to, or rich in sound.

example.es: El museo creó un mapa sonoro.
example.en: The museum created a sound map.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sonreír means ‘to smile.’ The short word me is attached to its end and identifies the person receiving the smile; the written accent on í remains.

example.en: She wants to smile at me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sonrojo is the present ‘I’ form of sonrojarse, ‘to blush.’ In this use it appears with me: me sonrojo.

example.en: I blush easily.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they support; they are compatible with
cardCatalog.noteEn: In a technical context, soportar means that a system can work with a protocol, format, or feature. It is not the physical sense of holding something up.

example.en: These browsers support the format.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This sense of soportar is about tolerating something unpleasant, not physically supporting weight.

example.en: I cannot put up with that noise.

cardCatalog.answerEn: support; technical ability to work with something
cardCatalog.noteEn: In technology, soporte can mean that a system is compatible with a device, format, or feature, not only help from a support worker.

example.es: El navegador tiene soporte para este formato.
example.en: The browser supports this format.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sospecha is the present form of sospechar used with él, ella, or formal usted.

example.en: Marta suspects that something changed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The written accent belongs on the first syllable: sótano.

example.es: Guardamos las cajas en el sótano.
example.en: We keep the boxes in the basement.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spam is a widely used technology loanword in Spanish for unsolicited or repetitive messages.

example.en: The filter removes spam.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Splaash is a stretched comic-book sound for a large object entering water. The extra a suggests a longer or larger splash.

example.en: The rock fell into the water: splash!

cardCatalog.noteEn: A run of s letters can represent a sustained hiss, such as air leaving a valve or filling a balloon.

example.en: The valve went “hissss.”

cardCatalog.noteEn: With formal usted, su can mean “your.” The same form can also mean “his,” “her,” or “their,” so context identifies the owner.

example.en: Ma’am, here is your coffee.

cardCatalog.answerEn: its; part of a su vez (‘in turn’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Su is the possessive middle word in the fixed expression a su vez. The expression can refer to a person or thing taking its turn in a sequence.

example.es: El segundo equipo, a su vez, revisó los datos.
example.en: The second team, in turn, reviewed the data.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Su comes before the singular thing that belongs to someone. Spanish does not mark the owner's gender in su; the surrounding context identifies a female owner.

example.en: Ana lost her phone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Su agrees with the possessed thing, not with the owner. The same Spanish form can mean his, her, its, their, or formal your; the surrounding context identifies the owner.

example.en: Carlos opens his laptop.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Su does not show the owner's gender. Here a singular institution or place is the owner.

example.en: The company changed its name.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Su stays singular because the possessed thing is singular, even when the owners are several people. Sus is used before a plural possessed thing.

example.en: The students know their subject.

cardCatalog.answerEn: your (formal or plural, before one thing)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here el subconsciente is used as a noun for the part of the mind outside conscious awareness.

example.es: El subconsciente influye en los sueños.
example.en: The subconscious influences dreams.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Subida can name an upward movement or an increase in a measured level.

example.es: La subida del nivel fue rápida.
example.en: The rise in the level was rapid.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Subirá is the future form of subir for one person or thing.

example.en: The balloon will rise slowly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Subyace is the present form of subyacer used with one third-person subject. It often takes a before the thing supported or explained at a deeper level.

example.es: Una regla sencilla subyace al sistema.
example.en: A simple rule underlies the system.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sucede is a present form of suceder for one event or situation. It says that the event happens or takes place.

example.en: That happens every summer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: follow one another; occur in succession (with se)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Suceden is the present plural form of suceder. With se, it describes things coming one after another.

example.en: The meetings follow one another quickly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sucedió is the completed-past form of suceder for one event or thing.

example.en: The change happened in April.

cardCatalog.answerEn: usually; tends to (before an action verb)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Suele is the singular present form of soler. It is followed by another verb in its unchanged dictionary form to describe a habitual action.

example.en: Ana usually walks to work.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Suelo is the present form of soler for the speaker. Before an unchanged action verb, it says that the action is habitual. This is unrelated to the noun suelo, meaning floor or ground.

example.en: I usually walk after dinner.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Suena is a present form of sonar. With me, te, le, nos, os, or les, it can say that a name, idea, or thing feels familiar to someone.

example.en: That name sounds familiar to me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Suena is the form of sonar used for one thing that gives an impression. A describing word can follow it directly; sonar a is a different pattern used before a noun or comparison.

example.en: The idea sounds interesting.

cardCatalog.answerEn: sounds; seems (before a comparison with a)
cardCatalog.noteEn: A form of sonar followed by a can compare the impression something gives with another thing.

example.en: That sounds like an excuse.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Suficiente describes an adequate amount or degree. After neutral lo, lo suficiente means “enough” or “what is sufficient.”

example.en: That is enough.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to suffer; to experience an unwanted condition

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sugiere is the present form of sugerir for one person or thing. In the stressed part of this verb, e changes to ie: sugerir becomes sugiere.

example.en: Marta suggests another route.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sumas is the familiar singular present form of sumar. With le before it, the small word can identify the value receiving the added amount.

example.en: You add two to the result.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Súper is an informal shortened noun for supermercado. The written accent distinguishes its stressed pronunciation.

example.en: I am going to the supermarket for milk.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Superficie is the outside or upper level of something, including the top of a body of water.

example.es: La boya volvió a la superficie.
example.en: The buoy returned to the surface.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Superó is a completed-past form of superar. It says that someone exceeded another person's level or performance.

example.en: The student surpassed the teacher.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you found out; you learned (informal singular)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Supiste is the completed-past form of saber used with one familiar listener. In a question about a source, it asks how that person came to know something.

example.en: How did you find out the news?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Supondrá is the future form of suponer for one thing. Here it introduces the consequences something will bring.

example.en: The change will entail more work.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Suponer can mean “to suppose,” but it also describes the result, amount, or consequence that something represents.

example.es: El cambio supone una hora más.
example.en: The change means one extra hour.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por supuesto (“of course”)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Surrealista has the same form with masculine and feminine singular nouns.

example.en: We watched a surreal film.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sus is used before plural things that are owned. It agrees with what is owned, not with the owner; with usted, it can mean formal “your.”

example.en: Sir, these are your documents.

cardCatalog.noteEn: When context identifies a female owner, sus means “her” before plural things. It agrees with the things owned, not with the owner.

example.en: Ana raised her hands.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sus can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or formal “your.” It agrees with the plural things possessed, not with the owner; context tells you whose they are.

example.es: El jefe llamó a sus empleados.
example.en: The boss called his employees.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sus agrees with the plural things owned, not with the owner. The same Spanish form can also mean “his,” “her,” or “their” in other contexts, so context identifies the owner.

example.en: The tree loses its leaves.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In aviation, sustentación is the upward aerodynamic force that helps support an aircraft.

example.en: The wing generates lift.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I replace her; I stand in for her (as a requested action)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Sysadmin is an English computing loan used for the person who maintains computer systems, servers, accounts, and related services. Spanish also uses administrador or administradora de sistemas.

example.en: The system administrator checked the servers.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tabla can mean a flat wooden board. The same written plural can also mean tables of information, so the pictured object determines the sense here.

example.en: They bought boards for the floor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: TAC abbreviates tomografía axial computarizada, a CT scan. The full name is feminine, so una TAC is often preferred; un TAC is especially common in Spain and among medical professionals.

example.en: I need a CT scan of my abdomen.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes qué tal, “how about...?”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tal completes qué tal, a common expression used to ask how something is or to suggest an option. It does not have a useful separate English translation in this expression.

example.en: How about tomorrow?

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; completes qué tal when asking how something went
cardCatalog.noteEn: Qué and tal work together as one question expression. Tal stays unchanged regardless of the event being discussed.

example.en: How has the trip gone?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a singular naming word, tal points to something of the kind just mentioned. It becomes tales before a plural naming word.

example.en: I know of no such rule.

cardCatalog.answerEn: just; exactly (as part of tal y como)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tal is part of the fixed connector tal y como here. Learn the three words together as “just as” or “exactly as.”

example.en: It happened exactly as you said.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tam is not a complete standard Spanish word. When the remaining letters are hidden or cut off, it can be the readable beginning of también.

example.en: We also want to go.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tampoco adds a second negative case. In a short reply, yo tampoco means “me neither”; the negative verb does not need to be repeated.

example.en: I do not know either.

cardCatalog.answerEn: as (before a description in tan… como)
no separate English word; adds emphasis in tan solo (“only; just”)
both; introduces the first of two linked items
cardCatalog.noteEn: In tanto X como Y, tanto opens the first item and como introduces the second. The two items can be nouns, descriptions, or longer matching phrases.

example.es: Sirve tanto para estudiar como para descansar.
example.en: It is useful both for studying and for resting.
