cardCatalog.answerEn: somewhat; rather (as part of un tanto)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tanto often concerns amount, but the fixed pair un tanto softens a description in much the same way as ‘somewhat’ or ‘rather.’

example.es: El final fue un tanto raro.
example.en: The ending was rather strange.

cardCatalog.answerEn: as much; to the same degree
cardCatalog.noteEn: After a verb, tanto can measure how much the action happens. With como it makes an equality comparison.

example.en: Ana works as much as Luis.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tarda is a present form of tardar for one person or thing. Tardar en followed by an action says that the action takes time.

example.en: The train takes a while to arrive.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tardará keeps the complete verb tardar and adds -á to place the time-taking in the future for one person, group, or thing.

example.en: The repair will take an hour.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tasa is a feminine noun for a rate, especially a quantity measured relative to a population or period.

example.en: The employment rate increased.

cardCatalog.answerEn: tautology; a statement that needlessly repeats the same idea
cardCatalog.noteEn: A tautología says the same thing again in different words or is true simply because of how its terms are defined.

example.es: ‘Entrar dentro’ puede sonar como una tautología.
example.en: ‘Enter inside’ can sound like a tautology.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The written accent distinguishes té, the drink, from te, a short pronoun meaning you or to you.

example.en: We drink tea with lemon.

cardCatalog.answerEn: marks you as the affected owner; English often uses “your”
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish can identify an affected owner with me, te, le, nos, or les and still use el or la before the owned thing. English often uses a possessive instead: te rompieron el móvil means “they broke your phone.”

example.en: I cleaned your computer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks you in te das cuenta
cardCatalog.noteEn: Darse cuenta uses a matching small pronoun: me for I, te for familiar you, and se for he, she, or they.

example.en: Do you notice the change?

cardCatalog.answerEn: yourself; marks the listener in darse un golpe
cardCatalog.noteEn: In te diste un golpe, te marks one familiar listener as the person who experienced the bump. Natural English often uses “yourself” or rearranges the body part.

example.en: Did you bump yourself?

cardCatalog.answerEn: you; identifies the person being estimated
cardCatalog.noteEn: With echar in its estimating sense, te points to the familiar listener whose age, time, or other amount the speaker is estimating.

example.en: I estimate you at about twenty years old.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to you; marks one familiar person as the person who likes something
cardCatalog.noteEn: With gustar, te identifies the person experiencing the liking. The liked thing controls the verb: te gusta una cosa and te gustan varias cosas.

example.en: You like those books.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Te can mean “to you” when you are the recipient or the person affected by an action. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.en: I’m sending you a message.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you; for yourself (small pronoun used with merecerse)
cardCatalog.noteEn: With informal singular tú, te is the matching small pronoun in merecerse algo. It appears before a form that matches the person and time, such as mereces.

example.en: You deserve a break.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks that “you” are the person who worries
cardCatalog.noteEn: Preocuparse is used with me, te, se, nos, or os. Te is the form for one familiar person addressed as tú.

example.en: Do not worry about me.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks a “you” verb used with te
cardCatalog.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs use te when the person affected is the informal listener. The meaning belongs to the whole verb pattern, so English may not translate te separately.

example.en: You stay here.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to you; for you (one familiar person)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Te can identify one familiar listener as the person who receives something or benefits from an action. It normally comes before a verb that has changed for the person and time.

example.en: I am bringing you a coffee.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; marks referirse for one familiar listener
cardCatalog.noteEn: Referirse is a pronominal verb: its small marker changes with the person. Use me refiero for “I refer,” te refieres for “you refer,” and se refiere for “he, she, or it refers.”

example.en: Are you referring to the report?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before imaginas, te identifies the informal listener as both the person imagining and the person pictured in the imagined scene.

example.en: You imagine yourself traveling alone.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to you; marks you as the person who finds something a certain way
cardCatalog.noteEn: With resultar plus a description, te identifies one familiar person who experiences that impression. The thing producing the impression is the grammatical subject.

example.en: Do you find the task difficult?

cardCatalog.answerEn: techno; an electronic dance-music genre (printed with the English spelling)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish commonly retains the international spelling techno for the electronic dance-music genre. It can be used as a genre noun without an article after verbs such as escuchar or comprar.

example.en: We listened to techno at the party.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Teclea is a present form of teclear used for one person or thing, or for formal singular “you.” As a brief action label, it reports that one person is typing.

example.en: Ana types a password.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tecleando is the -ando form of teclear, pressing keys to enter text. Context can make it typing at a keyboard or texting on a phone.

example.en: She crossed the street while texting.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The ending -a matches a feminine singular noun such as perspicacia.

example.en: We need technical help.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, técnica is a particular method or way of doing something. This is distinct from técnica used as an adjective meaning technical.

example.en: We tried a new technique.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Técnicamente describes something as true according to a strict or technical reading.

example.en: Technically, the shop is still open.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, técnico names a trained worker who installs, maintains, or repairs equipment or a service. La técnica can name a female technician.

example.en: The technician checked the modem.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tecnología can mean technology in general or one technological system or field.

example.en: This technology is still experimental.

cardCatalog.answerEn: tissue; a structural material in a living organism
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tejido can also mean woven fabric. In biology, it names a group of similar cells that form part of a plant or animal.

example.en: Plant tissue contains water.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tejón is the animal called a badger. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: A badger came out of the forest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Teléfono is stressed on lé, which is why it carries a written accent.

example.en: The phone is ringing.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Teléfono can name the device itself or the number used to call someone. Context distinguishes the two senses.

example.es: Apunté tu teléfono en mi agenda.
example.en: I wrote your phone number in my address book.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Teléfonos is the plural of teléfono. The written accent keeps the stress on lé.

example.es: Los teléfonos están sobre la mesa.
example.en: The phones are on the table.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Teletienda combines tele-, relating to television, with tienda, “shop.” It refers to products sold through television advertisements.

example.es: Compró el aparato en la teletienda.
example.en: She bought the device through television shopping.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tema can mean a topic, but in music it can name a recognizable melody or theme.

example.es: Reconocí el tema de la película.
example.en: I recognized the film's theme.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tema can mean a subject being discussed or studied. This is separate from its use for a musical theme or tune.

example.es: Es un tema difícil de explicar.
example.en: It is a difficult subject to explain.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In software, a tema is a coordinated set of colors, images, and styles that changes how an interface looks. In other contexts, tema can mean ‘topic.’

example.es: La aplicación incluye varios temas oscuros.
example.en: The application includes several dark themes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Teme is a present form of temer used with one person or thing.

example.en: The dog fears the noise.

cardCatalog.answerEn: warm; getting closer to the target in a hot-and-cold game
cardCatalog.noteEn: Templado literally describes a mild or warm temperature. As a game clue, it marks progress between frío, which is far away, and caliente, which is very close.

example.en: Warm... Come a little closer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Temporada can name a run of television episodes, as English uses “season.”

example.es: La próxima temporada tendrá diez episodios.
example.en: The next season will have ten episodes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ten is the positive familiar command form of tener. In tener en cuenta it tells one familiar person to consider something.

example.en: Keep this in mind tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it will have; he or she will have
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tendrá is a future form of tener for one person or thing. Tener changes its stem to tendr- before the future ending -á.

example.en: The building will have another entrance.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tendrás is the future form of tener for one familiar person. Tener changes its future stem to tendr- before the ending -ás.

example.en: Tomorrow you will have more time.

cardCatalog.noteEn: To make this ‘would’ form, tener changes to the irregular base tendr- and adds -ía. The following noun states what would be had.

example.es: El proyecto tendría un coste alto.
example.en: The project would have a high cost.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you all have (informal plural, mainly Spain)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tenéis is the present form of tener for vosotros or vosotras. It informally addresses more than one person and is used especially in Spain.

example.en: Do you all have the tickets?

cardCatalog.answerEn: to have; to have a certain quality about it
cardCatalog.noteEn: In questions such as ¿qué tiene de especial?, tener asks what quality or feature something has. English often phrases the idea as “what is special about it?”

example.en: What is special about this place?

cardCatalog.answerEn: to feel; to have (as part of tener miedo)
to have each other; to have us
cardCatalog.noteEn: The action word tener means “to have.” The attached nos normally means “us”; when the same two or more people both do and receive the action, context gives it the reciprocal sense “each other.”

example.en: It is good to have each other nearby.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they have (special form after a future cuando)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tengan is a special form of tener used after cuando when the event is still expected or hypothetical rather than presented as an established fact.

example.en: Call me when they have time.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you have (special form after puede que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tengas is a form of tener for familiar singular ‘you.’ After puede que, ‘may’ or ‘might,’ Spanish uses tengas instead of ordinary tienes because the idea is presented as possible rather than certain.

example.en: You may have time tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you have (special form after an evaluation)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tengas is a special form of tener for familiar singular ‘you.’ After an impersonal judgment such as es increíble que, Spanish normally changes the ordinary tienes to tengas.

example.en: It is good that you have time.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I am (stating age); literally, I have
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses tener, “to have,” when stating age. Tengo is the form for the speaker: tengo edad suficiente means “I am old enough.”

example.en: I am twenty years old.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tenía is a past form of tener. It presents a state or characteristic that held at that past time without marking its beginning or end.

example.en: The house had a garden.

cardCatalog.answerEn: had (the completed-action form used after he)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tensión can be physical tightness, emotional suspense, or mental strain that has not been settled. Its final syllable is stressed, so it carries a written accent.

example.en: The wait created a lot of tension.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tercera is the feminine form of tercero, ‘third.’ Its ending matches a feminine singular noun such as planta or puerta.

example.en: It is the third door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Terminado is the completed-action form of terminar, “to finish.” After a form of haber such as ha, it stays unchanged rather than matching the person or thing that finished.

example.en: The meeting has ended.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they end up; you all end up (formal)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a description of the final result, terminan says where people or things eventually end up. It is the present form used with a plural subject.

example.en: The roads end up blocked.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it ends; it finishes, referring to a future event after en cuanto
cardCatalog.noteEn: Termine is a special form of terminar used because the ending has not happened yet. Spanish commonly uses this form after en cuanto when looking forward to a future event.

example.en: I will leave as soon as it ends.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before an -ando or -iendo action form, terminó describes the final outcome of a process or series of events.

example.en: She ended up living in Madrid.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Terriblemente is formed from the feminine singular describing word terrible plus -mente. It strongly intensifies the manner or degree of what follows.

example.en: The train arrived terribly late.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tesis has the same written form in the singular and plural; surrounding words show the number.

example.es: Leyó dos tesis sobre el tema.
example.en: She read two theses on the topic.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Test is a widely used loanword in Spanish. Its plural is tests.

example.en: Tomorrow we have a test.

cardCatalog.answerEn: The (part of the English band name The Donnas)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tibiamente is formed from tibia plus -mente and describes a response lacking warmth or enthusiasm.

example.en: The audience applauded without enthusiasm.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tiburón is the general Spanish word for a shark.

example.es: Vieron un tiburón cerca del barco.
example.en: They saw a shark near the boat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In expressions about an earlier era, tiempos means the times or days in which something used to happen, not measured timings.

example.en: Those were different times.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tiempos can mean deliberately chosen timings, not only time in a general sense.

example.es: Ajustaron los tiempos de las señales.
example.en: They adjusted the signal timings.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you are (stating age); literally, you have
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish states age with tener, “to have.” Tienes is the present form for one person addressed informally, so tienes trece años means that the listener is thirteen years old.

example.en: You are twenty years old.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This sense contrasts land with the sea. It does not name the planet Earth or soil as a material.

example.es: Después de horas en el mar, vimos tierra.
example.en: After hours at sea, we saw land.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This sense names the planet rather than land or soil.

example.es: La Tierra gira alrededor del Sol.
example.en: Earth revolves around the Sun.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a political or geographic context, tierras can mean a people's territory rather than separate pieces of soil.

example.en: They traveled through distant lands.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish normally uses the plural las tijeras for one pair of scissors.

example.en: I need some scissors.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tinte can mean dye or tint. In an image-editing control, it refers to the hue or color cast applied to an image.

example.es: La foto tiene un tinte azul.
example.en: The photo has a blue tint.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tío literally means “uncle,” but in informal Spanish from Spain it can also refer to a man or guy. With an article, as in un tío, it normally names someone; used directly to a listener, it can instead work like informal “man” or “dude.”

example.en: A guy asked about you.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tío literally means “uncle,” but in casual speech in Spain it can address a male friend much like “dude” or “man.”

example.es: Tío, no me lo puedo creer.
example.en: Dude, I can't believe it.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tío literally means an uncle. Before a relative's name in direct address, it functions like the English family title “Uncle.” This is distinct from the informal Spain use meaning “guy.”

example.en: Thanks, Uncle Carlos.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Típicos is masculine plural. When one adjective describes a mixed-gender group of nouns, Spanish convention normally uses the masculine plural form.

example.en: We buy fresh bread and fruit.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In informal speech, tipo can refer to a man as “guy.” In other contexts, it can instead mean a type or kind.

example.en: That guy lives nearby.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In printing and design, tipo can be a shortened way to refer to a tipo de letra, a typeface or font. This is distinct from informal tipo meaning “guy.”

example.es: Elige un tipo fácil de leer.
example.en: Choose an easy-to-read typeface.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tipo can informally mean a person or guy. The plural tipos may refer to a group of men or a mixed group.

example.es: Conozco a unos tipos que trabajan aquí.
example.en: I know some guys who work here.

cardCatalog.answerEn: sleeping with; having sex with (informal, as part of tirarse a alguien)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tirar normally means to throw or pull. The pronominal expression tirarse a alguien is informal and means to have sex with that person; tirando is its -ando ongoing-action form.

example.es: La novela insinúa que se estaba tirando a su vecino.
example.en: The novel hints that he was sleeping with his neighbor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tirar can mean throwing something physically or disposing of it. The object and situation identify the discard sense.

example.en: Do not throw away that box.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to throw something at someone's property; le marks the affected owner
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tirar is the unchanged action form, and le attaches to its end for the person affected. Spanish can then use an ordinary article before that person's item, where natural English often uses “her” or “his.”

example.es: A Ana le tiraron pintura a la puerta.
example.en: Someone threw paint at Ana's door.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is someone's turn; falls to someone to do
cardCatalog.noteEn: In tocarle a alguien hacer algo, toca does not mean physically touching. It says that an action is now that person's turn or responsibility.

example.en: Today it is my turn to cook.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to annoy us; to piss us off (in a vulgar fixed expression)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tocar normally means to touch or play an instrument, and attached nos marks us as the affected people. In tocarle los cojones a alguien, the whole expression is a very vulgar way to say ‘annoy someone’ or ‘piss someone off.’

example.es: A esos vecinos les encanta tocarnos los cojones.
example.en: Those neighbors love to piss us off.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a comparison such as mejor, peor, más, or menos, todavía can strengthen the difference and correspond to English “even” or “still.” This is related to, but distinct from, todavía meaning that a situation continues.

example.es: La segunda opción es todavía peor.
example.en: The second option is even worse.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a singular noun without an article, todo can cover every instance of that kind. This differs from standalone todo, ‘everything.’

example.en: Every level requires practice.

cardCatalog.answerEn: everyone; everybody (as part of todo el mundo)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Todo normally means “all” or “everything.” In the fixed expression todo el mundo, the complete phrase refers to everyone.

example.en: Everyone arrived early.

cardCatalog.answerEn: part of a todo esto: by the way; speaking of that
cardCatalog.noteEn: Inside this fixed transition, todo does not simply mean “all” on its own.

example.en: By the way, what time is it?

cardCatalog.answerEn: all (completing después de todo, after all)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Todo completes the fixed expression después de todo.

example.en: After all, it turned out well.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before el plus a masculine singular noun, todo means the whole amount or extent of it: todo el día, todo el trabajo.

example.en: She studied the whole chapter.

cardCatalog.answerEn: all of them (masculine or mixed plural)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here todos stands alone for all the previously understood options.

example.en: I have tried all of them.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Todos can stand on its own for a whole masculine or mixed group. With a first-person plural verb, it includes the speaker and naturally becomes “we all” or “all of us” in English.

example.en: We all want to rest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Standalone todos can refer to all the people in a group. It is masculine plural for an all-male or mixed group; todas is used for an all-female group.

example.en: Everyone understood the warning.

cardCatalog.answerEn: take (a form of transport; informal command)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Toma tells one familiar person to use or board the named transport. It comes from tomar.

example.en: Take the bus.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tomando is the -ando action form of tomar. With juramento, tomar can mean to administer an oath to another person; the surrounding context distinguishes this from taking an oath oneself.

example.es: La jueza está tomando juramento al testigo.
example.en: The judge is administering the oath to the witness.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tomar has several uses. With a beverage or the vague object algo in a social invitation, it commonly means to have something to drink.

example.en: We are going to have a coffee.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With a vehicle or service, tomar means using it to travel.

example.en: We are going to take the train.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to have; to get yourself (a drink or bite)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tomarte is the familiar-person form of tomarse attached to the unchanged verb. Tomarse algo commonly means having a drink or light bite, especially as a social activity.

example.en: Do you want to have a coffee?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tomas is the familiar singular present form of tomar. In a procedure, it can mean choosing or starting with a value or object.

example.es: Tomas un valor inicial y aplicas la regla.
example.en: You take an initial value and apply the rule.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tome tells one person addressed as usted to take something. In a handover, it can work like English “here you go.”

example.en: Take this document, please.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we take; we handle (in a form used after a judgment or reaction)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tomemos is a “we” form of tomar used when the action is presented through a judgment, reaction, wish, or similar trigger rather than as a plain fact. The ordinary form tomamos changes its -amos ending to -emos.

example.en: It is important that we take notes.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Top is a common loanword for the highest positions in a ranking.

example.es: La canción entró en el top diez.
example.en: The song entered the top ten.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tostadoras is the plural of tostadora, an appliance for toasting bread. The word is printed across two lines in this comic but remains one word.

example.es: Las tostadoras están en la cocina.
example.en: The toasters are in the kitchen.

cardCatalog.noteEn: This French borrowing is used as a short reaction that admits the other person's clever reply or successful counterpoint.

example.en: “You did the same thing.” “Touché.”

cardCatalog.noteEn: Trabajo often means work or a job. In costar trabajo, it instead names the effort or difficulty involved in doing something.

example.en: Learning this technique takes effort.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to swallow; to buy or accept uncritically
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tragarse can describe literal swallowing, but it also means accepting a claim or story too readily. The attached se is part of this dictionary form.

example.en: I don't buy that rumor.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Trago literally can be a swallow or sip. In a count such as dos tragos, it commonly refers to alcoholic drinks.

example.es: Tomaron dos tragos en el bar.
example.en: They had two drinks at the bar.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Traído is the completed-action form, also called the past participle, of traer. It keeps the written accent on í.

example.en: I have brought water.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Traigo is the present form of traer used when the speaker says yo. The middle of the verb changes: traer becomes traigo.

example.en: I am bringing bread for dinner.

cardCatalog.noteEn: With hacer, trampa means cheating or breaking the rules.

example.en: Don't cheat.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Trans- is added to the beginning of another word to suggest crossing or going beyond a boundary. It stays attached to the word that follows it, usually with no space.

example.es: El vuelo transatlántico dura varias horas.
example.en: The transatlantic flight lasts several hours.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A transbordador transports people or cargo between points; transbordador espacial is a space shuttle.

example.es: El transbordador lleva pasajeros a la isla.
example.en: The shuttle carries passengers to the island.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Transcurre is the present form of transcurrir used for one subject, often a period or moment of time.

example.en: The afternoon passes quietly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Transfieren is the plural present form of transferir.

example.en: The pipes transfer the heat.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it will transmit; it will relay
cardCatalog.noteEn: Transmitirá is the future form of transmitir for one person or thing. The ending -á supplies “will”; the subject in the surrounding context tells you whether English uses he, she, it, or formal you.

example.en: The radio will broadcast the match.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is about; concerns (as part of se trata de)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Trata comes from tratar, but se trata de works as a fixed impersonal expression meaning that something concerns a topic or is about an action.

example.es: Se trata de una decisión importante.
example.en: It is about an important decision.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tratabas is a past form of tratar for one familiar person. With de before an action, tratar means “to try”; the -abas ending presents that attempt as ongoing or as background rather than as one completed event.

example.en: You were trying to open the door.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here tratado is a noun naming an agreement between governments, not the completed form of tratar.

example.es: Los dos países aprobaron el tratado.
example.en: The two countries approved the treaty.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we are dealing; we deal (with con)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Tratamos is the present nosotros form of tratar. Followed by con, it can mean dealing with or facing a person, problem, or situation.

example.en: We are dealing with a delicate problem.

cardCatalog.answerEn: part of a través de, “through” or “across”

cardCatalog.noteEn: Trepa tells one familiar person to climb. It comes from trepar.

example.en: Climb carefully.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Trepó is the completed-past form of trepar for one person or thing. It presents the climb as a finished event.

example.es: El gato trepó por el árbol.
example.en: The cat climbed up the tree.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A trilogía is a set of three related works. Its written accent belongs on í.

example.en: I read the complete trilogy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A trimestre is a period of three months. It is commonly used for stages of pregnancy and for divisions of an academic or financial year.

example.en: The course lasts one trimester.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Trío can name any group of three. In a sexual context, it means three people having sex together.

example.en: They talked about having a threesome.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Triunfaréis keeps the full verb triunfar and adds -éis for a future action by vosotros, the informal plural “you” used mainly in Spain.

example.en: With patience, you all will succeed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses the borrowed noun troll for someone who posts provocative messages mainly to upset people or attract angry replies. This sense is different from the creature in folklore.

example.es: El foro bloqueó a un troll.
example.en: The forum blocked an internet troll.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tropiezas is the present form of tropezar for one informal listener. The vowel changes from e in tropezar to ie in tropiezas.

example.es: A veces tropiezas con esa piedra.
example.en: Sometimes you trip over that stone.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A computer troyano pretends to be useful or harmless so that someone will allow malicious code to run.

example.en: The file hid two Trojan programs.

cardCatalog.answerEn: tunnel; protected route for network traffic
cardCatalog.noteEn: In networking, a tunnel carries one kind of traffic inside another connection, often to link a device securely to a remote network.

example.es: Los datos pasan por un túnel cifrado.
example.en: The data passes through an encrypted tunnel.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A turno is a scheduled period of work. Turnos is plural.

example.en: This week I am working three shifts.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tuve is the completed-past form of tener for the speaker. This completed-event past is called the preterite.

example.en: I had a meeting yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tuviera is a special past form of tener used when the thing being described is sought, imagined, uncertain, or otherwise not presented as an established fact. For example, buscar una casa que tuviera jardín seeks a house with that feature rather than stating that a known house has it.

example.es: Buscaba una casa que tuviera jardín.
example.en: She was looking for a house that had a garden.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tuvimos is the completed-past form of tener for nosotros, “we.” This completed-event past is called the preterite.

example.en: We had a meeting yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tuviste is the informal singular completed-past form of tener. It refers to something one person had at a finished time.

example.en: Did you have time yesterday?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tuvo is a completed-past form of tener, “to have.” The subject supplied by context tells whether it means she or he.

example.en: Ana had an idea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tuvo is a completed-past form of tener. Before que and an unchanged action verb, it forms a past version of tener que, meaning that something was necessary or required.

example.en: The machine had to stop.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Tuyo agrees with the masculine singular thing owned, not with the person who owns it. El tuyo means “the masculine one that is yours.”

example.es: Mi vaso es azul; el tuyo es verde.
example.en: My glass is blue; yours is green.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ueeeeeee represents an excited cry during fast or playful movement. The repeated e letters stretch the sound.

example.en: She shouted “wheee!” on the way down.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The initial u approximates the start of the cry, and the nine written e letters show that the vowel is held for a long time. This expressive spelling is playful rather than a standard dictionary form.

example.en: Wheeee, how fast!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ugrofinesa describes the branch of the Uralic language family that includes Finnish, Estonian, and Hungarian. It uses feminine singular -a to match familia.

example.es: El finés es una lengua ugrofinesa.
example.en: Finnish is a Finno-Ugric language.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Uh is an informal written sound showing hesitation, uncertainty, or puzzlement. Its spelling can vary in dialogue.

example.en: Huh... I don't understand.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a noun, último can mean the final or last remaining one, or simply the most recent one. The surrounding noun and situation distinguish those readings: el último superviviente is the last survivor, while mi último trabajo can mean my latest work.

example.en: I read his latest article.

cardCatalog.answerEn: a; an (before a feminine noun beginning with a stressed a sound)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Some feminine singular nouns beginning with a stressed a sound use un immediately before them. The noun remains feminine, so a describing word is also feminine: un hacha nueva.

example.en: She bought a new axe.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; Spanish commonly uses un before a percentage
cardCatalog.noteEn: A percentage can behave like a masculine quantity in Spanish, so it often follows un: un 20%. Natural English normally says only “20%,” without “a” or “one.”

example.es: Un 20% de los asientos está libre.
example.en: Twenty percent of the seats are free.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins un tanto, ‘somewhat’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Inside the softening expression un tanto, un is a fixed part of the phrase rather than an article before a noun.

example.es: La respuesta es un tanto confusa.
example.en: The answer is somewhat confusing.

cardCatalog.answerEn: one; a certain (before a masculine time word)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a masculine time word, un can point to one unspecified occasion rather than simply serving as the article “a.”

example.en: One day I will return to Granada.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Una can stand on its own for one feminine person or thing when the noun is already understood. It is not introducing a new noun in this use.

example.en: I want one that is comfortable.

cardCatalog.answerEn: one; a single (as part of por una vez)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Una agrees with the feminine noun vez. Together, por una vez means “for once” or “just this once.”

example.en: Listen to me for once.

cardCatalog.answerEn: one; a certain (before a feminine time word)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a time word, una can introduce one unspecified occasion rather than count several things.

example.en: She arrived one autumn afternoon.

cardCatalog.answerEn: one (feminine singular, before a counted noun)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses un before a masculine noun and una before a feminine noun for both the number one and the indefinite article “a.” Context shows whether an exact count matters.

example.en: Only one page remains.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here una gives the number of occasions rather than introducing an unspecified thing.

example.en: I tried it once.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Unen is the present form used with a plural third-person subject. With se and a, it means that those people join the following group or activity.

example.es: Muchas personas se unen al curso.
example.en: Many people join the course.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Único changes to única, únicos, or únicas to match the person or thing it describes.

example.en: It is the only open road.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In computing, unidad can mean a storage drive, as in unidad de disco. This is different from the general meaning “unit.”

example.es: La unidad guarda una copia del archivo.
example.en: The drive stores a copy of the file.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A unidad can be an agreed amount used to measure and compare other amounts.

example.es: El metro es una unidad de longitud.
example.en: The metre is a unit of length.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Uniéndome is the -iendo action form of unirse with me attached for the speaker. The written accent keeps the original stress after me is added.

example.en: I learned a lot by joining the project.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Unificados has masculine plural -os to match comandos.

example.en: They work with unified criteria.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Unirme is the dictionary-form verb unirse with me attached for the speaker. Unirse takes a before the group, organization, or activity being joined.

example.en: I want to join the team.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Unirte combines the dictionary form unir with te because the action is directed back to one familiar listener. A normally follows when the group, service, or activity being joined is named.

example.en: You can join the club tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Uno can stand for an unspecified person rather than the number one. Natural English often uses generic “you” or “people” instead of formal “one.”

example.en: You never know.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Uno can stand in for a masculine singular noun that has already been mentioned or is obvious from the situation, just as English can use ‘one.’

example.en: I need a pencil; give me one.

cardCatalog.answerEn: about; approximately (before a masculine plural amount)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a number, unos can make the quantity approximate. This differs from unos before an ordinary plural noun, where it usually means ‘some’ or ‘a few.’

example.en: We will take about twenty minutes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: some; a few (before a masculine plural noun)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Unos introduces an indefinite masculine plural group or amount. Use unas before a feminine plural noun.

example.en: I have some new books.

cardCatalog.answerEn: uptime; time a system remains available
cardCatalog.noteEn: Uptime is an English technical loan used by Spanish-speaking computing professionals for the time that a computer or service stays running and reachable.

example.es: El servidor mantiene un uptime muy alto.
example.en: The server maintains very high uptime.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Urgencia can name either the need to act quickly or the urgent situation causing that pressure.

example.en: They fixed the fault urgently.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A urraca is a black-and-white bird popularly associated with collecting shiny objects.

example.es: Una urraca se posó en la rama.
example.en: A magpie landed on the branch.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Usa is the affirmative command of usar for one familiar listener. The same spelling can also mean 'he, she, or it uses,' so context distinguishes the command.

example.en: Use this key.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Usa is the present form of usar used for one third-person subject. It can also be an informal positive command meaning “use,” but that is not this sense.

example.en: The machine uses little energy.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Usado is usar's completed-action form. After a form of haber, it helps say that an action has happened; it does not change for gender in that construction.

example.en: We have used this tool.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Usarías keeps the whole dictionary form usar and adds -ías for one familiar “you.” It presents the choice as hypothetical.

example.en: Which tool would you use?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Usé is the completed-past form of usar for the speaker. The written accent distinguishes this past form from the special present form use.

example.en: I used a blue pen.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here uso names the act or amount of using something. The same spelling can also be a verb meaning “I use,” so the surrounding words determine which meaning applies.

example.es: El uso del teléfono está prohibido.
example.en: Phone use is prohibited.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ustedes addresses more than one listener. It is the ordinary plural “you” throughout Latin America; in most of Spain it is mainly formal, while vosotros or vosotras is informal.

example.en: Do you all live here?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Usuario is a person who uses a service, device, or computer account. The feminine form is usuaria.

example.en: Each user has a password.

cardCatalog.answerEn: sighted people; people who can see (spelled out)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Read the separated letters together as videntes. Vidente can also mean a seer or clairvoyant, but here it contrasts people who can see with people who read Braille by touch.

example.es: La señal tiene texto para personas videntes.
example.en: The sign has text for sighted people.

cardCatalog.answerEn: appeals to; is someone's thing (in irle la marcha)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In irle la marcha a alguien, va does not describe physical movement. The fixed expression says that excitement or action appeals to that person.

example.es: A Leo le va la aventura.
example.en: Leo is into adventure.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ir can describe how a situation develops. Cómo va can ask how something is going or how it turns out.

example.en: We'll see how the project goes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is doing; is getting on (in ¿cómo le va?)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Here va does not describe physical travel. In ¿Cómo le va?, it asks about someone's progress, circumstances, or general wellbeing.

example.en: How are you doing at work?

cardCatalog.answerEn: is; currently ranks (in ir primero, “to be leading”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: In a ranking, a form of ir followed by primero, segunda, and so on gives the current position. Va primero means that one person or team is in first place.

example.en: Our team is in first place.

cardCatalog.answerEn: it leaves; it goes away (with se)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Va is the present form of ir used with one other person or thing. In se va, the added se makes irse and shifts the focus from movement toward somewhere to departure from the current place or state.

example.es: El dolor se va poco a poco.
example.en: The pain goes away little by little.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is going to (before a future action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Va normally means ‘goes.’ Before a and an unchanged action verb, it helps express what one person or thing is going to do.

example.en: Marta is going to call.

cardCatalog.answerEn: is; is meant (in va en serio)
goes by; comes to an end (with se, of time)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Va is the present form of ir used with one person or thing. When a period of time is the subject of se va, the expression says that period is passing or ending.

example.en: Summer is coming to an end.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Va is the present-time form of ir for one person or thing.

example.en: The train goes very fast.

cardCatalog.answerEn: runs; is running (a vehicle or machine)
cardCatalog.noteEn: A vehicle or machine that va bien or va mal is running well or badly.

example.es: El coche va bien después de la reparación.
example.en: The car runs well after the repair.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vacías agrees with feminine plural nouns. Masculine singular is vacío.

example.en: The boxes are empty.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In physics, el vacío is a region treated as containing no matter or air.

example.es: La cámara funciona en el vacío.
example.en: The chamber works in a vacuum.

cardCatalog.answerEn: are okay; are allowed; count as valid
cardCatalog.noteEn: Valer can mean “to be worth” or “to be valid.” In a rule or permission label, vale or valen can say that an option is acceptable.

example.en: Those options are okay too.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Valer can describe value or adequacy. In no valer nada comparado con, it says that one thing does not measure up at all beside another.

example.es: Estas copias no valen nada comparadas con el original.
example.en: These copies are nothing compared with the original.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The ordinary spelling is vamos. Five written o letters represent a much longer shouted vowel; the added letters are playful and nonstandard.

example.en: Cooooome on!

cardCatalog.answerEn: come on! go! (vamos stretched as a cheer)
cardCatalog.noteEn: The ordinary spelling is vamos. An extra o imitates a crowd holding the vowel while cheering; this is expressive informal spelling, not the standard written form.

example.en: Come on, team!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vamos is the “we” form of ir, “to go.” Speakers also use it to propose that the group go somewhere or begin moving.

example.en: Let's go to the park.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we are going; we are going to
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vamos is the present form of ir for “we.” Before a and an action verb, it can announce a plan or near-future action.

example.en: We are going to rest.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we are running; we are doing (in a current state)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vamos is normally ‘we go.’ With an adjective describing progress, such as atrasados, it reports how a schedule or group is doing rather than literal movement.

example.en: We are doing well with the project.

cardCatalog.answerEn: we are; we stand (at a current score or level)
cardCatalog.noteEn: A form of ir can describe how a game, result, or process is going. In vamos tres puntos por debajo, vamos reports the team's current standing rather than movement toward a place or a proposal to act.

example.en: We are two points ahead.

cardCatalog.answerEn: gradually go; are progressing (before an -ando/-iendo form)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before an ongoing-action form, van presents a plural subject's action or change as developing gradually.

example.es: Las tardes van haciéndose más largas.
example.en: The afternoons are gradually getting longer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they are going to; you all are going to (formal)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Van is the present form of ir for ellos, ellas, or formal ustedes. Before a and an unchanged action verb, it helps express what is expected to happen.

example.en: They are going to arrive tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Variado normally describes something as varied or assorted. Used alone on a menu, it can name a mixed selection or sampler plate.

example.en: We ordered an assortment of cheeses.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Varios before a plural noun means more than one, usually an unspecified small number or range.

example.en: We tried several designs.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vaso names an open drinking container without a handle. It does not necessarily say that the object is made of glass.

example.en: She filled a glass with juice.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vatio is the Spanish unit name for a watt, a measure of power. Vatios is plural.

example.en: The lamp uses ten watts.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I leave; I go (special form after deja que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After deja que, the ordinary first-person form voy changes to vaya because the action is being requested or allowed rather than stated as a fact.

example.es: Mi madre deja que vaya solo.
example.en: My mother lets me go alone.

cardCatalog.answerEn: goes; proceeds (special form after antes de que)
cardCatalog.noteEn: After antes de que, ordinary va changes to vaya because the event is still pending rather than stated as a fact.

example.es: Hablemos antes de que vaya más lejos.
example.en: Let's talk before it goes any further.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Used on its own as an exclamation, vaya can express surprise, admiration, or annoyance. This conversational use is distinct from vaya as a form of the verb ir, 'to go.'

example.en: Wow, what a surprise!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vd. is a traditional written abbreviation of usted, the formal singular “you.” Modern writing also commonly uses Ud.

example.en: You may come in.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ve is the irregular positive command of ir for one familiar person. It is different from ve meaning “he or she sees.”

example.en: Go home.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they see; they can see (with gente as the Spanish subject)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vea is a special form of ver used when the seeing is a purpose or desired result rather than a stated fact. Although gente refers to people, it is grammatically singular in Spanish, so it takes the singular form vea.

example.es: Abro la ventana para que vea el jardín.
example.en: I open the window so that she can see the garden.

cardCatalog.answerEn: let's see; let's take a look
cardCatalog.noteEn: Veamos is a form of ver, “to see,” used here to suggest that the speaker and others look or find out together. In conversation it often introduces the next step or a moment of checking something.

example.en: Let's look at the map.

cardCatalog.answerEn: that we watch; that we see (special form after a suggestion)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Veamos is a special form of ver used when seeing or watching is proposed rather than reported as a fact. The ordinary statement form vemos changes to veamos after a frame such as sugiere que. On its own, veamos can instead mean ‘let's see.’

example.es: El profesor sugiere que veamos el vídeo.
example.en: The teacher suggests that we watch the video.

cardCatalog.noteEn: In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

example.en: I tried it three times.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vecinos can describe nearby people or nearby things of the same kind.

example.es: Los pueblos vecinos comparten una carretera.
example.en: The neighboring towns share a road.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vehículos is the plural of vehículo, a means of carrying people or things.

example.es: Los vehículos esperan junto al puente.
example.en: The vehicles are waiting by the bridge.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Veis is the present form of ver for informal plural vosotros, common in Spain.

example.en: Do you all see that light?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ven is the irregular positive command of venir, ‘to come,’ for tú, the familiar singular ‘you.’

example.en: Come here, please.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vencen is the present form of vencer for a plural subject. The opponent follows a.

example.en: They always beat the champion.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vendí is the completed-past form of vender used when the speaker says yo. The written accent keeps the stress on the final í.

example.en: Yesterday I sold my bicycle.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Venere is a special form of venerar, “to worship” or “to revere.” After an expression of fear followed by que, Spanish uses this form to present the feared event rather than state it as a fact.

example.es: Temo que la gente venere al líder.
example.en: I fear that people may revere the leader.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Standing alone after a suggestion, venga can show that the speaker accepts or goes along with it. In other contexts it can urge someone on or come from venir, so those senses use separate cards.

example.en: —Shall we have a coffee? —Sure.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Venga is a form of venir, but speakers also use it by itself to urge or encourage someone. In that use it does not literally tell the listener to come to a place.

example.en: Come on, team, we can do it!

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vengo is the present form of venir for the speaker. With de or del, it identifies the speaker's origin.

example.en: I come from downtown.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to come; to come over (addressing several people)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Veniros is venir plus os, the marker for informal plural vosotros in Spain. After tenéis que, it stays in this unchanged action form.

example.en: You all have to come over this summer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Venta can name the act of selling or a sale transaction. En venta means “for sale.”

example.es: La venta de entradas empieza mañana.
example.en: Ticket sales begin tomorrow.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ventilación is the movement or replacement of air in an enclosed space.

example.en: The room needs better ventilation.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ver normally means to see. After a in the short expression a ver, it helps signal that the speaker is pausing to inspect, consider, or find something out.

example.en: Let's see, what is here?

cardCatalog.answerEn: connection; relevance (inside nada que ver con)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ver normally means “to see.” Inside no tener nada que ver con, however, it is part of a fixed expression about having no connection or involvement; translating ver alone as “see” would be misleading.

example.es: Eso no tiene nada que ver con el precio.
example.en: That has nothing to do with the price.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Verás literally has the future form ‘you will see.’ In conversation it can instead introduce a clarification, much like English ‘you see.’

example.en: You see, the plan has changed.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Verás keeps the whole verb ver and adds -ás, the future ending for one familiar person.

example.en: You will see the result tomorrow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: actually; really (as part of en verdad)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Verdad by itself means “truth.” With en, it forms the reusable expression en verdad.

example.en: In truth, it was easy.

cardCatalog.answerEn: real; genuine (as part of de verdad)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Verdad by itself means “truth.” In de verdad after a noun, the whole expression can mean “real” or “genuine.”

example.en: It is a genuine friendship.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Verde has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns; the plural is verdes.

example.en: The door is green.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Verdeazulado combines verde with azulado, describing a green shade that tends toward blue.

example.es: El agua tiene un tono verdeazulado.
example.en: The water has a blue-green shade.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Verde has one singular form for masculine and feminine nouns. Verdes adds -s to match a plural noun.

example.en: I bought green apples.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Verías is ver with the conditional ending -ías.

example.es: Con más luz, verías el detalle.
example.en: With more light, you would see the detail.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to see it; to check it
cardCatalog.noteEn: Verlo combines ver with lo, which stands for a masculine thing or an idea already mentioned.

example.en: You can check it with a magnifying glass.

cardCatalog.answerEn: Verónica (the name invoked in a mirror legend)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Verónica is a Spanish given name. In a Spanish mirror-invocation legend, it names the figure people try to summon by repeating the name before a mirror.

example.es: Cuenta la leyenda que Verónica aparece en el espejo.
example.en: The legend says that Verónica appears in the mirror.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you watch (informal singular, television or a show)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ver normally means “to see,” but with television, films, or shows it often corresponds to English “watch.” Ves is the present form for one person addressed informally.

example.en: Do you watch that series on Mondays?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vestirte joins the unchanged verb vestir, to dress, with te, which identifies one familiar listener as the person being dressed.

example.en: You can get dressed here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vetado is the masculine singular completed-action form of vetar. After estar, it describes the resulting state of being barred.

example.en: The player is banned.

cardCatalog.answerEn: turn; part of a su vez (‘in turn’)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vez ordinarily means a time or occasion. In a su vez, it helps mark the next corresponding step in a chain.

example.es: La lluvia llenó el río, que a su vez inundó el campo.
example.en: The rain filled the river, which in turn flooded the field.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; forms en vez de, ‘instead of’
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vez often means an occurrence or time, but inside en vez de it helps form the fixed connector ‘instead of.’

example.es: Fuimos andando en vez de tomar el autobús.
example.en: We walked instead of taking the bus.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vi is the completed past form of ver for yo. It can describe seeing a person or thing and also watching a film or program.

example.en: I saw that movie yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Viajan is a present-time form of viajar. It is used with ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

example.en: The signals travel very quickly.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A viajante travels for work, traditionally to sell goods. El problema del viajante is the conventional Spanish name for the traveling-salesperson problem in computer science.

example.en: The traveling salesperson visited five cities.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vidas is the plural of vida, a life.

example.es: La tecnología forma parte de nuestras vidas.
example.en: Technology is part of our lives.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Videojuego combines vídeo and juego into the standard word for an electronic game.

example.en: They bought a cooperative video game.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Videollamada combines vídeo and llamada for a call in which participants can see one another.

example.es: Tenemos una videollamada a las tres.
example.en: We have a video call at three.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vídeos is the plural of vídeo. The form with stress on ví- is standard in Spain; video without the written accent is common in much of Latin America.

example.es: Guardé los vídeos en el ordenador.
example.en: I saved the videos on the computer.

cardCatalog.answerEn: old; former (a place from one's past)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Before a place connected to someone's earlier life, viejo can mean the old or former place they remember, not necessarily a physically aged place.

example.en: She returned to her old neighborhood.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Before the name of a familiar thing, viejo can express affectionate or nostalgic familiarity. It need not literally claim that the thing is physically old.

example.es: Volvamos al viejo método de siempre.
example.en: Let us return to the good old usual method.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Viendo is the ongoing-action form of ver. It can mean seeing, watching, or looking at something, depending on context.

example.en: I am looking at the data.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Viendo is the irregular -iendo form of ver.

example.en: I am watching a film.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Viéndome is the ongoing-action form of verse with me attached for the speaker. In a romantic context, verse con alguien can mean to be seeing or dating someone. The written accent keeps the original stress after me is added.

example.es: Estoy viéndome con alguien desde mayo.
example.en: I have been seeing someone since May.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Viene is the present form of venir for one subject. In a phrase such as el mes que viene, the coming month is the next one.

example.es: Nos mudamos el mes que viene.
example.en: We are moving next month.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vieron is the completed-past form of ver for ellos, ellas, or ustedes.

example.en: They saw the notice yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vinculadas describes more than one thing named by a feminine noun. The usual link to the related thing is a.

example.es: Las cuentas están vinculadas al mismo correo.
example.en: The accounts are linked to the same email address.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Viñeta can also mean a small illustration or vignette. As a comics term, it names one framed panel of a comic strip.

example.es: La primera viñeta no tiene diálogo.
example.en: The first comic panel has no dialogue.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vino is the masculine noun for wine. The same written form can also be a past form of venir, but a drink or packaging context identifies the noun.

example.en: They served wine with dinner.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vinos is the plural of vino.

example.es: La tienda vende vinos de varias regiones.
example.en: The shop sells wines from several regions.

cardCatalog.answerEn: to violate; to break (a rule or principle)

cardCatalog.noteEn: Violeta can name the color or the flower. As a color after a noun, it commonly stays unchanged for gender.

example.en: I bought a violet scarf.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The written form virus is the same for one virus and several viruses; surrounding words such as el, un, los, or muchos show the number.

example.es: Detectaron varios virus en el equipo.
example.en: They detected several viruses on the computer.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Visible has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns. The plural is visibles.

example.es: La señal es visible desde aquí.
example.en: The sign is visible from here.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Visión can mean the ability to see, what someone sees, or a broader viewpoint. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: She has good night vision.

cardCatalog.noteEn: As a noun, visita names an occasion when someone comes to see another person or place; it is not the verb form “visits.”

example.en: The visit lasted two days.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Visita is the present form of visitar for one person or thing described as he, she, or it. When the visitor goes to see specific people, Spanish normally uses a before them.

example.en: Clara visits her grandparents.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Visitante has the same singular form for a male or female visitor: el visitante or la visitante.

example.en: Each visitor receives a map.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Visitó is a completed-past form of visitar for he, she, or formal you. The written accent distinguishes it from visito, “I visit.”

example.en: Marta visited the museum yesterday.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Visto is the irregular completed-action form of ver, ‘to see.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have seen.’

example.en: We have seen that movie.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Viva is the feminine singular form of vivo and matches one feminine person or thing.

example.en: The plant is still alive.

cardCatalog.answerEn: he lived; he used to live
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vivía describes an ongoing or habitual situation in the past.

example.en: I used to live near the sea.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Viviente has the same singular form with a masculine or feminine noun.

example.es: Es la persona viviente de mayor edad.
example.en: She is the oldest living person.

cardCatalog.answerEn: live; in real time (in en vivo)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vivo usually means 'alive,' but the fixed expression en vivo describes something transmitted, performed, or handled as it happens.

example.en: We listen to the program live.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Volador describes something that flies or is designed to fly. It changes to voladora with a feminine singular noun and adds -es in the plural.

example.en: They designed a flying vehicle.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Volantes is masculine plural to match platillos. In platillos volantes it forms the conventional name for flying saucers.

example.en: They saw two flying objects.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Here volumen means how much physical space an object occupies, not sound level.

example.es: Calculamos el volumen de la caja.
example.en: We calculated the volume of the box.

cardCatalog.noteEn: A voluntario offers to take part without being forced. The feminine plural is voluntarias.

example.en: They are looking for volunteers for the project.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Follow volver with de and a place or event to say where someone is returning from.

example.en: I have just returned from work.

cardCatalog.answerEn: you will do again (with a + action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Volverás is the future form for informal singular you. Followed by a and an unchanged action verb, it says that the action will happen again.

example.en: You will try again.

cardCatalog.answerEn: they became; they were to become (in an imagined situation)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Volviesen is a plural hypothetical past form of volverse, “to become.” The equivalent -ra form, volvieran, has the same meaning here.

example.es: Si se volviesen famosos, viajarían más.
example.en: If they became famous, they would travel more.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a familiar group that is masculine or mixed. Spain commonly uses it where much of Latin America uses ustedes.

example.en: Are you all coming tomorrow?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Online services may use votos for positive or negative ratings left by users, not only for votes in an election.

example.es: El producto recibió muchos votos positivos.
example.en: The product received many positive ratings.

cardCatalog.answerEn: I am going to (before a + action)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Voy is the yo form of ir. Before a and an action verb, voy a announces a plan or near-future action.

example.en: I am going to rest.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vrmmm imitates a motorized or vibrating machine. Sound-effect spellings vary because they represent a noise rather than an ordinary spoken word.

example.en: The engine goes “vroom.”

cardCatalog.answerEn: back; return (as part of de vuelta)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vuelta can name a turn or a return. In de vuelta a followed by a place, it presents movement or orientation back toward that place.

example.es: Estoy de vuelta en la oficina.
example.en: I am back at the office.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Vuelve often means “returns,” but before a description of a resulting state it can mean that something causes a person or thing to become that way.

example.en: The wait makes me impatient.

cardCatalog.answerEn: your (informal plural in Spain; before one feminine thing)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vuestra says that something belongs to several people addressed informally. Its feminine singular ending matches the one feminine thing owned, not the number or gender of the owners.

example.en: This is your table.

cardCatalog.answerEn: your (informal plural, before a masculine singular noun)
your (informal plural, before masculine plural things)
vulnerable; open to harm or attack
cardCatalog.noteEn: Vulnerable has the same form for masculine and feminine singular nouns. Use vulnerable a before the danger or influence involved.

example.es: El servidor es vulnerable a ese ataque.
example.en: The server is vulnerable to that attack.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Web is an English loan commonly used as a feminine noun in Spanish, as in la web. It can refer to the World Wide Web or to a website, depending on context.

example.es: Encontré la información en la web.
example.en: I found the information on the web.

cardCatalog.answerEn: webcomic; comic published on the web
cardCatalog.noteEn: Webcómic combines web with cómic. Standard Spanish spelling keeps the written accent because the stressed syllable remains có.

example.en: She reads a webcomic every week.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Wifi is used as a Spanish noun. It is often feminine because red, 'network,' is understood: la wifi. Usage and pronunciation vary by region.

example.es: La wifi del hotel es lenta.
example.en: The hotel's Wi-Fi is slow.

cardCatalog.answerEn: so; and (as part of ¿y qué?, “so what?”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: At the start of ¿y qué?, y does not merely join two listed items. It challenges the relevance of what was just said, much like conversational English so.

example.en: —They do not agree. —So what?

cardCatalog.noteEn: At the start of ¿y si...?, y helps introduce another possibility for someone to consider rather than simply joining two items with ‘and.’

example.en: What if it rains?

cardCatalog.noteEn: A standalone ¿y? asks for the point or consequence of what was just said. This is different from ordinary y joining two items with ‘and.’

example.en: —I'm going out. —So?

cardCatalog.noteEn: In a short follow-up question, y before a person or topic asks for the corresponding information about that person or topic. English often uses “what about” instead of a separate “and.”

example.en: I prefer tea. What about you?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ya often means ‘already’ or ‘now.’ Before a negative expression such as ni siquiera, it marks a change from the past and is naturally translated as ‘anymore’ or ‘no longer.’

example.en: He does not even call anymore.

cardCatalog.answerEn: adds impatient emphasis in venga ya (come on!)
you know; as part of ya sabes
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ya usually relates to “already” or “now.” In ya sabes, the two words work as a conversational aside meaning “you know.”

example.en: It's difficult, you know.

cardCatalog.answerEn: in due course; then (in ya veremos, “we'll see”)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ya has several uses. In ya veremos, it suggests that time or events will reveal the answer later.

example.en: We'll see what happens.

cardCatalog.answerEn: no separate English word; begins ya que, because or since
cardCatalog.noteEn: Ya and que form a causal connector. This fixed ya does not mean “already.”

example.es: Me fui, ya que era tarde.
example.en: I left because it was late.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ya often means “already” or “now.” Before no, it instead marks a change from an earlier situation: ya no means “no longer” or “not anymore.”

example.en: I no longer work there.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spoken on its own with a pause, ya can show that the speaker has just understood what is happening. This differs from its time meaning ‘already.’

example.en: I see... now I understand it.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Said alone with a flat or doubtful tone, ya can acknowledge what someone said without fully believing it. This is different from its time meaning ‘already.’

example.en: —I don't care anymore. —Right...

cardCatalog.answerEn: that's it; nothing more (as part of ya está)
indeed; adds emphatic agreement in ya te digo

cardCatalog.noteEn: Ya often means ‘already.’ In a question about an expected change, natural English commonly uses ‘yet’ or ‘by now.’

example.en: Does the printer work yet?

cardCatalog.noteEn: Yema can mean an egg yolk, a plant bud, or the soft tip of a finger. The body-part meaning commonly appears in la yema del dedo or las yemas de los dedos.

example.es: Toca la pantalla con las yemas de los dedos.
example.en: Touch the screen with your fingertips.

cardCatalog.answerEn: self (as a noun in el yo interior)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Yo normally means I. With an article or possessive word, it can instead be a noun meaning a person's self: el yo, mi yo, or tu yo.

example.es: Su yo adulto entiende la decisión.
example.en: Her adult self understands the decision.

cardCatalog.answerEn: me; myself (self-reference rather than a sentence subject)
cardCatalog.noteEn: Yo normally means “I” when it is the subject of a verb. When someone identifies, labels, or addresses their own self, natural English may use “me” or “myself,” while Spanish still uses yo.

example.es: La persona de la foto soy yo.
example.en: The person in the photo is me.

cardCatalog.noteEn: The repeated u letters show that the vowel is held for a long time. Written sound effects can vary in spelling and length.

example.en: Wheee, how fast!

cardCatalog.answerEn: zappa-; a deliberately fake metric prefix
cardCatalog.noteEn: Zappa- is not an SI prefix. The comic substitutes the musician Frank Zappa's surname for zetta-, the real prefix for 10²¹.

example.es: Zappa- no aparece en la lista oficial de prefijos.
example.en: Zappa- does not appear in the official list of prefixes.

cardCatalog.answerEn: zeppelin; printed without the accent required in standard Spanish
cardCatalog.noteEn: The visible label says ZEPELIN. Standard Spanish writes zepelín, with one p and an accent on í; the German/English proper name is Zeppelin, with two p's.

example.en: The zeppelin crossed the sky.

cardCatalog.noteEn: Spanish uses the borrowed noun zoom for changing how close or enlarged an image appears.

example.en: Increase the map's zoom.
